Division of Research and Statistics
October 21, 1935
Highly Confidential
INTERNATIONAL GOLD AND CAPITAL MOVEMENTS
The current movement of gold from Europe to the United States began
early in September with small shipments from London. On September 17 the
first gold arrived from France, and on September 23 shipments were re-
ceived from the Netherlands. In the five weeks ending October 21 about
$370,000,000 of gold arrived in the United States, and $50,000,000 more
is scheduled to arrive during the next ten days. Of this $420,000,000
France has shipped $195,000,000, England $125,000,000 and the Netherlands
$55,000,000. The remainder has come largely from India and Canada.
This heavy movement of gold does not reflect an excess of payments
due to the United States on ordinary transactions with the world. Recent-
ly this country's merchandise exports have exceeded its imports by only a
small amount. Largely because of agricultural developments the surplus of
exports has been cut down from an average of $32,000,000 a month for the
first eight months of 1934 to less than $4,000,000 a month in 1935. This
small excess, together with income from foreign investments, has been more
than balanced in 1935 by tourist expenditures abroad, immigrants' remit-
tances, and freight payments to foreign vessels. That gold nevertheless
has flowed to the United States during the year is attributable to the
heavy movement of capital to this country. The volume of gold imports has
been held below the inward movement of capital by purchases of silver abroad
for account of the United States Treasury.
VOLUME 267
PAGE 19
During the crisis in the gold bloc countries last spring, the move-
ment of capital was largely in the form of short-term balances. Speculative
and flight funds were being transferred from these countries to New York.
There was also a large return of New York funds from London, where the dis-
count on forward sterling made the continued holding of balances unprofit-
able. During the summer forward quotations on sterling and gold bloc cur-
rencies continued to be at a discount, and there was little return to Europe
of funds that had come here in the spring crisis. There was, in fact, a
considerable net inflow of short-term funds, reflecting liquidation of
German short-term indebtedness to the United States, and a movement of
balances to this country from Latin America and the Far East. In addition
there was a large movement of European resources into the New York security
market. Purchases were mostly of American rather than foreign securities.
From the end of the spring crisis until September the greater part
of this inward movement of capital was offset by purchases of silver abroad
for account of the United States Treasury. There were, however, imports
of gold amounting to about $60,000,000 during July and August, half of
which was shipped from the Netherlands during the week in which the Dutch
Cabinet was overturned. The movement ceased with the passing of the
Cabinet crisis.
Aside from the Dutch shipments Europe lost little gold to the United
States during the summer months, but losses in reserves suffered by commer-
cial banks in Paris and Amsterdam during the outward movement of gold in
the spring were not restored and these centers continued to carry the in-
debtedness incurred at their central banks at that time. Early in September,
when the current gold movement began, reserves were still at the lowest
level reached since the international crisis in 1931 and indebtedness
was near the spring peak. The cost of this indebtedness has been lowered
in France, however, by successive reductions in the rate charged by the
Bank of France. From 6 percent on June 20 the bank had lowered its rate
by August 9 to 3 percent. The Netherlands Bank, after reducing its rate
three times, raised it from 3 to 6 percent during the crisis in July and
thereafter reduced it to 5 percent. On September 17, in the face of the
renewed gold outflow, the rate was again raised to 6 percent. In view
of the substantial volume of indebtedness to the central banks, the course
of central bank rates has largely determined the course of open-market
rates in Paris and Amsterdam.
The fact that the current movement of gold to the United States led
only the Netherlands Bank to raise its discount rate is attributable to
several peculiarities in the situation. Pressure on European currencies
developed toward the end of August as silver purchases abroad by the United
States Treasury diminished in volume. During September there was little
further activity of the Treasury in foreign markets and consequently the
movement of capital had its full effect upon the movement of gold. The
direct shifts in capital between countries, however, did not correspond
with the flow of gold. Throughout the month funds continued to be trans-
ferred to New York for Far Eastern account; and, although gold began mov-
ing in heavy volume from the Netherlands and France, the transfer of funds
on Continental account was largely for Switzerland and the smaller European
countries. It appears that the Japanese, Swiss, and others who moved bal-
- 4 -
ances to this country were for the most part transferring London balances
to New York. In addition the British themselves were building up balances
and buying securities in New York. As a result the pressure of the capital
movement was concentrated on London. The British Fund transferred this
pressure to France by selling francs obtained through the release of gold
earmarked in Paris. The sale of francs depressed the franc to the gold
export point and nearly half the gold received in the United States has
consequently come from France. But it has come, not from reserves of
the Bank of France which have increased during the movement, but from
holdings of the British Fund. In addition substantial amounts of gold
reaching the London bullion market from South African mines, Indian
hoards, and other private holdings have been transferred direct to the
United States. Recently there has been some evidence that the Fund it-
self has been selling gold in London. It is in the nature of the Fund's
operations, however, that they cannot affect either the reserve position
of the Bank of England or of the London clearing banks, for its gold
transactions are automatically compensated by its purchases or sales of
Treasury bills. Hence not only has the Paris money market been unaffected
by the gold flow from France to the United States but the London market
has also been unaffected by the heavy outward movement of balances and
gold together.
The movement of balances from London to New York appears to reflect
the disturbing possibilities of the existing situation in Europe and the
prominent rôle played in it by England. On the other hand there is little
- 5 -
evidence that the movement of gold from the Netherlands in September was
attributable to the same cause. Dutch exports of gold began on the eve
of the reconvening of Parliament when there was considerable chance that
the Catholic Party might withdraw its cooperation with the Government and
overthrow the economy program. When the Catholic Party failed to develop
a program of its own and voted for most of the Government's measures de-
signed to balance the budget, the gold outflow practically ceased, Dutch
shipments of gold to this country during October have been negligible,
and the Netherlands Bank has been able to replace through purchases in
Paris some of the gold lost in September. On October 17 it reduced its
discount rate to 5 percent.
Gold has continued to flow to the United States, however, from
England and France. The movement has been moderated somewhat by renewed
purchases of silver abroad for account of the United States Treasury.

Mr. Charles S. Hamlin, Special Counsel,
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System,
Washington, D. C.
Dear Mr. Hamlin:
Thank you for your letter of February 13, 1937, in which you
suggest that a careful examination be made of the effect of so-called
easy money on the small merchants and shopkeepers throughout the
United States.
There is enclosed a copy of a memorandum to the Board on the re-
cent survey of rates of interest paid on deposits and charged on loans
by member banks. This shows interest rates most commonly reported by
member banks as charged on various kinds of loans. Separate figures
are shown for country member banks excluding those in non-reserve cities
of over 100,000 population. A textual discussion based upon this study
and other data appears on pages 295 to 298 of the April issue of the
Federal Reserve Bulletin.
As you know, the Board has not before obtained reports on rates of
interest charged on loans by member banks other than those located in
the larger centers. It is not possible, therefore, to determine accurate-
ly whether the average country banker has lowered his interest rates
materially. It is possible, however, to compute from condition reports
and statements of earnings and expenses average rates of interest on
loans by relating interest and discount on loans to total loans and dis-
counts. The table below shows these averages for all member banks from
1928 to 1936, inclusive. The table also shows corresponding average
rates computed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston covering approximate-
ly 200 New England member banks outside of the City of Boston.

The ratios given above show a distinct downward trend in the rates
of interest charged by member banks as a whole. The figures for country
member banks in the New England States also show a downward trend, although
not as pronounced as in the case of all member banks. Corresponding ratios
for country member banks in other districts have not been compiled. Be-
gunning in 1932, however, the annual reports of the Comptroller of the
Currency have shown earnings of country national banks separately. On the
basis of these figures and computed in the same manner as the ratios shown
above for all member banks, the average rate of interest and discount on loans
of country national banks was 5.3 percent for the year ended June 30, 1932,
and 5.3 percent also for the year ended June 30, 1936.
Prior to 1932 it is possible to compute similar ratios for country
national banks only in certain States. The attached table shows such rates
for country national banks for 23 States for each of the fiscal years ended
June 30, 1928, 1932 and 1936. This table shows lower average rates of interest
in 1936 than in 1928 except for Wyoming, Oklahoma and Nevada. For the 23 States
as a whole the average rate of interest fell from 6.2 percent for the year end-
ed June 30, 1928, to 5.6 percent for the year ended June 30, 1936. These ratios
are, of course, averages reflecting all types of loans and discounts on which
various rates of interest were probably obtained. Nevertheless, they seem to
show that a definitely lower rate structure prevails at country banks now that
a few years ago. It is interesting also to compare the figures for 1936 with
the rates of interest most frequently reported in the recent survey by country
member banks as charged on the largest volume of commercial and industrial loans.
These rates are given in the last column of the table. You will note that in
several instances the average rate of interest obtained for the fiscal year 1932
was lower than for 1936, materially so for Oklahoma and Nevada. This may be
due to a number of factors, one of which is perhaps the transfer of some of the
larger loans to banks in reserve centers for the purpose of obtaining lower
rates than the country banks are willing to quote. Another possible cause is
the fact that most country banks keep their books on a cash basis. Thus, certain
1932 figures may be abnormally low because loans and discounts at that time were
inflated by the inclusion of some loans on which interest was not being received
in whole or in part. Similarly, the 1936 figures may reflect the receipt of
more than a full year's interest on a certain portion of loans and discounts.
You are undoubtedly correct in your feeling that the smaller banks have
not reduced their interest rates on loans to local merchants in line with re-
ductions in rates charged to large corporations by banks in the financial cen-
ters, where the pressure of surplus funds has naturally had its greatest effect.
The recent survey as of October 1, 1936, indicates, in fact, that even in the
large cities the rates charged to the largest number of borrowers (which would
include the small shopkeepers) have not declined nearly to the level of rates
at which the large corporations can borrow. The fact that manufacturers and
other large businesses in money centers have been able to borrow at relatively
low rates of interest from banks in such centers has, however, enabled them to
extend credit to their customers on more liberal terms than would otherwise be
Mr. Hamlin - 3
the case. It is quite possible, therefore, that merchants in the smaller cities
have benefited from easy money to a greater extent than would appear from com-
paring rates of interest charged by country banks over the past ten years.
Very truly yours,
Marriner S. Eccles,
Chairman.

It is my desire my dear children to avoid in your
education every thing I think erroneous -- mine &
there is nothing I wish more fervently, than to
make the acquisition of knowledge & the
practice of virtue delightful to you -- At present
Sunday is to you, the pleasantest day of all
the week -- In the morning you are dressed with
more than ordinary care, you are sent after
breakfast to visit my good neighbour Mrs. Holt, to
the same pleasant walk -- we are all most happy
on this day; as it is the only one your dear father
gives with us -- after dinner the children have to take
their supper in my dear father's for the hour that brings them
to sunday cakes, is saved to divide with them.
When they come, I collect them all around me, I find
here the hour says their lessons, in reading or telling
I show the little ones to play, when their cakes
finished their lessons, the little ones are called in
to my fires; I make it a rule that they should
all have seats, as I remember how weary I used
to be of standing -- when this little circle
seated around me, I make each repeat one of
Watts hymns, & explain in a familiar way
the precepts contained in them. There is no mode
of instructing I have found more useful than that
of asking the children questions concerning what
they have read -- of rectifying their ideas & language
after teaching them these excellent hymns, which
contain all the principles of Christianity, enough
in the most pleasant style, I sometimes read them
a story which is instructive & entertaining, &
inverses with them in with a familiar & amusing
manner, that they receive, my instructions without
turning it. I make patient inquiries of each
concerning the past week, in order to know how
they have passed it -- what faults they have committed,
enjoining on each the necessity of telling the truth; I have
found this an excellent mode, & I am to be assured
we had the best effect on her children, making
them more obedient to her & kind, to each other.
After this little course of amusing instruction is over
they all go to play, & eat fruit, cakes, & eggs, &
something of the kind is distributed. This summer
I have a swing in the yard & a little wagon
both of which afford great pleasure.

July 4th— How pleasing is it to receive even the least testimony of gratitude from a slave, for my part I think I have
so much injured that I never feel as if I had a claim to their affection or voluntary good offices— Just now I gave
harry the key of the milk house to get out some butter to drop Tabby's rabbit for her, it being one of the
dog had caught a bright day, I after wards, as it was the conclusion of harvest I had worked hard all
day, sent him tea biscuit & butter for their supper, aiders as I gave them to harry, now with Tabby's
rabbits you will have a nice supper, she went out with this message, but when she delivered it, it shant be fixed, said Tabby,
no, no, added the other, we wont eat it but save it for your son, as it is a rarity—
It has most sweet with this rabbit taste to me, thus reasoned with the good will of
these poor slaves.—
During the last week or two, I have had my feelings almost agitated at the sight of the suffering of one of these unfortunate
creatures— Lizzie, a fine, good natured, active young Man, had been hewed by Mr Smith most of last winter; in the spring his master died
to be used as for sale by the executor. He solicited Mr Smith to buy him, but the interest seconded his request, my excellent hus-
band would not sacrifice his principles, which were all adverse to slavery.— He was bought
by Major Beans; but was so discontented with his
situation that in a few months he again came
to Mr Smith with the same request, this
was again denied. The poor fellow, separated
from all those whom he loved, with
a cruel master, was so mistaken, that
he ran away. After concealing himself about
a week in the woods, he at last ventured
here, I again besought Mr Smith to lay him.
His eyes were sent in his head, his cheeks
were hollow, I he looked almost worn
out with watering & hunger. I felt
extremely affected, I to persuade him, seemed
in clearly the dictate of humanity, that Mr
Smith consented in case his master would
part with him promising him at the
same time to set him free at 35 pounds
in case he behaved well. Pepy was always
so said he would leave nothing undone to please
Mr Smith. He did persuasion to
remain here until Mr S. could write to his
master & get a to answer; believing him, however
that he would run the risk of being taken
as his master would learn from the letter
where he was. This will he was willing
to run.
He was here two weeks, 2 rop pay 2 safety that
he was singing from morning to night, his feet
often stepping company with his voice. He was
so obliging, a quiet demeanor, so affectate I loved
to the children, that I became quite attached to
him. I don't think Major Beans called on me,
he was alone, & unarmed, so that his appearance
reappeared one as to his profession -- He told me
he & Mr Smith had not yet agreed about the
price, but that he thought they would & that
he intended to return to the City for that purpose,
but that mean while he would to talk to safety,
I was so free from suspicion that I directed
him to the spot where he was at work & he
rode off -- not long after safety came running
to the door. Our hands clashed 2 carried out & came
come Mysteries, safety begs you will come, they
have got him bound to a tree! I was the
way the streets, but I encountered a lot I saw
him at a distance, found a conductor along
several men. I stopped, but asked as bad
as I could to Major Beans to come to me,
he saw me, I changed my signal, -- I was quite
out of breath when he came, but after
recovering myself, Sir said I, it is your interest
& not your humanity that I address --
you may take for granted that you will not be able
to keep him, he has solemnly declared he
will not live with you & that if he cannot
escape, he will take his own life, -- & salt
in his aversion to being your slave, & in his
own hatreds, I make no doubt but he will --
I then you will have the power to offer
to your slave to -- You smile sir, as if such
a thing had never happened, but within a year
I know several instances, of it was but last
week that Genl. Osborne's man threw himself
overboard, to save himself from punishment,
& it is not a great while since, a poor old
man, when his son was torn from him
to be sold, in distress, hung himself in my
house -- And her son escaped from the hands
of the purchaser, threw himself into the river,
thus did you see what I say is founded on
experience. Or as he said he, it was
not in that account I smiled, for I have known
many instances of the kindyer opinion, but
I will not suppose I mean to set him down
to the Georgia negro-buyers & thus he may
escape. This is treason & being himself an
son of the President, and in it respectable
sir, that for the sake of a hundred more dollars
than Mrs. will give you, that you will sacrifice
the happiness, perhaps the life of a fellow creature!!
I continued to talk & urged every motive interest
& humanity could suggest -- but all in vain &
the poor wretch was taken away -- I remained

dog about 30 lbs. & 2 a pig -- Julia was
afford of the pig & cried, "What you cry for
said the child, don't be afraid, pig ain't
negro-buyer, no negro buyers take you, I don't
any --
Nothing -- to prevent them from obtaining

Her character is yet one had proof beyond doubt
that she was guilty of the theft laid to her charge.
She is a most extraordinary woman, amplying the
character of virtue divine with a proud intellectual
value would have triumphed over her has the most
humane & tender disposition. She has a most
refinement bordering of mind, great activity & vigour
of body, very inventive, full of experiments, a

Seventeenth of September, in a hospital, into which
rapidly does time pass & thus few visitors dare to leave behind.
I am not able to get in contact with them, I seem to have done
nothing. The happiness of a family in every day adds, every day
to home is to be put in order the two principal
to clothing made a model. -- From it then require to
whole of life to support life, few are exempt from
the necessity -- at times how inconvenient it has been sometimes
to these domestic arrangements cause it with difficulty
I seem to admit my mind to this kind of existence a woman
it not for the animal spirits a constitutional good
humour & contentment with which I am endowed often
would this contrast between my duties & melancholy
make me quite miserable -- This evening I have
enjoyed a most pleasant portion of placidity
& cheerfulness; few days have occurred in which I have
not felt an almost to discharge to duties in which
I have not enjoyed the greatest temperature of mind,
but this sunshine has been more & then overlanded in
moments when have occurred when my mind has refused
to be trained to the memory of family business & has
found to secure in to the regimen of intellectual existence,
feel within me an activity & self-possession thought,
an elevation of soul, a overflowing of imagination,
which quite unfit me for the lively duties of
my humble situation. The limited circle which
it is prescribed for woman to tread, seems like
that of the house chained to the wall, while
the unlimited sphere of man is like that of the
front course, who overlooks every obstacle,
I am no bands opposed to the expansion & exercise
of his powers.— So how at each moment, obliged
to explore this scene, to try other paths, to give
full scope to that active & venturesome power that
feels within me, to break through the narrow of
the little cage that confines me, to extend my
vision & rise far beyond the mere possibility
of what I now see. But I am a woman, and society
says, thus far & no farther shall then come.—
Why then has nature given me a mind so
active & ingenious, an imagination so untrammeled
& free, qualities are not necessary to the discharge
of female duties? But why this agony, it
cannot charge my destiny as rather my own, I must
see a woman! I have only to try to describe
my duties faithfully.— How delightful would
be even table & quiet full scope to the powers
of mind, to plunge into all the actions, the sensations
the strong contradictions of life—to meet with certain
stars & objects that would call forth exercise
all the noblest qualities of the soul.— But
what to what end and how are these thoughts, I cannot
say, that mountains about me rise and spread in
horridness in this wild valley at its foot—
well, the valley has its charms & when I do not raise my
eyes to the summit of the mountain, I am befoged entirely
in calling the flowers that are scattered in my path.
I have often said & said with truth, & at this moment
say, I never knew any woman so happy as myself. But
what to a reflecting mind is the happiness which human
life can afford; Its comforts, its joys, its splendours, are
often mitigated, or magnified, that the immortal soul
turns with disgust from them, finding them a spectacle
for its desire to an individual & more individual existence.— I have every thing which this
world can give, it is impossible in this life for
me to have more source of happiness, a yet I
feel within me the capacity of being happier.—
Does not this speak the soul to be of higher origin
than the body, does not this prove that it is destined
to a distinct existence.— If we believe in the
goodness of God, it does prove this—in this case
is found whatever is necessary for the well-being
& enjoyment of the body, but can the soul find
in the whole world of human life, objects that
can satisfy its desires, objects that can exercise
its faculties? The labour of the body can obtain
the sustenance clothing & shelter necessary to the
preservation of animal life, but the most active
& entertaining soul cannot desired objects vast enough
to exercise all its abilities, or give scope to all its
energies. These are the reasons why I am
content with my present situation, I
have not the power to acquire
more, I have not the desire to acquire
more, I have not the means of acquiring
more, I have not the opportunity of acquiring
more, I have not the inclination to acquire
more, I have not the ability to acquire
more, I have not the desire to acquire
and cannot be fostered beyond the narrow limits of this
little garden. Without the support of this small
but most important garden, I would not have been
able to pursue the work of my life, which is the
description of plants for the Royal Gardens at Kew.
Poor indeed would life be, even to the richest
in its enjoyments, if it was not connected with
the life to come. The seed which the farmer
holds in his hand is small in quantity &
of little value; it is for the sake of it produced
that he labours his labour & experiences anxiety.
Thus the circumstances of life are in themselves
but of little moment, but on their cultivation depends
the harvest we shall reap in futurity. I
think of this, & of the husbandman labouring
the winter or the summer in order to obtain his small & precarious
harvest, state not I cheerfully discharge the duties
of this life, in order to gain a hoped immortality.
As one of the ancient writers has observed, life
is a stage, on which our parts are given to
us, & it is not he who acts with the highest character
but he who acts with the lowest that defains
the affrontation of the Manager.
Oh my children remember this, & however humble,
the part allotted, endeavour not
only to act it well, but to act it willingly -- A willing
mind makes labour easy & a cheerful heart makes duty
pleasant. -- seldom have I to struggle with discontent,
or despondion of spirit, & when I find myself enjoying
a questionary the pleasure & duties of life, generally
check this habit of the soul, which is indulged, leads
inevitable to discontent. -- I have been thinking
this morning, that it would amuse, & perhaps
interest me, to read a brief diary of my
unseasonable occupation, state of mind, a state of the
weather. -- I know not if I shall find either method
& leave to pursue this, however I will make
the attempt -- This little record may instruct me
to do better, when I think it will be read by
my dear daughter. -- The weather for a few days
past has been so oppressively warm, that it
has interfered me for every creation. Now have
to order men, necessitise with a long continued
strength, we have had scarcely any thunder or
rain to clothe summer & many streams & things
are dry, so that all the mills for many miles
round are stopped & the flour I have been able
to obtain has been from a windmill.
The weather oppressively hot. -- None at breakfast after 8 o'clock found
it necessary to get up and neglected their usual part in the morning
while at breakfast, received my temper by reflecting that I should
make some allowance on account of the heat. After breakfast
James and I went to town -- I went the whole distance in

little business. I went to town -- I went the whole distance in the comfortable carriage which I have so often found so comfortable. I went to the office to
given her pieces of candy, which I observed her now

The rest of the evening passed while Mrs Smith

The day was dark & cloudy & had a few little

The letter of Mr. Jefferson was written
soon after the Attack upon him by the
"native Virginian"; and when there was a
strong expectation of a War between Russia
and Turkey:-- This explains some Allusion
in them.
From Mr. Jefferson to Mr. Adams.
Monticello, June 1st 1822.
It is very long my dear Sir, since I
have written to you.-- My Dislocated
Wrist is now become so stiff that I write
slowly and with pain; and, therefore,
write as little as I can. -- Yet it is due
to mutual Friendship to ask once in a
While how do you do? -- The Papers tell
us that General Starke is off at the age
of Ninety three. -- He still lives,
at about the same age, Cheerful, and
Plenish as a Grass-hopper and so
much without memory that he scarcely
knows
2.
recognizes the Members of his household.
An intimate intimate Friend called upon him
not long since. it was difficult to make
him recollect who he was, and Sitting
one Hour, he told him the same
Story four times over. — is this Life?
with Labouring Step to tread our
former Foot-Step! Pace the Round
Eternal, to beat, and beat the beaten
Track — to see what we have seen —
to taste the tasted, — O're our
Palates to decant an other Vintage?
It is at most, but the life of a
Cabbage surely not worth a Wish,
When all our faculties have
left, or are about leaving us one by
one, Sight, hearing, Memory, every
Avenue of pleasing sensation is
closed, and Debility, and Malaise
left in their place, when the Friends
of our Youth are all gone, and a Generation is hushed around us whom we
know not, is Death an Evil?
When one by one our Ties are torn,
And Friends from Friend is snatched forlorn;
When man is left to morn
Oh! then, how sweet it is to die!
When trembling Limbs refuse their weight,
And Films slow gathering dim the Sight,
When Clouds obscure the Mental Light
Tis Nature's kindest Bood to die!
I really think so. I have ever
dreaded a doating old Age; and my
Health has generally been so good and is
now so good, that I dread it still. The
rapid decline of my Health during the
last winter has made me hope some
times that I see Love, during Summer,
I enjoy its Temperature, but I
should
14 thunder at the approach of Winter
and wish I could sleep through it
with the Dormouse, and only wake
with him in the Spring if ever.
They say that Starke could walk
about his Room. I am told that you
walk well and firmly. I can only
reach my Garden, and that with sens-
ible fatigue I side however, daily;
but reading is my delight. I should wish
never to put pen to Paper; and the more
because of the treacherous Practice
some People have of publishing our
Letters without leave. Lord Mand斯field
declared it punishable at Law. I think
a penitentiary felony; yet you will have
seen that they have drawn me out
into the Arena of the News Papers.
Although I know it is too late for me to
buckle on the Armour of Youth,
yet my indignation would not permit
me passively to receive the kick of an Adj st .
To return to the News of the Day,
it seems that the Cannibals of Europe
are going to eat one another again.
A War between Russia and Turkey,
is like the Battle of the Kite and
Snake; which ever destroys the other
leaves a destroyer the less for the
World. - This Pugnacious humour of
Mankind seems to be the Law of his
Nature, one of the obstacles to too
great Multiplication provided in
the Mechanism of the Univers. The
Cocks of the Hen-Yard kill one an
other; Bears, Bulls, Rams, do the
same, and the Horse in his wild
State, kills all the young Males, until
worn down with age and war, some
vigorous Youth kills him. xxxxxx

Thus is hardly a principle of the
human mind more extensive in its
influence; & none more necessary or
useful than gratitude. Accustomed
as we are to appropriate the word to signify, almost exclusively, a disposition to
reciprocate favours between individuals,
we will hear with surprise -- that it
is the only true foundation of our duty
towards our Creator & towards our fellow-men -- that it is essential to the existence of
our Society -- & is the source of patriotism
of filial & paternal affection, & friendship.
Thus useful, it is assisted in its operations
by the auxiliary & kindred passions of love,
pity & interest. Although the idea of
the great importance & extended utility of
gratitude presented itself almost as soon as
I had turned my thoughts to the subject,
I was happy to find in Ciceronian sentiments
perfectly coincident with my own.
I could wish (says that illustrious author
rendering him for Miss Anna & not occupying
unnecessary space with the original) "I
could wish that I were endowed with every
virtue but with none rather than with grat-
-itude. For it is not only itself the greatest
virtue, but also the parent of all others.
What is filial affection, but a grateful
disposition towards parents? Who are good
or useful citizens but those who bear in
mind the benefits of their country? Who are
holy & religious but those who ever mindful
of the favours of the Gods, offer up to them in
return their grateful yet suitable acknowledgements? What pleasure could there be
in life without friendship? And what
friendship between ungrateful men?" (Ca-
It must be self evident that the
adoration which is prompted by inter-
-est or fear cannot be acceptable to
the Deity. "My Son give me thy heart"
is, according to Solomon, his language.
Those therefore err who attempt to
work upon the minds of men by repre-
senting the Almighty - as an unjust
judge condemning to everlasting anguish
those who neglect his ordinances, and
rewarding with endless enjoyments
those who regard them - as that being
who rides upon the whirlwind, and
is heard amidst the thunder and
tempest. Such inducements to religion
are the inducements of interest & fear, &
surely there is no occasion for these.
When we consider that he, who hath
endowed us with lofty faculties, with
the ability to distinguish between
good & evil, & with interminable des-
-tinies, might with equal facility
have made us less than the worm
which perishes under our feet: that
he, who hath placed us in a world affording
abundantly all that is necessary for our
subsistence & happiness, who has spread
abroad on every side the fruitful field
and tilling stream, the verdant lawn
and stately forest, might have cast
our lots in aightful waste amidst
eternal darkness & winter. When we
consider that to God, the author of our
existence, the guardian of our infancy
and protector of our mature years, we
owe the light & warmth of the Sun by
day, & the moon & stars which adorn
the night, the fertilizing showers of
spring, the cooling breezes of summer
& every blessing we enjoy. What
is the man whose bosom is not filled
with grateful emotions, prompting him
to yield in return every thing he can, his
love and veneration to the author of
every good & perfect gift.
Nature has given to man,
neither the acute ness of smell
or hearing, nor the fleetness, nor the
weapons of defence, nor the strength
which she has given to other animals. Helvetius has asserted
that this defective construction
of the human frame is the source
of all our excellence. And he
is no doubt right: not only because
the human capacity as well
as that of other animals is measured
in proportion to the emergency: but
more especially because, conscious
of the insufficiency of his unaided
exertions either for his support or
defence, man is compelled to seek
assistance from his fellows. The
foundations of society are laid in
our necessities: & most of our im-
provements spring from society.
The boasted endowments of speech &
reason are not inherent in man,
but acquired from intercourse with
his fellow men. "We have instances
(says Rattel) of persons, who, having
grown up to manhood among the bears
of the forest, enjoyed not the use of
speech or of reason, but were, like the
brute beasts possessed only of sen-
sitive faculties." Society, thus im-
portant, and arising from the necessity
of mankind for mutual assistance,
could never exist without gratitude
which implies an interchange of
favour. To judge of the import-
ance of gratitude in Society,
we need only imagine to ourselves
the wretched condition of a com-
munity where no man either re-
membered or returned the
the obligations he had received.
Gratitude creates obligations
in proportion to the benefits received.
Most love, most veneration, most
attention is due where we have received
most favours. Thus our duty to God com-
prises as being our first & greatest
benefactor. Then comes our duty to
our Country, our Parents, our Friends,
our Relations, our fellow citizens,
& last of all the whole human fam-
ily. Man is a being so constituted
that he seldom looks to second causes
or to what is without the range of his
sensitive faculties; & hence it is, that
seeing most of the benefits he enjoys
to come from his country or his
parents, his patriotism & his filial
affections are usually stronger
than his love of the Duty, which
he does not consider as the ultimate
source of all good. We can never
love, either that Country, or that
parent, or that friend, or that man
who has done little for our good
& much for our injury. And
in proportion to the goodness of the
government under which we live
to the parental attentions we
have received, to the love of our
brother or our friend, so will be
the ardour of our patriotism, &
the strength of our filial & fraternal
affection, & friendship. For these
affections are, as we have said,
founded in gratitude & gratitude
increased with the increase of
the favours confended.
I have but entered upon my
subject. But it is an old saying that
we never know our weaknesses till
experiment discovers them nor was
I aware of my incompetency to write
an essay on gratitude suited to
a Ladies portfolio until I had attempted
it. I shall cast that dry remark
upon a title topic with the observation of Cicero that "There is no Duty
more necessary than gratitude."

Seems not the ship like an island of rest?

Like a heart— cherished home on some desolate plain.

Spreading her wings on the bosom of night,
More on the deep, as the moon in the sky.
Or phantom of beauty— could deem, with sighs,
That so lovely a thing is the mansion of sin,
And souls that are omitted lie bursting within?
Who— as he watches her silently gliding
Remembers that wave after wave is devoting
Bodies that scream and guilt could not sever,
Hearts that are parted and broken for ever?
Or deems that he watches, affront on the wave
The death bed of hope, or the young spirit's grave?
Like a rebel at sea, amid sunshine and song!

Gaily we glide, in the grace of the world,
With steamers afloat and with canvas unfurled;
All glad of, and gay, to wandering eyes,
Yet chartered by sorrow, and freighted with sighs—
Fading and false is the aspect it wears,
As the miles we put on part to our own loss;
And the withering thoughts which the world cannot know
Like heart— broken spirits, lie burning below;
Whilst the vessel drives on to that desolate shore
Where the dreams of our childhood are vanquished and dies!

The Heirship's Complaint.
Why tell me with officious zeal,
That I am young, and rich, and fair,
And wonder how my soul can feel,
The pangs of sorrow and of care?
Why dost thou court the golden store,
The sparkling jewels that are mine,
And name the suitors 'er and o'er
Who breathe theirincesse at my shrine?
Know that I scorn the sordid train
Whose loveless vows are bought & sold,
Know that the heart I sigh to gain
Despises, spurns, my worthless gold.
I love — I dare not breathe his name,
The son of genius, of mind;
He climbs the sleepy path of fame,
Content to leave the crowd behind.
Wind while in halls illuminated bright,
I hear the same false flatteries o'er,
The patient wastes the midnight light
In studious toil, in learned love.
Seldom he seeks the giddy throng,
And then he stands retired, apart,
And views the dance, & hears the song,
With listless look & joggle heart.
He turns from Love's all speaking eye,
His mind to fame, to science clings,
Throned in a world of visions high,
Of deep, & vast imaginings.
My vaunted wealth, my flattered face,
The praise of coxcombs may employ;
But he regards that drops as base,
He holds that beauty as a toy.
Yet must I still reluctant wear
These flashing gems, these robes of state,
And nightly must submit to share
The futile vanities I hate.
Oh! never shall the world deride
My passion with unfeeling jest,
While smiles of more than Spartan pride
Can hide the tortures of my breast.
My tears flow fast—Now judge if gold
Can banish anguish from its shrine,
And say if ever tale was told
So sad, so sorrowful as mine.

Solomon, and the Queen of Sheba.
The Rabbins tell of an ingenious
invention, which in the Talmud
is attributed to Solomon; and the
story shows that there are some plea-
sing tales in that immense compila-
tion.
The power of the Monarch
had spread his wisdom to the remotest parts of the known world.
Queen Sheba, attracted by the splendour of his reputation, visited this
poetical King at his own court; there
one day to exercise the sagacity of the
monarch, she presented herself at
the foot of the Throne; in each hand
she held a wreath; the one was
conspicuous of natural, & the other
of artificial flowers. Art, in the
labour of the mimetic wreath,
had exquisitely imitated the lively
hue of nature; so that at the dis-
stance it was held by the Queen for
the inspection of the King, it was
deemed impossible for him to decide,
as her question implied, which
wreath was the production of na-
ture, & which the work of art.
The sagacious Solomon
seemed puzzled, yet to be van-
quished, though in a trifle, by
a trifling woman, irritated
his pride. The son of David,
he who had written treatises on
the vegetable productions, "from
the cedar to the hyssop", to ackno-
wledge himself outwitted by a wo-
man, with shreds of paper, and
glazed paintings! — The hon-
our of the Monarch's reputation
for divine sagacity seemed di-
minished, and the whole Jew-
ish court looked solemn and
melancholy. — At length an
efficient presented itself to
the King; it must be con-
fessed worthy of the naturalist.
Observing a cluster of bees hover-
ing about a window, he com-
manded that it should be
opened; it was opened; the bees
rushed into the court, saluted
on one of the wreaths, while
not a single one fixed on
the other. — The baffled Sheba
had one more reason to be astoni=
shed at the wisdom of Solomon.
This would make a pretty
poetical tale. It would yield
an elegant description, and
a pleasing moral: that the
Bee only rests on natural
beauties, and never fixes on
the painted flowers, however
inimitably the colours may
be laid on. — Applied to the
Ladies this would give it
generosity.

"Write a few lines, 'tis all task"
"Fill but a single page."
Laura, 'tis an easy task
For youth — but not for age.
Know you not that Spring has flown
That all its lovely bloom has gone?
Know you not that Summer's past
And Autumn breathes its chilling blast?
When in you walk and look around,
Withered leaves beset the ground;
Tasted is the lovely green,
And when sunset clothe the scene.
This you know, no hope to find meet;
Violetts springing round your feet;
This you know — no hope to find,
Luscious fruit of summer kind.
Know you not the life of man,
Refashioned on the selfsame plan?
That on its youthful, venial hour,
Sportive Fancy strews her flowers;
That young affections of the heart,
Their genial power to mind impart?
Then, the thoughts as freely rise,
To warling birds in summer skies,
When this inspiring warmth has fled,
Our thoughts are chilled, our fancy dead.
Then vain dear girl what you require,
Fancy denies her kindling fire.
I feel the approach of Autumn roll,
Its chilling influence on my soul.
Well be it so — I'll not repine,
While Autumn richer store is sowed;
The richest store kind heaven sends,
Domestic love, and faithful friends.
— Louisa, when your spring is flown,
Your summer days and joys are gone,
When cold autumn days shall come,
Be yours as dear and calm a home,
A husband suited to your mind
Is true, so tender, and so kind
That when your youth has passed away,
And your maturing decay,
This love like some bright evergreen,
Shall screen, and cheer life's winter scene.
Louisa, round your cheerful hearth
May you enjoy as harmless youth
With objects to your heart as dear
As those you've often met with, here.
And when from us you're far away
Sometimes recall the cheerful day
When gathered round the quilling flame
Our hopes, our fears, our tasks, the same.
The years may pass, and sorrows come,
Do not forget the evening hour
When Sidney's neighbours used to meet,
And pass their time in converse sweet.
No yet forget, how oft you've stayed
On sunny hills, — through forest shade
How happy with your friends you've been
While summer smiled upon the scene.
How often plucked its glowing rose
To twine around your youthful brows.
That youthful brow so smooth and fair!
Unfavored yet by pain or care,
And must it bear the deep impress,
Of dimming age, and dark distress?
That fragrant rose, without a thorn
Sparkling in the dew of morn;
Must it then wither drop and die,
Beneath a cold and flowering sky?
That sunny hill, that woodland shade,
In Nature's loveliest hues arrayed;
How bright they seem! as if decay
Could never wear their charms away.
Those evenings cloaked with social mist
Those cheering friends around the hearth
Those devout joys I wish for you
These - these, alas must vanish too!
Since charms and joys, which spring from earth
Return to whence they take their birth.
— Yet sigh not at the sad presage
Since there's a charm to brighten age
Since there are joys which in decay,
But last when Time has past away.
Then let me dear Louisa say
Forget not these when far away,
When to kind heaven your prayer ascends
Remember then your Sidney friends.
M. H. S.

To my dear Mother
With the first Viollets of the Spring 1823.
With what delight in childhood's hour
I've watched the Spring's advancing foot,
With her who loved to mark and trace
Sweet nature's every charm and grace—
Each leaf and every bud that burst
Bore hail and every bud that burst
Were hail with rapture as the first
But to the viollets humble shade
Were our first visits always made,
Searching the earliest bud to find
To shield it from the stormy wind
That soon it might rise and bloom
And yield to the its sweet perfume.
But sometimes to our surprise
A flower unnoticed would arise
The one we thought would soonest blow
Had still to bear the frost and snow.
Oh with what fond and eager haste
The first flower on thy breast was placed,
That breast where all the virtues meet
And blest religion finds her seat.
But she who loved the opening spring
And loved to see its flowers to bring
She whom we loved is now no more
Our earthly hopes for her are over.
Oh! can we ever cease to sigh
For those sweet hours, alas, gone by.
Those days of pleasure and of joy
And happiness without alloy
Oh no! in memory they dwell
To be "remember'd oft and well"
Time can her image nier efface
But death for her remembrance trace.
Let the sweet humble widow's fate
Be emblematic of her state.
Perhaps you did not think that she,
The youngest of our little band,
That she the first would gather, be
By your heavenly Father's hand.
Yes she has first been called away
To the bright realms of endless day
Like the fair flower, this left below
The stormy wind and winter's snow,
Removed to that celestial home
Where earthly blisses can never come
She has exchanged a world of light
For one of glory and of light
And on her Heavenly Father's breast,
Her soul enjoys eternal rest.
The sentiment of filial and sisterly affection
Which animates these simple lines, I know will
be sufficient to recommend them to my sweet home,
because in her bosom are the same chords of
love, that will vibrate with the touch of sympathy.
Long, long may you enjoy all the delight
which flows from these affections, and be spared
the anguish which arises from bereavement.
But when it last the swearing stroke shall
come, may you be sustained by that hope
which looks beyond the tomb.
J.B.

The strong hold of Friendship is lasting,
And firm as a rock in the Heart;
But Love is delusive swaying,
And owns all its beauty to art.
Tho' it beams like a brilliant Lightning,
It shines over its own distant tomb,
Like the flash of the Heaven's redlightning,
Encircling the darkness and gloom.
Let me claim then a spot in your bosom
To Friendship and Memory dear;
Where the buds of remembrance may blossom,
Their fragrance embalmed with a tear.
The pleasures of life are but fleeting,
They pass like the rays of Spring,
And the heart that with anguish is beating
May soon throb with agony's string.
Let me hail then the joys which have broken
The dark recollections of sorrow,
But this record, alas! is the token
Of long desperation tomorrow.
January—Oh! it flames as if parting,
Were like the last beam of the light,
That's left, like the day star, departing,
To rest in the darkness of night.—

Oh! why does the Heart the reflection retain,
Of the Sunshine whose Splendor has fled,

When their blossoms are faded and dead?—

Recollections of days that are gone,

The flame of affection be wasted away,

The sigh of remembrance that mourns its decay,

And gladdens the desolate heart.—

Sleep.
"Praise be to him who invented Sleep." Sancho Panza
When baling Sleep its soothing influence sheds,
And lulls in blissful dreams our aching heads,
No longer then by toil or pain oppress
We sink in sweet repose and quiet rest.
For then removed from every anxious care,
We breathe in brighter worlds a purer air,
Range fancy's fairy realms on wing sublime
Free and unfetter'd by the lapse of time.
Mute, in peaceful slumber, long and deep,
The sage-the Shepherd-and their Sovereign sleep,
No longer then the Ambition and the Brave
Pant for the Victor's laurel or the grave-
Een Hated sleeps! yet guiltless of the blow
Which waking dooms to death his hapless foe,
And hopeless Love-forgets its dark despair
In vision roos and wins the beautious fair.
Come sweet sleep! thy powerful aid impart
To soothe the sick, and cheer the sinking heart,
For soon Life's fitful fever will be o'er.
And eyes that weep, will close to weep no more;
Then shall the Spirit wing its upward flight.
Beyond the Stars which girt the brow of Night,
To worlds of light in living verdure dress,
The abodes of peace—the mansions of the blest.

has misruined our styles;) but Dante and Ariosto
were ambitious of conveying to the minds of others
the impressions on their own, with force and persua-
siveness, and to affect this they could not
refuse to stoop to the meanest images.
Indeed, in spite of all his romance, Ariosto is the poet of
Nature; his images, and he abounds in them beyond almost
any other writer, are from things which seem all to
have come under his own observation. They have all the
simplicity and spirit of proof impressions. They are not
refined from ancient and improved artists, which by
transformation through various hands have lost
the most delicate features of the model,
but they are original drawings by a most original
master. Hence the mighty mixture of the new
and magnificent which they sometimes present,
because it is only by exhibiting natural objects
in unnatural proportions that this can be kept
out of sight. Hence, again, the distinctness of their
images, which when they are introduced for the
purpose of occasion to make use of a lion or a
bear (and what poet has not?) he exhibits them
them in a circus or a cage, or with a rascal about
their necks, more frequently than amidst their
natural haunts; because in the one situation
he had probably seen them with his own eyes,

Chinese method of propagating various kinds
of fruit-trees:
They strip a ring of bark, about an inch
in width from a bearing branch; surround
the place with a ball of fat earth or loam,
and fast to the branch with a piece of mat-
ting; over this they suspend a pot or horn,
full water having a small hole in the bot-
tom, just sufficient to let the water drop,
in order to keep the earth constantly moist;
the branch throws new roots into the earth
at above the place where the ring was
stripped off. The operation is performed in
the spring, and the branch is drawn off and
put into the ground at the fall of the leaf:
the following year it bears fruit.

Notes on management
of Green House Plants —
Geraniums, are very culture, requiring
a sort of loam with a little peat must
have little water when not in flower
They require more light than ever
green plants with coriaceous leaves & woody
stems, such as the myrtle & camellia, when
they grow large & strong, they should be
cut down, or cut off, for the smaller the plant
in general, the more vigorous the flowering
leaves — The seeds should be sown in
soil of light earth, no sooner as germination
is over they come up a seedling, for seed
may be transplanted into soil of the smaller
size. Seedlings from seeds sown early
in the season will flower the succeeding
autumn, & none will be later than one
year in showing their flowers. To obtain
new sets another way is to put plants home
where they will be influenced by other plants
in flower, produce to same effect.
All those which have not fallen
away or other their roots are propagated
by cuttings of the wood taken off at a
point where the it is beginning to refer
all the thick wood tends to dry up great
difficulty is that one plant will half
with stand above ground — Cuttings from
the root may be taken off at any time
during the Summer season & if the
Summer pots or tubs they are planted
are plunged in a hot bed, they will
become handsome plants in 2 or 3 months
time. Many gardeners plant their cuttings
in the open ground in a shady border
& take them up & pot them in autumn.
In some gardens a number of cuttings
of the hardier kinds are every spring planted
in open borders, where they make a
fine show during summer & though they
are killed by the first frost it is easy
to plant them in the spring. Old
plants, unfit for the green house, may
whenever be planted in open ground &
produce a favourite display of flowers
before they perish.
Chrysanthemum.
As these plants are so
easily cultivated some should always
be kept in a green house, 2 be grown in
small pots. They are propagated by dividing
at the root, or by cuttings taken either from
the flowering stems, or from the ground roots,
The cuttings from the stem make the neatest

To preserve a collection in a small space
the best way is to grow the plants in
single pots of a small size, from 2 to 3
inches diameter & never to allow more

order to have strong flowers, pinch off all

Mode for cultivating early Potatoes.
We take up all intended for seed next
year before they are ripe, just when
the outer skin feels off, and before
the stalk or stem begins to wither; they
are then laid upon a gravel walk,
fully exposed to the sun, for a month
or six weeks, when they becomes quite
green and soft, as if roasted, and often
much shi p pedled; they are then
put away, and protected as other pota-
toes are. In February we examine them,
when we generally find every eye full
of long sprouts fit to be planted; they
are then cut as described by R.W.; but
less economically, as we seldom make
more than two sets from each tuber,
— the eye, or tip part, and the root or
bottom part. We plant them as descri-
bed by him, the eyes upwards in
both parts; and we observe, as des-
cribed by him, that the potatoes from
the eye or tip sets are earthen by a
fortnight, and that those planted in
the common ground. And let me
observe, in by no means the warm-
est or richest part of our country, the
writer had a dish of ripe potatoes at
dinner last Whitsunday the 14th of
May, and the same every day since,
from successiveal crops, until the
20th of July, when the common
potatoes come in use.
You will perhaps wish to know how
we secure the successiveal crops of
the same variety. In February 1818, the
writer purchased the above variety
from town, &, they were planted the
latter end of March; although
treated as the other potatoes, they
were three weeks or a month earlier
than the general crops. Before they
were ripe, as before described, every
other row was taken up, and the potatoes
exposed to the influence of the
scorching sun; the other rows were
left until ripe, and were laid up
with those taken of unripe, care
being taken to keep each sort separate.
In December they were examined.
Every eye of those taken up unripe
had a sprout almost an inch long, yet
the tuber itself quite soft, was as
hard and all wrinkles had dis-
appeared; while those left to grow
ripe, were as hard as when laid up,
showing no appearance of vegetation.
In February they were again examined.
Those taken of unripe were covered
with sprouts from six to eight
inches long; those taken up ripe began to show sprouts. Each sort was
then cut harrasline fashion, and
planted the same day in alternate
rows of ripe and unripe; and also the
tops and bottoms of both sorts were
set separately in alternate rows. In
the beginning of April, every plant
from the unripe sorts was earlier
than the others; the plants from
the ripe set were only beginning
to appear; the eye sets of those
were evidently earlier than the
bottoms. When planted on litter and
stable dung, they were all covered
with earth, about two or three
inches deep, and were not earthe'd
up, as is usually the case.
Brevity being essential to render
your miscellaneous interesting, I will
not at present enter into further details,
but state to you how they were taken
up. The early potatoes last earthe'd
up, grew close round the stalk or stem,
like eggs in a nest, and at near
the surface, that they may readily
be picked off with the finger,
leaving the stalk or stem standing
uninjured, to produce more potatoes
from the runners. From the eye set
of the unripe tubers we had a full
supply every day for a fortnight,
when those from the bottom set of the
unripe seed came into use for another
fortnight; at that time potatoes from
the eye or top sets from the ripe seed
came into use, and were succeeded
by potatoes from the bottom sets of
the ripe seed. Those kept for seed or
for the table, were earthed up as usual,
and each row produced almost as large
a crop as any two of the rows not earthed
up—the luxury of an early potato
being a greater object than the quantity.
The writer has this day examined
the potatoes preserved for seed (taken
up unripe) of the three varieties
laid in the garden-house, northern
aspect, upon a stone floor, and the
spouts from the eye, on the eye
end of all are nearly an inch
long, vigorous and strong.
By earthing up the potatoes, they
become three weeks later earlier . I
could add much more, but fear-
ful that I shall exhaust your
patience, as well as that of your
readers, I will now conclude.
Most of the sorts of Chrysanthemum succeeded admirable,
and continue in beauty for
a long period, trained against a
south wall; the late-flowering
sorts grow more vigorously and
flower better in this situation
than in pots under glass. Whether
against a wall or in pots, reducing
the number of flower buds, as recom-
mended by Mr Joseph Wells, enlarges
the size of the flowers. In training the
shorts to a wall, combine to have the
branches of different lengths, so that
the flowers which only grow at their
ends may not all appear at the
extremities of the plant.
The best sorts for an open border
are the peple, changeble
white, buff and rose.

of the Milk during the nursing of Calves. By

From the Bibliothèque Physiologica Rominonique,
it has been supposed, in most countries,
that the best and most effectual method, either for
stimulating or for the milk, is to make
the calf suck the mother's milk; it is not so
certainly, that the following is the preferred
method. The calf can drink. When it is three
days old, two-thirds of oatmeal (spurry,
corn meal as good) is made into a paste, and
fed for a minute. It is then left to suck it
until it has drunk as much as it can, which is
one or two quarts of milk that has stood twelve
hours. Then it is given a second time, stir the whole,
and give it to the calf to drink. This method is
designed to make the calf drink by preventing the
fetus from being irritated by the milk, thus
help, and will grow incomparably fatter than by
the other method. This method is not only a
theoretical truth, but its success is not doubted.
The economical advantages that result from it
are striking. According to the old method,
a calf finished at the age of three months is to
suck for three weeks, and times intended for
grazing are left empty. This is supposing
the cow gives only a moderate quantity of milk.
The value of the milk in these three weeks to the
mother is the value of the calf. If, in the new method, we
consider the calf according to this new method, we
consider it as having received only three
quarts of oat-meal, at most, and the elementary
milk.
M. Schune adds, that he has practiced this
method himself, and that his calves have been
always as healthy, and as strong as the others,
and not subject to disease. The only alterations
he has made in the method, is to prevent them
to suck at all, but give them the pure milk of the
mother, and the same quantity every day; because,
he has observed, that the separation of the
mother from the calf is more painful to the mother than when the
calf is taken from her at the time of birth. He
makes no exception, only when the cow calves
for the first time, he has found it has observed that in this case the latter vessels of the
mother, and the cow is more easily milked, if
the calf is allowed to suck for a few days.

expressively. The lady had no positive information to give those
who had requested her to inquire whether Mr Jefferson would receive
company, but watching his motions, found that after a little
while he had left the orderly stilled through the crowd --
left the room. This she communicated to the company, who
with one accord determined to follow him to the President's
house. It was evident that he had not expected this attention from his friends & fellow citizens, as his whole interior-hall
had gone forth to witness the ceremonies of the day -- he was alone --
not therefore the less happy, for not one of the eager crowd
that followed Mr Madison, was as anxious as himself, to show
every possible mark of respect to the new President.
How memorable was this last interview! -- Every one present seemed
to feel it so, & each in turn shook hands with him, their coun-
tenance expressed more forcibly than their words the respect
they felt on leaving one who had been the uniform friend of
the city & the citizens with whom had lived on terms of hospita-
lity & kindness.
In the evening there was an Inauguration Ball.
Mr Jefferson was among the first that entered the Ball-
room; he came before the President's arrival -- "Am I too early?"
he said to a friend, "You must tell me how to behave -- for it
is more than forty years since I have been to a ball."
On the course of the evening, some one remarked
to him, "you look so happy & satisfied Mr Jefferson, that you
won't the President's appointment; & Mr Madison looks so serious
not to say, sad, that a spectator might imagine that you were
the one coming in, & be the one going out of office."
"There's good reason for my happiness & his sorrow looks,"
replied Mr Jefferson, "Shane got the barther off my shoulders,
while he has now got it on his."
Thus closed Mr Jefferson's eight years residence in
Washington. The constant interest he had taken in the improve-
ment of the city -- the frank hospitality he had extended to
the citizens, made his departure the subject of general regret.

The following oratory was pronounced at the
funeral of Cadet Lieut. Schloff, of Independence,
Louisiana, who died at the Military Academy
in Charleston, S.C. — Feb. 12, 1865.— By the
Rev. W. Colson, Chaplain to the Academy.
But a few days since and Schloff moved among us as the man he is
for all— the years of his career closed— the movement of his
army over— the banner of his military head— all still held
strongly to his devote within him— but how he has since passed
it down under the cold hand of death!
He will never again be seen gliding from his apartment
to fill his place in your minds— the voice of his footsteps will
never again answer to the deep roll of the marching drum!
But never will he be dead, but it will not cause him from his
rest, the battle that sends his mortal death for the cold despair
of the game! Schloff I who can think of thee— of thy untiring
hours— the province of thy many virtues— the pledges of thine
united work— and not dissolve in grief over the nation's griefs
but who has now heard, and heard thy latest prayer— but
thinks of prayer— dear departed one— no parent with him—
being separate from over the dying couch! no sister with under
obstinately anticipated the enemy's want— thy dying words were spoken in
a stranger land— but there were those around thee, strongly
attested by thy worth— those who thinned at every hope of thy—
and who spoke for strongly and just when they stood
up— and there are those who with breaking hearts, will hold
their in long remembrance. Soldiers!— Scholar!— Friend—
Companion— rest in rest!
Comrades of Schloff! ye who arose with him at the earliest
light, and with him stood on the solemn parade where we kneaded
our morning prayer to heaven— ye who with him leaped
over the barrier of light in the deep drift of thought— and with
him kindled the lamp over the march of some mighty mind—
come up around his grave, gather close about his coffin's edge—
for though he died, he speaks to earth of you— What thou doest do
quickly? Who can understand the energy of those words? Then
pale circles of death! I were treason not to hear thee now!
"What thou doest do quickly" for there is an emphatic in those
words redoubled by their grace is going in life to the cold want nothing
of the thread.
Who is there among your ranks, men vigorous in your army
more courageous in your hope of many days than Schloff? None!
he was a strong man, that seemed to hold an party with Liberty no
compromise with the infamy of our nature.
But he is there released in death! He must go and convey
him to the universal judgment— we shall awake even from
our wildest dreams— but he will sleep on— till the
humility of God enwraps him in the judgment seat.
Who then, among you, is not prepared to follow Withoff?
Have him for he speaks to you— What then do you do by
your thoughts unrepresented and unrepresented you may be the most
unfortunate companion here in the grave— Then that sense of sin
and death— that undying soul— that spirit stamped with
the immortal courage of its Maker— Is it ever passed for
heaven, whether with all its boundaries, or parties can or

create its enthusiasm -- but give it constancy to its reflec-

'Twas evening, once the setting sun
Boke from the cloudy West,
Athwart the misty sky it shone
And gladdened all the East;
There, on the clouds which dense and low
Stung up the humid sky,
A beautiful majestic bow
Of nebeys met the eye.
The thunder seals were harn'd no more
The lightnings ceased to glow,
The winds had rushed its assistant rear
Along the vale below—
Nature, just bursting from her chain
Of winter, fresh & fair,
Set on her robes of liveliest green,
And fragrant was the air.
So may this life of toil and storm,
At evening passed me by:
So may my sun break out, anasform
To rainbow in my sky.—
May gratitude and love and praise,
Thin fragrancy impart,
To cheer the errings of my days
And fill my haptur'd heart.
And when life's latest beams recede
From earth and time away,
May glory, bless and blest endure,
In bright suffulgency:
Then, as the colors of your rocks,
Are blended in all in one;
May I with Christ's triumphant breath
Compose an everlasting arch
To rainbow round his throne.

I can scarcely believe that a whole week has passed since I wrote
you my last letter. This is the third time I have written from this
place, & I have at yet received no answer to my first letter. I cannot
avoid some apprehension I begin to fear that some one of the family
is ill. Oh, my dear sisters do be punctual in writing, you cannot
conceive how the value of a letter is increased by our seifer attempts
from all our friends, & being as we are in a land of strangers. The last
week, Mrs S. had a letter from Mary & John, I welcomed them most
sincerely, but still I felt sadly disappointed that first after first
arrived without any intelligence from Brant. Since this day week,
my good husband, has not been an hour free from a violent toothache
It keeps him awake, almost the whole night & incapacitates him for
business or society through the day. In attempting to extract it the dentist
had it, & in endeavouring to get out the broken parts, he said he has
eructated the gum, so much, that his whole head is affected. -- He suffers
so much pain, that it produces a slight fever. The indisposition, has so
depressed my spirits, that for this day or two, I have been quite
good for nothing. I find it impossible to fix my mind sufficiently
for reading or writing. On wednesday evening last, we were just
seated at our tea-table, when the door was opened & brothers
& Sister entered. I felt most truly rejoiced to see them. They
passed the next day with us, I left this on Friday morning.

Here my dearest sister, seated beneath one of the finest trees in
Willow I have ever seen with orchards, woods & meadows extending
bide around me, do I take up my pen to act after years
concerned to give you some account of my own. Maria's
last letter informed me one from you, of which I have been
in daily expectahin. Since you last heard from me, I have
experienced the most trying anxiety. My little Julia has been
very ill. During the few days when she was at the worst,
in how did I wish for you! I thought that your presence would
have helped the danger, almost banished my fear, it would
at least have rallied my heart & enabled me to undergo
any trial with which I might have been afflicted.
She made every exertion to get lodging in the country &
at last the house kindly offered as the use of 2 rooms
on his farm; which I most gladly accepted. While my
little one was ill, all my friends were most kindly attend-
ing. Mrs. Tupper & Mrs. Thornton called every day to see me, Mrs.
Stoddard, Robinson, Robinson & others all who expressed an interest
in my situation; but all this was not equal to the right
of my dearest sister Jane. When any thing ails my child, I think
respectfully of you, I wish continually for you, because you would
feel for me as a daughter & I should confide in your care
& sympathy as in a mother. The only society from which
my heart derived any gratification was that of the St German
& Hudson Picher. Stewart died to give the tendency, the
sympathy expressed by their conduct & their means.
The theft of a little darling, is the greatest trial of my fortune
I ever met with & I could scarcely have supported the
evil apprehension which tormented my mind, had it not
been for the
for the tender cares of my own then ever beloved husband
when the heart is oppressed by sorrow, how sensible is it to
every mark of affection or kindness? even in a character
uninterrupted prosperity is hard to render the feelings calmer
& inseparable to the wants & sufferings of others. These I
find easy to be exempt from suffering.
Many wrote me word that your little Elizabeth had
been sick for several days previous to the appearance of a
tooth, I could not but regret that she had not described to
me the symptoms, in which case I could have compared them
with Fulton. Her gums were not seared, she had no fever, breath
more than usual, but was extremely fretful & restless; her breath
was much diminished & the complaint seemed to be attended
with great pain. During 3 or 4 nights Mrs Smith & myself
slept deeply, but were up, administering warm baths, injections, etc., which I have no doubt improved her. The day
before the tooth appeared she lay in a kind of lethargy, during
her sleep only a minute at a time, making no noise, taking little
or no nourishment & her legs, arms & face cordial in, with
furious red sweat, while her head & body were burning.
I cannot describe to you my sensations when the next day
I finally perceived a tooth. What a load of anxiety are removed!
I now knew the cause of her sleep & felt the alarm.
Every unpleasant symptom gradually disappeared, her ride here
was of great service to her, every day since our arrival her more
her Stock of health. She eats a great deal of meat & milk
every day, besides taking other food. The black girl, Mitty,
whom I have brought with me, is one of the gayest best
humoured creatures in the world. Liz is always running, painting or
dancing with her on our little flagga or beneath the trees.
Sam again suffies 2 gay as ever.
My solitude is seldom interrupted, Mrs Thornton's family are the only
persons I ever see, & they are seldom at their place, which
is a charming farm about a mile from this. They have been
extremely kind, & gave my lodging a room with them, which when
they & I declined they offered me every thing their house required
could afford & gave me almost every day sent something to me.
The cottage in which I am, is a small building of one story
with four rooms, two of which I occupy, & the tenants the others.
The walls of my room are made in which time has made
many a chink, my window have no glass, (except one
for Smith has dismounted) but are protected by shutters.
I brought out, what little furniture is here & have
to find my ingenuity to work to make that little room
all my wants. The stairs serve as a dresser on which I place
bottles, cups, saucers &c are displayed to the most advantage. The
chimney in my mud walls serves as a book case, in which
my table library is fixed to the front entrance; a post to give
about me an air of quiet room, a small bake oven, serves as a pot,
an oven for griddle & frying pan. My tea cup serves as sugar pot,
in which I steep my coffee, salt cellar a potter box &c. These
little continuance please me. I have a bench under the
noble willow which shade the front yard, where I pass most
of my time & I assure you it looks quite romantic to see
me seated on this most beautiful, with my cradle & my bed &
a small table before me. Here too when I have visitors, I
spread my tea table. There is a novelty in my situation, which
confers a degree of pleasure which compensates for every inconvenience.
As for solitude, every day trial but attaches me the more to it.
I spend my time in reading, writing & seeing & never feel lonely
or weary. Sam carried me to a most beautiful country, surrounded
by orchards, cops fields, meadows, fields & woods. Already have
I wondered this came of the most romantic scenery, where one
human fabrication reminds me of the vicinity of man. It first
I was charmed with my solitary ramble & preferred them
to having any company, but when my dear husband came
I, quickly abandoned a most sensible difference. United as we
one, not only by the most fervent affection, but by a consciousness of mutual
a similarity of taste, a powerful love action in myself. Every opinion
seemed to gain some new charm when he was with me, and I never
had a double power to please. He left me yesterday, after saying
three happy, incommensurably happy days. He left though I felt he
behind him & gave himself up to the charms of solitude &
grief, of love. The weather was very cool, & I am sometimes
afraid the whole morning in wandering thru woods, where the
silence was only interrupted by the wind mothing among the
leaves, at home he read aloud, while I seemed to enjoy myself
with fiction in the yard. All my old romance & Enthusiasm seem
to be revived & my heart responds with more than common
tenderness. -- What a transition from my situation one week
ago! --

behind the houses a fine wood extends to the river, which is
about 3/4 of a mile distant. Our lot will contain some fine
oaks & hickory, & plenty of black berries & other vines & briars.
We went through the houses, the office was to be finished suf-
ficiently for use last night, as for the rest of the buildings,
I do not expect they will be done, in less than three weeks.

dividing the house as we please, of having closets, windows, &c,
