December 10th 1817.
A variety of little matters, in a different
way has so occupied my time, since I received your letter my
dear Harpster, that I have not been able to devote that
quiet hour to you which is essential to the execution of
philosophy converse. By this time I suppose you are quite
blind in the city -- and have completed your winter prepara-
tions. I hope you will pass an agreeable season -- but so
gay I presume as the Lord's Short -- will hardly
be in time be in time for general society -- but you may
easily compensate to her -- any loss sustained in that way --
indeed from what you say, if her present views retirement
will be the most acceptable. A heart that is occupied with
a new affection touched by grief -- and awakened to religion can
not find enjoyment in gay errands. This has been an interesting season to me -- I sincerely hope it may continue in her
lasting happiness. It will be delightful to you to have settled
near you -- and see her united to an amiable and deserving
young man. Her entering the family just at this moment
must endear her greatly to the parents -- She will fill up
the place in their hearts and be adopted as a daughter.
-- It would gratify Mary exceedingly to be with you again --
but at present -- I can not say when, nor how -- Robert's
Bayard returns in safety, and makes a prosperous voyage he
may complete his much wished for excursion to Washington &
take Mary with him. But this is all uncertain. As to
Gov. Ro. he says it is impossible for him to leave home
for another he has so much to do in his office.
I regret it exceedingly - for I am sure he would enjoy it
and he really wants some recreation - he rarely denies anything
to his family - and as rarely indulges himself.
Brother Samuel is appointed by the Committee of the
Bible Society to go to U. S. Edition borough - for certain
favour to the U. S. I hope he will be successful. It is not
quite so unpleasant as begging for money directly. I think he
is a suitable agent - for he has great zeal in the cause and
great activity & perseverance. I imagine you will not find
the collision of political sentiment so sharp as it was when you
were here - there is a very great change, generally characterized
the present President has conciliated the good opinion of many
by the gentleness and candor of his manners while on his tour
and has pleased in his late appointments. Every one I have
heard speak on the subject think that Mr. Dick & Biblical
hom do honour to the Presidents judgment and to their
country. That will be the effect of the refusal of the inter-
nal taxes on Mr Smith's office? Will it be absolute? or shall
continued in case of contingencies? I hope if this place is
disposed of - that will be some other opening for him.
I am now looking for heavy - by the next stage that
comes in - Elizabeth is to remain in D.C. with her cousin
June Stevens, this winter. She has commenced taking lessons in
drawing - of a teacher that is very much celebrated - Mrs Johnson
profits from her - objection - and recommends him highly. If C. has
as much taste as you had she might make great improvements
this winter - I hope she will acquire so much that she can
hereafter prosecute it at home, with more pleasure & advantage.
Do your girls go to Dix's Stone this Winter? Does their
improve in music? - As to their dress - I do not think
you need to make any change. I do not think otherwise
expect it - perhaps not notice it. If I did, the excuse you
give is quite sufficient.
I expect to pass a few days with our friend at
prisonation toward the close of this week. I have not seen
sister since the painful scene of Susan's death. I will receive
many affecting recollections. but I hope it will be a salutary
sorrow.
I do not know what to make of the strange
accounts you give of Littledon. I hope you will see more of
him now you are in town - so as to form more accurate
judgment. Have you said anything to Mr Baldock about him?
Does he consider his late poem as proceeding from religious
impressions? I long to know something more about him.
He writes very seldom to us, and when he does it is in a way
that affords no weight into his sentiments or feelings. His
other validity that he is living - and that is all.
We have had the pleasure of hearing from King.
He arrived at Eutawja on the 23d of Sept. and was obliged to
perform guarentine - he appears well - and in good spirits
but does not say when he will return. We now begin to
look for him and hope he will be with us by Christmas.

I have been reviewing its events -- I have been recalling the hopes & fears wishes & anxieties, many of which have been fulfilled, & many of which have been disappointed -- the expectations have failed yet I persevere, clearly percipient in all that has befallen me -- the goodness of my God -- the tender mercies of my Heavenly Father -- and so deep is the conviction that I require that his will be not mine, from every event of my life -- then, I am perfectly thankful for disappointment, believing that often our own wishes give us not our wish, & thinking it more than probable this would not have been my case -- Oh how often do I repent that sweet sacrifice I made of my religion, when all my mercies of my God, my saving soul surveys, transported into the new I am lost, I wonder how I came to be so -- All my life has been a life of misery -- and yet how little want, how cold, has been my cause to be so poor a divine person? What then, is shortening necessary to make us love a father? I would fervor answer in the negative, but when I see the effects of application on the human mind when I see that prosperity is a gladness, happiness the heart, that sorrow & suffering distresses it, I must believe the charitable Lord chastens whom he loves, because it is necessary for their spiritual well fare -- How strange it is my dear Sister that a heart of any generosity or tenderness should be insensible to goodness -- I will give to severity -- I have often condemned on this, & I loathed myself otherwise for my ingratitude & insensibility to the mercies of my Heavenly Father -- It is not that I forget him -- I have not -- it is my sole duty to feel his constant presence & to recognise his providence. pending even a thought or hope on what may be decreed, certain

nesses, never has my belief & trust, in an all directing &
special Providence, been weakened or clouded. God reigns! thy
kingdom come & thy will be done on earth, as it is in Heaven,
I can say with my whole heart & soul. Would that all the
other points of Faith, were as obvious & soul convincing.

done to arouse so much enmity"? & I tell you my sister what
it does, (at least that system taught in our churches) it re-
quires us to sacrifice our reason, that best & distinguishing
& brightest gift of the creator to his creatures. It opposes
itself to that instinctive, moral sense of justice implanted by
the creator in the hearts of his creatures. Our natural
powers of intelligence & our natural feelings, (& is not nature
God's ordinance?) are opposed to such doctrines as the Trinity.

Once more dear sister do I date my
letter from dear Sidney -- How much more like home
can it feel than the city of Sydney, the society is
now changing -- here, my friends they know a friend is killed,
a friend is dead fast & unchangeable, & being separated
with the severest recollections of many, many
years I feel united to them by the closest bonds of
sympathy, I have with them a companionship which
if I did not feel, I never should imagine exist between
the heart & inexorable nature -- But for the first
week I felt sad & lonely without Anna, whom I left
at Kalarama -- but because of her absence, but the occasion
of that absence -- I went for Julia & when she came was
saved from that childish & disloyal feeling -- Her situation
awakened a more than usual degree of tenderness --
indeed we both felt, we had never loved each other
so perfectly before -- She was so full of activity, so
crazy to spend me, that I could not make her sit
quiet, & Mrs. Drake who was with me, advised me
not to restrain her from her usual exercise -- The first
week she was so perfectly well as she was happy, but
one day when I let her ride into the city she went
about all the morning in the hot sun -- stuck with some
other independent foolish consequences which disapponted
my fond hopes of having a grand manner -- She was taken
ill the evening day -- but soon recovered -- I would not however
allow her to leave me until a day or two after I am so sorry
Anna is now better than she has been for
many months. The air is perfumed with the
scent of thousands of flowers in the unending foliage
of trees, & it seems to me most perfect a healthy
& balgamic quality, peculiarly calculated to benefit
the lungs. Still, she is very delicate & feeble, a little
too much excitement of pleasure or occupation or exercise
brings on fever & a sinking or fretfulness of strength.

I regret my dear Hazard that I have not been able
to write to you for so long a time -- and fear you will think me remiss yet I
think you must from long experience felt that confidence in my sympathy -- which will
cause you to think I never could night you lose your son especially in your present
circumstances -- But I have been much indebted -- Washington has been possessing
a pretty powerful sense of treatment -- as the complaint seemed so many times --
which has affected my whole frame -- yet has not exalted the malady the is assisted
the febrile symptoms. sometimes I feel distressed but I should have the same
obvious satisfaction of former years but yesterday -- and today I am in better order.
It is not always an easy attainment to live by the day. Many will make flight
into futility and bring back unworthy apprehensions. Except of myself I trust I
shall do well. At last I will enjoy present comfort which divine providence
has so graciously bestowed beyond all expectation.
It is more than twenty days since the date of your last -- Dear Anna was
thus more comfortable -- and not hearing either from you or from Hazard unless
we hope the remission of painful symptoms is still continued -- and that the
same such warm expressions are still continued to you. What proofs of goodness
are there bunched mitigations of suffering! At a distance we think only of
what is painful and distressing -- but when with a patient we see how many
real pleasure and gratifications -- thus the gloom and sadness as position
habits itself as health itself can ever taste. The comforts of devotion -- the
tenderness of friendship are related in a manner known only to the sufferer
and then the minor gifts of kindness -- the visits of friends -- of a physician
from the apriority of something afford so much satisfaction that pain is
often bequited by its potency, and a sweet feeling is diffused over the sorrows
of disease in the being the object of so much love and care. I must afford you
my dear sister suchlib gratification that you are in circumstances to command all
that comfort for your beloved child -- and that her complaint alone will
mitigatome. I feel very anxious to hear from you -- and from Regard that
has prevented him from writing. He is thus letter in debt to me, and I was deeply
interested in not hearing from me. He did not know how much I needed his prompt
attention -- when you can him inquire if he has not written I think probably he has
written by a private opportunity and that the letter is bad. Every day I have been
expecting he would bring me some mission.
Being shut up in my room -- I have not much to say -- you know there
is a sort of stagnation of mind when cut off from society -- I have omitted only
a few friends -- and when at all interested in conversation have always suffered
from Monday I had quite a leave -- or rather succession, and gentlemen too. I find myself
a venerable elogeeman (real existence) an agent for Belongings. I made an earnest
pleasure visit. He talks as a great and about the prosperity and prosperity of the
Besa Cove settlement -- and appears to think that humanity has every thing
to hope from the appearance of success in all their plans. Before he went
he made a most sweet and soothing address from some corner in the 45th Psalm
where God's care of the kiddos & fatherly is spoken of -- and in an art of liberal
portion recommended as to that case. It was really astonishing! -- I have called
soon after -- and was very kind and cheerful. I had a few female friends also
so that it was quite a legal day in my calendar -- but since then I have had to
practice abstinence --
You speak of Miss Jane -- I believe she is a relation of the Governor
and if the Governor has I wonder not that you love her. I am sure you do
debates with Mrs B. and I am also certain I should admire your wife Jane.
My body is in a very bad state this summer and always came most kindly

a mother can feel; -- a sense of homœomie
almost equal to in some respects more insufferable

I have been wanting to write to you
my dear Sister - but I could not - my pen will
not move unless carried onwards by a current of
thought, or impulse of feeling - unless as a means
machine - a useless implement - I neither like to
waste or receive such mechanical letters - or as I often

tranquility - that usefulness & agitation have subsided
into quietude, though accompanied as it is by
an indifference that deadens all my faculties -
My dear Bayard has been very anxious that I should

the original why is omitted 2 it required greater

so at a loss, that I think I shall assume a
copy something else 2 perhaps offer a whole

been called on to watch the dissolution of this mysterious
tie -- I passed great part of last month by the bedside
of my young friend Dolley Cath -- she had no mother,
no closely friend to watch over her (for her aunt Mrs

Yale, Cambridge, New Haven, Dec 23d 1808.
Dear Parents:
As it is now my turn to write you I have found little time to do it, I received a letter from Bishop in sufficient time informing me that your letter was read I was very sorry to hear it & regretted the departure of Mr. Goddard as I was very glad to hear that you had read this fatal letter. I am sorry I began to fear it was lost. Eddie & myself are very well, I still contented I have not missed prayers but once & recitation, no once. The term has almost expired it was but 13 weeks. In my duties I have been thru 3 books in reading almost thru the 6th to the Epistle in Horace, to thru Epistle in the 5th Vol. Georaphy. Mr. Grimm did not take the Candills to you left for him to have him on a or twice, just before he left began to regretted him to order take them but he has not done it. I have not told him his either, I am sure nothing that will hurt us, & do not know what I shall do with it. I wish to receive some information respecting Harward college, I have not received a single letter from any of my acquaintance there, I heard Goodman, Ward Walker, & others, I have written a long letter to Goddard but have received no answer, I wish if you see him you would request him to write me, Ward likewise I wish to hear from him very much. I have not received a letter from him since I have been in New Haven. Barnes too is expecting a letter every day from him, I hope he has not forgotten me, I shall write him soon.
In Fairfield County a large pieces of stone were contained in it & lay scattered round a mile of miles, Mr. Silliman went with Mr. Kingsley to see a piece of this stone he applied a magnet to it & by its attraction found it to contain iron; the explosion was very loud, it was heard here in New Haven while the students were in to prayers, I heard it at the same time. I will try to obtain a piece of the stone of Mr. Silliman & keep it to bring home for a curiosity. Friday Dec 28th I again have found a little time to answer my letter for I have been engaged for a few days part in writing a 2d composition to use before my class. I am most anxious to get out of this place & to go to Mr. Valuel's house in the country. I have been to Mr. Valuel's house in the country. I have been to Mr. Valuel's house in the country. I have been to Mr.
as we are pretty strict with him about returning our clothes I think he will be
more regular in future. I feel as thankful as you do that I am not
at Cambridge College I would not exchange for a great deal; there are no
disturbances here all goes on regular & the students are pleased with the
authority & the authority with them. We had an ugly affair here
the college books were arraigned before the tribunal of the students consisting of
a committee of 11 from each class no college; I was chosen as one of the
committee from the 2nd Honourable class, we sent for two of the worst of the
books, & were all Saturday afternoon in trying them, found them guilty of
several charges, such as being insolent to the students, not excusing them-
selves to cook clean for us, in concealing pies which belong to the students,
having supper at midnight, & inviting all their neighbours & friends to sup
with them at the expense of the students; & this not once in a while but
almost every night; we extorted this from one of them, that the reason they
were so neglected towards us, was, because there had been no disturbance in
college for 7 years, that the students, & the authority, not taking much no-
tice of their conduct, they meant to do as they please: The committee
after arranging the charges in their proper order, presented them to the
President, he has had the authority together & they are now considering
the subject: this afternoon (Tuesday Decr. 29) they have been together & I with
many others have been with them all the afternoon, there was no restitution
at 4 o clock, they were so busy engaged, I know not how this affair will end, but
I expect in the expulsion of some if not all the books: it is now 3 weeks
since the students convene to appoint their committee, & since that we
have lived extremely well, indeed, for me, past I think we have lived
very well this term, the fault is not so much in the food as in the cooking
for our bill has general been in the following way, chocolate, coffee & hashed
meat every morning; at noon various roast beef, 2 a week pudding & times Vienna
& geese upon an average once a fortnight, baked beans, occasionally Christmas
and other merry days, turkeys, pies, & puddings more as we wish for, at night
for supper we have chocolate tea & pies 1 in a week; I thought to have added that in suc-
tures we are to have beef steaks & toast twice a week; before the books were too large
to cook them I will inform you of the result of this affair as soon as it is complete
I have now as much as I can do; my leisure moments are employed
in composing, reviewing, Geometry & reading history; I am now reading Winterboth-
ams China, I have read Cars stranger in Ireland, & intend soon to read his North-
ern Summer; I am very much pleased with him as an author: I began to read
Robertson's Charles 5th but finding several leaves in the book missing I have depr-
ived it till another time. I do not think I have been extravagant this
term in my expenses, I have lost frequently apples, oysters, cakes &c. but not ex-
travagantly I have been in the custom of having such things at home & this year
Do not think it improper that I should have them now once in a whiles nearly
2 thirds of the scholars spend double of the money that I suppose things, & I suppose some of them do not spend so much; But this I know by experience that the more I study the less I am inclined to desire such things. I hope you will find by my expenses (of which I have kept an accurate account) that I have not been so extravagant as I was last term, & if there are any things which you think I might have dispensed with I will amend in future; in the vacation I will send you a list of my expenses
We sleep very comfortable I am warm, have plenty of clothing. We are early to bed & early to rise, which makes us healthy, wealthy & wise.
The season here is very mild we have had no snows, & in many places the grass is quite green, it seems more like spring than winter.
I enjoy myself very much, feel quite contented & very well pleased with my studies; The past term (for it is almost gone) seems to have run away very fast, & if the next passes as fast, I think I shall be at home in less than a week. Remember us to Richard in particular, I wish I had time to write to him but he must excuse me I believe as I have so little time to spare; if he feels home sick at all he must think of the great distance we are from home, & must think how he will feel when he comes on to college. Remember us particularly to Grandma Ma & Aunt Abby, & to "excusing" Mr. & Mrs. Woodroof & in short to all who are solicitous for our welfare & enquire after us.
It is almost bedtime do I think Somers is alone the christle, & bid you Good Night
Please to execute the writing of Blots
I remain your affectionate Son
S. F. B. Morse.
Rev'd W. J. Morse Charlestown

Dear Parents,
I have just received yours of the 12th inst. by Betsy
Allot & intend to send this by him with a no. of others to
my regret inance in Charleston & then South. I
had safe & sent the little trunk which you sent us some
time since, but was obliged to pay a monstrous price for
carriage & toll. We are very much obliged to Hannas
for sending us the cake & raisins, we have eaten them all.
I have given up the idea of having Major Hirst for a
sett has just been purchased for the Brothers' library & I
can have the use of that. I have not been to the President's
house yet to visit him, I will go soon; I don't wish to visit
much during the vacation as I have my hands full;
I am pursuing my Frenchy & Mr. Valued says, if Petition
I can nearly acquire the language in 3 Months
In the affair of my gun I don't think I made a very bad
bargain, I had used it considerably, it wanted many repairs,
the lock was out of order, & as I had not used the gun
for some time, it was getting no better by being kept in my room
The principal book I read was Young, Right Tho'k, the rest were plain
wh. I consider as trash & only took them that I might sell
them again.— The result of the Cooks trial is, one has been
dismissed, 2 remain on trial for poor behavior, the rest are
in their former standing— I have not got any trunk from
Williams yet, this I have asked him for it a no. of times—
We have had but one day in which there has been good
slighting; the winter has been uncommonly mild, the grass
is green in many places. This letter is rather short for a
private opportunity, but as I have so many to write I hope
you will excuse me. I think it is better to write all my
intelligence by this opportunity than to send them by mail. I am
Your affectionate Son S.G.B. More

Sabbath evening Yale College, New Haven Jan. 31st 1808.
Dear brother,
As I have a little time left this evening I improve
it by writing you a few lines. Edw. & B are both well & very
much contented, altho so great a distance from home : Our
vacation is just out ; next Wednesday will be the first day
of the term, & I feel very glad to see the vacation so far gone,
for I wish to pursue my studies, altho the hardest studies of
my college life will then be studied, Enelid, God. Webber, &
Gracia. Majoram. I hope the next term will pass away quiet
for I want to see home agains very much. I long for the
time when you will come on to college, I hope you will
study hard so as to make one of the first in your class.
I have been pursuing the French Language this vaca-
tion & hope I shall gain a thorough knowledge of it
by next commencement. I would write you a longer
letter but have not time. Mr. Abbott goes early in the morning
& it is now past 9 o'clock.
I am very much troubled with chilblains this winter
& so is Edw. the winter is very mild here, there has been
but one day in which there has been good sleighing.
I remain
(Give our love to Papa & Your very affectionate
Manma when you write)
Samuel T. B. Morse.

Yale College Feb 18th 1808
Dear Parent,
I have again found a little leisure to write you
a few lines; my time is wholly taken up by my studies,
especially Mathematics; Trigonometry requires very deep
that at first to understand it, but as I have got the me-
niments of it perfect, I find but very little difficulty
with it. My leisure time is chiefly taken up by
studying French, but sometimes I find time to read a
little in other books: I have been reading the Prophecies
in the Bible to day & find the prophecy of Bonaparte
& have found one which appears to me to be the one, it
is the 11th Chap. of Daniel & beginning with the 21st verse
"And in his estate shall stand up a vile person &c. in
the 25th verse it says "Then shall stand up in his estate a rais-
er of taxes &c. but he shall be destroyed neither in anger nor in battle." This I conceive to be Louis 16 who raised heavy taxes which caused his death which was neither in anger nor in battle: in the succeeding verse it mentions after, "(shall stand up a vile person);" that he should obtain the kingdom by flatteries which agrees with the manner in which Bonaparte gained the kingdom. In the 24th verse "He shall enter peaceably upon the fattest places of the province," &c. So I think this must mean his popesping the countries about France such as Germany, Austria, Rusia, Switzerland, &c. it then mentions 2 Kings, the kings of the South & North this I conceive to mean Bonaparte &
Alexander & in 27th v. it says "both these kings hearts shall be to
do mischief" this seems to correspond with their actions at
present. Then in the 30th verse it says "for the ships of Chit-
lin shall come against him" & this passage seems most to
confirm my belief that this is a prophecy of Brionaparte
For I take "the ships of Chittlin" to mean "the ships of Eng-
land" & that this part of the prophecy & the remaining
part is yet to be fulfilled therefore I can't explain
the rest, only in the 36th verse it says "he shall exalt him-
self & magnify himself above every God" & in the 24th He shall
do that which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers fathers" &
all this seems to apply to him. I wish you would write
me your opinion of this subject & correct me when I am
wrong. Another thing concerning Brionaparte I will
mention to you; in the 13th Chap of Revelation & 18th verse
it says "Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understand-
ing count the number of the beast, for it is the number
of a man, & his number is Six hundred three score & six"
that is 666. Now Brionaparte read in Greek & spelt accor-
ding to the Italian or Corsican manner is Bonaparte
& the amount of this name is exactly 666.
I have read Newton on this subject but he supposes,
with another writer that this passage refers to one
Latinus & Lateinus the famous kings & or of the
Latinus &c. &c. I only mention this, perhaps it may be of some importance.
Editors & myself are very well yesterday
I had a very bad headache & was not able to study.
Adieu! I have a lesson to get & it is 10 in the evening
Excuse my hurry & the bad writing.
Yours &c. S.F.B. Moore

Sabbath evening. Yale College New Haven March 6th 1815
Dear Parents,
I have a little leisure time I improve it by
writing you a few lines. Dr Dwight is quite aware
he has been unable to attend to his college duties for some
days past; he is very much distressed in his eyes & I fear
he will lose them; on this account there has been no
exercises in the chapel to day I was not able to go
out to meeting on account of my hat it is cracked and
torn in such a manner that it is totally unfit to wear
Mr Twining seems always to recommend me to the worst
places in town to get my things, he once recommended
me to a barber (who is known to be a drunken & profane
person,) to get my hair cut, & likewise to a shoemaker (who
is the worst in town) to get a pair of shoes & lastly to the
hatter of whom I purchased my hat who is the greatest
cheat in town, & tomorrow I must purchase
me another hat, before I have worn my hat, half long
enough to pay for it; I shall let Mr Twining go himself
& get one out this time. I hope you will not
think that it was owing to my carelessness that my
hat has lasted so short a time; for no person could
taste more pains to make it look well, than I did;
I was cheated, & I am not the only student who has
been cheated by the same man. I find it impossible to live in College without spending money;
at one time a letter is be paid for, then comes up a great
tax from the Class or Society which keeps me constantly
running after money; when I have money in my hands
I feel as tho I had stolen it & it is with the greatest pain that
I part with it. I think every minute I shall receive a letter from
home blaming me for not being more economical & thus
I am kept in distress all the time.
The amount of my expenses for the last term was
$15.10 & is founded in the following manner
For my expenses I do not include my
wood, tuition bills, board or washing
bills -- my washing was last term $8.00
Prince does not wash for me now, but
Mr. Moultriep; the washes very well indeed --
Edwds & myself are very well & I
believe we are doing well, but you will
learn more of that from our instructor.
In about 2 months I hope I shall
have the pleasure of seeing home once
more, the time passes away very fast.
I must now bid you Adieu for
I am rather tired at present. Give my love to Grand Mama, Aunt
Richard, & Nancy. I hope I shall see
them soon.
P.S. The students are very fond of flying
balloons at present; I will (with
your leave) when I return home
make one they are pleasing
sights. Edwds carried the
latter part of your letter to Mr. Evarts
I have not received any answer from
Mr. Evarts since.
Yours etc.
S.F.B. Moser

Dear Parents,
I have but a moment's time to write you a few lines by Mr Huntington who goes immediately, I received of the 12th inst. a letter to take this opportunity to answer it -- The Post is not so bad as I think it was when I wrote, he was able to attend his toller in office the next day after I wrote you, Norris is in good health at present, as fast as I can team. P. Dana is quite unwell, & is not expected to live. Eliot & myself are in very good health, & enjoy ourselves very much. You ask us if our clothes look shabbier, I think I shall need a new light suit soon by the time I come home, I have had mine mended once since I have been home, & it is almost in need of being mended again. My class have studied since this commencement. Ishamous, No 2d vol. Geography, Buckid & Horace, (for the first term,) (2 terms) review Euclid, Horace, & study 2d vol. Webster Math. & have got as far as Euclides in it, I wish when you write me you will inform me who it is that is coming from Cambridge to this college -- The large box you mention I was not able to sell, I placed in the entry & it was broken some of it was carried off for kindling wood, so I brot it in & burn it -- I have not the pamphlet you mention & likewise the paper I have not time at present to write more "multum in parvo" Abeel years to
S. H. B. Morse

Dear Parents,
Since your of the 1 inst. some time since, I
take this opportunity of answering it, I shall be quite
overjoyed when vacation arrives for I feel myself in need
of some respite. I never studied so hard before, as I have
since commencement, & I feel much happier for it. I think
I should feel quite happy if I had kept a regular account
of my expenses for this last term, for I have been so taken
up in my studies, & I must confess have been a little too
negligent, that I can give but a very superficial account
of them, but if you will pardon this neglect for this time,
I will be more careful in future.
I am at present reviewing my studies for the 2 last
terms, Horace, Exelixis, & 2d Vol. Webster; we have only
proceeded as far as Navigation in 2d Vol. Wilks on Heights
distances, & Surveying an very amusing subject, a few
days since the whole class accompanied by the tutors, went
to find the height of East Rock, found it to be 337. feet higher
I have read composition 2d time upon my division, 2d poetry
Last Sunday there were 21 persons pronounced to enter Mr.
Stuart's class -- I was told this by some of the students, but is
not known for certain that it is true. I have been quite un-
well a few days past but have recovered Edward & I am quite
well at present. -- My clothes are quite worn out I am
you much afraid they will not last me till vacation, I shall
need a new coat as soon as I get home & likewise a pair
of trousers, I look very shabby now, & you may judge
how I must look at the expiration of 3 weeks. I shall
be ashamed to go thro' Boston looking as I do now.
You will please to excuse me from writing
more at this time.
Your affectionate son
Sam'l T.B. Morse.

Yale College New Haven June 10. 1808
Dear Parents
I have just received your letter & parents
by Revd Mr Jackson of Philadelphia, viz. a
sett of Geographies & an atlas for Mitchell, & a
no. of Panoptist Subscription papers with a letter
Mitchell had just purchased a sett together with
an Atlas, but I believe he is about to sell them
again. We arrived here safely on Thursday
evening after we departed from Boston, we were
neither of us in the least homesick & have not
yet been. I am a little indisposed to day with
a violent headache, therefore I hope you will
exercise the brevity of this letter, I hope I shall
feel better the next time I write. I have not
yet been to see Mr Swining, Evarts, or Beers
concerning the business with you mentioned to
me I will go soon. Mr Silliman has
given me a receipt to make liquid blacking
it is the best & cheapest of any I have seen, I
will copy it here, thinking it may be of
great use to you,
Receipt to make good Liquid Blacking.
Take 1 quart of sharp vinegar
1/4 oz. of Gum Arabic
1 gill of Molasses
2 ozs. Sweet oil
2 ozs. Sulphuric Acid
1/2 lb Ivory Black
Remember to pour in the Sulphuric Acid last as that
will set it a boiling, be very careful not to let any of
the Acids touch your clothes or hands, as it will burn them bad-
ly. After it is mixed you can either keep it in a bot-
tle or a bowl, the Ivory black will keep at the bottom
remember when you use it to stir it up well; the virtue
of this blacking is that it requires less brushing than
the common liquid blacking, & there is a fine gloss
remaining on the boot or shoe, it is also cheaper than
any other, 1/6 will get all that is necessary for making
a quart.
I must now bid you Adieu! as my head
aches so bad that I can scarcely tell what I
write. on that I hope you will excuse all
blots & mistakes.
Edu:ts is very well
Your affectionate Son
J. B. Moore

During my first night at the camp, I was much at a loss to find a subject on
which I might write. I composed myself to sleep, in
expectation that a dream would disclose to me some
incident from which I might be able to extract matter
sufficient to form a passable composition. Accordingly,
after the usual confusion which takes possession of the
senses immediately on falling into a sleep; a beau-
tiful prospect of New Haven and its delightful harbour
gradually opened to my view; from surrounding objects
I soon perceived that imagination had placed me on
the summit of East Rock. Among the various scenes
which then attracted my attention, the sun half sunk
beneath the horizon, gleaming with its setting rays a
dreadful cloud, was among the most interesting. I had
scarcely time to contemplate this awful sight before
the approach of the threatening storm warned me
to seek some shelter from its fury; I accordingly bent
my way towards the thickest part of the forest, in hopes
that I might meet with some humble shed in which
I might repose myself until the strength of the
blast had spent itself; but I searched in vain; the
darkness increased; the tempest roared; and the light-
ning, flashing at short intervals, served but to disco-
ver to me the gloominess of my situation: I thought
of returning, but instead of pursuing the way thro' which I had entered the wood, I turned into a different
path.
path and thus became more perplexed than ever. It
was then that I felt real terror; all the horrors of de-
spair seized upon me at once; death seemed invi-
table, and I was just closing my eyes for the last time,
when a sudden and dreadful flash of lightning dis-
covered to me the ruins of some building but a short
distance from me, this sight inspired me with fresh
vigor, and leaping up, I directed my course towards
the place, which I reached in a few moments. I found
it to be an ancient castle, to all appearance unin-
habited, one part of it was entirely decayed, the other
seemed to be in a tolerable state of repair. This unex-
pected discovery of a castle in a place little suspect-
ed of containing such a building, for a moment
filled me with surprise; But I was soon roused from
my meditations, by a dim light suddenly gleaming
from one of the grated windows of a decayed turret
of the castle, which attracted my whole attention. The
ancient tales of castles, spectres, &c. which I had
frequently read in old romances, now rushed forth
to my memory, and I concluded from these that
I was destined to be the performer of some great
exploits. Taking courage from this conclusion, I de-
termined to explore this solitary mansion, and sum-
moning up all my firmness, I proceeded across the
court and entered an old Gothic porch, seemingly
the only entrance to this lonely building. The storm
had now subsided, the clouds were dispersed, and the
moon rising over the tops of the trees, gave me an op-
portunity of viewing the castle in more advantage.
It was constructed entirely in the Gothic taste with two
turrets one of which appeared to be entire, the other
nearly fallen to ruins, it was in this last turret that
I perceived the light which surprised me so much a
few minutes before this tended in some measure to in-
crease my astonishment as in all probability if the
castle was inhabited by human beings, they would make
choice of the most convenient part of it to dwell in.
I now opened the great door of the building with
conducted me into a spacious chapel, I passed softly
by several large pillars, when stopping I could
distinctly hear footsteps approaching me. Scarcely
venturing to breathe, I turned, and by the pale light
of the moon, rendering the gloom of the place just
visible, I perceived a tall, unacciated figure, slowly
walking towards me, as he passed me he beckoned me
to follow him, I, not daring to refuse, followed him
thru the chapel, down several pairs of stairs into the
vault beneath the castle, my guide then taking a
dim taper from the last staircase walked on some
distance; he then turned to the right, and applying a
key to the door of a gloomy dungeon, we entered it;
at the same time my conductor extinguishing
his light disappeared, leaving me in total darkness.
I stood for a moment considering what was best for
me to do: I turned to open the door which I had
just entered, but it was fastened, as I retreated
a few steps back I struck my foot against some
soft substance on the ground. I stooped down to
discover what it was, when to my great astonish-
ment and terror I placed my head upon the
cold face of a corpse; this was more than my
overstrained senses could bear; struck with horror
at my situation, I fell senseless to the ground.
How long I remained in this situation I am un-
able to inform you, but when I recovered I
found myself to me no small joy safe upon my
bed.
S. S. B. Morse.
June 13th 1808.
Yale College N. Haven July 21st 1808
Dear Parents,
I have received 1 or 2 letters from you
lately, which, I fear, we have been too negligent in
answering.
I have not been at all well this term
I have felt extremely languid, & very much inclined
to sleep; I have felt no disposition to study, I cannot
relish my food; the cause of all this I am pretty
confident, is the sultriness of the season; want of
exercise, and slemeness of food; I have some hints of
requesting leave to return home, which, upon after
some deliberation, I think would certainly be best
for me; the term is now nearly half gone, the
Senior class were dismissed yesterday, and there is
but little for my class to study between this &
Commencement, Murray's Exercises, 2d Vol. Webber's
Grace Majora, & perhaps Priestly's Lecture, if we get
this Murray, now then I can study at home
but I cannot here; I feel very low spirited, & un-
less I can find some thing that will raise the
spirits I fear I shall be but poorly at Commencement;
Literise if I am at home I may be able to assist
you in various ways, I can write for you; &
can have more time to compose for myself; I hope
you will not infer from this language that I am
discontented with College, it is quite the converse, I
never was more pleased with it; yet I think it for
my own interest to be at home; if I stay here I
shall certainly do nothing, but if I am at home
I shall soon feel inclined to study. However, in this
business I shall not proceed rashly, I intend going to
consult Dr. Dwight concerning it, and shall do as he
advises me; I think I would give you this informa-
tion lest you should be surprised at seeing me of
come home in such a sudden manner.
There is nothing of importance that I can
mention to you, the College is in a prosperous state;
There has been one instance of the yellow fever in this
city & four or five of the putrid fever, it is now in
this place, but I know not whether we are in much
danger of catching either of them -- Adieu!
Yours etc.
P.S. Edwds is well.
J. S. B. Morse

Col. College New Haven July 23d 1808
Dear Parents,
I wrote you a few letters, two or three days
since informing you that it was not improbable
that I should be at home in a short time. I have
not seen Dr. Dwight on the subject yet but shall if
I do not feel better in a few days. In the
last letter I forgot to mention some things which I
ought to have done. Mr. James Dwight requested
me to buy & get him one or two copies of Col. Pick
ering's last letter to Genl. Sullivans; I wish you could
procure them for me & send them on as soon as possible.
They are not to be obtained in New Haven.
The Seniors were dismissed from college a
few days since, the classes have chosen rooms. I
did not choose with them, as I intend rooming
with a tutor if possible; I have spoken with Mr.
Dwight on the subject; If I can do this I shall
think myself highly favored. It is now late in
the evening; I will finish this some other time.
Monday July 25th 1808.
I have just received your letter of the 15th. I
hope you have received mine before this time. I never
said so much hurt, as when I heard of the misconduct
of Elisha Goddard, I know not what excuse he has to
fallate his crime, & I therefore cannot judge whether
he is to blame or not; but after all that I have said
to him I think he might have employed his time better
the 1st Sunday in the month of February, 1820, in search of John Cooper;
I now despair of reforming him; I christen great hopes of
making him, in process of time, a perfect companion for myself;
But these hopes are now blasted; However, I do not know
but, reflection, (if he is not entirely hardened) with a parting letter
from me, may not have a good effect on him, if it does
I hope you will not deprive me from encouraging him to
ample & advice when I come home. In any rate I hope
you will not forbid my visiting the family, you will not
hear my being led astray by Eliska, & I have too much regard
for my own character, to be seen walking the streets
with him. I shall at first receive him very coolly, and if this
has no effect on him, I shall abandon his company altogether, or
special with him no farther than is consistent with civility. Ward & Walker
shall in future be my most intimate intimate friends; I wish you would
tell them by some means, that I do not forget them as little
I do not write them; they will see me as receive a letter
from me in a short time. Campbell has been here, and
has obtained liberty to be examined for my class, he has since
returned home & concludes not to be examined until
commencement. Barnes & Edmonds are well, I am still
the same as to my health & think it very probable I shall
be at home in a short time. I feel myself very much
to blame for not writing you often, than I have done
hitherto, I will mend in this particular.
Please excuse me from writing more
often. Yours, etc
S.S.B. Morre

Dear Parents,
I have just received to my great surprise
a letter from you, answering me for not writing
oftenier than I have done; I really cannot
conceive the cause, why you should suspect I have
done any thing wrong, I am not in, the least difficulty
in any thing, except feeling a little unwell &
very much hurt on reading your letter; I am just
in as good standing in my class as I was last
term; I had a quarrel with one of my classmates
a few weeks ago, but that has not injured me
in the least, the blame was entirely on his side
I complained to the authority, & the young fellow
who quarreled with me (Grumball) is to
be sent from college for this, & other crimes.
You need not think that this has had the least
effect in injuring my character, for I was
perfect last it would, & went to Mr Day, he
told me I need not be under any apprehension
on that account, I was not consider at all blameable,
if this is not sufficient to satisfy you on
this head, you can write to Mr Day and he
will give you the particulars, or I will tell you
when I come home, they would take up too much
time to repeat them now. The affair is entirely
over closed closed & you need not be under any apprehension
on that score.
I am really surprised to hear you say
you have not received but two letters from me
I have written no less than six this is the 7th
& I sent by mail, then 1 by Mr Townsend then
1 by mail & 1 by Goddard, wht I hope you will
receive before this reaches you
Goddard has been here, and behaved very well; I write
however, give up his company, for I see many things in him
which has disputed me. His father wrote him a very
long & serious letter; he read it to me, it was similar
to many of your letters to us, giving him a great deal
of good advice, and one would suppose from the contents
of the letter that he (Dr Goddard) was a Christian; I did
not know before, that, Dr G. was such a serious man, if Elisha
is not entirely hardened. That letter must have affected
him some -- I suppose the family must be in great distress,
for I really believe they are a very amiable family,
to take them generally -- Elisha's letter was enclosed in
one to me, written by Dr Goddard, thanking me for the
good advice I had given Elisha, & wished me very much
to give him some suitable to his situation, &c. I accordingly
did, but I doubt whether it will have any good effect;
I feel very well today, and am now pursuing my studies with redoubled ardour to
make up for the time in which I have been unwell.
I should think you ought to make some allowances
for my not writing you; I have been so unwell that
I have not been able to do any thing at all, for two
or three days, at a time -- Edwards has not written
but one or two letters this term; & he is not censured,
whereas I have written 6 and it appears that 3 have
miscarried & 1 is on the road; I hope you will get
them all soon, & relieve me from my pains, I wish you
would answer this as soon as you receive it; for I
shall be very much hurt until, I know that you
are convinced that I am not to blame -- I am now
perfectly contented & happy, am more & more pleased
with a college life; have not missed prayers nor recitation,
for our week past (the time I began to feel better) and
shall not again till commencement.
I inform you with a great deal of joy that my voice
is entirely changed; I have now spoken like other people,
I obtained it I believe only by singling I have sung on
great deal this term.
There is no news in town I believe, I see by a
New York paper that there has been a rumor that Bue-
naparte has been assassinated at Bulegne by the
Spaniards.
I hope you will not be under the necessity of writing
another letter to me; this I shall expect one, if this
miscarries like the rest of my letters which I have sent by post.
I must now bid you Adieu!
as I have little exercises to attend to
Your affectionate and ever dutiful Son
Sam'l B. Yosse

Yale College New Haven Jan 1st 1809
Dear Parents,
As I have a little leisure to write I impose
it by writing a few lines; my studies on week days occupy so much
of my time; that I never get an opportunity to write them, I
am forced to do it on Sabbath evening. I heard a few days ago
by Ward that I had a sister, but this month I heard from
Mr Dwight that she lived but a short time, which grieves me
very much for Mama's sake, for I know it must afflict her
children who have been spared will afford her comfort, suffice
to overbalance the affliction, I will endeavor for my own
part to behave in such a manner that you will have no reason
to complain of me, indeed I trust you will find no cause
for blame in my conduct this term; I have not been
absent from prayer this term, nor but once absent from recitation,
by that unavoidably Edwards has neither been absent
from prayer or recitation to my knowledge this term, he stands
high in the esteem of his class from what I can learn, and
in short I hope the conduct of us both this term has been such
as will meet with your approbation: The appointments at
the end of this term will be given to those who merit
them, in my class, a great many are in dread of the
judgment expecting who will doubtless be dis-appointed
as for my own part I do not feel very anxious, if I deserve
an appointment, I hope I shall have one, if otherwise I will
cheerfully yield to those who are my superiors.
Mr Kingsley received your letter sometime since he desired
me to acquaint you that he was so much taken up in
business that he was unable to do what (you requested) or (he promised)
till some future period; Mr Filliman likewise wished me to
inform you that he wrote you a few days ago & wished to know
if you had received it. Tutor Hooker has arrived here
to take charge of his division of the Freshman Class, he had en-
gaged a roommate a long time before I applied to him & so I
am unable to room with him; Ward is without a room-
mate he rooms out of college now but the Bos. has told
all those that room out that they must come into college
the next term, therefore Ward will be obliged to come in, if as
he is very anxious to room with a stranger he is very desir-
ous of rooming with me & wish you would write to Mr Dwight
& obtain leave for us to room together next term. I shall
leave Mr Dwight next term as he only engaged to keep me
one term, and as it must be inconvenient for him to have Bin
his room. I am very fond of S. Wards and should be
very much pleased at rooming with him; he is well, in good
spirits, & very much pleased with the College, thinks it far superior
to Cambridge. The disturbances are all over here now, & we
are restored to order again. I feel very well, & enjoy myself ex-
traordinarily, am more & more pleased with my situation in college.
I am very much pleased with "Chemistry" it is very amusing
as well as instructing, there are many very beautiful and
surprising experiments that can be performed, which are likewise very useful
I intend (with your leave) getting me a "Chemical Trough," of small
apparatus, when I come home, Ward & I to bear the expense
together; you will find our experiments very entertaining. --
There will be a no of articles which we shall want, which we shall
be obliged to get him, on account of their being obtained here
cheaper such as furnisette, retorts, &c, the cost of which I will
explain to you hereafter. Vacation commences in a week from
next Wednesday; & then I shall have some respite from my
labors; there will be a great number of students who will re-
main here & keep me company, so that I shall not be liable
to feel homesick.
I hope you will excuse me for not writing you often
than I have done this term, for you know how busy I am
employed in studying. You mentioned in a former letter that
you hoped we visited at the places you told us, but I had
not been out of the college yard before I came here, when I
went to see him at Butler's tavern it was the first time I
had gone out of the yard. So you see I have no time for vis-
iting; indeed it is not a popular thing among the students to
go on visiting; they think the person is more pleased with
company than his "Books"; now I don't wish to be that
of in this way until I get out of college I will then
visit as much as you desire me to but whilst I am
in college, I should desire to be free from such cares, for you
have often inquired upon me this maxim, "Do one thing first."
now whilst I am studying I wish to make a business of it
and when I visit them I will visit.
Give my love to all the family especially Nick,
his clap is a very good one, & makes progress as I have no doubt
he does; Edw's will inform him of their studies as I have
other business to attend to. This letter must last a long while
for it is a long one. I wish you all a happy new year.
I hope mama is well; write me soon. Edw's & I am well.
I may possibly find a letter in the office for me from you I have
not received one this long time. I must bid you Adieu as it is late
and I am considerably fatigued. Your affectionate son
Samuel F. B. Morse.

My Dear Parents,
Owing to some unforeseen incidence I did not go till to-morrow morning (Wednesday) I therefore improve a few moments in writing you longer,
as I intended write but a short letter yesterday.
The "appointments" come out to-morrow morning I therefore shall leave this letter unsealed & will give you a list of them at the end of this letter;
I cannot say but I feel a little anxiety on the occasion but I have prepared myself for a disappointment.
I received last evening a couple of pamphlets from the Office, for which I thank you, I delivered the Panoplist to Mr Kempsey who was wishing it very much.
There has been a gentleman named Colly with a subscription paper for Hon Fisher Ames' Works I saw your name on the list & therefore declined subscriptions I wish you would send me the work as soon as it is published; I understand it will be an excellent thing.
I have been reading the 1st Vol. of Professor Silliman's journal while the rest during his passage to, & residence in, Europe I am very much pleased with it; I long for the time when I shall be able to travel with improvement to myself and society, and hope it will be in your power to offer me. I have a very ardent desire of travelling, but I consider that an education is indispensable to me, & I mean to apply myself with all diligence for that purpose, "diligentia vincit omnia" is my maxim, and I
shall endeavor to follow it.
I hope you will write to Doctor Dwight on the
subject of my rooming with Washo, I shall have to
room with some of my own class who are disagreeable
fellows, unless, I can be so fortunate as to get Wan for
a roommate; I wish you would attend to this subject
as it interests me very much.
I wrote you some time since concerning some
books for Mr. James Dwight but I have heard nothing
of the fate of the letter which contained the request.
I be wished me to inform you that you need not send
them now, as he has got them from NewYork. They
were concerning the Theological Institution.
There is no news in NewHaven, I hear nothing but complaints
of the "scandalous embargo"; I have received no papers from
you if late; I should be gratified to see some of Boston
news.
Please to write us soon and often this vacation
as it will serve to heighten our spirits, as they are a
little depressed at the approach of a vacation which
we are not destined to enjoy in I find it a difficult
task to do nothing." I shall be employed in the vacation
in the Philosophical Chamber with Mr. Dwight who
is going to perform a no. of experiments in Electricity.
Next term the studies will be more difficult
than at present we shall study Dialling, Spheres,
Gracia Majora, (which by the way is a hated book here) and
Philosophy; besides an o of small duties such as, disputing
declaring, composing, &c &c. so you see that I have
my hands full.
Give my "best love" to Richard, I thank him for his
kind letter a few days ago, and would answer it, but
at present have not time.
I must now bid you Adieu!
Your affectionate Son
Samuel F. B. Morse

Of all the subjects, which are discussed by mankind,
no one affords more real satisfaction than the contempla-
tion of Beauty. Whether we consider the beauty of the
human form and features or the beauties of nature &
art, each of them are equally interesting. However with-
out dwelling any great length of time, on either of
these abstractedly, it is my intention briefly to con-
sider them all promiscuously.
The principles of beauty are three, viz. Variety,
Proportion, and Uniformity. It needs little
demonstration to convince a person that the continued
repetition of any one thing, is disagreeable; a person
cannot view with pleasure, a painting, where the only
object that strikes his eye is water, he would imme-
dately pronounce it insipid; but if a ship, or a rock
were introduced, it would then afford variety, and
of course have a great claim to beauty. From this
it might seem that the greater the variety, the more
beautiful the scenery would appear; but this is far
from being the case, for a confused assembly of
objects, without fitness or connection is quite as dispris-
ing as an unvaried sameness. The eye with respect to
variety is very analogous to the ear: you may all have
unmasked the disagreeable sensations, which are felt by
hearing one unvaried & continued strain upon a musical
instrument; it tires the ear and compels it to wish an
immediate change to relieve it: And this change pro-
duced in an agreeable and skilful manner constitutes
the beauties of Music. On the principle of Variety
Landscape is the most beautiful of all scenery, as it
affords us an infinite variety of forms & colors; a land-
scape however is considered as defective unless water is
introduced in some part of it: the water by reflecting and inverting the objects
which are near its borders, occasions a pleasing vari-
ety, and gives a degree of lustre to the whole.
The human form and features are excellent
examples of variety, the oval form of the face, the
dissimilarity of the ears, eyes, nose, & smooth, & the other
membes of the body to each other, are fair proofs of this;
but I shall have occasion to mention the human
figure in an after part of this composition, I will
therefore leave it for the present.
The next ingredient of Beauty is Proportion,
this is a term given to that law of nature which
establishes the length & breadth of objects. Proportion
is a principle which we have all derived from experience
we have in a manner acquired a knowledge of
judging of the due proportions of an object wherever
we see it; thus for instance if we see a part might be
suspended by a slight thread it immediately occasions
in us a sensation of pain, so likewise should an
enormous pillar employed for the support of a tri-
fling burden it would excite in us a sense of
Convenience and habit given to the idea of pro-
portion, thus a person who is accustomed to see the
mechanism of a clock, forms within his mind an
idea that all the wheels are proportionate, because
each one does its duty and on the contrary if he
should see a clock with some of its wheels of a lar-
ger size than ordinary he would immediately
form the idea of disproportion in his mind: Many
other instances of proportion might be adduced, but
those already mentioned, I fancy will suffice.
I therefore, proceed to the next and last
ingredient of Beauty with I mentioned viz.
Variety. It may appear in some degree
paradoxical that Variety and Uniformity two
opposite characters, should be placed together to con-
stitute a part of Beauty: But by Uniformity I
would not wish to be understood, sameness, that is
far from being my meaning; by Uniformity is meant
a pleasing regularity, harmony, and similarity of
parts to each other. To illustrate this principle by ex-
ample; we know that a well constructed edifice is
usually composed of three parts viz. two wings and a center
now to have these constructed according to the strict rules
of uniformity, the wings should be perfectly similar to each
other, should have a due proportion to the center and
the entrance should be in the center at equal distances
from the sides, this constitutes uniformity,
but if the door instead of being placed in the middle
should be thrust in at one side the eye would directly
perceive the defect and indicate to the mind
that something was wrong. Thus much for the
principles of beauty considered abstractly, it now only
remains to find a character most suitable to exhibit
all these principles combined; and when shall we
find a better example than man? The dissimilarity
of the eyes, nose, ears, and mouth to each other are exhibits
of variety; the elegant construction of the limbs so well
calculated to perform their respective offices as fair examples
of proportion, & the similarity of one eye, ear, arm, &c. to
its fellow are excellent specimens of Uniformity; So that from
what has been said we may draw this conclusion, that
real Beauty cannot exist without Variety, Proportion,
and Uniformity; and that man is consequently the
best standard of Beauty, as he possesses all these qualities
in a high degree of perfection.
February 21st 1809.
Samuel F. B. Morse
Yale College New Haven, July 1809
Dear Parents
I have neglected writing you for some
time, in daily expectation of receiving a letter from
you, but as I have expected in vain I think it
my duty to refrain no longer, from informing you
of our situation here: Edwards & myself are
both well, as this is a very sickly time in this
place; the typhus fever rages here without con-
troul, there are a number of the students very
sick with it; 3 of them a few days since were
not expected to live; viz Rice, (with whom papa
is acquainted;) Fish & Parkins, all of the Se-
nior class; I am happy however in now stating
they are considered out of danger & are slowly
recovering: Wells of my class belonging to Hart-
ford, was sent for home a few days since, with
the melancholy news of his mothers & only sis-
ter's death; they both died of the spotted fever
of which the typhus fever is a genus. Wells was
the person with whom I roomed the latter
part of my September year... I hope, however,
you will not give yourselves unnecessary anxiety on
our account, as I think we are entirely out of danger. I expected that I had taken this fever
a few days since, as I had the symptoms very strongly; it however proved nothing more than a
violent turn of my accustomed complaint, the headache; it has now nearly left me; it has occasioned
my being absent from prayer & recitation a number of times when I regret very much.
I have left Mr. Dwight's room, as it appeared so inconvenient for us to room together, the
measure was advised by Mr. Dwight & he has recommended me to a good roommate by name
Grainke brother to the person who visited us in Charleston some time since with Dr. Durghm. I am
very much pleased with him.
I have nothing of importance to relate to you; my class about a fortnight since sent unanimous
petition to the authority, to permit us to study something in the room of Grace Majors
it was granted, and we are permitted to study Homer & that our studies are comparatively
easier than they were last term.
The class met a week since to choose the managers to the may balls, I trust you will not
object to my attending it as it is in my class; if con-
venient I wish Mama would please to send me on
a white jacket, and other clothing with she may
think suitable for such an occasion; I should wish
to look as well as the generality of my class there,
whom I have no doubt will most of them attend
as is customary. It is true, I request these things
of you in season, but I think it is better to be too
early than too late."
Give my particular love to Richard, I
hope he is well & doing well, I long to see him
very much, but the time I trust is fast past
on when I shall have my wish realized. I
write him a letter if time would permit me
for at this I have more time to spare than I had
last term yet I have not sufficient to write to
many friends I could wish to correspond with;
however I expect he will find as much enter-
tainment in those letters while I write to you as
in one directed particularly to him.
My studies are at present Optics in Philoso-
phy, Dialling, Homer, besides disputing, composing,
attending lectures &c &c all which I find very interesting,
and especially Mr. Day's believe who is now believing
on Electricity. Adull! my letter is full I will write more
another time.
Yours &c. Sam'l F. B. Moore.

1809 Yale College New Haven March 3d.
My Dear Parents,
I now sit down with pleasure to write you a short letter. I have not received one from you this long time, I am trying to conjecture a reason for this long delay but cannot, I hope nothing has happened which you are afraid of informing us of, however I ought to know better than to think that any serious circumstance should happen relative to the family or the public, without immediate information of the same from some of you I am in daily expectation of some news from home I hope I shall not be deceived.
I informed you in my last letter that Wells my former roommate had lost his mother and only sister by this terrible fever which rages so much near this place, late news from Hartford informs us that he has lost his only brother in addition to these, and it was currently reported here a few days since that he himself was dead; however this was a false report, although he runs a great risk of his life, his father is the only person left of the family. This fever is really a horrid thing, a person is dead, at the farthest period 24 hours after he is taken, it is now within 12 miles of this place, and raging all over this state in every direction; if it makes its appearance in this city in a single instance, college will without doubt be dismissed, do you must not be surprised to see us home if that is the case, for there is no place in the country where we shall be free from danger. If we wait for the symptoms to die us, it is then too late to think of going home, there is no help for us, we must
It Hartford a few days since a student left that
place, and asserted that the day he left the city, there were
six persons lay dead, Buried, and there were 21 new cases.
A few days before he started there was a family consisting
of five persons who were all taken at the same time, the
next day a neighbor having occasion to go into the house
found them all dead; this is what I heard from this
student.... At Berlin the fever rages very bad, 9 die
in one day last week, a young lady coming home from
meeting last sabbath, at the same place, on pulling off
her glove discovered that her arm was entirely covered
with purple spots, her mother told her it was the spotted
fever, and she died before the next morning.... Rice, Fish, and Parkin are slowly recovering they
have been sick a long time. The students are in some degree
sickly, but principally with colds, there are two more
cases of the typhus fever in college, very Dwight and Brown
of the Senior class, Dwight however was but slightly taken,
and he is now able to attend college duties.... I was confined
to my room all the last week with a very bad
cold, and a slight fever, Dr. Ives prescribed for me ain't
have now perfectly recovered; I had a very violent
headach all the time I was confined.... The students look
melancholy, and feel alarmed at the approach of this
contagion, The whole aspect of public and private affairs
looks gloomy, but I will drop this story it is bad enough
to think of it....
I can't say as formerly, "I have not missed prayers
nor recitation this term," for I have, more than a dozen
times, however, you know the circumstances and circumstances alter cases; so I hope you will forgive me for it.... I generally find this to be the case, that if I am absent
from prayers even once at the beginning of a term, it is always
the cause of my being absent oftener, but if I can make
out to attend punctually for one week I am pretty certain
not to miss prayers during the whole term. Another
thing likewise has a great effect on me, and that is the
place where I spend my vacations, if it is here I feel
no relaxation from study, and do not feel myself rested
but feel during the vacation and the succeeding term
very unfit for study, this is in some degree the case now;
however I am determined not to give way to those feelings
but suppress them and study as hard as I did last
term: If I had spent my vacation at home, besides
the strength I should acquire by the ride, I should
come back with the pleasure of having seen my friends
and the that would inspire me with fresh vigor, &
I should be able to study as hard as the rest of my
class.
My studies are quite easy to what they will last
term, Homer is quite easy, Optics in Philosophy, are in some
degree hard but interesting, and Siberies in the 2d vol. of
Webber, is very hard; Our disputes and compositions require
a great deal of hard thinking and close application, and
I hope they do not want from me. Our Chemical Lectures
at present are not very interesting, Mr. Silliman is
now lecturing on the Earths, and this part has always
been considered very dry. -- Mr. Day's Lectures are very
interesting, they are upon Electricity, he has given us
some very fine experiments; the whole class taking hold
of hands formed the circuit of communication, and we
all received the shock apparently at the same moment.
I never took an electric shock before, it felt as if some
person had stuck me a slight blow across the arms.
Mr. Day has given us two lectures on this subject and I
believe there is two more remaining, I will give you some
account of them as soon as they are delivered, which will
probably be in the course of this week.
I think with pleasure that two thirds of this town
evening about 2 o’Clock, by the crew of the vessel Union
is a rumor that there will be bloody works to night
in the harbor, as the sailors in town are determined
to take the 16 gun vessel belonging to the U.S. Station
off this harbor.
Give my particular love to Richard, I
would write more but Mr. Mallory goes to move
you moving early, so I hope you will excuse the
brevity of this.
Yours sincerely
Samuel P. B. Moore.

Yale College, New Haven April 21st
My dear Parents.
I am surprised that scarcely any of my
letters have reached you: for my own part I have written
regularly once a fortnight and the two last letters were quite
long, I cannot conceive the reason that you do not get
them more regularly. I have received but 2 or 3 letters
from you this term, and was very particular in answering
all your questions: yesterday Mr Dwight told me
that he had received a letter from you requesting him
to inform me that you had not recieved a letter
from either of us for 6 weeks. I wrote one
about the middle of march, and another on the
3d day of April, what has become of them I cannot
tell; indeed I feel very much hurt that every letter
I receive from home instead of acknowledgements
of letters, I receive nothing but reproofs for not writing
often, when I take so much pains this term to write
long and regularly, I really hope this will reach
you before I get home; or I shall be induced to write
letters and carry them myself rather than have them
misseasy in this manner. The mails have been
very irregular this term, Dr Dwight has received yours
of the 13th March but not the other of the first he is unable
all to answer it on account of his eyes.
I have been looking over all the letters I have received
from you this time to answer all the questions contained
in them for I have answered them once and must now
answer them again. You mentioned in your letter of the
15th of March, to us, we received some time since
and has been acknowledged and answered a dozen times
that you were surprised that the letters you sent us
by Mr. Mallory were not acknowledged. We had not received
them when we wrote your letter neither did we
get them till 3 or 4 days after Mr. Mallory had again
set out for Boston, they lay in Mr. Beech's store at this
time, so we could do not acknowledge what we had not
received: In my two first letters I gave you an account
of the sickness in and about New Haven: I painted
it in stronger colors than I perhaps ought to have done, I hope
you will allow for the state of my feelings at that
time, as I was sick myself and did not feel in every
high spirits at the time: The sickness has entirely subsided:
those students who were sick have entirely recovered
and are attending to their usual exercises, there is not
the least apprehension that the malignant fever will
reach New Haven.
I have been absent from prayers and recitation
a great no of times this time but it was impossible for me
to remedy it, I have been more unwell this time than
I ever was before, however, I have not lost a single lesson
this term: I have used the Baltimore and South water
some the latter part of this term and I find it does
me good, I feel in better spirits and am more
able to pursue my studies.
I have found my watch again; one of the students
had taken it for a short time merely to play a
joke upon me.
The PHOENIX Society has fallen!!!
We receive newspapers from the office once in a while,
I presume all that you send.
The vacation is near & I rejoice to think
that I shall once more see home, it is a fortnight
from next Tuesday.
Next Thursday is my birthday, 18 years old.
I received a letter from Goldard yesterday the 2d.
I have received his letter, from his sister I learn
that his sister Miranda was quite sick; I wish
you would write me soon, and inform me how she
is.
Edwards and myself are well and in good
spirits, as is Warder, we are all preparing for examinations.
A report was received here last evening that
the British had resented their orders in counsel; this
news is true, but fear it is not. Give my particular
love to Rich. and the family, can't stay to particular.
Remember me to inquiring friends.
Understand that Aunt Abby is soon to be married; give her
joy for me.
Yours in haste
S B. Moser.

My Dear Parents
I wrote you a letter the Monday after you left this place, with I suppose
you have received this time; My leg has got entirely well, and my head also has almost entirely
left me; we are all of us well here; and pursuing our studies. The term has nearly
expired & I hope again to see home soon.
I employ all my leisure time in painting I have a great number of persons engaged
already to be drawn on ivory no less than 7 they obtain the ivoies for themselves I
have taken Professor Kingsley's profile for him it is a good likeness of him and he is pleased
with it. I think I shall take his likeness on ivory and present it to him as my present at the end of the year.
Mr. Mervin goes to morrow morning to Boston and I improve the opportunity of writing one or two lines to you, I have
taken two letters out of the office for Paper for one of which I paid 25 1/2d as postage.
There is nothing new in New Haven all friends are well and send love to you.
I have finished Miss Leffingwell's miniature it is as good likeness and she is very much pleased with it.
In some haste,
Samuel T. B. Morse

[96421] I arrived in this place on Sabbath
evening by Packet from NewYork, I left
Philadelphia on Thursday morning at 8 o'Clock
and arrived in NewYork on Friday at 10,
I went immediately to Mr. Coits where I
was treated with much attention, I was in
introduced to Mrs. Malcom's family and also
to Mr. Stouts and Mr. Marsh, from all
whom I received great attentions I sailed
in NewYork but one night I found it quite
insipid after seeing Philadelphia I went
on board the packet on Saturday at 12
o'clock and arrived as I before stated on
Sabbath evening We had on the whole
a very good set of Passengers from
NewYork to this place on Sunday we had
two sermons read to be, one of them Dr.
Hawley of this place; and in the evening we
sung 5 psalms, and during the whole of the
exercised the passengers conducted with perfect de-
corum, though one of the summons was 1 hour in length; we came
in the Maria Capt. Bradley, I found him a
very pleasant man he said he was acquainted
with you, I was on board at Mt Ogdens till the
term commences; I met a young Englishman
there who appears of a different disposition from
most of his countrymen whom I have seen, in-
stead of finding fault with every thing he sees
he appears pleased with every thing; I have got
acquainted with him and as he appeared to be
a stranger, I have offered him my services
to show him round New Haven, he is travel-
ling thro' the country, and expects to visit

him; I suspect you will find him worthy of

I think it necessary to give you this short account
of him as what I write in a letter of intro-
duction is exposed to his inspection as it is the

rected me; I shall not be very reluctant to go to
Philadelphia again whenever it shall please you
to let me go: I was desired by all the good folks
to send a great deal of love to you when I
go. I saw Mr. Hooker in New York he was well
and his wife. Mr. Dullas goes back to Phil. this
evening by him I sent my letter to Matthew R.
Edwards & Kickb. join me in love to you all.
I remain your affectionate Son
Sam'l J.B. Morse
