Bloomingdale January 6th. 1812.
My dear Sir,
I have to acknowledge the receipt of five letters from you; one
was off Sandy Hook one from Liverpool, & three from London, on Sept. 30th, & the third of Nov. 9th 1811, the last of which I received the day before yesterday. As I am so far distant from town, I never hear what ships are about to sail for England, and this I trust will accoust to you sufficiently for my not having written sooner. But waving apologies I return you my hearty thanks for the entertainment which I have received from the formal of your packet of Sept 30th. The subject of painting is always interesting to me, and it becomes still more so, under your sun. I hope you will take a copy of the Egyptian Hieroglyphics in the possession of Lord Elgin. What you say of Mr. West delights me. I have something or other, felt for a long time, a strong attachment to that man I have often hoped he would visit America, that I might have an opportunity of seeing him. I saw one of his first pieces in Philadelphia, painted with as much care as Lord Elgin can take of his Athenian & Egyptian antiquities. Pray have there not been engravings made from some of his best Scripture pictures? If so, during your stay in England you will confer upon me a great obligation by making a selection of the best prints from Sacred History, whether copied from him, or the works of other great masters.— As for paintings, they are too far above the reach of my purse for me to think of them; but a collection of such pictures as shall pass the ordeal of Mr. West's judgment would be to me invaluable.— Your observations on the English customs amuse & gratify me. I say gratify because they are so minute. A traveller who writes for the public usually puts his mind on the rack to discover something which will surprise or astonish. But it is not prodigious or uncommon events which I seek. Your letter, are just what they should be.— You tell me of incidents in that easy natural way, which the incidents themselves occur to your mind. In case you leave England what
route shall you take? Will you go directly to Calais or pass this Holland?
I know not what to think with respect to the differences between our government
& the English. I find the opinions of people in general seem now to lean to
wards the probability of war. I cannot but hope, however, that we shall continue
at peace. We have so long enjoyed peace that we know not all its
blessings. On the subjects of politics however, I cannot find anything new or interesting.
You doubtless see the American papers of a much more recent date than
that of this letter. Does it not amuse you to hear the observation which are
made on the state of parties in this country -- or rather does it not make
you ashamed that all the abuse & ribaldry vented in our papers should ever
meet the eye of a foreigner? Pray is there as much violence in the disputes
between the ministerial & opposition prints? -- It would I think be an interesting
subject of speculation, to trace the features in which the English & American
represent each other & those in which they differ? So far as the latter are derived from the former it would enable us to perceive the effects
produced by separation, and local circumstances. -- And when there
is a measure of other nations we should be better able to trace the progress
and influence of their respective peculiarities. --
But no more of England, let us now talk of America. I am afraid my
dear sir, you will not find my letters a source of great satisfaction in this
head, because I cannot give you those details with a correspondent in the
city courts. We live a very secluded life -- cut off from almost society but
our own. Mary Shaw spends the winter with us. We have at present
but one or two near neighbours, and my whole parish (excluding about
60 young masters & pupils in the neighbouring boarding schools) consists
of but six families. I have not (indeed not one of us has) been into the city
for three weeks. Every morning I spend in my study, & the afternoon when
the cloth is removed in reading to Mrs. J. & her sister. This is almost
my constant routine, & therefore since I have no company, nothing new
or strange or surprising, to defecate my standing pool you must expect
to find me rather dull. It is now some days since we have received letters
from Connt. When we last heard all was well. I forwarded your letter
to Saybrook agreeably to your request, a day or two after it came to hand.
Your friend Miss Jacobs spent the Christmas holidays with us. She is
very well, and desired me when I should write, to include her compliments
& kind wishes, with those of my family. Capt. P. M. Hunt I have
never seen since your departure. I intend, if possible, to call upon them
the next time I go to the City. Mr. Hogan the younger was
time since, I said they were both very well.
It gives us all great pleasure my dear Mr. Moser, to learn
been received into the Royal Academy. Your having thus
a subject as the Lacocinin renders your reception so much
honourable and of course the more satisfactory. I
will shortly attend you, and may your name be enrolled
in the list of those worthy who have, by their talents
added the American name.
You mention Mr. Palmer. I have received a letter from him, as
to him immediately, to send however by another ship, which will
enable of sending a duplicate. When he arrives in London, you
goodnly to say to him that I have answered his few of the questions
of my letter was to request him to purchase for me -- For the
Outham de Sacrificiis. Raphetic Annotations. Hammond's works. Campbell's translation
of the Gospels. Marsh's Michaelis. Pearson on the Creed. Watson on Infant
Baptism. Burn's Eccles. Law Leslie & Thiberg. Works, & Ready edition of
the Ecclesiastical Historians. -- Cloth for two Bails of clothes, bedding -- in case
Mr. Palmer delay his return I am more speedily directly opportunity presents
itself. I will be much obliged to you my dear Sir to send me the letter together
with information thro' whose hands I may remit to you the money with you
Samuel F. B. Morse Esquire

pool sometime ago but we find by the papers

sure and be acquainted with him and attend constantly
on his ministry Mr C says he wishes he was with
you. they plague his life out where he is but he will give
superior to them he is a good man sends his love to you
as do all your Friends whom you have mentioned in
your letters we read your letters so often to our Friends that
I expect we shall get them by heart. You will draw the con-
clusion from this that we do not forget you as yet. - Mr
Godman asked me whether you do not make your own
Tea af a morning, I could not tell him, he said he always
did as it was not safe to let it be made for you as you would
probably be cheated out of a great deal of Tea & Sugar by the
Servants how ever honest the people themselves might be
he said he always kept his Tea & sugar Under lock & key
the people Boiled his tea in a kettle for him and bought his
rolls, or crumpets & butter, for him and he made his own
Breakfast in the morning and Tea at Night. I told
him I would write you how he managed his money
and I must now bid you Adieu Nancy Betty & Joe &
Cardines all beg to be kindly remember to you a remain
as ever
Your affectionate
brother E A More

Charlestown Jan 18th 1812.
Dear Brother,
Capt Holmes was detained a
week longer than he at first expected, and as he
went by the way of Liverpool, we troubled him only
with a single letter; the rest we send by the Plato
Richard says we shall garden you with reading
letters, but notwithstanding his remonstrance Papa
insists upon my writing you this second, although I
am obliged to do it in the parlour surrounded by
prates, and harassed by messages flying in all
directions.= Under these circumstances you can expect
nothing but apologies -- and the the have I am
sitting in the parlour in the arm chair, on
the right of the fireplace and as I hold my paper in
my hand, with my feet stretched out before the fire,
and with my body reclining in an oblique position
against the back of the chair, I am penning you a
letter, such as it is, and for the inverted portion of the
letter I beg to apologize.
As I turn my eyes upward, I perceive
I behold the family picture painted by an ingenious artist
who I understand is at present residing in London. If you
are acquainted with him, give my love to him, and my
best wishes for his prosperity, and success in the art to
which if report says true he has devoted himself with much
diligence.
Richard sits before me, writing to you, and Mama
says (for I have just asked her the question) that she is engaged
in the same business- Papa is up stairs, very nicely
engaged in the self same employment. Your hands
are now at this instant uniting to produce give
you at some future moment the pleasure of perusing the
present products of their present labor. Your imaginations
are now employed in conceiving of a son or a brother in
a distant land - Therefore we may draw the conclusion
that you are not universally forgotten, and consequently
all do not forget you.
I have written you this long letter because
I knew that you would be anxious for the infor-
mation it contains, because Papa told me I must
write, because Mama said I had better write,
because I had nothing else to do, and because
I hadn't time to write a shorter. I trust for these
special reasons you will excuse me for this one,
especially when you consider that you asked me
to write you long letters, when you consider that
it is my natural disposition to express my sentiments
fully, that I commonly say most when I have
least to say, that I promise reformation in future,
and that you shall hereafter hear from me on
this subject.
As to news, I am sorry to say we are
entirely out, we sent you the last we had by the
Sally Ann. We hope to get some ready by the time
the next ship sails, and then we will furnish with
the country affords.
Mr S. D. P. Mosse

My Dear Son,
I wrote you a few lines this
week by the Sally Ann (capt. Holmes) for Li-
verpool - I now write by the Plate for London
direct Capt Smith - by whom I shall send
a parcel containing letters from your
Mama's brothers containing the informa-
tion concerning many things, which will be
interesting to you; also a large number of
the Newspapers, from which you will
learn all the public news of the day.
Togeth er , the letters' Newspapers, will furni-
sh all that is passing here, + will super-
cede the necessity of my saying much -
I am now wholly engaged in preparing
the Geo. 9 for the press, + reading the proofs.
Four presses are employed, which print be-
tween 60 & 70 pages a week - Your brothers are
both at home expecting me but will return
to N.Haven in about a week - Edw d has
been of great service to me & excites
good judgment and great dispatch in preparing the copy for the press. The work will be
out I expect in April. The Vol. which treats of America, I shall revise after it is out, I send it to
you to have reprinted in Eng. for your benefit. Probably you may secure the copy right
in your name. More on this subject by the Galen. In the mean time you can enquire of
the proper persons what can be legally done in such a case. You can make a conditional contract
with some honest & responsible individual. This new arrangement will be certain enough to interest the British public.
Much is said about dear old Great Britain but I have no belief that the Govt. is
in earnest in the business, notwithstanding all that is said in Congress that looks that
way. Our legislature, as you will see by the Govt. speech, & the doings of the legislature
are prepared to go great lengths. They have inserted an entering wedge in regard to the
College (by calling on the Corporation for a statement of the College funds) what will be their
future course, cannot be foreseen. They keep their plans to themselves.
The Bodman has put to press a collection of papers which contain the whole history of
his difficulties. I will send you a copy of the Galen. It will be an interesting pamphlet of
about 100 pages &c. The features of the opposition
are marked with a malignancy, & wickedness
altogether unparalleled in this country. To
find balance are the attacks on the characters of those
at the seat by their opposers, that I know not but
it will be necessary for us all to vindicate
ourselves by publishing the truth.
Things remain in this town pretty much
after the old sort. The talk made for a time
some noise in consequence of the violent opposition
made to it by some individuals. And
within a few days I learn that a petition is
in circulation, to be presented to the Legislature,
to let aside the act incorporating this Parish.
I have very little anxiety about the issue,
it will be what it may. Every thing appears to
be in an unsettled & in calculable state.
Our children are our greatest earthly comfort.
Your affectionate concern for our happiness has returned
for ours in regard to you, yielded us much
consolation under all our disappointments. Truly
what are not a few -- Your letters have afforded
us much satisfaction -- continue to write us -- We
cease not daily to remember you in our prayers. For
if not my son, to remember your parents, brothers in
spirit, be virtuous & be happy.
Your friends here remain much attached to you &
enquire after you affectionately. I wish to be remembered
to you. I enclose you the $100.00 bill -- 1st P. J. Ford -- before I shall write
you by the Galen -- Regards to Mrs. H. Clinton. Your affectionate father

My Dear Parents,
It is an opportunity to write to you a few moments for the purpose; I wish I had been able to write you a longer and more particular letter, which I intend doing soon, for I can scarcely find leisure at present to eat my meals; I feel every day an increased enthusiasm, and encourage you that I had received your leave by the Baltimore and Liverpool packet, and have also sent you letter No. 12, by the Miss Lynders, Gen. Lemans daughters who embarked for Philadelphia in a few days in the ship Aurora Maria.
I delivered your parcels to Mr. Burder, he is a very friendly good man, who receives me very kindly; -- Mr. Duncan Smith likewise, Mr. Evarts's clasmate, is very attentive to me, and desires remembrance to Mr. Evarts. On Tuesday last I dined at Mr. Wests, who requested to be particularly remembered to you he is extremely attentive and polite to me; I have just purchased a sketch of his face from it and send it to you; when I return home I shall bring it with me as I consider it very valuable -- Mr. Hurd and Mr. Parkman are still here, they are often in and out at my lodgings and are well. -- I have changed my lodging to No. 82 in the same street, and have room with Mr. Leslie of Philadelphia who has just arrived, he is very promising, and a very agreeable gentleman, we are in the same stage of advancement in the art. I have painted 5 pieces since I have been here, 2 landscapes and 3 portraits, one of myself, one a copy from Mr. Wests copy from Van Dyke, and the other a portrait of Mr. Leslie, who is also taking mines. I find a short time since at Dr. Lettsom's who requests his remembrance to you. I delivered my letter to Mr. Vaughan who is a very hospitable
I shall write my brother shortly.
man, I was invited to dine with him on the day that my
letter arrived, and took that opportunity of delivering it upon
reading it; he took me by the hand, and said, "tell Mr. Gore
his letter came too late," I had been invited without having
been introduced to him; he is so hospitable that no American
whom he hears is in London passes unnoticed by him; he
called on me yesterday to see my pictures and appeared
pleased with them.
Besant called a day or two since on Sir William Beechey,
an artist of great chineness, to see his paintings, they are
beautiful beyond any thing I ever imagined; his principal excellence
is in coloring, which to the many, is the most attractive
part of the art, Sir Wm is considered the best colorist

and even the best, What is Mr West's great excellence, Mr West
is a bad colorist in general, but he excels, in the grandeur of
his thought; Mr West is to painting what Milton is to poetry,
and Sir William Beechey to Mr West as Pope to Milton;
so that by comparing with the other I can give you a better idea of the art by
the other, I can give you a better idea of the art by
the other, I can give you a better idea
since William the conqueror, also the crown which the
king wears in Parliament the value of which is estimated
at 1000,000 of pounds sterling or 4000,000 of dollars; and
also the golden sceptres, of king, and queen, the gold eagle
which holds the consecrated oil and the spoon of gold into
which the oil is poured at the coronation, &c. &c. the whole

ourry, the kings of England with each his suit of armour

cient times; also the axe which beheaded the Earl of

invincible armada; and many other curiosities, too

My dear Son, I am informed that a rebel U.S. sail for Ireland on Tuesday
offered to take charge of a letter to put on board for you. (Hope the boys Mr K. has a fine for a few days old. Your
remembrance of them by name was grateful as it was to them named) Your Mama wrote you a long letter two days ago, to go by the Missouri for Liverpool, to sail also on Saturday. We improve both opportunities, as we know it will gratify you to hear often from us and we once you thin attention, in return for yours to us we have received all your letters, mentioned by you except the one by the West-ship written at sea we did not notice in any of the papers, that you were spoken with at sea. Mrs in her last letters to her friends speaks of you in favorable terms, which gave us great pleasure. We are, as you know deeply concerned in every thing that concerns you - I am made very happy when we hear well of you - All our sons are giving us much comfort & pleasure by their good behaviour. We regret the failure of Mr H in London, his efforts here on the other branches of the house, while I desire to give them with suitable feelings, the hand of Providence in this event. Persecutions still continue of the old kind as bitter as ever - The Lord however greatly prosper the benevolent plans of the present, for bevailing
pursuing which, with success, the preceding spirit has
been exerted. — The late Act (1810) changing the
Board of Assessors has been repealed within a
few days. That Board is now as it has been since
the Adoption of our Constitution. — The Common-
wealth has been strangely Districted for the choice
of Senators & Members of Congress, to answer po-
litical purposes. — The burghers has probably been
overdone — The candidates for Gov. & Lt. Gov.
are Gov. Strong, & Dr. Phillips (very popular nomination,
likely succeed) — Gov. Gerry (from Wm. King, an
other side) & Gen. Tracy having declined.
Congress are doing strange things also, what they
will open the eyes of the people, to effect a change in
the Administration I have never for a moment
believed we should declare war agt. Great Britain
The people, I believe, are generally agt. all po-
litical parties. The restrictive system, I hope
is nearly at an end but we are in an incalcula-
ble state — Earthquakes have been felt
in many places very severe & alarming in various
parts of our country viz. Connecticut river, particu-
larly on the Mississipp river in some of the
Southern States — a volcano, it was lately S.C. had
burst out in one the western counties of S.C. Carolina
& changed the course of Broad river — This is doubtless
however — It is, on many parts, a wonderful period in
all we live in & I have often thought of late that
you had chosen a profession remarkably suited to the
present times, to preserve you from party feeling,
I am engaging in the contest, that are deluding
the world in misery & blood -- If my dear son, you
will unite with your profession, the choice of the
one thing helpful the poor part, which shall never
be taken away from you, you will fulfill the most
desires of your parents. That your fortune
may prosper this good by portion, is their daily prayer.

My Dear Parents,
I have the pleasure to inform you that I
have just received your good letters by the ship Pluto
for which I thank you; I must relate a circumstance
however, with respect to my getting them; Mr Brownfield wrote
to me and said there was a parcel for me, in the Post Office
which he supposed contained newspapers only from home, and
that the charge of Postage was 2s 5d or 10 dollars, wishing
to know if I would take them at that enormous charge
or let them remain in the post office; I immediately
waited on him to see about it, and told him there were
several letters in it, wishing to know what I could do; he
told me he would go with me to the post office and see
what could be done; I then went with him, and stated the
case to them, telling them, I was willing to pay the postage
of all letters contained in it, and told them they might open
it, which they did, but, as good luck would have it, they
found a corner of the letters which were in the newspapers, they
told me as there were no letters I might have it by paying
15 shillings, I was going to decline, when by accident I discovered
a corner of the letters, and wrapping it up, lest they
should make another search, I paid them the 15 shillings and
took it, although that was a great sum for postage being about
a dollar a piece for each letter; I hope you will not blame
me for paying this neither than let them stay in the office, when
you consider the case, that I do not very often hear from home
and how great the temptation was, knowing that there were
several letters directly from home, and that if I paid 15 shillings
I could take them and not without, but I will not palliate,
I know you won't blame me, they were letters from home.
But to remedy this in future, you will find it the
least expensive to put the letters separate into the letter box,
the postage then is only 1 penny each letter, and perhaps you
will not expect me to pay postage on letters which are
not intended for me.
With all my love to your family
Ever affy
W. B. A.

Mr. Allston is very busily engaged about a very large
picture, and requested you to tell you that if he has
not received the other mention in my letter as soon as he does
he will write again, he and Mr. Allston desire particular remembrance to you, they are both in excellent
health, and spirits. -- Mr. Allston regularly meets all men, that aim improving
very fast, and getting along very well.
I have called twice on Mr. Taylor about Papa's business, he is a man whose time like Papa's is very precious, he
has appointed, next Tuesday a week, to settle the business I shall call on him then and inform you of the result immediately after, he is an honest, good man, from all accounts
and will act honorably.
I thank you for the letter from Mr. Filliman to Col. Inman
bull, but I should wish not to have any more letters of introduction to any body else, I have not yet delivered those which
I have received. I find they only retard my progress, for were I
to pay the due attention to every one I have had letters to,
all my time from morning till night would be taken up in preserving the acquaintance, I begin to wish I had
brought but one or two; I think letters of introduction are less necessary to a young artist than
to any other class of people, for his attention to his art ought never
to be diverted; now a young man studying divinity or physics
or any thing else can bear to have his mind diverted, and it
would seem necessary, but it appears to me it is not necessary for an artist, he can find amusement enough and dancing
too, in his art, for my own part I feel sometimes, that I should like to live entirely abstracted from society, and devote myself solely to painting, but that I know it is impracticable. If I should wish for letters of introduction to any
particular person, or to any particular place, I will write you
for them.
I am glad to hear the Geography is going on so well, I
am afraid, I shall make but a poor bargainer, but I will
do my best when you send it.
By this time, you have probably received notice of
my receiving the draft safe, it is accepted and all is right
I am afraid my expenses will exceed my allowance for
the first year, but the next will make them even again, if
I exceed it, it will be but by a few pounds; Mr Bromfield
said he expected it would be so, on account of my necessary
expenses in establishing myself; I shall use all my inducement
to economize as much as possible, and reduce my expenses
to as narrow a compass as possible.
We make our own tea and coffee just as Mr Codman
used to do. I mentioned to you in a former letter that I have
removed my lodgings to No 82. in the same street where I am
much better situated with a young american artist from
Philadelphia by the name of Leslie, you heard me mention him
when I was at home, he is the young man who gained so much
reputation in Philadelphia by taking the likeness of Cook in his
celebrated characters, he is a very agreeable industrious, steady,
young fellow, and our best together makes my absence from home
very agreeable; Mr Parkman returns in a few days to America and
will tell you all about us, he was quite socialable, and intimate intimate
with us, I like him very much.
I have delayed this letter until I should have seen Mr Taylor on Papa's business, I drank tea with him last evening; Mr Bruder was there; after tea we looked into your account which I give you at full length, you can perhaps understand it, though I confess that my mind has been so habitually employed in works of fancy and imagination, that I found myself perfectly stupid, the moment I thought of the plain, dry matter of fact, book accounts, and I was perfectly lost in the business, and
understood it about as well as I did Chinese, this is the account however, which I copied from his books;

You have ordered several books to be sent you, all which
orders I have received, and, as soon as it is practicable
to send them will do it, but you will easily see that, it
is not possible in the present state of affairs; those who go
passengers have always more than they can take care of,
of their own property, and refuse to take charge of any thing
the captains likewise say they will not risk their self
by taking charge of anything so you see that it is
impossible in the present state of things to do anything respectively
them but as soon as I can get an opportunity I will send

state of affairs. The book Smith on the Prophecies
which you sent me, I have submitted to Mr Burder
who understands these things better than myself; for I am
entirely separated from all things of that kind, being 3
miles distant from booksellers or printers, and my time
being wholly employed from daylight till midnight, in
pursuing my studies, I should lose a great deal by
going that distance.
I thank Mama for her kindness in sending me
prescriptions, I have not had occasion for them having
been in perfect health ever since the first term at the hotel,
and have felt nothing of the rheumatism since I left the
ship. I am now in excellent spirits, and health; and
Mrs Allston says I am growing fleshy, this climate, although
disagreeable suits my constitution very well.
Mr Hurd is still here and visits me often, he is well
but is a little lowspirited, since Mr Parkman has left London
that I must be well returned to the country of the Americans
and that I must now be returning to the United States, where I will
continue with my knowledge of the arts and sciences, and with
my family, and with my friends, and with my country, and with
my countrymen, and with my countrywomen, and with my
particular change thro' the whole progress of it; every thing
in nature must be studied in the same minute
manner so you see that it is not so easy a thing
to be a painter, as some are apt to suppose;
I mention these things, that you may not raise your
expectations of my progress too high, for it must be slow
and sure; if within 8 or 10 years I can paint tolerably well
I shall think my time has been well employed; I am deter-
mined if application and study will make me a painter
to be one, no difficulty shall discourage me, the more
they increase, the greater is my desire to overcome them.
The most disagreeable part of the whole
is the necessity of my being so far from my friends; if
there were only a few more Miss Rupells in America,
American artists would not be obliged to leave their
own country; Tell Miss Russell she possesses an en-
graver of Leonardo da Vinci; that print cannot
be purchased here under 25 guineas, the painting
itself is considered as a masterpiece of painting, and this
print a masterpiece of engraving. But I must close
this letter; I am going to write my brothers soon: "Give my
love to all friends." I wish S.D.Ward would write me
he cant think how it would gratify me. I mentioned before
that I had received a letter from Mr. Vose of Charleston, I answered it a few days after I received it, remember me to him.
I have a great many things to tell you, and indeed too
many for a letter, so that I must wait untill I come home,
and then my visit will be made more interesting, as I shall
have so many things to tell you of

My Dear Friends,
I have long been waiting in anxious expectation
for an answer to some of my letters, this is the fourth I
have written to Miss Dannette and an one to Miss Mary Isaac, the two last with one other to
you went by the ship Louisa for NewYork in Octr. last, we
have heard of her arrival at this port, I hope you have received
some of them, I wrote one by the Lydia the ship in which
she has been to NewYork, and has arrived again at Liverpool
but I have received no intelligence since I have been here from
NewYork altho' I have no less than 6 correspondents and some
too my clafmatip and have written them all once and
some twice -- but I will not complain, I never can suppose I am forgotten; the distance is great and there are thousands of accidents to which a letter is liable in passing such a
distance; my letters have probably miscarried or are delayed on the way, I am still on the expectation I am
not so particular as some who never write a second letter till their first is answered; so I will improve an opportunity that offers for the purpose, and write my fourth
letter.

My dear Son
Three days ago we received your acceptable
letter of the 30th June 7, your 14th. The two preceding ones by
Miss Lyman's, 2 Novr 13, we have not yet received. You do well
to number your letters, I to write often as we feel a
deep interest in every thing which concerns you, as well
as our other children. We have not numbered our
letters to you but shall in future -- we suppose we have
written you about as many as you have written
us -- We are pleased to find that your ardor for your
profession continues. A line from Mr Alston's brother
as to your proficiency would be very grateful to us.
We hope the change in your lodgment, & your connection
your self with Mr Leslie, will be for your advantage
but at this distance we cannot judge for you -- I trust you
confer with Mr & Mrs Alston, Mr Bromfield, & Mr Smith, in all your important
movements, & especially in the choice of your companions,
which is of infinite moment to you -- We are unacquainted with Mr Leslie, but presume
he will be helpful to you, not only in your professional pursuits, but in all virtuous counsels.
I in every thing which will tend to promote your best interests, your eternal welfare. We feel, my dear son,
be assured a very deep & tender concern for you
continually in regard to these things -- By regarding
our wishes in these things you will give us the most
comfort in neglecting them your will help to bring down
our body hardy in the honor of the brave.
We observe that you do not mention Mrs. Astor in your last letter. You will take care always to
mention them particularly in future that I may inform their friends, who ask after them. Request him to write
me, I remember us particularly to them and to all others who ask after us, especially to Mrs. West. Dr. Lettsome. I hope
before this you will have delivered all your letters. You do not have delayed them so long as the gentlemen
think themselves neglected. You do not mention having received Mr. Van Hope's last fall
draft on him. It is mentioned in your letter by Miss Hyman's. I know not when I shall be able to send you more,
as we every day expect an embargo, I expect, war with Great Britain but I hope the elections of this day, will
convince our distracted government, of the inexpediency of folly of such a measure. The state of this
country was never more critical. The result of today's elections will produce almost important effect but
only on this State, but in our country. The language is strong. Peace, Gen. of War. I believe this correct. I have 3 neat copies of
your letter. I shall send you by this opportunity the proofs of the American Geog., new Edttn., as far as printed.
A few sheets will complete it, and I shall send as soon as I have offshl. -- I wish you to confer with Mr.
Smith on the subject of securing in your own name the copy right of the work in Eng. -- I engage
Badell, or some other bookseller to print the work, I make you a proper allowance. In this way
you may get something to support you it may be handomely, without depending on me. Before it is printed in Eng. -- particularly the Art. of the U. States, you
may want to receive some additions & corrections
from me, of importance relative to our Manufactures & Commerce which could not be obtained in
Season to be inserted in their place. – Beside I have sent an unredacted copy of the new Edit o of the
U.S. takes to the seat of Government expect to receive shortly the corrections I remarks of
Members of Congress from every state. – Here I shall send you who will make the London edition
much improved – write me immediately by my vessel to the U.S. states what success you meet with
in bargaining with a bookseller. – It may be very important to you to make something of this book,
as it may be the only means of your support. You may give it such a title as you, Mr. Smith or the
bookseller may think proper to give it. – It may be best for him to begin at the 89th page unless the
bookseller presents himself in introduction also, which is new. Possibly he may think it expedient to
publish the Western Continent as a great part of the Eastern continent is new. – I send for this
bookseller inspection, the first part of the Vol. describing the Eastern Continent you may contract for both
Vols. if you can to advantage.
I wish you, my son, to be very cautious how you introduce with spotlights or you may ruin
yourself in serious difficulties. You had better keep your own opinions, whatever they may be
to yourself, I not make them a subject even of consideration. It may be pretty clearly hazardous
to commit them to writing. I am so well known at present personally only in your profession as a painter
I leave you only feel at your ease in any conversation in any company. I am sending you
your name to writing this letter. I am your affectionate father & brother

My very Dear Son
It is very long since we have had any accounts from
you, which occasions much solicitude. We are anxious to know how
your healthy spirits are, and hope you succeed in your profession your
last letter was dated the 14 Sep. 1813 your success as to the reception
of your statue of Neptune was flattering & I hope your success
since we have announced your expectations. The little cast
you mention sending has not yet come to hand we wish much
to suit it but fear we shall not very soon for we are very desirous
of giving you this summer but do not wish it in such a way as
to have you injure yourself greatly in your profession to gratify
us, especially if by continuing a year longer you can get into
such business as will enable you to support your self afterwards
which I hope is an object with you, we wish much to see
our three sons in the situations to support them in comfortably
& as fast as should we need their help in our old age, and to
be able & willing to do good to their fellow creatures as opportunities
occur, you know perfectly our feeling on this subject and
that we would much rather see you all good & useful in every
situation into which your lot may be cast, than rich & great,
without a heart to do good & be useful to all your brother Common
has begun a letter to you but is prevented from finishing it just now
by a painter that you know he is a little subject to. I hope he will
be able to renew the letter before this goes. Richard is at Utica at
your Uncle's at Arthurs. We had a letter from him yesterday he was
well and in good spirits, he talks of going with Cousin Sam Brown
to Sackets Harbour, merely to see the place. We are pleased to find that
he appears to enjoy himself so well as he was rather despondent when
he left home he intends going to Andover in the fall & study. During
Edwards will go to Litchfield some time this summer & study. Last
if we live till next winter we shall be quite happy not having any
of you with us unless you should come & keep us Company. The
letters we write to each other are liable to be read by the officers of
the Government, we shall therefore say nothing on public affairs, in
the news papers which you doubtless see every Sunday in American
newspapers to go into particulars. – Then did I page on Aunt M r
Wilberforce? M r Thornton? Dr Lettsom? M r West? M r Alston
& other good Friends! Remember us very respectfully to them
when you see them & particularly to M r West & M r Alston
who we hope are quite well, M r & Mrs Botterill William, I have heard
is going to marry his Cousin Miss Gibbs, probably next month I
believe the family are well. – I hope you have painted the three
handsome pictures that I requested you too, one for Mrs Dr Bentlett,
one for Miss Huskill, & one for your Aunt Salisbury, I know not
when you will be able to send them such is the state of things
at present, but be sure you do not venture them till there is a
prospect of there getting safely to us, your Papa is publishing a pamphlet
which occupies much of his time at present to liberty to the Public
how he has been treated by Miss H. Adams & her Abbotson S. Higginson
& Shaw & others. When he has an opportunity he will send one or
two Bills, that your Papa has sent you lately & one small one
some little time ago, we wish to have M r Broomfield's statement,
of the manner in which our accounts stand. I hope my son you
are extremely careful that Company you keep. I hope you will keep
yourself from the Gay, the Disputation of the Prophane Reminiscences dear
to your early Education, & how very much depends on the manner
in which you spend & improve the present moment, that an eternity of
happiness or misery will be the consequence. I intrust you to think much
of the all important truths contained in your Bible & pray to meet
your God in peace. that if we are not permitted to see each other in
this world we may meet in that better World above & spend an
eternity in celebrating the praises of redeeming Love. This is the daily
prayer of your affectionate parents for your own other love make it
your own or it will be in vain for us to make it. I have been confined
the greater part of the Winter with the Ague in my face hair had
two teeth extracted but still wear a bandage of any face your paper
wishes me to tell you that he wrote you a fortnight ago by the
way of Halifax, by a Cartel, and sent the Bills mentioned to
Mr Broomfield, to whom he wrote also. We wish you to have
a letter from Mr Alston & Mr West with respect to your con
tinuance another year.— we wish a description of your house, to Ex
ford & Bristol &c &c and what pieces of Painting you are engaged in
at present.— Your Friends are continually asking about you and
are pleased to hear of your success Mr James Frothingham has taken
the likeness of your Father it is thought to be very good wish
we could have the likeness of Miss Hannah Moore & Mrs Wilberforce
& Dr Buchanan. Your Father Nancy Betsey &c join with me in
love to you Miss Russell Mr Evans Mr O Brown &c a great many
others beg to be remembered to you. We all want much to
hear from you much often than we do it is longer than it
ever has been. I must now bid you good bye my dear Son &c remain
your affectionate E. A. Betsey
Mr. Winter.

Mr Vinton.
Letter of Introduction.
Dear Brother
We have received no letters from you since
November. Your last was dated in September We have improved every opportunity. We are all well in good spirits.
Mama has been troubled with a pain in her gums & face in consequence of the extraction of two teeth. Richard has spent the winter at home. He has been very dull & low-spirited. A few weeks since he went to Utica in company with cousin Sam Breeze, We have received two letters from him since. He writes in remarkably good spirits, & appears as happy as a King. - Cousin Sam has just returned from a cruise in the Congress; the third since the war, but he has met with no frigates or armed vessels of any description.
Papa has published an Appeal to the Public, on the subject of Miss H. Adams's charges. He is now publishing a pamphlet which will contain all the particulars & details of the controversy as connected with the True Reasons, and Harvard College.
Richard has not yet fixed upon his professor. I am still studying on Mr Rockwood's Office but shall go to Litchfield soon.
Mr Abner Rogers whom you well know & where brother is in London, died a few weeks since. He had been very inattentive to his health, and suffered his disorder to increase till it was beyond his control. The immediate occasion of his death was a copious bleeding at
lengy. - Judge Parsons died a few months since of a
pulmonary Shock.-
You will be astonished to hear that Mr Dexter
is the democratic candidate for Governor in opposition
to Caleb Strong. He has expressed himself in a letter to
the Electors as decidedly opposed to the whole course &
conduct of the General Government. He styles their
measures "unconstitutional, unjust, oppressive, demon-
atizing." He says, "They cannot be executed, & if they
could they would be ineffectual; that they make
perjury familiar; that they aim a fatal blow at
our prosperity; that they sacrifice our dearest rights
& interests." Yet the democrats will support him. The
great point in which he differs from the Federalists
is this. He says "it is our duty to submit implicitly to
every violation of the Constitution, and every species
of oppression." Federalism I need not tell you will
never go to advocate such Toryism.
The New Hampshire election has issued in favour of
Federalism. Our Charlestown Meeting for the Election
of Town Officers took place about a fortnight since. The
Federalists carried their ticket by a majority of 50.
The democratic majority last year was 37. Charle-
town has been democratic till now for 13 years.
Massachusetts has an overwhelming majority of Federalists
Last year 14,000.—
Nanny Rayner is dead. She left her property,
between 5 & 10,000 Dollars, to George Bartlett.—
Elizabeth Hooker, the daughter of Mr & Mrs Hooker
who were with Papa & Mama in Carolina, is now
living with us. She is about 10 years old, and is a very
lively, figgetty, horty-torty kind of a baby.—
Cousin Betsey Breeze has spent the winter in Boston
with Aunt Salisbury. She is well, and all our Utica relations
Grandmama is at Utica.— Grandpapa Morse has been
confined to the house by a blouse which he received in a
fall. He will never perfectly recover.— Uncle Jonathan talks
of selling his farm and removing into the Western country
under Wilkinson. One of Uncle Calvin's sons is in the army
Elisha Goddard has not arrived in America. We
have been waiting with great impatience to see your statue.
Write us more frequently.— Your friends here constantly inquire
after you.—
I am your affectionate brother
Sidney E. Morse.
Mr Samuel J. B. Mosse
to the care of
Henry Bromfield Esq

out, sent by the first american packet which you will by this
time have received, you ask if you are to expect me this
next summer? This leads me to a little enlargement on the
peculiar circumstances in which I am now placed, Mr. Allison's
letter by the same postal (as mentioned) will convince you that an
admission and application has not been wanting on my part, that I
have been made greater progress than young men generally, &c. &c. End
of how great importance it is to me to remain in Europe for some
time yet to come, indeed I feel it so much myself, that I shall be
delivered of all risks, if I find I cannot support myself, that I
am contracting debts, which I have no prospect of paying, I shall then return
home, and settle down into a more practical painter for some time, but from
certain difficulties to return to Europe again, for I cannot be happy even
if I am pursuing the intellectual branch of the art, portrait painting
is, landscape has some of, but History has it wholly, I am
certain you would not be satisfied to see me sit down quietly spending my
time in painting portraits, throwing away the talents which Heaven has
given me for the higher branches of art, and devoting my time only to
the interior; I need not tell you what a difficult profession it is an
undertaker, it has difficulty in itself, which was sufficient to deter any
man who has not courage enough to go through without all hazards with
out meeting with any obstacles aside from it; the more I study it, the
more I understand well it, and the greater my progress, the more am I
struck with its beauties, and the perseverance of those who have dared
to pursue it, through the thousands of natural hindrances with which
the art abounds, I never can feel too grateful to my parents for having
assisted me thus far in my profession, they have done
more than I had any right to expect, they have conducted with a liberality
towards me, both in respect to money, and to countenance, me in the
pursuit of one of the noblest professions, which has not many equals
in this country; I cannot ask of them more, it would be ingratitude.
I am now in the midst of my studies, when the great works of art
and use of the utmost service to me, political events have
just thrown open the whole continent. The whole world, will
now leave war and bend their attention to the cultivation of the
arts of peace, a golden age is in prospect, and art is probably
destined again to revive, as in the 16th century; the American artists
at present stand unrivalled, it is my great ambition (and
it is certainly a commendable one) to stand among the first, my
country has the most prominent place in my thoughts; how shall
I raise her name? how can I be of service, in refuting the
calmings industriously spread against her, that she has produced
no men of genius? it is this more than anything (aside from thanking)
that inspires me with a desire to excel in my art, it arouses
my indignation, and gives me tenfold energy in the pursuit of my
studies, I should like to be the greatest painter, surely out of society,
but what a damper is thrown upon my enthusiasm, when I find
that the moment when all the treasures of art, are before
me, just within my reach, that advantages to the artist, were
never greater than now. Paris with all its splendid depository,
of the greatest works, but a day or two's journey from me,
and open to my free inspection, what a damper, I say, is it
to find that my three years allowance is just expired, that,
while all my contemporary students and companions, are reveling
in these enjoyments, and rapidly advancing in their noble
studies, they are leaving me behind, either to return to my
country, or by painting portraits, just to be able to live through the
year. The thought makes me melancholy, and for the first
time since I left home have I had one of my desponding fits.
I have got over it now for I would not write to you in that
mood for the world. My object in stating this is to request patronage
from some rich individual or individuals, for a year or
two longer at the rate of £250 per year, this to be advanced
to me; and if required, to return it in money, as soon as I
shall be able; or by pictures, to the amount, when I have
completed my studies. I ask for 250, because two hundred
has but barely been sufficient; and has left me nothing to
purchase prints, casts, &c. so indispensable at the present
time; if Uncle Salisbury, or Mrs. Russell, could do it, it
would be much more profitable to me than from any others.
This may seem to you an odd request, but I really do not
see any other alternative, if you wish me to be a great painter;
if you wish me to be merely a portrait painter, I can
return and obey you, but I should be miserable. Perhaps,
there would be some delicacy of feeling, in requesting such assistance,
but it might be done in the form of Commission, as
McLellan, has in some instances; for instance let some one
commission me to paint a picture for any sum, when I can
conveniently do it, and advance the sum; this is not perhaps,
strictly mercantile, but I rely on their confidence in my
integrity, I hope I have honorable feelings, and it could
be only consistent with the basest ingratitude, and total
want of honor, to deceive in such a case. But I leave
the management of this to you, whatever can be done to enable
me to prosecute to the end, my favorite studies, I shall
require see in, but do write soon and relieve me from a state
of great uneasiness. The box containing my plaster cast
I found in enquiry, is still at Liverpool, where it has been, to
my great disappointment now nearly a year. I have given
4 orders to have it sent by the first of opportunity. Mr Wilder will
tell you that he came near taking out my great picture of Hercules to you, it seems as though it is destined nothing of mine
shall reach you; I packed it up at a moment's warning and
sent it to Liverpool to go by the cartel, and I found it arrive
the day after she had sailed, I hope it will not be long, for
before both the boxes will have an opportunity of reaching
you. I am exceedingly sorry you have forgotten a passage
in my former letters where I wished you not to feel anxious if
you did not hear from me as often as you had done, I take
the reason, that opportunities were less frequent, more circuitous, and attended with greater interruptions, I tell you that
I should write at least once in three weeks, and that you
must attribute it to any thing but neglect on my part; Your
last letter has hurt me considerably, for owing to some accident
or other my letters have miscarried, and you will aid me
with neglect, and fear that I am not as industrious or correct
as formerly; I know you don't wish to hurt me but I can't help feeling hurt when I think that my friends
have not the confidence which I thought they had in me, that
some interruptions, (which all complain of, and are natural to
a state of warfare,) having prevented letters which I have
written from being received, instead of making allowances for
these things to have them attributed to a falling off in
industry & attention, wounds me a great deal. -- Mrs Allston to
her great surprise received just such a letter from her friends, &
it hurt her so that she was ill in consequence -- I have written
long letters and as frequent as formerly, but you must allow
that having long letters miscarry, which have taken so much time
to write, is but slender encouragement to continue them. --
My Oxford excursion contained I think 5 sheets & an 1/2
which by this time I hope you have received. I wrote 3 I think
from Bristol, 1 just before, which is the last you say you
received, one since my return, via Lisbon, or Halifax 2 for
which, a good long one by the Fair American cartel, and one
which arrived too late at Liverpool to go by the cartel and which
will go by another opportunity. For one of those from Bris-
tol, or the one since, I gave you a slight account of my ex-
cursion to Bristol, Please write me if you have received
it, if not I will write it over again. This will probably go by a cartel from Gotterburg to Boston, to touch here.
The Exhibition at Somerset house opens to day at 12, I shall
go then and give you a little account of it, where my pictures
are placed No. 40, send you a catalogue, and any critiques,
which may be made on any of our pictures Mr. Allston's
Mr. Leslie's or myself. I dine at Mr. Macaulay's at
5 o'clock to day, and shall attend the House of Commons
to-morrow even, when I expect to hear Mr. Wilberforce
speak, on the Slave Trade with reference to the property of making there an article in the pending negotiation
if I have time in this letter I will give you some account
of it. In the main time I will give you a slight account of some scenes of which I have been a happy witness
on the great drama now acting in the Theatre of Europe.
You will probably before this reaches you, hear of the
splendid entry of Louis 18th into London; I was
a spectator of this scene; On the morning of the day
about 10 o'clock, I went into Piccadilly, through which
the procession was to pass, I did not find any great con-
course of people at that hour except before the Pallmey
Hotel, where the sister of the Emperor Alexander resides
6. on a visit to this country, the Grand Duchess of Old-
enburg. I thought it probable that, as the procession would
pass this place, there would be some uncommon occasion
to take place before it so I took my situation directly opposite
determined at any rate to secure a good view of

carriages began to thicker, the windows & fronts of the
houses began to be decorated with the white flag, white

My friend and benefactor.
Your letter of the 28th February I received enclosing
two pounds, and should have answered it before, but considering the
nebulous situation, as I had nothing particular to communicate.
I have been in a great degree of distress, and my situation has been preserved
through a long season of miserable captives. I have not every occasion in my power to do anything for myself, and thus far
have made my situation more comfortable than could have been expected, with the means. I have waited with patience the
will of an inevitable providence, by which all things are overtaken for the best possible good, and have been flattered with the hope
that the late events in Europe would effect a universal peace, and that my liberty was not far distant. At present I cannot form no opinion as to the result of the negotiations, but hope to hear your opinion, and that you will have the goodness to inform me if any thing appears favorable. I find my health
and strength gradually dying, and in consequence of it, have laboured under much affliction for the month past. The French prisoners are now about to return to their respective homes, and the prison is in a state of revolution. We are soon to be removed from this to another prison, it is said on board the prison ships at Baltimore. I hope I shall not suffer so much on the journey as before -- If it is in your power, I hope to receive a little more assistance, as my situation is now much altered by ill health, and, the departure of the French prisoners. I am much in want of your kind attention, as I have not received any letters from America, -- the Point informed me the other day that he had not letters by the Ship Fair America by which any friends would get information concerning me --
my situation I am sorry my friend to trouble you with
my unfortunate case, but your goodness will be speedily
rewarded and ever gratefully remembered by one
who wishes you every prosperity and happiness, with esteem
your very sincerely Henry Barnard

My dear Sir
On my return from Connecticut where I left most saving
and our Son, I had the pleasure of finding your letter dated
Sep. 3d. 1813 and sent by the fair American Castle. I had written
you a letter by Mr. Armstrong, who was to have sailed in the postscript
Brig. Illinois protecting the trade of this month. On my arrival
day before yesterday I was surprised to find she had not yet
sailed. I have therefore one hour in which to acknowledge
the receipt of your favour and to thank you for having procured
for me the books you mention. I cannot but hope that
we shall soon have peace so that you will be enabled to
send them. I am told the Custom House Officers in Boston are
much more polite than in New York, since here they insist
upon duties being paid on Articles brought out for private
use. You will be pleased to give your father an order
on me for the Amount. Walk on Infant Baptism I have
obtained if you should meet with Outland I will thank
you to procure it. When shall you return to America
I have heard that your friends in Boston expect to see you this
Autumn. If you should not come so soon I will avail myself
of your kindness to obtain some other works of importance, and
which I cannot get here. – But, my dear Sir I should much
rather see you sooner though perhaps in the expression of such
a desire I consult the gratification of my own feelings rather
than the promotion of your good. – Your friends expect much
from you, and it is important that no opportunities for im-
provement be lost. – In case of your return next Autumn
I trust you will not bid a final Adieu to Europe.
Mr. Fairbanks will not have his portrait taken, for she refuses
herself she says to become a subject for your pencil.
She & I sometimes have doubtfully this morning praised your
letters which I sent yesterday. – I forgot whether I
mentioned to you in the letter which accompanies this
that I have purchased a house in the City (No. 489
Broadway) in which I shall hereafter reside. I
should be glad to consult your taste in decorating it with
prints. (for paintings I cannot aspire to) but as my
time is so limited I can only say that I will write
again to you by the next opportunity, and till then
I must beg you to accept the assurance that
I am,
Dear Sir,
Your affectionate friend
Sam'l F. Jarvis.

Cumberland June 10th 1814
My dear Son
The receipt of your very welcome letter of
May 14th together with the very interesting letters
of Mr Wilder before I Mr Alston. They were a
very great treat to us. We had had no letters or
intelligence in any way from you for about
seven months, I began to grow quite anxious.
I can now only make a short reply, as it is uncertain whether this will ever reach your hands but a short time to write you.
I wish you to thank Mr Wilder for his very acceptable letter which was deemed so important just at this time, as that Mr Everitts provided on me to give him a copy of it for the Campplot. I shall answer it soon. Present him my respectful & affectionate regards and the same to Mr Alston. I am much obliged to him for his highly satisfactory letter, I feel both him & Mrs P. for their attention to you. His account of your progress in your art of your general conduct has given us much comfort & pleasure. We hope God will continue to prosper & bless you, I keep your family in my thoughts & pray for their recovery. Mr Wilder arrived without your picture. I had arrived at Liverpool when the vessel sailed.
Goddard has not arrived, what has become of the
box with the plaster cast, we know not but hope
it is at Liverpool where Goddard left it.
I have written to Mr Richard Brn to boldly
throw open take them in to his proposition I find
them to me. You has better write him or
Capt. Beatt at Liverpool on the subject I
see that they do not get lost We regret the
disappointment in not receiving these evidences of
your improvement but hope we shall in due
time be gratified. The recent astonishing changes in
Europe give us hope that we shall in the approaching
of general peace, but this is uncertain.
We approve of your determination to remain
in Eng for the present We make the sacrifice which
is not a small one, of the pleasure of seeing you
often so long an absence for the sake of your own
improvement. I shall try to make you another
small remittance in the course of this journey,
I shall do what I am able to do but I have found
it extremely difficult to defray all my expenses
apudst so many copies of appointments which I
have sustained. The Indian state is myself
cannot be told with a great sacrifice till a
heal be established. — You must write me how
you succeed in supporting yourself It will do you
no harm in the end to be obliged to depend on your own
creation for support.
Your Grandfather Moore is yet alive — a well
as he has been in a year past — your Court may think I have
is in a decline -- There have been no deaths lately that I attended
among your acquaintance -- You will find the book seller (your
brother) shot himself with a pistol by accident a few days ago in
pleasant party down at Sandwich -- If Walker is in the Eng. you may
tell him that his uncle Genl Walker is dead & to be buried to-morrow
the mother is recovering from a violent attack of fever -- We are
all in usual health. Jefferson is now with us for a few days &c
I do not have yet yet gone to Littlefield -- We hardly know how to
part with him -- Rich. is yet in doubt about his profession
Mr. & Mrs Taylor of N. Haven have just p.r us a pleasant visit --
our & my Webster also has been to Ansonia in this state --
is a representative from that town -- Our Wednesday night is to be
a religious celebration of the recent events in Europe which we
hope are introductory to a general peace throughout the world.
These events yield to all good people here the highest felicitations.
We hope that our own unhappy country will not speedily participate in the great & most desirable blessings
of such a Peace. Present my most cordial congratulations on these events to Messrs Colburn & Thompson
Macaulay & Dr. Litchmore as you may have seen -- I have
not time to write further of them by this post.
My dear son -- your affectionate parents rejoice
in the great event above alluded to as on other accounts
especially on and for your dear children, as they give us
to hope that they are to act their part on the stage
of life in a calmer period of the world, more favorable to enjoyment & improvement in the fine arts &c
than those in which we have lived -- Our daily prayer to God for you all in that you may remember
your Creator in the days of your youth that you
may early choose the good part which shall never be
taken from you that your named may all be found
in the book of life -- that in the day when God shall
make up his terrible score of your transgressions -- My
dear son -- I am with you in all your afflictions &c
in the apple of his eye -- I pray for you in all your
happiness &c -- I am your loving father

glishman, he will not, at all. I wrote you about a month since

by what vessel it went but Mr Jack can tell you, if you have
received it. I should have been glad to have stayed there

exchange it for one untried. Whatever step I have taken hitherto,

They ask us frequently of you & by putting in their entertainment gentlemen 's name with the rest, show that they still con-

Papa & Mama & Safford are writing you all that is interesting

In my jaunt to Utica, I had an opportunity of learning
the particulars of Perry's victory, the most distinguished affair
of any of our naval achievements & deserving a place by the
side of Nelson's, tho' not so important as those. There is an
interesting account of him in the Port Folio (the March 1814 No.
or thereabouts) which you may come across. I have seen a
Panorama of the Battle in two views. I send you a key to the defeated
Com. P. was first in the Lawrence & outsailing the rest of his
fleet was exposed to the whole fire of the British line, the vessel
was a perfect slaughter house, not one being unhurt except himself & a little brother. He then left it & went in
a row-boat to the Niagara with which he broke thro' the line & took the bold attitude exhibited in the second
scene, separated by the enemy from the rest of his fleet
encountering single handed their two principal vessels. In this position they struck to him, successively
followed by the rest. The Trippe of 1 Gun tho' at the end of the line sailing up had come first to his assistance
& encountering the Lady Prevost of 13 guns, that vessel struck to her! the Caledonia going to engage her
did not arrive in season. He distinguished himself on and, in this respect resembling Nelson, as also in his letters
containing the account of his victory. He is remarkably modest & shuns attention. He returned from the Lake
in a plain habit with no other badge but a button on his collar, on horseback. He rode in company with Uncle Sidney
about ten miles, who took him a Midshipman & converted with him desultorily as such. He was known first at Utica
& there a dinner was given him. To avoid the gaze of the crowd whom the news of his approach had drawn together in all
the towns along the river, he took a batteaux & sailed down the Mohawk to Schenectady accompanied by two or three
gentlemen & ladies. I saw him in Boston. He has a very engaging & interesting countenance. Let me stop here.
Your affectionate Brother R.E. Morse.

My dear Sir,
I have had the privilege of reading or hear-
ing read the letters which you have written to your
parents since your residence in England. They have
afforded me much pleasure, as they are written with
ease and elegance, contain important information, &
exhibit the character & prospects of one whom I highly
esteem: and in order to make some adequate returns,
I almost wish, that I had the exclusive right of
communicating intelligence to you from your
native country: a country which, with all its con-
fusion, political division, degradation, & misery, is
still dear to you. But your parents & brother have
a previous claim, and you will consider my letter
as valuable no farther, than as it is a testimony of
my affection & esteem. The news of the glorious events
which have recently taken place in Europe has
just reached us. We rejoice that, that man who aspired
at nothing less than universal dominion has been
humbled, & tied back by the way in which he came;
that the nations of Europe, after having suffered & bled
for more than twenty years, may at length hail
with transport the return of peace. We rejoice especi-
ally, at the noble spirit of magnanimity, of chris-
tion benevolence, and, I may add, piety which has
prevailed all the proceedings of the Civil Powers, in
bringing about those events which command the
patitute and admiration of the world. He must be
blind indeed, who does not see the hand of God, in these
events; and he died to the happiness of his fellow creatures
who does not ardently desire, that they may be
introduction to that glorious day when man shall
cease to be the enemy of man, when the Prince
of peace shall commence his universal reign.
But we rejoice with trembling, while the destiny of
our own country hangs in awful suspense. But
we do hope, that the time is not far distant when
we shall be freed from anxiety by the return of an
honorable & lasting peace. There is not time to dwell
on this interesting subject.
I have spent my time since I graduated principal-
ly at New-Haven. For about a year I have
been sick and unable to make any progress in
my studies. But I have not forgotten that
my life has been spent, and that I have the prospect
of soon enjoying my usual state of health. Then
have been considerable alterations at N.H. since
I have been there. Several large buildings have been
erected -- two of the Meeting Houses, the Brick and Fair
Haven, have been pulled down -- three new ones are
now going up; one of which, that in the place of P.B.
is almost completed. This & that of the United States
stand nearly in the same places when the old
ones stood. The Episcopalians are building a large
stone house after the Gothic order, on the corner
opposite Mr. Selfingwell's. When completed, they
will be quite an addition to the town. A Medical
Institution connected with the College, has been established.
The Professors are Dr. Munson, Smith, from Hanover
Oves, Knight, and Mr. Hillman. Dr. H. was Tutor, I think,
when you were in College. He is professor of Anatomy, and
is said to be a very good lecturer. Dr Smith is said to be
the first physician in the country, now Dr Rush is dead.
The number of students is about forty. This inconsider a
good number to begin with. They occupy Mr. Hillhous's
large stone house opposite the burying ground. During
last year there was a society formed in Coll. called the
Benevolent Society of Yale College: the object of which is
to aid indigent young men of good character & talents in
obtaining a liberal education at that College. Our fund
amounts to about 2500 dollars. We hope they will soon
be greatly increased. Your father has contributed 200
dollars and your brother each of them 25. Many
people have died in N.H. within a year past. Mr. D. Knox & Co.
Booker Allen & D. Cook, Booker Allen, Mrs. Hillhouse, Mrs. Woolsey,
Mrs. J. Dwight, Gen. Merriman, Capt. Linus, and many
others have gone to the hour appointed for all their living.
Perhaps these things are none of them new to you. They
will however show you that I have a disposition to

My Dear Friend,
My last by the Van American cartel I trust you
have received before this, you see I am not ceremonious, for
without waiting an answer, I take advantage of a kind passage
to one of your letters, viz. that to hear from me at any time will
give you great pleasure; and improve a good opportunity by a
cartel to Boston, to write you a short letter.
The present time, in this part of the world, as you
will have heard before this reaches you, is a very interesting
and full of events, London was never gayer than now, it was
never so crowded with strangers of all descriptions, and more
especially of the greatest character in Europe, the Emperor
Alexander of Russia, the King of Prussia, the Marshal
Blucher, and the Kettman of the Czapsky, Count Statoff, are
all here, with a numerous tribe of foreign Princes, such
a visit from such Illustrious personages, you may well
think, produces no ordinary bustle; I have had the good
fortune to see them all a number of times, the Emperor
Alexander, I have seen 14 times; so that I am quite familiar
with his face; he is a man of good stature, stout, and handsome,
his countenance has much dignity, and is expressive
of great benevolence, his complexion is naturally fair, but
a little browned by the fatigues of his campaigns, his hair is
light and combed from the side towards the middle of his
head, which is bald, his forehead is high; in his manners he

suffused with tears, and his mouth seemed expressive of
the greatest gratitude, he often lifted his hands, as if to bless
the people.
I am sorry I am under the necessity of breaking

Your favor of 6th inst. has reached me

England for a further Period, it is problematical
whether an inference may thence be drawn that he

be willing to sacrifice much for your improvement, and it behoves you to consider how far his financial means may enable him, in addition to what he
has already done for you, will facilitate to furnish the requisite means of enabling you to go with comfort.

to judge upon the subject. Mr. Austone will best be

you imagine of your Father's means doubt you suppose

My Dear Parents,
Your kind letters of June last, I have received
and return you a thousand thanks for them, they
have relieved me from a painful state of anxiety
with respect to my future prospects, I cannot feel
too thankful for such kind parents, who have univer-
sally shown so much indulgence to me, accept
my gratitude and love, they are all I can give.
You allow me to stay in Europe another year, your
letters are not in answer to some I have subsequ-
ently sent requesting leave to reside in Paris, Mr. A-
as well as all my friends think it by all means
necessary I should lose no time in getting to France
and improving myself for a year in drawing, a branch
of the art in which I am very deficient, I shall
therefore set out for Paris in about two weeks,
unless your letters in answer to those sent by Dr.
Heyward & Cushing should arrive, and say otherwise,
since coming to Bristol I have not found my prospects so
good as I before had reason to expect, (owing in a great
degree to political irritation) I have however contrived to
make sufficient to pay off all my debts, which had
given me some considerable uneasiness, I can live much
more reasonable in Paris, (indeed, some say for half what
I can in London) I can improve myself more, and there-
fore all things taken into consideration, I believe it would
be more agreeable to me to remain in Paris than
to return to London, I shall be happy to hear from
you, and I am your affectionate son

Dear Breant,
I arrived in Litchfield yesterday at 12 o'clock,
in perfect health, met with no accident on my passage from
St.Haven. Immediately after my arrival I engaged my
board at Mr Lords, the lady recommended by Mrs Hooker.
I have spoken to Mr Beecher for a room. He can accom-
modate me at the end of a week; mean while I
have put up at Mr Lords in the same room
with a Mr Hotchkiss a young gentleman from St.Haven
who accompanied me in the stage and who offered me
a part of his room till Mr B could accommodate one.
My board will be $2,,50 per week. Room rent I
have not yet ascertained. Hotchkiss gives $1 per week.
I presume mine may be estimated at $40 per annum.
For the privileges of the office we give $100 per annum.
This morning I attended one of Mr Goulds lectures
and was very much pleased. My situation here is much more
agreeable than I had anticipated.
Hedges of my club is here and Cook is expected to return every
day. brety of Richards club Churles, Hotchkiss, Perkins, Devereaux
of the club which graduated last years.
When I left St.Haven I thought it doubtful whether he should be able to go to Boston this
season. If he should go I would thank Richard to call at

My dear Sir,
We wrote you about a month ago by the
Packet ship which brought the Dutch Minister who was to leave at
some English port. In that letter I informed you that I wish
to have 80000 for this year, that was all I could do for
you, this is done with great exertion on the part of your friends
for the purpose of giving you all the advantages & encour-
agement in our power -- you must henceforth depend on
your own exertions -- I do hope you will, with proper in-
telligence & economy, find no insuperable difficulties in doing
it. We wish much to see you as soon as it will be for your
advantage to return which will not probably be the case till
the return of peace, & this is still a very doubtful event
however earnestly desired. Our country is on the verge of ruin
never at any former period in so gloomy a state.
Our legislature are now in session, (extraordinary) & are about
adopting measures to call a Convention of the N. England
States first, then a Convention of all the States, to here
organize the Govt. -- or rather to alter the Constitution so
as to secure a just equal representation of the States.
Nothing but a speedy peace or a separation of the States, can
save M. Engd. & the U.S. indeed from bankruptcy & ruin.
This state of things, deeply affects all my property & income,
& your mother & me are sometimes seriously apprehensive
that we shall, in our advanced age, & if we be separated, be de-
pendent on our children from support. It. this be the case
& they shall be blessed with the means, we can have no doubt of
the dispositions of all of them -- I mention this, only to
prompt you to your utmost exertions to study the strictest
economy in all your expenditures. I have nothing to write
I send this by a Dutch Ship, via Holland. We have enjoyed
good health in the family for a length of time. I am going to Con-
necticut Haven with Edwards, me, with 7 others, were over set in the night
at Berlin, 10 miles from Hartford, the stage dashed into a wood
side— Providentially none were materially hurt. I was given
by my brother in law, the more Rogan, came to our house last Thursday,
left us this morning— The Dr gave us two very excellent famines
yesterday— Edw. I went from NH. after Convenement to Pitts-
field, there he is pleasantly situated with spend a year— He was
chosen Tutor, with Emerson, Danielson & Witten— but did not
accept he may the next year— Emerson & Witten accept— Colby
is flourishing, 82 graduated— nearly that number, it is thought
will be added this autumn— Harvard Col also is flourishing
as it Number, upwards of 100 are added this year— The controversy
about Miss A. I the College, is thought to have closed trium-
phantly on my part— Opposition is dilumed by "Remarks"
on this controversy, a pamphlet of about 30 pages, who has
read? uncommon applauds for its ability— I will send you
a copy by the first conveyance in one time let you know
the author in whom you have no common interest— Your bro-
ther Richard has concluded to go to the Theological Seminary
at Antioch to commence his Course of studies in 4 or 5 weeks,
so we shall be left alone— Nancy, Betty & Caroline are
still with us— Betty will leave us soon as our family will be
diminished— so that we shall soon have but 4 in family as we keep two
boys— You see that for the sake of supporting our children we are ad-
opting the strictest economy in our living.
Conkling have been dispatching a visit from the British fleet to de-
stroy the 740 stores in our Charles town Navy yard. In consequence, a body
of 7,4000 or 5000 of militia have been called out from the country, of the
several companies, 1200 make a very fine appearance who with the
neighbouring militia, who can be collected in 24 hours will make
a body of 25 or 30,000 of the best militia in the world.
Many strong fortifications have been erected, in great part by
voluntary labor, of all classes of citizens - Many people have
removed their furniture, & done their families - but the alarm
is now over - they are returning - confident that any attack
will be effectually repelled - You will have heard of the final
victory of Mr. Donough on L. Champlain & Macomb's
land - The present news is, that Pickett's Harbor is to be attacked
& it is feared will fall - A few days will determine if fate
will probably be known here, so as to be conveyed by the vessel
that will carry this - Congress are now in session - There is likely
to be a total change in the first officers of administration
if the President & Sec. of War have
the patriotism to resign, as many of his own party, will
agree, earnestly wish, there is no doubt we shall have an
Honorable Peace immediately -
The last letter we have received from you is dated
in June 24th - Mr. Lyman has just arrived, but we have
received no letters by him - We are desirous to hear often
from you - With much to see the plaster cast, I think
will be the last article were at Liverpool -
Mr. Stewart has just arrived from Andover & writes me to add to this
