Mr. Sam F.B. Morse
My dear friend
My heart is so full that
I do not know how to utter its emotions.
Thanks all thanks be to heaven and
our glorious heroes! My satisfaction
is full; it is perfect. It partakes of
the character of the victor and wants
nothing to make it complete. I return
your felicitations upon this happy
and heart cheering occasion, and hope
it may serve to suppress every sigh
and to enliven every hope that animates
the bosom of my friends at
Bristol. Give Mr. Allston a hearty
squeeze by the hand for me in token
of my gratification at this event and
my remembrance of him. Sent to you
all your feelings; I enjoy your triumph
as much as if I was with you may
it do you good and lengthen your lives.
Really I think it is much more worth
my regard to live now, than ever it
was before. This gives a tone to ones
nerves, a zest to ones appetite and
a reality to existence that pervades
all nature and exhibits its effects
in even word and action. Among
the heroes whose names shall be
inscribed upon the broad base of
American Independence and glory
the names of the heroes of Lake
Erie and Lake Champlain will
be recognized as brilliant and
every way worthy. And it will here-
after be said that the example and
exertions of New York has saved
the nation. At least 25,000 of her
Militia must now be in active service
at N.Y. 12 at Erie 3 at Sackets H. 2 at 3
at Plattsburgh 2 at 3. Perhaps you may
double the number at the two latter
places. These are corps amounting to
40,000 more which can be moved and collect
ed upon any point of attack in 7 or 8 days,
and in case of a hard and protracted
fight she can bring 50,000 more troops
completely equipped in the field.
What becomes of Massachusetts now?
and its sage politicians? Oh! What
the picture! I cannot bear the
contrast. Like a dead carcass she
hangs upon the living spirit which
animates the heart and inspirs
motions. Her consequence is for
me sorry for it because I have
been accustomed to admire the noble
spirit she once displayed and the
virtue which accorded her
highest days. Your letters
were very acceptable. I thank you
for them. Give my best wishes to
Mr. Rice and family. I am heartily
rejoiced that Eliza is getting better.

My dear Brother,
We have received your packet of letters
containing an account of the crowded heads in London
I am much obliged to you for the pleasure they afforded me. I
paid extracts from them to Louis I sent them to the Daily Advertiser. We all enjoy you
the happiness of having been in London at such an
extraordinary scenes. I am looking out for some account from you of the Duke of Wellington which will
wanted to complete the catalogue. I hope you have
seen him. Your proposal of going to Russia struck us
with surprise. I suppose they have no very distinguished
artists there. I suppose you expect to be more conspicuous
there. Believe me I could not help fancying you as going to be the first, to be at the head of the Art in
that barbarous & uncivilized Nation. However your
task I think, would be no very easy one, for according
to Dr. Clarke they have a mean sort of state for
Paintings & other collections making the same use of
them as of money to get conveniences & necessaries
of life &c.
I have nothing very interesting to tell you of your friends here. Edw. is gone to Litchfield & I am going next week
to Andover so that the family will again be separated
You must not expect of courts that I am going to be a
Minister; I am admitted (at all) on favor. It year
perhaps, or at farther two or three will determine the
result of this experiment. I am no better now than when
you knew me but mama says, a great deal worse. The
fact is, I am in want of some pursuit if any one should
tell me now that I should adopt this, I should think there
was no truth in the old saying "That every man is
born to some particular pursuit," for there are twenty
that I might be brought up to as easily as to that of a Her
junman. If this plan is adopted, so; if not I must
seek some other employment. But enough of myself.
There is no change for the better in our National
affairs. Peace is still in prospect. There is more hostility in
the National Government towards New England than towards their other enemies. They consider her as an alien
or rather a tributary & refuse to admit her to any stand in their councils, or to appropriate money to her defense.
Our motto now is "Millions for defense, but not a cent for tribute" & there is a Convention of the U.S. States appointed to seek redress of grievances & restoration of
our rights. We have been lately called upon to defend our Capital Boston. Presidents Warren & Calhoun Island, which have been occupied by Militia! there has
been a Fort (named Fort Strong) erected by volunteers on Noddly Island, opposite Watertown Wharf, if you recollect.
Turks were provided to be sunk in a line asteward the channel. The 74 also Constitution & the navy yard all
had directed down the Harbor. These preparations were made by an expedition by water. My land, also
we were prepared for an attack. General Orders were issued & 6000 troops were marched down to the capital
detached from every part of the State. They encamped at the foot of Dorchester Heights (South Boston) Notification
were thrown up on Dorchester Heights, at Dorchester point, across Boston Neck. The troops were reviewed several times
I went to see them & men who had seen 20,000 French & 10,000 English troops said, they never saw troops equal
to these 6,000.— President Lincoln, all citizens in Boston & the Trinity, were formed into companies & had a cockade
as the badge of their company. Companies of Sea Penitents, Riflemen & were formed by exempt. Boston was in
some respects a Camp where every day companies were out drilling, tall ready to march at a moment's warning.
These preparations have subsided now, for the winter. The troops have been disbanded & their place is to be supplied by a State Corps of 10,000 who will take the
field if necessary next Spring.— There were several of our College friends attached to the drafted troops. Winckley
was aid to the Gen. of one Brigade & George Wilkis of my class, aid to the Gen. of the other Brigade. John
Duright of my class was a Sergeant in an Artillery
Company.
I think you will find enough in the events of the last
summer to satisfy your pride as an American
Com. Mc Donough's victory is the most brilliant event of
the most important of the war. Captain Sam. Breeze was
in the field but escaped unhurt. If you have seen
the Mc Donough's act of the battle you will have a
clear view of the whole action. It is there given so
distinct that I set it down on paper. Uncle Arthur
writes that he shall wish you to paint a view of it
when you return.
Papa wishes me to make enquiry of you whether Zerah
Bolburn's father is living His wife has written Papa a letter
stating that she has heard he was dead, but nothing more
Perhaps it is only rumor. with you to inform us on the subject,
I what has become of the extraordinary Car
have not been informed of a narrow escape Papa
met with in the Stage, going on to N. Haven commence
They set out from Hartford about one O'clock at night, dark
& rainy, they got about 9 miles & found the driver was un-
acquainted with the way having never been on it but once
a road dangerous too, built in many places on the sides
of hills -- They were driving slowly on a walk & found the
carriage sloping ruinously going of one of these declivities.
They called to the driver who turned the horse into
the road, but not in time to bring up the carriage which
tipped, & fell ten feet with 9 passengers, to the ground & dashed
into a thousand pieces. But wonderful to relate, none of
the passengers were materially hurt. Dr Worcester of Salem
was alboard & received a sprain on his wrist. Eder had anticipated
the danger & being on the upper west side threw his
feet thru the canvas & was unhurt. Papa was so much jarred
by the fall that his limbs were sore for some weeks, but
the effects of it have passed off. The Stage happened at the instant to
come up be behind them ( tho' they were told falsely that no

My Dear Sir
Your last letter that we have received was dated January
2nd and anxiously looking out for letters from you by every avenue
that we knew of in any of our seaports -- and next to hearing that you
had become a real Christian on his of an inheritance incomparably und
filed and that faith not away would be the pleasure experience
from hearing that you were industriously maintaining yourself by your
own earnings it appears to us that you have obtained so much celebrity
by what you have done in the way of your profession as that if you have
been and are prudent in hoping the friendship of Mr. West Mr. Alston and
others who appeared disposed duly to appreciate your talents that by
this time you must ought to be in a situation to do every thing for your
self that we could wish which would be a great relief to us at this
trying time, but your goodness and gentle father has seen proper to give to
less you a thousand Dollars for this year which I know not how or where
he will obtain it but he bid me be of good Cheer the Lord will provide
and our own one dear wife, he often says has conducted so well as
has been of trust will continue to be an honour to his family of
to his country and will most cheerfully support us when we are on
the decline of life if not able to support ourselves that we must exert
ourselves to the utmost to spirit just at this moment though it comes
very hard upon us at this time Edwards has gone to Kentucky to study
law he was invited or rather appointed a tutor in Yale College but
he did not except he took his second degree we have not heard
from him this six week, he is not asked in writing us frequently of
long letters as you or Richard are but his a great comfort to us of
I hope will be a great blessing to his country & in all his connections
Richard goes to Andover to-morrow to commence his theological studies
Edward Hooker & his sister Mary are here on their way to Andover
When they expect to live their Father whom you knew was settled at
Norwich he died about 20 months ago his Widow has last week
married to Eg. Favore who thid to live with Madame Phillipps
of Andover and the family of course have removed there we think
it quite a pleasant circumstance to have them so eligible settled so near
us as we have a great regard for them. We wish to know what the
plan was that you said you was maturing for our Arbitration in
regard to the Emperor of Russia. You must not be a schemer but determine on a
steady uniform course it is an old adage that a nothing
stone never gathers any Moss so a person that is driving about for
Millar to put very seldom lays of anything against a vaining day
you must be wise my son and endeavour to get into such business as
it with the Divine Blessing give you a support secure that first and
then you will be authorized to indulge your taste & exercise of your
genius in other ways that may not be immediately connected with
a living. You mention patronage from this Country but such patronage
is not known here unless you were on the spot and not then indeed
but for Value received. You must therefore make up your mind to
labour for yourself without leaning on anyone & look up to God for
his Blessing upon your endeavour this is the way your Parents
set out in life about 25 years ago they had nothing to look to for
a support but their salary which was a House 20 cords of wood,
570 dollars a year the reception & execution of the Geographies
was an experiment not then made with the Blessing of heaven on
these resources we have maintained an expensive family kept
open doors for almost all who chose to come & partake of our Host
talities. Enemies at Wallan Bridges have been welcomed. We have given
you & your Brothers a liberal Education have allowed you $4,000 are al-
lowing your two Brothers about $300 a year supporting our remain-
ing family at the rate of two thousand dollars a year this is a pretty correct
statement and I make it to show you what can be done by Industry & economy
with the blessing of Heaven which last alone makes the rich add no-
torious there with our present situation calls loudly on our Children to make
every landable exertion to relieve us from every case of spending thime
with regard to them I hope you will not ever in debt as that makes a
man feel mean and is a stvish business, take care of money when you have
earned it & especially of wasting small sums if you wish to obtain a living
& Affluence is so plain but neat thin plain but let your food be wholesome

are comforted in the good conduct & proficiency of

peculiarly perplexing -- there are a great
many failures in Boston almost every day

them is your acquaintance, Young Beers.
We expect to have paper money issued &
will at once depreciate & the consequences
cannot be foreseen -- I know not that this

tecipations -- we leave ourselves in the

My dear Sir
Having just heard of a good opportunity to write to you via Lisbon
I avail myself of it to enclose to you in bill of exchange on London
for twenty five pounds sterling. The other I shall enclose to your father from
whom I have just received a letter informing me of his receipt of your order
for £24-12. I could not procure exactly that amount, and therefore beg you will
add to the books already purchased the works of William Tillinghast Lond
1740. Ed. in 10th Edition with his life by Birch in 1742. which I find by
the Catalogues may be purchased for seven shillings. -- I will make no
apology for adding the following books to the Catalogue of those which you
have already had the goodness to procure because your kind offer makes me
confident you will not consider it as too great a liberty. -- Critici Sacri seu
Dottissimum virorum in SS. Biblia Annotationes et Tractatus. Lond 1660 et
Amstelodami 1798. I do not know exactly the No of Vols. tho I believe 9. -- The
works of the Rev. C. Carneid John Lightfoot, D D. Revis'd & corrected by George Bright
D.D. Lond 1684. 2 vol. Fol. -- If the war continuing you will oblige me by having
them carefully packed in a light case I sent out by land yesterday in
the spring under convoy to the care of Mr Robert Foster of Montreal
for Mr Henry Fisher. Mr Fisher is a merchant of this city & Mr Frostle
his correspondent will forward them to him, perhaps free of cost since
Dr Rommy's books which have just arrived have been much damaged
from being packed so that the salt water could penetrate to them,
and if mine are sent to Montreal they will be transported a considerable
distance by land & exposed to danger of being robbed.
I am sorry so long a time has elapsed between the payment of the
books and the reimbursement of your money. Is there not some
quicker way of transmitting money to you?
Since I wrote the above I have received your favour dated Bristol
September 9th 1814. from which I find you are probably at this mo-
ment in Paris; consequently the request contained on the other page may
be impracticable. -- We had letters yesterday from Mrs Hull at Cork-
mouth. Jannette is with them at present, and has perfectly regained
her health which during the summer was not very good. -- I do not
remember at this time what I wrote to you in my letter of May 4th.
I hope it was not more than I ought to have said for I would not for
any consideration trifle with your happiness by the encouragement of
falter hopes -- I believe you worthy my dear Sir of her affections and it
would certainly gratify me to see her yours. But while I think you ought
not to dishearten me I am fully sensible that your absence for so long a period
and the uncertainty of your future settlement in life, may prevent that at-
tachment on her part which I am inclined to think your presence and
the constancy of your affection might create. -- You will I am sure duly
appreciate the motives which lead me to use the language of caution.
I am not surprised at the feelings you exhibit with regard to England
or America. The English in general I have so contemptuous an opinion
of us, I am so exalted of themselves that every American must feel a virtu-
ous indignation when he hears his country traduced and vilified.
But my dear Sir it is natural on the other hand for an exile from
his native land to turn with fond remembrance to its excellencies, I
forget its defects. -- You will be able some years hence to speak with
more impartiality on this subject than you do at present. The
men who have involved the country in this war are wicked, corrupt.
A systematic exclusion of all federalists from any office of
trust is the leading feature of their administration; yet the federalists
comprehend the majority of the wealth, virtue & intelligence of the com-
munity. It is the power of the ignorant multitude by which they are
supported; and I conceive that America will never be a respectable
nation in the eyes of the world till the extreme democracy of our
constitution is done away, and there is a representation of the prop-
erty rather than of the population of the country.— You feel nothing
of the oppressive despotism sway of the disunionist republicans. But
we feel it in all its bitterness I know that it is far worse than that
of the most despicible Sovereigns in Europe. With such men there can
be no union; I mean no permanent union.— The repulsion of British
Invasion is the duty I will be the pride of every American; but while I
stand in defence of his much wronged country against a
arrogant & in some instances a cruel foe,
he cannot be said to be the unprincipled conduct of the internal
enemies, & such he must conceive the present ruling party to be.—
But enough of politics.— Mrs. Jarvis desiring to be particularly re-
membered to you. I know not whether I mentioned in my last that
she has made me the father of a fine Son who was 9 months old
the 5th inst. & is the picture of health, spirit & good nature.
Now that you are in France you will I hope have more frequent
opportunity of writing; and I beg you will believe that to
none will your letter be more acceptable than to
Dear Sir,
Your obedt: humb. Servt
SAMUEL F. GARDINER.

Dear Sir
To these passages of D' Morses
letter respecting his son to which you
have directed my attention I hasten to
reply without any form because it will
satisfy me to relieve the anxiety of the
parents of my friend. His religious
and moral character unexceptionable
good. He feels strongly for his country
and expresses those feelings among British
friends with great deservibility. I do not
know that I ever undertook any investigations
in the Company of Englishmen
which are calculated to injure his
standing among them. But my dear
Sir you will know that an attack
cannot escape the sting of illiterate
and false charges against his country
and even its moral character unless it be
almost entirely withholds himself from
Society. It cannot be expected that any
human being should be so perfectly as
to suffer and dignify in total silence.
But I do not think that any political
collisions which may incidentally and very
unfrequently arise can injure him as an
Artist, for it is well known to you that
the simple fact of his being an American
is sufficient to prevent his rising rapidly
into notice since the possession of that character does the firm of superior genius
and established talent. The extent of the
prejudice has been developed in a case of
peculiar interest in which an exhibition and
offer of sales of pictures by an artist known
infuriated to keep himself totally failed and
left in debt a man whose modest worth and
towered genius with out star cast a ray of
glory over his country and his own soul
the heart and bright as the glowing touch
of his living spirit. In addition to this
the unfair and illegal conduct of certain
Directors clearly evinces the difficulty it is not
the hopelessness of endeavors with jealousy
and deep-rooted prejudice. But the feelings
and present situation I must give
to this communication the character of sacred
secrecy. I advised Samuel to go to France
and bring himself for six months in the Louvre.
I would then send him to Italy, the seat of the arts.
He inclines to the first part of the plan, and
then to return home, but before putting
it in execution will he heard from his father.
Mr. Elliston intends to winter in London.
Morse has a fine taste, and colour well.
His drawing is capable of much improvement.
but he is anxious to place himself
at the head of his profession and with
a little anxious encouragement will
probably succeed. That patient industry
which has in all ages characterized the
masters of the art he will find it of
interest to apply to his studies. The
painting he advances in them. His
success has been moderately good. If he
could sell the pictures he has on hand
the mails would probably pay his way

into France.
very respectfully
Your friend
Samuel Hearick

my Dear Son
This Day is the Sabbath of the Lord our God we have attended divine
worship heard your good father expound from a portion of the word of life
in the internal affections of worship I have rested myself alone in the parlour to
converse a little with you on your present situation, as I suppose this letter will
find you in a land where this holy day is abolished and where there is none
of the means of religious instruction that you have formerly enjoyed let me
ask you my son how this deprivation when you are so satisfied to have it now
is it a trial to you? do you long to get through with that part of your education
in your art that obliges you to be separated from privileges which you
truly ought to I hope will always hold dear, you dear as your immortal soul
I beg you to answer these questions in your next and let me know how you
spend your Sabbath, for I hope you will always remember the Sabbath Day
to keep it holy, wherever in the province of God your lot may be cast
and whatever thorn around you may grow so contrary think to Oh my Dear son
what shall I say to you? how shall I write you as to induce you to make
the one thing needful your chief concern shall I set before
you the flatting unsatisfying nature of all things here below does not every
day experience say more on this subject than I can in a column, what an
victorist do they not take to them silver things and fly at a Bird? What
is honour or fame hear what Pur Thatch says on this subject.
"Honours a Pass of dying Breath
that men expose their Blood
"And Venture everlasting Death
"To Gain this living Good
oh! then my Dear Child take that honour that cometh from God only
by a due observance of all his commandments let them not be
previous unto you but like the pious patriot extime all his command
ments concerning all things to be right, and hate every false way
that shall you be happy in life and Death through an Endless Eternity.
We wish you would write us your thoughts on this all important subject
and let politics entirely alone leaving them to those whose business they are
feel extremely anxious about you know not that I ever felt more
I know you are surrounded with the worst of temptations that can infest
a youth like you let me therefore be very important to you to be sure
on your Guard to keep your Bible for your constant companion to read
daily especially the proverbs of Solomon the praiser & the New testament
leave not to beg the protection guidance & direction of that God to whom
have been most Solomon by dedicated by your Afflictionate parents in your
infancy by prayer & by a strict observance of his holy commandments
nothing short of this will through the merits of our Blessed Saviour secure
his favour which we are bound to esteem more than life & his loving kindness
which is better than life and all its Honours &c. – The Sabbath is now over –
This is the beginning of Monday Dec. 19th I have many things to say to you my son
than can be compassed in this letter but the Question of every kind that has to do with
to answer as particularly & fully & speedily as you can after receiving this Letter &c.
Why did you not mention Mr James Russell of his family in any of the three letters
ten to us from Bristol two we received yesterday dated Oct 11th Mr Russell thinks it singular that
he did not just say they were well with him if that was the case if you say nothing about
his likeness which chiefly concerns him not how to account for as you said in
a former letter you had taken it as a present for her. It would be the most gratifying
to me to hear that you could make her if it is a good like nep. I am sorry you do
feel the importance of fulfilling your engagements with more punctuality &c
must be more attentive to your Friends, on God will grant to love them. – How do
you propose to be in France not more than six months I hope and then return
London from which place or Liverpool I expect you will embark for Boston next
Summer and be sure you leave not a single debt to be paid by your self or any one
when you come back I was not a little astonished to hear you say in one of your
letters from Bristol that you had earned money enough there to pay off your debts
if cannot help asking what debts could you have to discharge with your own
earnings after receiving one thousand Dollars a year from us which we are
sure must have afforded you even by your own account of your expenses ample
means for the payment of all just and honourable Debts and I hope you will
not either we are informed by others that they made six hundred Dollars
year not only pay all their expenses of clothing boarding training learning
French language &c but they were able out of it to purchase Books to read
and actually sent a large trunk full of Elegant Books now the person that
told us that he did this has a Father that is said to be worth a Hundred
fifty thousand Dollars therefore the young man was not pinched for
means but was thus economical out of consideration to his parents and to
show his gratitude to them as I suppose, now think my son how much more
your poor parents are doing for you how good your Dear Brother are to be
satisfied with so little done for them in comparison with what we are doing for
you I let the thought stimulate you to more economy & Industry as I greatly
fear you have been falling off in both since the elicit you received for your
first performances it has always been a failing of yours that as soon as you find
you could excel in what you undertook to be timed off and not humble yourself any
further about it I was in hopes that you had got over this fickleness in thin in
your letter in which you ask leave to stay longer in Europe you mention a large
picture that you were going to paint for the exhibition in Paris in hopes of obtaining
the prize; is this plan given up? and if so why is it? I think if you could get
one or two hundred pounds in Guineas it would while trying for it when you leave
France your papa wishes you to purchase a very handsome good combo black cloth
for a suit of clothes for himself & a cloak & also a suit for each of your Brothers
it will take I presume 15 or 16 yards if you should get it let it be perfectly neat
put up so as to keep it from being injured in coming home do not forget it and
look over your parents letters before you return and endeavour to comply with
their requests made at different times to you for Books &c &c bringing home pictures
paintings & include those at Liverpool and come with a good repellent
behave by self next if possible you must not expect to paint any
thing in this country for which you will receive any money to support
you but portraits therefore do every thing in your power to qualify you
for painting & taking them in the best style this is all your hope here is to
be very obliging & condescending to those who are disposed to employ
you our circumstances are altered much for the worse since you left
us we cannot keep but half the help we Used to do and have sold some of
our furniture to purchase Bills for you I have offered more for sale for the
same purpose so you see our deprivation are not small but we do it
with pleasure when we have reason to believe that you are exerting yourself
to relieve us from the great burden which we are labouring under and are
taking it on yourself I think young fester is a very estimable young man
to be as I am told he is supporting himself & assisting his widowed mother
by his Industry this is considerately does him honour I trust your feelings are
equally good if you had suffered it as necessary as it really is at present
to relieve us I must now conclude my Dear Son with wishing you every
happiness that our heavenly Father has best for you in this life & everlasting
happiness in the life that is to come all had a great deal of love to you from
your loving father
Brother Hill

My dear Sir
On the 12th inst I wrote to you for the Criterion via Lisbon
in answer to your favour of Sept. 9 which I that day received, and enclosing No. 4 of a set of Cachanges for £25. Sterling. Having another
good opportunity by Mr Chk King who will go direct to England, I embrace it to send you No. 3 of the same set. The first two numbers
I transmitted to your father, on the 15th in my letter above refer to, I requested you to purchase Chillingworth's works which would
make up the sum of £25. without considering that there might be some expenses attending the packing & transportation of the books.
I hope you will pardon this forgetfulness, and the trouble which I put you to, for my sake. Be assured that I very sensibly feel your
kindness. As you are now in France, I hope I shall hear from you often, and that you will give me an detail of your
occupations. I enlarge more upon your own private views I feel injsy. Whatever you write concerning yourself will be interesting.
Do not be afraid of Egotism; all such fear should be banished between friends. Mrs J. & our little son are well. She begs again
to be remembered to you, I unitly heartily, in the good wishes of
Dear Sir
Yours very sincerely
Sam'l A. Faris Jr.

My dear Parents,
I arrived yesterday from Bristol
where I have been for several months, fast endeavors
to make a little in the way of my profession,
but have completely failed owing to several causes, find
the total want of anything like partiality for the time act
in that place, the people there are but a remove from
brutes; a Bristol hog, is as proverbial in this country
as a Charleston man of the same species is in
Boston; their whole minds are absorbed in trade, cattle
and gain, and interest, is all they understand, if
I could have painted them a picture for half a
quintal by which they could have made twenty, whilst
I starved; I could have starved; secondly, the vulnerea
of national prejudice, which rages now with brutal
acrimony, they no longer desire, they hate the Americans,
the battle on Champlain, and before Plattsburgh, has de-
cided the business, the means and bewailings for this
disgrace are really to an American quite comforting;
after their arrogant boasting of reducing us to uncondi-
tional submission, is it strange that I should feel
a little, the effects of this universal hatred? I have
told it, and I have left Bristol after six months
perfect neglect, after having been invested there with
promises of success, I have had the mortification
't leave it without having from Bristol a single com-
mission; more than that and by far the worst, if I have not
gone back in my art there six months I have at least
stood still and to me this is the most trying reflection of
all; I have been immersed in the paralyzing atmosphere
of trade till my mind was near partaking the infection,
I have been listening to the growling, avaricious devotes
of mammon, whose souls are narrowed to the studious
contemplation of a hard earned shilling, whose leaders imagine
a hundred thousand, I say, I have been listening to their
misery being, till the idea did not seem sufficiently, of
lowering my noble art to a trade, of painting for money,
of degrading myself and the soul enlarging art which I professed
to the narrow idea of merely getting money; for on myself I am ashamed of myself; no, never well I degrade
myself by making a trade of a profession if I cannot live a
gentleman I will starve a gentleman -- but I will discuss this unpleasant subject the particulars of which I
can better relate to you, than write; suffice it to say that
my ill treatment does not prey upon my spirit, I am in
excellent health and spirits and have great reason to
be thankful to Heaven, for thousands of blessings, which
one or two reverses shall not make me forget: reverses so
I call them, how trifling are my troubles, to the millions
of my fellow creatures who are afflicted with all the
dreadful calamities incident to this life, receive
with I call them, no, they are blessings compared the miseries of thousands; indeed, I am too ungrateful, if a thing does not result just as I wish, I begin to deplore, I forget the load of blessings which I enjoy, the health, parents whose kindness exceeds the kindest, brothers, relatives and friends, advantages with no one else enjoys for the pursuit of a favorite art, besides numerous others, all which are forgotten the moment an unpleasant disappointment occurs; indeed, indeed! I am very ungrateful.
With respect to Peace, I can only say I should not be surprised if the Preliminaries were signed before Jan. my reasons are that G.B. cannot carry on the war any longer, she may talk of her inexhaustible resources, but she well knows that the great resource the Property tax must fail next April, the people will not submit any longer, they are taking strong measures to prevent its continuation, and without it they cannot continue the war; another great reason why I think there will be peace, is the absolute Fear which they express of us, they fear the increase of our Navy, they fear the increase of the Army, they are in dread of the further national displace of their character; Mr. Munroe's plan for raising 100,000 men went like a shock through the country, they saw the U. States assume an attitude which they did not expect and the same men who cried for war, through the Americans now cry most bitterly for peace -- the Union of the parties also have convinced them we are determined to resist their most apparent pretensions. Yours very affectionately
Samuel M. Spencer

Dear Sir,
Noticing the Reason which
has interfered with your calling upon me, as I had
looked for, I now enclose the Twenty Pounds
requested in your Letter of 16th. of this Month
requesting to be at your Post of the Town, I then call
upon you, I further entreat upon the Situation
you have mentioned until I have the pleasure
of your call -- in mean time however I cannot but
express how extremely grieved I have been on
the very melancholy Event to which you refer.
I pray present me with friendly Regards to Mr. Heston
& pray that I must truly condescend to call upon him -- it has
been continued in my Mind to call upon him for some days past the higher to permitted --
you will very sincerely
H: Bromfield
Mr Sam. P. Mosse
8 Buckingham Place
Vitroy Square
My dear son,
This is to go by the Galena, which sails to-morrow
to write you a long letter some weeks ago, to go by the Liverpool
packet but by mistake my letter was not put on board, it
is to go by the Galena so that you will probably receive both
together, with some pamphlets & other papers. We suppose you
are now at Paris though we have no information from you
since your letter by Dr. Romayne. We are now very anxious
to hear from you I am daily expecting letters from you
You will not fail to improve every step I to write up, & be particular
Mr Wilder expects to go to France in a
few days, via N. York, perhaps via London, & we hope will
meet you & then he will be able to communicate to you
many particulars what we cannot write He is much disposed
to be our & your friend & to patronize you. Mr.
he offers you any assistance, in away of funds by loan
take no more than is absolutely necessary for your use
as it may perplex your business both you have to run further
into debt. We have been obliged to provide ourselves more
than we wished in order to support you & your brothers in
settling your professional education but we shall be
satisfied to have thus exerted ourselves if you behave
well & succeed in your profession, & become useful to
your fellow men Your brother Edwin we have just
heard, is very well at Litchfield, wholly engaged in
his professional studies, who already acquired a high
reputation in that town His mind we are very happy
also to hear, is very seriously impressed with religious
concern for his own future happiness This is also
the case with your brother Richard, in a still greater
degree He spent the last Sabbath with us, I returned
to his studies (in which he says he has great enjoyment)
yesterday His mind is very tender, amiable & affectionate,
I we had great comfort in our interview with him
We daily think of them & you, my dear son, in our prayers
How happy would be our meeting next fall, if God
preserve us all to that time, I wish to bring us together
if all our sons should have come in the best
sense of the phrase "children of God" sons of the
Almighty, & we meet not only as parents & children
very dear to each other but also as Christians, fellow heirs
of the heavenly inheritance Oh my dear son amidst the
scenes of dissipation, & allowing temptations with which
you are surrounded & to which you are exposed, think of
these things - Remember your Creator - Let his fear be
before your eyes - Call to mind the advice of your
affectionate parents - how deeply they are concerned
for you - Daily read your Bible - neglect not to open
your morning & evening sacrifice to God, from a devout
heart - Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy - In-
clude yourself from improper company on that sacred
day - If you can find a suitable place of worship,
attend upon it steadily & devoutly, I get what
good you can from it. Will God preserve your
son, in health, from sin, prosper you in your professional
pursuits, & return you in safety, to your affectionate
parents & numerous friends.
I have written you on the subject of bringing home
all your paintings & of the importance of finishing your large
picture, in order that you may exhibit them in Boston
on your return, I am thus only raising something for your
support - as Mr Sergeant has set you the example of
led the way, by exhibiting his "Landing of the Fathers,"
by locked at 25th each. We think you might in this
way do something clever, & perhaps make a beginning
for a gallery of paintings in Boston, & awaken in
that town, & in N. Eng'l a spirit of emulation, not
to be out-doned in patronage of the fine arts, by
Brit. a or N. York - Now peace has come, they
may feel better able to do it - At least you had
better come as well prepared as you can for
executing such a plan - We wish, if practicable
to have our children planted near us, if they can
do it to advantage - We hope Edw. D will settle
in this town or Boston -
On second thought, I have concluded to send this
letter by Mr Wedder, as you will have one by the
Galen, & I shall not have time to write another
by him as my time is much occupied always at this
season, as we have in addition to the usual fast (on
the 6th Apr.) a national thanksgiving on the 13th -
I have just received a letter from him with an affectionate one, in which he speaks
of you in terms of great kindness & friendship -- I express a desire to cultivate your acquaintance
not on my account only, because you are the son of his friend, but on your own account. He says that
you feel that his attentions to you, which have not been much of the kind he desires to pay to others
because he is wont to pay to those whom he wishes to call his friends, have not been understood
by you -- that you had been as he thought rather shy of visiting him, that he had been in this letter
dated 4th Oct. 98 he felt concerned to have it returned & requested me to write you on the subject. I have
written to him, that I would have apologized for your return to London, if I had not been
so embarking for home, by all means to call at Medlarthwaite, Thront Macarplay, Bunderstone
Lettsomes & give them all an opportunity to write to you as to me. I will explain all more fully on
your return. If we are spared to meet we shall have much to communicate on both sides, which will
deeply interest us -- The religious controversy is commencing openly at the election. Dr. Warren is in
taking a very interesting turn as we think favorable to the cause of evangelical true
But we can see but a little way before us
Apr. 2d 1811. Sabbath Evenings
The Collier has just called & informs us that he goes to New
York Monday for N.Y. Steam to France & allows a few minutes
only to prepare a little panel for you -- A larger one has gone to
the Beneficents for you by the Galen -- Mr. Collier will tell you
all about them as to what will be interesting to you -- what we
wish you to do -- We have just had a visit from Rich Salt
ten from Ford -- both are in excellent health & spirits -- pursuing
their studies with great vigor diligence & success. Ebd. has
a high reputation among his fellow students -- Your mother &
I are very well for this season -- Many, Gregory & Caroline
all well -- Miss Russell is just recovering from a severe illness --
Boston friends & relations are well -- All join in love to you
I can add no more - write as often & fully give
your letter to Mr Wilder to forward
You ever affectionate father
Samuel Wilder
Paris
P.S. You will have a cloak made for me, bring it
with as mention'd in a former letter - The other articles of
Clothing we have requested Mr Wilder to get, as he

This will be handed you by
Mr John W. Webster, son of Dr. Redford Webster
of Boston, a young gentleman who has just
completed his medical studies, passed an
examination before the Faculty of the University
at Cambridge. He goes to Europe with a view
to attend a course of operative surgery in the
London hospitals. On your return from France
I hope you will meet him in London, provide
this should this be the case he will inform
you particularly how aware he is of the state of
the family, as he very politely, called on us for
the purpose of ascertainings for your own sake
Mr W. will wish to see such places & objects
of curiosity & improvement as you may be
acquainted with. You will oblige him & me
by directing, 1, as far as your engagements will
admit, accompanying him to such places
& objects especially those that relate to your
own art, I show him all that civility &
kindness, which in like circumstances, you would
wish to receive yourself.
Your affectionate father & most
affectionate son

My Dear Son
Your last letter was dated Oct 12th of Bristol your intention there
was to go to Paris in a short time from that date, we hope you went, and that
the letter we have received from you making the request for leave to go, have been
received by you & retired from mind, and left you at liberty to pursue your own
course – We now have the heart felt pleasure of congratulating you on
the return of peace between our Country & great Britain may it never again
be interrupted but may both countries bring the things that make for honor
& love as Brethren – Your Friends here are often asking whether we shall
not see you in the course of the Summer or Fall since peace has come, we
answer we hope so, we all long to see you very much indeed. We hope to receive
your pictures, viz. the Heracles by Mr James Knell, portrait for Shipley
& a handsome Landscape for Dr Bartlett & the Plaster Cast if not broke
to pieces are it gets here, by the first good opportunity that we may get
some of your improvements in your Art which will be a great gratification
to all your Friends. I hope you are going on with your large picture
& that you will be able to bring it home with you after gaining
the 200 guineas for its Exhibition. You must try all in your power to
clear what money you can in the way of your profession to help yourself,
as we are becoming very poor in consequence of what we have done
& are doing for our Children & others, we have been put to a vast deal
of trouble in our pecuniary concerns, they do not end with the War
we live quite Economically only four in family, your Papa & myself having
no condition make our present family, We hope to hear from you every
often till we see you, when you return we wish you to bring some excellent black or
Corbeau cloth to make your good Father & Brothers each a suit of Clothes,
Your papa also wishes you to get made a handsome black cloth Cook
for him one that will fit you he thinks he'll put him before I attend to this
Your mama would like some grain colored silk for a gown if it can be had for
but little don't forget that your mother is no stranger & that a large pattern
fits her better than a small one, -- I hope my son will see all your Bills
discharged and leave Europe free of Debt when you embark for home your
papa has been this week getting Bills for you to the amount of five hundred
dollars which makes out your allowance from us all to one or two hundred
dollars which he hopes to be able to procure in the course of the spring
or beginning of the summer you will when you get this last have had
from your parents since you left them 4 four thousand dollars we do not
regret it, as all the accounts we have had from others as well as yourself
have afforded us much satisfaction with respect to your improvement in your
art & your otherwise good Conduct, continue & increase in well doing my son
and may that Almighty Power who said let there be light and there
was light shine into your heart with the light of divine truth and make
you his own by that news & bring way pointed out in the Gospel of his Son
Jesus Christ, there is nothing which can afford your parents so much joy
as to see their Children walking in the truth. Your Brother Rich and I
are studying Divinity at the Theological Institution at Ansonia and is increasingly
pleased with his studies his health & spirits are much improved I believe
is at Litchfield studying Law & attending the Law lectures & a
course of Theological lectures given by Mr. Buchin once a week to the young
lawyers Edwards is much Blessed with them I think they must do them good
I should feel terribly when I think of your situation my dear son as that
out from these precious means of grace was it not that I know you are
in the hands of continually under the Eye of that good being whose you are
and whom I hope you forever served love, we are very anxious to hear from
you & hope we shall hear from you by the first arrival. -- Capt. Smith's
family expect to embark for Liverpool some time this spring to render
there a number of years if you should return via Liverpool you will
see them of course they shall try to see you as soon as they
possibly can, I have read Mr. Smith's many a number of your letters
they appear very friendly to you I hope if it is not attended with more expense
that you will try to see them before you embark but you must do as the custom
say out your Coat according to your Cloth and not go to any expense beyond
what would be prudent for the sake of saving them - Mr. Court has another
daughter they have now three Daughters & a son besides Daniel Barnes
Mr. Evans son by her former husband, I shall leave this side of this letter for
your paper to fill up with any opportunity good long letters but nothing
of politics.
Mr. G. L. Your poor mother has left one little trade. We have today had our March
meeting and decided the election for the year The Democrats cannot compete by an increased
majority inasmuch as they are in some measure for the Union. I hope the good effects
of peace will be to do away party spirit in some measure at least as it is the basis of
our happiness & prosperity -- You strongly urge the Federal candidate for Gov. & Vice-Genl
agt. of the Democrats -- It must have surprised you to see them between candidates for

Mr. John E. G. Colville
to the Genl. Staff, Washington
10th Oct.
New York City
Genl. Colville
My Dear Parents
Three of your letters are now before me which
I have this moment received, of the following dates, Nov.
23d, 1814, Dec. 19th 1814, & Jan. 25th 1815, so that one,
you will perceive, has been 5 months on the way.
Your letters surprise me in Paris, but I am
not there; you hope that I went in Oct. last. I intended
to go and wished it at that time exceedingly, but
I had not leave from you to go, and Mr. Bromfield advised
me by no means to go until I heard from you, you
must perceive from this case how impossible it is for
me to form plans and transmit them across the Atlantic
for approbation, thus letting an opportunity slip
which is irrecoverable; I wish I could persuade my
Parents that they might place some little confidence
in my judgment at the age I now am (nearly 24)
an age when in ordinary people the judgment has
reached a certain degree of maturity; it is a singular
and I think an unfortunate fact that I have not that
I recollect since I have been in England, had a turn
of low spirits, except when I have received letters from
home, it is true, I find a great deal of affectionate
solicitude in them, but with it I also find so much
complaint and distrust, so much fear that I am
doing wrong, so much doubt as to my morals and principles,
and fear lest I should be led away by bad
company, and the like, that after I have read them
I am miserable for a week, I feel as though I had
been guilty of every crime, and I have passed many
sleepless nights after receiving letters from you, I shall not
not sleep to night in consequence of passages in your letters
just received. I will quote some passages from them; Mama says
"I am sorry you do not feel the importance of fulfilling your
"engagements with more punctuality, you must be more attentive to your friends or you will grieve and loose them." In another
letter after giving an instance of a young man living for 600 dollars
per year in London out of consideration to his Parents and gratitude
to them, who were worth 150,000 dollars you say, "now think my
"son how much more your poor parents are doing for you
"how good your dear Brothers are, to be satisfied with so little
"done for them in comparison with what we are doing for you"
"and let the thought stimulate you to more economy and industry
"as I greatly fear you have been falling off in both these"
"since the relief you received for your first performances, it
"has always been a failing of yours that as soon as you found
"you could excel in what you undertook to be tired of it and
"not trouble yourself any further about it, I was in hopes that
"you had got over this fickleness ever this." Now as to the
young man's living for 600 dollars, I know who it is of whom
you speak, it is Dr Parkman, who made it his boast that
he would live for that sum, but you did not inquire how
he lived. I can tell you, he never refused an invitation
to dine, which he used to obtain often by pushing himself
into every body's company, when he did not succeed in
getting invitations, he invited himself to breakfast, dinner
or sup with some of his friends he has often walked
up to breakfast with us a distance of 3 or 4 miles,
if he failed in getting a dinner or meal at any of these
places, he either used to go without or a bit of bread
answered the purpose till next meal. In his dress
he was so shabby and uncouth that any decent person would
be ashamed to walk with him in the street, and above all
his notorious meanness in his money dealings, his sticking
with his poor washerwoman for a half penny, and with others
for a farthing, and his uniform stinginess on all occasions,
rendered him notoriously disgusting to all his acquaintance, &
affords, I should imagine, but a poor example for imitation.
But all this is not to the point; you must perceive, that
the object of your sending me to London, was improvement
in my art, to the extent of 200 pounds per Ann. now I should
conceive I was abusing your goodness if I did not employ
it all for that object; suppose, instead of purchasing frames,
carts, &c. paying models, &c. I should at the close of
year write you word that I had the happiness, to say that I
had expended but 100 pounds, that I had found very cheap
lodgings, but my room would not answer for painting because
it was small, had a low ceiling, and I had my bed in it, that
I lived on little and to save expence of cooking, I was my
own cook, but that most of my day was employed for that
purpose, in purchasing my food, dressing it, and clearing away
my cooking utensils; that I made out to paint with few
colors and cheap ones, and cheap tools, but that the
colors and tools were of inferior quality; suppose I should
say this in a letter, would you be satisfied with my years
work, would you not say, why did you not get a more
convenient room, when you were allowed ample means
for the purpose; and also better colors & tools; and why
did you expend your time in cooking, when you had
sufficient to pay others to do it for you? The fact is I
could live for 50 pounds a year if my only object was to live
cheap, and on the other hand if I was allowed 1000 pounds
a year I could spend it all without the least extravagance
in obtaining greater advantages in my art; but as
your
96912
4. goodness has allowed me but 200 pounds, (and I wish you again
to receive my sincere thanks for this allowance, for my
sole endeavor be to spend all this, to the utmost advantage,
to keep as closely within the bounds of that allowance
as possible, and would not economy in this instance consist
in rigidly keeping up to this rule; if this is a true statement
of the case, then have I been perfectly economical,
for I have not yet overspun my allowance, and I think
I shall be able to return home without having exceeded it, a
single shilling, if I have done this, and still continue
to do it, why, in every letter I receive from home, is the
injunction repeated of being economical; it makes me exceedingly
unhappy, especially when I am conscious of having
used my utmost endeavors, ever since I have been in England
to be rigidly so. — As to Industry, which means
I am falling off, I gave you an account in my last
letter (by Mr. Kalston) of the method which I use in parcelling
out my time, since writing that letter, the spring and summer
is approaching fast and the days increasing, of course
I can employ more of the time than in the winter, Mr. Leslie
and myself, rise at 5 o'clock in the morning, and walk about
a mile and a half to Burlington House, where are the
famous Elgin marbles, the works of Phidias and Praxiteles
brought by Lord Elgin from Athens, from these we draw
3 hours every morning, wet or dry, before breakfast,
and return home just as the bustle begins in London
for they are late visitors in London, when we go out of a
morning we meet no one but the watchman, who goes
his rounds for an hour and a half after we are up.
Last summer Mr. Leslie and I used to paint in the open air
air in the fields, 3 hours before breakfast, and often
before sunrise, to study the morning effect on the landscape
now, being conscious of employing my time in the most industrious
manner possible, you can but faintly conceive the mortification,
and sorrow with which I read that part of
Mama's letter, I was so much hurt at it, that I read it to
Mr. Allston, and requested he would write to you, and
give you an account of my spending my time, he seemed
very much astonished when I read it him, and authorized
me to tell you from him that it was impossible for
any one to be more indefatigable in my studies than
I am! —
Mama mentions in her letter, that she hears
that Mr. Leslie supports his mother & sisters by his labors,
this is not the case; Leslie was supported by 3 or 4 individuals
in Phil: till within a few months past, about
a year ago he sold a large picture which he painted
(whilst I was on my fruitless trip to Bristol for money)
for a hundred guineas, since that he has had a number
of commissions in portraits and is barely able to
support himself, indeed he tells me this evening that
he has but 20 pounds left, he is very economical
and a most excellent young man, his expenses in
a year are on an average from 230 to 250 pounds,
Mr. Allston's (single) expenses not less than 300 Pounds,
and I know of no artist among all my acquaintance
whose expenses in a year are less than 200 pounds.
Mama accuses me of neglect in not mentioning Mr.
Russell and family in my letters from Bristol, this was
certainly an oversight in me in not explaining the cause
the fact is I saw Mr Russell but seldom, or the family
they were exceedingly kind and hospitable to me, but I
lived between 5 or 6 miles from them, they in Clifton and
I at the other end of Bristol, the way to them was very
dreadful and considered not altogether safe for a single person
at night; night was the only time when, from the nature
of my studies I could visit them, it being winter and on
little daylight, beside the dreadful state of the weather
in the winter season, if I had visited Bristol in the
summer I should have availed myself of every oppor-
tunity to call on them for they were a charming
family, and I feel very grateful for their kind atten-
tions to me; as to the portrait which I painted of Mr
Russell, I am sorry you mentioned it to Miss Russell, as
I particularly requested you would not, because in case
of failure it would be a disappointment to her, but
as you have told her, I must now explain, in the first
place then it is not a picture which will do me any
credit, I was unfortunate in the light which I chose to
paint him in, I wished to make it my best picture
and so made it my worst, for I worked too timidly
on it, it is a likeness; indeed, a very strong likeness,
but the family were not pleased with it, I had not flat-
tered him, and made him too old, so I determined I
would not send it, indeed, I promised them I would not
send it, but notwithstanding, as I know Miss Russell
will be good enough to comply with my conditions, I
will send it directly, for as it is a likeness, every one
except the family knowing it instantly, and Mrs Allison
saying that it is a very strong likeness, it will on that
account be a gratification to her, but I particularly
and expressly request that it be kept in a private
room to be shown only to friends and relations,
and that it may never be mentioned as the painter
and moreover that no artist or miniature painter
be allowed to see it; on these conditions I send it,
taking for granted they will be complied with
and without waiting for an answer. I did not
know you had even hinted it to Miss Russell,
and I intended to let the thing die away.
May 3. 1815.
With respect to returning home, I shall
make my arrangements to be with you, (which
my life be spared) by the end of September next
or the beginning of Oct. but it will be necessary
that I should be in Eng. again (provided, always,
Providence permit) by the Sept. following, as arrangements
which I have made will require my presence, this I will
fully explain when I meet you, the moment I get home
I wish to begin to work, so that I should like to have some
portraits bespoken in season, I shall charge 40 dollars
less than Stuart for my portraits, so that if any of
my good Friends are ready, I will begin the moment
I have said "how do ye do," to them, I wish to do as
much as possible in the year I am with you; if I
could get a commission or two for some large pictures
for a church, or public hall, to the amount of 2 or 3
thousand dollars, I should feel much gratified, I do
not despair of such an event, for through your influence
with the clergy, and their influence with their people, I
think some commission for a scripture subject, for a
church might be obtained, it may perhaps be said
that the country is not rich enough to purchase large pictures;
yes, but 2 or 3000 dollars can be paid for an entertainment,
which is gone in a day, and whose effects are to
demeoralize and debilitate, whilst the same sum expended
on a fine picture, would be an ornament to the country,
which would be lasting, it would tend to elevate and refine
the public feeling, by turning their thoughts from sensuality
and luxury to intellectual pleasures, and it would encourage
and support a class of citizens, who have been
reckoned among the brightest stars in the constellation of
American worthies, and who are to this day compelled
to exile themselves from their country, and all that is
dear to them in order to obtain a bare subsistence;
I do not speak of portrait painting, had I no higher
thoughts than being a first-rate portrait painter, I would
have chosen a far different profession; my ambition is
to be among those who shall revive the splendour of the
15th century, to rival the genius of a Raphael, a Michelangelo,
or a Titian; my ambition is to be enlisted
in the constellation of genius which is now rising in this
country, I wish to shine, not by a light borrowed from
them,
but to shine the brightest; if I could return home and stay a year visitors my friends in various parts of the union, and by painting portraits make sufficient to bring me to Eng. again, at the end of the year, whilst I obtain commissions enough to employ me and support me while in Eng., I think in the course of a year or two I shall have obtained sufficient credit to enable me to return home if not for the remainder of my life, at least to pay a good long visit; all these plans I wish you to understand me as always taking into consideration the will of Providence, and in every plan for future operation, I hope I am not forgetful of the uncertainty of human life, and I wish always to say should I live, I will do this or that.
Will you be so good in your next letters as to repeat all former orders for books, &c. (as many I am confident from your late letter must have miscarried) that I may in season get every thing together for home; you had better not write me after the end of June or beginning of July as letters may be detained, and I shall endeavor to get away as near the beginning of Sept. as I conveniently can.
About my finances I don't know how they will hold out in the various great and small expenses of returning home, I calculate they will exceed considerably what I have got left; should this be the case I will refund to you what I expend on my own account the rest of course will be yours. I perceive by
96915
10 your late letters that you suppose I am painting a
large picture; I did think of it some time ago
and was only deterred on account of the expenses
attending it, all this I will explain to your entire
satisfaction when I see you, and why I do not
think it expedient to make an exhibition
when I return: I percieve also that you are a
little too sanguine with respect to me, and expect
a little too much from me; you must recollect I
am yet but a student, and that a picture of any
merit is not painted in a day; Experienced as
Mr West is, (and he also paints quicker than any
other artist,) yet his last large picture cost him
between 3 and 4 years constant attention; Mr
Allston was nearly 2 years in painting his large
picture; Young Haydon was 3 years painting
his large picture, is now painting another on
which he has been at work 1 year and expects
to be 2 years more on it; Leslie was 10 months
painting his picture, and my Hercules cost me
nearly a year's study; so you see that large
pictures are not the work of a moment; all these
matters we will talk over one of these days, and
all will be set right; I had better paint Miss
Rufelli's Aunt Salisbury's and Dr Bartlett's pictures
at home for a very good reason I will give you.
Love to all. I must close abruptly. With affectionate
Yr Affectionate Son
D. H.B. More.
Bristol, 3d May 1815
My dear Sir
I did hope before this to have given
some more favorable reply to yours of 27 ulto but
until this hour I could not make out how far
Mr Haythorne carried his notions of prudence
in the indulgence of a favorite passion, indepen-
dent of his late experience in London as to
the present valuation of pictures, he retains so
high an opinion of Mr Allston's landscape that
he declares 500 Guineas should not take it from
his wall was it once hung up there, yet with
this feeling he tells me that, having a large family
he cannot indulge his fancy at a great expense &
his respect for an artist who could point such a
picture he would not think of offering him such a
price, as would, if named by the seller, tempt him to
purchase, he did in conversation say that was it
to come in his way at £100 he should think himself
justified in buying it if he would never part with it
for any sum. It is mortifying to me to mention such
a price, but you will understand it not at all to apply
to the merit of the Artist but to Mr. It's means he is so
much of a Gentleman as not to divulge any thing which
passes on this occasion -- May make my best respects
to Mr. Allston whom I will at all times give me great
pleasure in rendering any service in my power
I am
Very sincerely
Yours very sincerely

Mar 5. 1865.
My dear Son,
Capt Rogers of this town is to sail to-morrow
for Corwin, & thence be expectd to go by land to London
& kindly offers to take a panel for you. I prepared
in great haste. We have rec'd a few days ago your
letter of Decr. 22, just after your return from Boston.
Also yours of the 314th of Feb. announcing the
melancholy tidings of Mrs Alston's death. The
enclosed letter to Mrs McChanning was immediately
handed to the family whom I have since seen.
Everything proper has been done to soothe their
gloomy sorrow. They are most obliged to you for your
sympathies & kind attentions to Mr Alston & feel
toward you very affectionately. You will express
& Mr Alston our tender sympathies under his
afflictions. Your letter arrived was received
as I was going to the funeral of our friend
Mr Rockwood, who died of a rapid consumption
after about a month's confinement. His loss is
deeply felt & lamented. Mrs R. will go back
to her father's at Phila in a month or 6 weeks with

Dear Sir
Your Letter of 15th Mr. having come
to hand at a time of many engagements, having required
some attention in order to answer the Enquiry made in it,
a delay has occurred beyond what was intended.
Below is a statement of the D. P. side of your Actio from your
2 years, whereby it appears that in the year 1812 (the year in
which the Brooks were paid for) the Amo did not much exceed
that of one thous. dollars, but the following year did
considerably exceed, so that in except of the two years more
than balanced the Bill received in pay for the Brooks,
consequently, the Amo did must be considered as already
absorbed in your expenditure –
The Expenditure of the present year already amonts to £131.9.1
to which is added the sum now called for 20.—
the sum you mention as being for 60.—
and you will perceive that their united Amo 211.9.1
added to that of the preceding years 704.0.9
will exceed the four thousand dollars 915.9.10
attested by your Father – This will undoubtedly
prove a satisfaction to you, but still what you may
want for your Experiences shall be furnished, it also
the sum necessary to procure the Articles requested by
your Father, who in his Letter to me supposed that the
Commissioners
Remittances he had made would be sufficient to pay
all your Bills & your Passage home, & also to purchase
some Books & Articles of Clothing, but during, if there
should be any Deficiency, thus I will advance it.
These are all the Particulars he has given me & I trust
your Wish that what is advanced for articles to be procured
for him be kept separate from your Own & you
will at the time of receiving it let me know to which
& how to place it.
The Revolution you have formed of returning to America
is in my opinion tedious, for the Multitude of Competitors here in the Line of your Profession is so great as to render the Chance of Success in it much greater than
altho the Field of Improvement may not be so extended.
There also you will be in the Midst of your Friends, an
Intercourse with whom will enhance the Enjoyment of
Life, while it will tend to mitigate the adverse Occasions
that must be calculated upon. The difference between
the two Countries in the Expenditure of living is not an immaterial object.
The Letter for your Father shall be forwarded when
any opportunity offers. The Galen I hope will get away
in about three weeks whether any will be going to
Boston sooner from Liverpool I am not informed.
I enclose the Twenty Pounds you have requested
Sincerely wish you success in the object of your present
Engagement remain as truly
Yours Your Friend & etc etc
C Bromfield

Dear Son
Received your Letter of the 21st of March was happy to find
by it that you were in health and industriously pursuing your Profession
we were pleased to find that you were receiving some money to support
yourself we hope your means will increase and that you will be able to
do as Mr Leslie does, and be independent, in time we were relieved from
any further responsibility as to your support if Providence should enable
us to do as much for each of your Brothers as we have done for you
we shall be thankful that , but we know, not what is before us, in the
Cities we received from you during the two first years of your bringing
London you appeared pretty confident that by the end of the two years
you should be able to support yourself, this you find has not been the case, we
give you reason to expect that we would allow you $300 a year for three
years we have since added 200 a year to the thre fourth year also a 1000
for a fourth year, all of which except 100 or 150 have been transmitted to
you making as you will see $4000 which we have hired and are now
paying interest for, to gratify you in the permit of your favourite
Profession – I don't mention this by way of complaint, in the proportion
you have made in your Profession, from the reports we have had, and
with the accounts of your correct conduct otherwise we are well pleased
and also with your expressions of gratitude in your former letters to
us for making the many sacrifices which under our many circumstances
we have carefully made to aid your views, you requested in
some of your first letters that your affectionate parents would continue as
they ever had done to counsel, reprove and advise you from time to time
as they should in their wisdom deem necessary and give us reasons
believe that what we should be improper to do in this way would be received by you as
a wise & dutiful son ought ever to receive advice & reproof from affectionate fa-
thers, whose constant language to their children has ever been to yourselves
no harm. With the strongest feelings of the importance of the utmost prudence
in a young man who had his living to obtain from his profession we have felt the necessity of advising you not to meddle with politics, which
your sentiments coincided exactly with our own we should have advised you
to keep them to yourself your busying yourself with such things, could do no good
to anyone, and was calculated to do yourself, more harm, than any other person
could do you, by making enemies of those who might have it in their power, to serve you
spiritually, in the way of your profession, did you not offend their prejudices: I do not charge you with being so imprudent as to have
caused any alterations of the kind which have suggested, by expressing
such sentiments to those around you, as you have, from time, to time, expressed in your letters to us, but fearing you might in your zeal to defend
the character of your country, drop an unguarded expression, which would
injure you as to your prospects, we have thought it our duty to advise you, to
be prudent, in this respect, and not give your tongue, as much latitude, as
you did your pen, we should love you much less than we do, if we thought
you capable of not loving your country, with all the ardour which you
express for it, we consider this as a very amiable trait of character,
which we have not the least desire to eradicate, but would cherish,
still a person may be placed in a situation in which it is best to keep
this to himself. We have never in any letter we have written you given you the
least reason to believe we thought you criminal in regard to your politics, or
company, as your last letter intimates we have cautioned you with regard to
what company you kept, and what amusements, you attended, but have
never impeached the moral character of Mr. Bayne, in the slightest
degree, as you intimate to look at our letters when you undertake
to answer them, & then your letters would be more correct recollect saying
of Mr. Haynes, in one of my letters to you that I understood that he maintained
a very good Character, but hoped being acquainted with him would not lead
you into the company of men of that profession, as they were not generally
the best sort of Characters -- in short all the advice we have given you
has been such as you ought to thank us for with as much filial affection
as you ever did for any remittances of money we ever made you as
you can have no doubt that our object in both is the same to do you
the greatest possible good -- and here let me give you a word of kind advice
and receive it kindly let your letters be in future fraught with the
same tender affectionate expressions of duty and love and all that is good
that they Used to be, before you had your mind so soured by the state of
publick affairs, let your letters, and your actions, both show that you are
of a truly gratefull disposition, and be ready to fulfill any Commission
that your parents may request of you, even if you should have to stand
still in your Art till you had accomplished it, to me, were it in your
place the heart felt pleasure I should feel from having done a kind
act, to oblige my parents would more than make amends for
all the time spent in executing it. we do not intend to be troublesome
to any of our Children or Friends. You wish to be known in this country
as a painter in order to this you must send pictures of your own painting
as yet not the slightest thing has ever been seen of yours since you left this Country
except the little portrait of yourself in India Ink. -- You will recollect I do not blame you for
this but ascribe it to the times but now it is peace times will show be

of greatly disappointed in not seeing you this Summer, as does your Friend,

you may be desirous of enjoying, as knowing far better than we poor short sighted

It is therefore our Indispensable duty to beg daily, that God will may be done

the best good of our own souls & the souls of our fellow mortals. – Indeed my

you profess of that honour that cometh from God, than all the facing
praising honours, that are derived from fallible man, these last,
are not to be desired as but they may have a tendency to place
us in situations to be more abundantly useful to our fellow men
but they are by no means to be sought for merely to gratify our ambition
of distinction, and the pride & vanity of our own foolish hearts, we
ought daily to be searching into our motives and making the public
of thealmest. Hearch me Oh God and know my heart try me
and know my thoughts and see if there is any wicked way in me and
lead me in the way everlasting, – Hope my son that you remember
the Sabbath day to keep it holy and that you constantly attend the publick
Worship of God both parts of the day let no such early and highly important
habit, even if it were nothing more than a habit, be ever laid aside, but
with you I hope the attention to the ordinances of religion, will be attended
with far higher motives than can exist from mere habit and early education
I wish to hear from you on the subject of religion, or your own views
on this all important subject, believe you attend church, and that is going
on in the Religious World write us on these subjects, as much as you
can spare time for, We were much pleased with your letter giving an
account of the Death of Mrs Aston as discouraging a tender of prosperity
in the affliction of that family which was great. We need not tell you that
we take no comparison more satisfaction in commending and approving
and having others that are good people like him commended & approve
the conduct of our sons than in having the slightest reason to curse
or condemn them, and we acknowledge them with gratitude to our Heavenly
Father for his protecting & restraining grace granted you all that you
have afforded us the highest satisfaction that we are capable of enjoying
next to having the assurance of your all having been the subjects of
the renewing and sanctifying grace of God, which we hope if it be the will
of God we may yet live to see or hear of it. – In perfect consistency with
the feelings towards you all above described we may and ought to
tell you and that with the greatest plainness of any thing that we
seem improper in any part of your conduct either in a civil social
or religious view and this we feel it our duty to do and what we shall continue
to do as long as we live, and it will ever be your duty to receive from
us the Advice counsels and support which we may from time to
time favour you with, with the most perfect respect and dutiful obser-
vance and when you differ from us on any point whatever let that differ-
ence be conveyed to us in the most gentlemanly manner
and let this be done not only while you are under age and dependent
on your parents for your support, but when you are independent and
then you are head of a Family and even of a profession if you even should be
either, this advice that I have now given you rely on it will recommend you
more by far to your fellow men as well to him who has made it one
of his Command to honour your parents that your days may be longer
than any distinctions that may be acquired if this be wanting. I have
dwelt longer on this subject as I think you have in some of your last
letters but somewhat deficient in that respect which you are good
since will at once convince you was on all accounts due and which
I know you feel the propriety of without any further observations.
Your Parents & Friends here are very anxious of seeing your paintings
that we may mark your improvement the seeing some of your perform-
ances, and approving them is as you say the only way of obtaining
celebrity in this country Your Father & myself have had thought,
of having your Heracles & Castor exhibited for your benefit in Boston
they tell us that Mr Sargent who has lately finished a picture, the
landing of the Fathers, is doing very well, by having it exhibited at
a 4/8 each for grown persons, half that for Children, if you would have
Remember more such as your picture of Mrs Payne & Barathia and any
others which may do you credit, little collabour, and try and think
to mind the landscapes for Dr Bartlett, of your Aunt Salisbury, the
portrait of Mr Russell, for Miss Russell, the seeing these pictures, in the
houses of these persons will go a great way in recommending you as an
artist. – Several gentlemen have expressed a strong desire to see for them
selves, your performances. You must be at some pains to see these things
sent to us, or they will not get here of themselves, Eliza Goddard has returned
