to write you, will save me the labor of
writing you long letters by an app. 4 to direct
good, that we cannot omit it. I am glad
to be spared this labor at this time, as it is
the close of Election week which I have been
always with me a busy week has been un-
commonly crowded this season. I am very
tired. I have written by Mr Gallandett
a few days since I sent a small parcel
of papers, which I shall send you will give
you an account of our Spring Elections
of the news of the day. Of which we have
very little, that is interesting -- we wait for
important news from Europe --
We have just received a letter from your
Uncle James E.B. Finley of Carolina He fears
you will remain in Europe but hopes you
have "so much amor patriæ" as to return
& display your talents in raising the military
& naval glory of the nation by exhibiting
on canvas some of her late naval & land
actions & also promote the fine arts among
us -- He is, you know, an enthusiastic re-
publican & patriot & a warm approver of
the late war -- but an excellent man
I am by no means certain that it would not be
best for you to come home this fall, I find a few
or two in this country in painting some portraits,
but especially historical pieces & landscapes -- You
might, I think in this way succeed in getting something to support you afterwards in Europe. London, June 26th 1815.
My Dear Parents,
I just drop you a line by the Gales
to inform you that I am well; I am making
my arrangements to leave about the end of
August; my time is now very precious to me
and this must therefore be short; you must
be aware that I shall be under the necessity
of drawing in advance for many of next year
expenses such as clothing and printing materials,
all which I shall expect to refund you, as well
as what I may exceed in my proper allowance
for the 4 years, I trust it will not
be much though I fear it will be a few
pounds. There is one thing I wish to notify to
you; my friend Lieut. Newcomb of our Navy
went to Paris a short time since, I gave
him a commission to get me a large lay figure,
which will cost 30 to 100 guineas; the prices
are from 30 to 100 guineas; my reason for
deciding on such a step without previously
notifying you of it, was that they are to be obtained
no wheres but in Paris so cheap & so
good, that a dreadful campaign was about
to open in France & that the Allies threatened
to destroy every thing before them and to burn
Paris; that this state of things, would render it
next to impossible to obtain anything from France;
a lay-figure is absolutely indispensable to an artist.
I have got along since I have been in England by
borrowing one, of my different Friends, but I shall
be deprived of that indulgence on returning home.
Lieut. Vinromt promised to execute the order, &
to pay for it himself, and he would receive the
money in America whenever I could make it
convenient. it will be shipped for Boston
from France; so do not be alarmed if you
should open a long box and see a figure in it.
I thought I never should have a better opportu-
nity, and was unwilling to let it pass. The price
is not to exceed 30 louisines. This sum I con-
sider as borrowed from you and will refund it
you from my first profit should it be necessary.
You will have heard of the dreadful
battle in Flanders before this reaches you, the
loss of the English is immense indeed, almost
all their finest officers and the flower of their
army, not less than 800 officers, and upwards
of 15,000 men, (some say 20,000) but it has been decisive, if the
news of to day be true that Napoleon has
abdicated. what the event of these unpar-
allelled times will be, no mortal can pretend
to foresee. I have much to tell you
when I see you. Perhaps you had better
not write after the receipt of this, as it
may be more than two months before an
answer could be received.
Love to all
Good Bye.
Your affectionate Son
Sam. J. Moser.
P.S. The Paper of to-night confirms the news
of this morning; Bonaparte is no longer a
man, he has abdicated; and in
prorbility a Republican form of government will be the future government of France, if they are capable of enjoying such
a government. but no one can foresee events
there may be a long peace, or the world may
be torn worse than it yet has been. --
Revolution seems to succeed revolution so rapidly
that in looking back on our lives we seem to have
lived a thousand years; and wonders of late seem
to scorn to come alone, they come in clusters. a
P.S. 2. I have just received your letter of 20th May which
gave me much pleasure, I still intend returning by the
end of Augt though I cannot be sufficiently grateful
to you for your kind offers of encouragement & support for
another year. I shall tell you my plans when I get home.
Excuse me for not enclosing as I am in a great hurry.
Yr most affectionately
Sam Moser

I have arrived thus far on my way
home, I left London the 5th and arrived in this
place yesterday the 7th at which time, within an
hour, 4 years ago I landed in England, I have
not yet determined by what vessel to return, I
have a choice of a great many, the Ceres is the

the Liverpool Packet sails about the 25th and
as she has always been a favorite ship with me

I have seen Capt. Pratt and family, by whom
I have been rec'd with great attention, some of
them (the young ones) have grown quite out of my
recollection, I need not tell you with what pleas-
ure I saw my old acquaintance Miss Mary,
she has grown quite a fine polished girl, Charles-

Bloomingdale November 2. 1815
My dear Sir
It is but a few hours since I received your letter
announcing your arrival in your Native land, and I hasten
to express my heartfelt pleasure at an event to me so unexpected
and so desired.— The intelligence gladdened our evening circle and
Mr. Jarvis and myself made it the occasion of recalling many
grateful recollections of the past, as well as that of anticipa-
ting pleasures which are still in store for us when you
shall become once more an inmate under our roof.—
We have lately removed to Bloomingdale, and are within
sight of the house in which you visited us just before your
departure for England. This of course brought to mind all the
associations connected with that visit and we could hardly
believe, so rapidly has time flown, that more than four
years had elapsed since you walked with us over the
lawn.— Your time must be so much engrossed by those
friends who have a stronger claim upon you than
we can possibly have, that I am afraid it will be
some time before we shall see you in New York. I
can only say therefore that there is a room for you
whenever you shall choose to occupy it and I am sure
I need not add, what I trust you know full well already,
that the sooner you take possession of it the more will
you enhance our pleasure. - It is not impossible indeed
that I may see you in Boston in the course of a
couple of weeks, as I promised my sister Mrs Hull to
pay her a visit this autumn; and though I have hitherto
been prevented from fulfilling it I have not laid
aside my intention. - A clergyman however is so con-
fined, that he cannot wander at will, and should it
so happen that I shall be disappointed, I hope you will
not let the winter pass by without paying us a visit.
Upon casting my eyes upon the date of your letter when
I had before overlooked, I find to my great surprise
that it bears date Octob. 19th. - Where it has been all
this time I cannot positively divine, but it fills me
with regret to think that you have been a fortnight
arrived without receiving my congratulations, and
what is still worse that I had seemed so negligent
and cold hearted. - Do my dear Sir, let me hear from
you by the next mail. - I have a thousand questions
to ask you.
As to the Books you have had the goodness to bring me,
I cannot at present say anything, as I am ignorant con-
the safest mode of conveyance. I will make the necessary inquiries and inform you in my next.
Mr. J. intends to add a postscript herself, and would have done so to night had it not been for the lateness of the hour.
She says, for fear I should not have an opportunity in the morning, you will say that I send my kindest good wishes and congratulations.
Have the goodness to present my respectful compliments to your father, for whose happiness on account of your return I most sincerely rejoice, and believe that Mrs. J. & myself are as well. Your warmly attached, & affectionate friend.
Sam F. Jarvis

My dear Sir,
Having just heard of a private conveyance for this letter,
I embrace it merely to tell you that your favour of October 19th was
read and answered by me the 2d of November, I put into the of
office the 3d. I presume therefore you see it the beginning of the
last week. At the time of writing it I indulged a hope which
I have now in great measure abandoned of seeing you in
Boston this season. In that case I should have taken
charge of the books myself. As it is, I am at a loss what
to say. The Navigation from Boston is not I suppose
very safe at this inclement period of the year. On the
whole therefore, I must beg you to direct them to the care
of Henry Fisher Esq. and give them to Capt Hull. He
may probably know of some safe conveyance. There
may possibly be some officer coming to New York by
water to whose care they may be entrusted.
In hopes of soon hearing from you, and begging you
to excuse this hasty Scrawl I remain as ever
Yours truly
Saw F. Jarvis

My dear Sir Copied
There seems to be a fatalilty attending our correspondence.
At least your letters to me constantly miscarry; mine to you I
hope are more fortunate. Your favour of November 29th 1815
I did not receive till the 12th inst and while I was making
arrangements to send you a draft for the amount, I received
a letter from Capt Hull mentioning that he had paid you
and drawn on me. As he observed it was at your request
I am afraid you thought me remiss, but this letter will
explain to you the cause of my not having written you
sooner. I feel under many obligations for your kindness
in putting yourself to so much trouble on my account,
and I would not be so ungrateful as to neglect for a mo-
ment any account you should present. Be so good in
future as to direct to me, merely at New York, as I am
persuaded your letters have failed of immediately being re-
ceived on account of the name "Bloomington" which is probably
not known beyond the bounds of this City.
You are now I suppose unmittingly engaged in the pursuit of
your profession. It will gratify me much to hear what you are
doing. Portrait painting alone is profitable in this country;
out rich men not having yet obtained that relish for the fine
arts which would lead them to admire a painting for its own
sake or to patronize Genius from the noble principles of love
for excellence, & love for country. The Bostonians probably will
patronize you however because you are their fellow citizen,
and though the thought of being indebted to that motive cannot
be a very pleasing one to you, yet it may in time lead to just
views. You know I presume that Col Trumbull has seated
himself down in this city, and his collection you are prob-
ably well acquainted with. Our Academy of Arts is at present
in rather a languishing state: but I trust we shall soon be
able to make it worth attention. The Corporation of this city
have given or are about giving a large lot near the new
City Hall in Broad Way, where it is proposed to erect a
building to correspond with that noble edifice (not to vie
with it of course, but as a sort of appendage) which is to be
devoted to our literary, scientific, elegant institutions. We
are to have in it, the City Library, Scudder's museum. The Academy
of fine Arts, a Chemical Laboratory, and apartments for the learned
Societies. The NY. Histor. Soc. The NY. Lit. & Philos. Society
&c &c. I hope they will institute an Academy of Painting
and it would give me great pleasure to see you one of the
professors of it. -- Why will you not let us have the pleasure
of seeing you, when we can talk over these matters at our leisure?
I am reserving the printing of my thing for your present, and as they
tell me I look best in the winter, because tallest, you see it is of great
importance that I see you at this season. -- Have you attended as often
to architecture? That is with me a favourite science, tho'
I know but little about it. I hope some time or other to be
a Gothic church erated here, and I must consider your taste
concerning the plans. That has been a Gothic Church erected at New
Haven since you were there; and it is my intention to put up a
monument in it to the memory of my father, which I wish to have
correspondent with the style of the building. As you have probably
noticed the principal monuments in England, it may be on your power
to furnish me with a design. I wish it to be attached to the wall
in the Chancel, near the Altar, and I think of some such inscription
as the following: "Hic sub altare jacent Mortales Ecavius, Abrahami, Jacobus
S. T. D. nuper Eccl es ia Connecticutensis Episcopi, qui Natalis Maii V. MDCXXXIIIA
S.V. annos prope LXXXIIi visit, quorum XV et dimid. in Cathedrâ Episcopali sedebat
et mortuus est Maii 3 d die AD. 1813: -- In memoriam patris & quam dilectissimi
parvuli hujus Ecclesie quam diu magno animi ardore & cæsurgentem spicata
videtur (Eben non sibi oculis mortalibus) filius marens & Ha c Manner affatus

Dear Sir,
Your letter of the 29th instant was duly received & I write to you
in such a state of mind & heart that I can with reason beg that no part
of this letter may be made known to any one — I shall as much as I am
able endeavour to repress the feelings under which I am labouring & commu-
nicate my ideas with betraying as little of my weakness as
the nature of the case will permit me — The Portrait, intended to be
my last letter, is a full length one as large as life of my beloved
daughter whose existence in this world will very soon terminate.
She is in a deep consumption her frame is wasting very fast & the destroying hand of this incurable
disease has at length reached her face which is generally the last part it touches — In two days after you receive
this you will either find her at Mrs Coleocks or learn where she may be found — I will give you the price you require for the picture say
six hundred dollars and pay you two hundred dollars of it as soon as you finish the head; the arms & hands you must not attempt to finish but
only take a sketch of, as it will be impossible for you to determine the
attitude (on which my very soul is fixed) without the most mature deliberation & the finishing of them at this moment would be injurious.
You perceive the necessity of finishing the head with as little delay as the
difficulty of it will admit, in accomplishing it I trust it is unnecessary for
me to say that no consideration whatever ought to hurry you in the
least bit that you ought to take as much time literally as if you
had nothing else to do. I trust I have no appeal — I wish I could write as I feel — I trust that on such an occasion you
will put forth all your powers — that you will make the canvas
speak — I have seen several of your portraits before one of which I
often sit & admire, but I will not have you believe it as which tells me
it is, far from it, I admire only in it the genius which it could inspire
form were it pressed — In the countenance of my daughter you
must give all the animation in your power, you must let from
her expressive eye her soul distinctly speak — Every muscle of her
face must be full of motion and expression instead of the flat & com-
municative expressive likenesses that are & which are usually denominated
(though falsely) striking ones, you must exhibit a picture
truly animated — It is not possible for you to have such another opportunity of placing me under such obligations to you as the present,
Is there a spectacle more interesting to humanity than that of
a father imploring from your genius an image of his departing
only daughter, that daughter too the representative of his
deceased wife? As soon as you will inform me that the head is
perfectly finished & that you have no further occasion for her attendance
I will then call to see it — The extent of the landscape I have already described — It must be divine — May you exhibit in this picture the learning of Michael Angelo, the grace of Corregio, the coloring of Titian, but
above all I will invoke the spirit of "the divine Raphael" to inspire you
with the attitude — How often shall I leave the grave of my child

for the society of this picture — It shall be placed in a room where
none shall enter but myself — More prostrate value I shall offer to
the humble tribute of my gratitude — Little did I think when on
youth while I hung with rapture on the eloquent accents of your

Dear Sir,
Your favor of the 4th ulto was duly received
& I cannot find words sufficient to express my gratitude for
it - To have such an appearance from you, on a subject of such
importance to my feelings, is more gratifying & acceptable to me
than anything else in the world that could be offered to me,
upon the reception of this picture (the full length likeness of my
daughter as large as life, of such a description as to the size of the
Cannons & Landscape) it will only remain for me to testify
my gratitude in a manner worthy your pencil & my
honor - I have already said to you, that in order to give you full
time to accomplish my object, this picture is not to be delivered
until twelve Months from the time I made application for it,
or longer if you choose. - My Daughter is at the boarding
school of Miss Fraser & will attend you at any time, & should you
experience any difficulty in her attendance I request you will
acquaint me & I will have it removed. - You have been
good enough to promise to execute a full size half Portrait
of each of my Sons with hands & landscape, & Sam to pay you
for each of them 150 dollars; It is proper for me to apprize you
that my Sons will return to the country on the first of April
& will remain during that month & very probably may not
return to Charleston until the end of May, your time may then
be too limited to their pictures - The object of this letter is
to beg the favor of you to finish the heads of each during the
present month, so perfectly as never again to require their atten-
dance for them - I shall send them to the North this spring
to remain for some years & I do not think you will have another
opportunity of seeing them — As they may never return to me
I feel extremely unhappy about these pictures & I beg the favor
of a line from you about them as soon as convenient; will
you finish them before you leave Charleston or take them to
the North to complete? Should you intend to take them with
you, I beseech you to finish the heads perfectly as you perceive
you cannot again see them — I wish the heads finished at
any rate as soon as possible for should you conclude to take
them with you & they are executed late, upon being packed
up soon after & excluded from the air so long, they will cer-
tainty turn yellow & get otherwise injured — excuse, my
Dear Sir, this freedom, & impede it only to the affection
of a father — You had hardly reached Charleston bar last
year before my youngest son was given over by the Physi-
cians, he was near expiring in convulsions to which he is
subject, & should this again occur I may lose this picture,
the first thing I thought of when he was in peril was
the likeness you had taken of him, and this, on account
of your desire to gratify me you have condemned, so that
had he died I should not have had a fine likeness of him.
I wish to be assured against this misfortune — I wish
you to let me know what will be your price for each of the
small portraits of my sons which I hope you will finish
before you leave here, I make the request merely because
it will be necessary for me to give my factors directions as
to their payment, I have forgotten to request the price of
the small Portrait of eld2 Dunkin which I beg you will
not fail to execute — My Sister will attend you on a
few weeks — I thank you for the impression of the seal you
sent me, it will probably be the subject of a communication soon
time hence — Accept, Dear Sir, the appearance of my respect & regard
Y. T. B. More humble
John A. Hotton

Charleston S.C. Mar. 26. 1819.
My Dear Parents,
Two of your letters have been lately
reached, detailing the state of the parish & church; I
cannot say I was surprised for it might be expected from our people.— Before saying anything on this
subject, however, I will just say that Lucretia is just
recovering from a severe bilious fever, which has confined her to her bed for several days, she has, however, by the blessing of God on the means used for her recovery, safely passed through it, not however without considerable alarm on my part and indeed on the part of Uncle Finley and our friends generally, in consequence of her delicate situation, she is now comfortable and recovering fast, she exhibited a pattern of patience through all her sickness, making no complaint, and expressing no unreasoning; as to returning home in the way I mentioned Mama need not be at all uneasy on that score; it is necessary I should visit Washington, as the Pres' will stay so short a time here that I cannot complete the head unless I due him in Wash. (by the bye the City council have passed a unanimous vote to request me to paint it for the City Hall and have agreed to give me more than Dashed, 750 dollars,) I therefore, propose leaving here for Baltimore by water, leave Lucretia in the case of Nancy at B. and go on to Wash. to complete my business there, then proceed to B. and soon to Phil.
by steam boat and stage, stay a few days there, or a day as may be, then to New York by steam boat and stage, a day or two there, then
by packet to Providence, from there home by easy stage; there can
be no danger but rather benefit I think by such a plan there
will be very little land carriage, and plenty of time to rest, after
every short journey. Aunt Finley thinks there will be no danger
but rather benefit, and she, you know, is a good judge in these
matters.
Now as to the Parish and Church business, I hope all things
will turn out right yet, and I can't help wishing that nothing may
occur to keep you any longer in that nest of vipers and conspirators;
I think with Edio's decidedly that on Mama's account
you should leave a place which is full of the most unpleasant
associations to all the family and retire to some place of quiet
to enjoy your old age; why not come to Charleston? here is
a fine field for usefulness, a pleasant climate especially for
persons advanced in life, and your children, here I
seriously think of settling in Charleston, Lucretia is willing
and I think it will be much more for my advantage to remain
through the year? Ricl. can find a place here if he
will, and Edio's can come on, and be Bishop or Presb, or Professor
in some of the Colleges, (for I can't think of him in a less character)
after he has graduated: If I wish seriously, you would
think of this, your friends here would greatly rejoice if an
opening could be found I have no doubt Christians want
their hands strengthened, and a veteran soldier like Papa
might be of great service here in the infancy of the United
States, who finds its easy and fascinating tenets.
to receive any character well disposed to receive any character
with its easy and fascinating tenets.
I have not received any money lately of sufficient importance
to send you, but hope to send a remittance soon; I shall not
make so much this season as last, from a variety of causes all
of which I cannot explain in a letter, one is that Lucretia's
illness has caused a considerable expenditure of time to me
and there have been several pictures which I painted last
year that I have redeemed by painting them over again.
Will you be so kind as to inquire of Mr. Arthur Benjamin in
Broad st. Boston whether he has obtained for me the Kremlitz
White which he was to get from Germany for me; I hope he
has; I found a small quantity in Charleston and have sent for
more from Germany through a German who informed me there it was
manufactured, it is at a place called Kremlitz in Silesia,
which is famous for its manufactories of this pigment; I
tell Mr. Benjamin of this fact, as he was ignorant of
place where it was to be obtained. -- Has not my last
figure been heard of yet? I sensibly feel the want of it.
Please give my love to all; will write again soon; this is
written in great haste. -- The Surf-Times arrived safe some
time since 344 days passage, we got the bundle of kinns, but no
books; I shall go and inquire again particularly for them. --
Good bye. Lucretia sends a great deal of love.
Remember me particularly to Mr Alston, shall write him very
soon; have not got his picture.

My dear Son
Your letter of 26th ult. in reply to that
given us much satisfaction as it informs us
of the recovery of our dear daughter from her illness.
Had we known of it at the time she suffered
I had prayed for her, particularly in reference to
her situation though we never forget you both in our
daily prayers I have comfort to believe that you
forget nothing in your prayers. Your plan of returning
via Baltimore we on the whole agree with
have written Nancy to wait for you. If any alteration
in your arrangements write her and
Your feelings in respect to the affairs of
this City, & the conduct of some of its members, are
natural I do not wonder that they are though the
whole spirit of their proceedings, were they fully
known, would not make you full up. The details must
be left till I see you. I can only say that their
design, with they were even cunning, almost as
if accomplishing is complete, is most wonderfully
frustrated. I am sure as they are constrained
to describe it to special Divine intervention. The
measures adopted for its execution to defeat
this purpose (which way my removal at all events
have been in every instance, such as they cannot
conceive, a yet in many instances completely successful
The course of measures which they apparently
with high hopes of success has terminated in their
deportment, is an thing which is at
present, they must rally & regain which with pretty
dignified & disheartened members. Wilber to the
Lord hath helped us & has been a refuge in time
of trouble. The grave is broken & we are escaped
into the spit then had digged for us, them selves
have fallen -- The trial has been very severe,
never one, from Unitarian influence (on this has
evidently been) more so -- but we have had, corres-
ponding supports. You & your brother & my dear
son, I am loved Kentucky, have been among our
chief earthly comforts. We have had abundant
comfort, & trust, from the Fountain of
all consolation.
Your can be sure has arrived, & was shipped
for your letter arrived -- Before the bill of lading -- The cost of shipping
which I shall pay, will be about 18250
dollars -- Mr Wilders letter, will keep till
you return.
A very friendly letter from Mr
Bromfield informs, that he had not funds to
pay Leslie for the Canvas -- If he has not
returned, per haps you had better make him
a remittance of £25 from Charleston -- I
have put the balance due Mr W. to that
debt in off my hands -- Prospects in respect
to all other debts are favorable -- What you
can conveniently spare as a loan will thus
afford effective relief.
A letter just received from President Coffin, mentioning
you with much regard.
I have done your Message to Mr Benjamin
no well will -- as he was not in -- except one word.
Shall write you by the Swift once a
few lines We all are in tolerable health,
I unite in love to you & Lucretia Your
mother I me wish to be remembered to all
our Charleston friends have not time to
name them - Your affectionate
father J. Morse

Georgetown April 10th 1819
Dear Sir,
Your favor of the 31st ult. was duly received, & I would
have answered it immediately, but was desirous of seeing your Por-
trait of my Daughter before I did so; four days ago I had the pleasure to
view it I have been since then too ill to write to you, I hope you will
deem this apology sufficient. — I wrote immediately upon the receipt
of your favor, to Messrs. Kirshaw & Lewis, and requested them to pay you two
hundred dollars, according to my promise, as part payment for the full
length Portrait you are to execute of my Daughter as large as life,
& I also requested them to pay you sixty six dollars for the frame of
the small Portrait you have just sent me, both of which payments
I suppose they have by this time made you. — The account you
have been pleased to give me of your painting of the head of my Daughter
together with the numerous reports of others on the same subject, has
so completely overwhelmed me that I shall not express to you my
feelings or my gratitude. — My obligations are eternal, they shall
long, very long, be substantially expressed to you — There is nothing
I have, or can have, so near to my heart as this Picture — My soul
hovers over it even in imagination, & should it meet my expecta-
tions, it will cling to it as to the Angel of mercy — Your first
letter consenting to undertake this Picture shall always be preser-
=ved by me, it reflects as much credit to your head & heart, as any
of your productions will to your pencil — Let the suitableness of the
drapery, the variety, the contrast, be beautiful
in perfection — but above all, so peaceful, that it may never
be equalled by any one — Whenever you will inform me of any
of the rest of the Pictures being ready for delivery, I will direct Messrs.
Kirshaw & Lewis to receive such pay for them — Is it your
intention to take any of them to the North to finish, & if so which
of them? I ask this because I shall in such case insist upon
paying half of the price, as there is to be a beautiful landscape to the full sized half Portraits of my Sons, & also to the
full sized half Portrait of my Daughter, I fear it's being done
here — but this I leave to yourself — Though my letters are
dated at Georgetown I reside eight Miles from that place — Your
Portrait of my Daughter was left in Georgetown at the house of a
friend — Nearly all of the citizens have seen it & I really think
it will occasion you some applications — I found several looking at it & even his honor the judge who happened at that time
to be holding the Circuit Court — everyone thought himself at
liberty to make remarks — some declared it to be a good likeness,
while others insisted it was not so, & several who made such remarks
I knew had never seen my Daughter — At last a rich Gent
leman observed "it was the richest piece of painting he
ever seen" this being so much in character, that I assure you
Sir, I could contain myself no longer, which speaking among the
audience occasioned not an unpleasant moment —
I am extremely pleased with it — There is certainly very consi-
erable likeness, & the more I examine it the better pleased I am
but I do not think the likeness quite as striking as I could have
wished — with regard to the painting, you know, nothing can
exceed it — as a painting alone I would have given much
more than it cost me, & considered myself fortunate in me-
eting with it — Some of my friends think the likeness extrem
strong — I am satisfied it is the best ever taken of my Daughter —
I should be much gratified to see the fine Picture
of Mr Washington Allston, but must decline the purchase
of it — It has always been my intention to procure a piece
of Mr Allston's painting & I am sure I shall do so even though
it cost more than the present one — but I would greatly
prefer some of his figures to a Landscape, & would wish
more over to have one of his last productions as
every one will constantly improve — I certainly shall
at some future day apply to him — I assure you Sir, I feel
much flattered & gratified at your kind letter in assisting
me to procure these fine paintings — it will induce me
to take the liberty of getting your assistance at some time
hence, which otherwise I should not have ventured upon
With regard to Mr Fisher's painting of the fall
of Niagara, I wish you when you next write, to have
the goodness to state to me his price & the length & breadth
of the picture & will then determine upon it — In the
mean time receive my very best thanks for the prefer
you have been pleased to give me — His fame has reached
me — it is as loud as that Cataract — Believe me
Dear Sir, with much respect & consideration —
Your obliged subser
John H. Allston

My Dear Son
I write you a few lines by Mr. Drews, your pastor preached
yesterday at Charleston for Mr. Homer that Decham might be superseded
In Council preached here three times yesterday. I hope our people
Will be well pleased with him as to give him a call, but I do not know
that this will be the case your father wishes him to settle on a
place for a year or two or less to give him the opportunity to reconcile
the two parties so as to have them all united in Mr. C and also to enable
him to settle all his affairs in this region so as to quit with the
least disadvantage to all concerned. I hope Mr. C will if applied to by
them, make this stipulation that Mr. M shall do this. Your father has
probably informed you that 20 of the church who met in regular
Church meeting (the meeting consisting of 30) voted by Ballot to
propon to your father to call a mutual council and choose a Com-
mittee of seven to make out their charges against their pastor with
their proofs to be first submitted to him, and then to the Council if
he agrees to it, if not they mean to have an extra-legal Council
the Committee are the three opposing Deacons with Dr. Warren John Riley

My dear Friend
I received your letter this evening, and have had a long and full
conversation with my father on the subject of it; and I think I shall be
able now to give you precisely the state of their feelings.
The course which my father would prefer before all others would
be this: that you should come and be the minister of Charleston, and
connexion with his people for sometime to come as colleague pastor
for some time to come. – Discouraging his wish would be that his connexion
might be as nearly nominal as possible – the responsibility and direction
of affairs to belong to you. – The advantages of this course he thinks are
the following.
1. He believes it is the only course which will secure the union
of the church and society. His reasons for this belief are as follows:
2. You would wish to revise the discipline of the church, and to
introduce a change in this practice which would be in the interest of Baptists.
My father thinks that he could not sustain the change without remaining
connected with the people he could assist you in their plans, and render the
revolution less hazardous.
3. With respect to himself personally, it would be desirable that the law relating to Overseers of Harvard College will
be repealed – and then the proposed plan will give two orthodox overseers
from Charleston.
4. – On the proposed plan my father retains his connexion with
the Anderson Institution, the Prudential Committee, and the various
donations to which he belongs.
5. With respect to himself personally it would be grateful to
his feelings – because it would give him an opportunity to wind up his
affairs, and gradually to deliver the church and remove this region.
It would give the occasion for the admission of an enemy to triumph. He
now feels that the public impression will be that he is driven away.
It would be much more pleasant to leave the impression
under which he will learn in that case he will be much more likely to his feelings.
He thinks it would effectually destroy all the
animosities in the happiest manner possible between
him and this people.
On every account, therefore, with as regards the property, & good
of the society, & your usefulness, & his own reputation, he
believes that the plan is desirable
With respect to the practicability of the plan, my
father believes that if you are willing it might easily be effected
through the instrumentality of the Professors to whom he wishes,
you would communicate this view of his feelings, & take their
opinion as it is wisdom upon it. -- This is the course with
me & his views.
If the Professors should be of opinion that this course is
impracticable and should be unwilling to use their influence
to accomplish it -- my father would say that your decision to
come to Charlestown would meet with his cordial approbation,
and that so far as his personal feelings and those of his
family are concerned, he would rather you would come here
than go to Salem. He would much prefer you to any other
man -- If the plan of colleagueship is impracticable
whether you come as colleague or sole pastor or either as
mother proposes that you should occupy the passage to either as
boarders --

"The Bishop's Pastor to provide a Candidate for

be convenient; so much of my salary redeemed,
as shall pay the expense incurred for supplying

Explanation.
So much of the salary of the Pastor, is to be
reserved as shall pay Candidates for settlement in
ministry in this place & Society who may be
employed by the Committee appointed for the purpose;
which Candidates will supply the pulpit by my
consent during the period for which they may be
respectively engaged. When Candidates are not
employed, the pulpit will, of course, be supplied,
as usual by the Pastor. When the Committee wish the
Pulpit for a Candidate -- it is expected they will
make it known to the Pastor, who will cheerfully
comply with their wishes, agreeably to his proposal -- The person whom they may employ -- need
not be explicitly informed that he is a Candidate, --
if in fact he is so heard of that it is understood
between the Bishop & Committee The person employed
it is presumed will be one who is in a situation to speak
as a Candidate, & who will be at liberty to settle, & the
people by united vote appoint him, I give him a call
to the Vestry & who are not allowed to speak as Candidates, the Pastor
will readily indulge them by asking them to speak for
him. This will give the desired opportunity to the Congregation
to judge of their talents & qualifications for settlement.

inform you, that in their opinion, it would be better
to defer the execution of the portrait, until a more
convenient opportunity may occur. During the winter
he will be constantly at this place, and as the seat
of government offers much more inducement for
a visit at that season, than at the present, it
has occurred to me, that it might be equally
agreeable to you to postpone it for the present.

My Dear Father,
I improve a moment to write you in answer to
your letter we have received from you, we are all well and send
you many love, Lucretia is fast recovering, and dear little Susan
is healthy and thriving. As to the concerns of the old Parish I
shall devote the greater part of this letter to that subject; and I
have proceeded to the statement of circumstances without preamble,
the project of friends which you were so much interested in,
will not, (in all probability) succeed, the project was intended to
appear immediately, (how we know not,) and we have reason
to believe that we have taken efficient measures to counteract it. I never
could feel satisfied myself as to the propriety of this measure,
it looks, under hand, I hope, you will excuse me if I say, I wish
you had not continued it, the motive was unquestionably
good, but the end does not justify the means, your friends
and family all know how to account for these things in you, but
does it not, my dear father, give occasion for your enemies, and
those that have been warning, to ventilate the cry of "a plotting
deserving man," and will not the constant failure of schemes in
this business at length induce the few remaining friends, to say
that you are desperate, and will cater at any thing to support
you and will tread so near to the line of honorable, of course necessary
that enemies will easily mistake, and friends can scarcely dis-
luciate you: Excuse the freedom I take in being so plain, my dear
Father I do not intend to express any thing which will wound you
in the least degree, or lead you to think I am wanting in that respect
which is gratefully due from me to you, but as this is entirely between
ourselves, and I know of no friend who would feel authorised
to tell you all their hearts in this subject, I have ventured to do
it but I hope in a manner that is proper for you to refer to your
a beloved and respected parent. I have conversed with Mr
K. U. with Mr Q. D. K. & Mr B. -- the two
former told me plainly they did not think it would do for you
to think of staying, or that any measures that looked like it should
be adopted, it keeps alive the opposition, by giving them an object to
aim at, keeps those men in power, who have all along been so ob-
vious. -- Mr Hay preached last Sabbath 3 times to great accept-
ance, the audience were solemn and seemed much affected, I
was myself exceedingly pleased with his manner, style, and doc-
trine and think him well calculated to unite the good friends
of this Society, and I find that the friends of both sides
as far as I have heard, speak in high terms of him; now my dear Father, is not here an indication in pro-
vidence of union in this Society, and union too complete that
very influence, which we now feel it our duty to oppose, will
those men be likely to retain influence, under such doctrine
and with a phalanx against them composed of all the friends
and well disposed in the Society; let the Lord send by this hand
of him whom he will send, it does appear to me as plain as
the sun that it is your duty, as well as your interest to leave
this spot and that too immediately, or at any rate sooner than
May next, you say, wait and see the result of the number of friends,
what has been heretofore the result, and what is now the result; nothing
has occurred in the least encouraging to the success of the method you
propos of destroying this influence: "Vengeance is mine I will repay
with the Lord," is it therefore duty for us to devise any measures
against adversaries, who shall put them into disgrace, except by preaching
the truth, especially too when it calls into exercise such passion
from the opposition: what if the child "behave himself proudly
against the ancient, and the base against the honorable," is it not
by permission of God, and is it not for wise purposes to humble
us: and by resisting in the way we do, are we not whipping the
rod instead of humbling ourselves under it, should we not let
Providence punish our enemies in his own time and way.—
In view of things at present I should suggest this course, to acquire
excuses, and encourage in your friends the disposition to settle Mr.
F. to rejoice that your end was at length accomplished, that you
left the Chk. entitled under a good man, one whom
would build them up in the faith; and as for
them, would you were willing to think that most of
them were guided by good motives, that as for those
whom you believed to be your enemies, you forgive them
and pray God to forgive them by taking this noble
father, it does seem to me you come off with honor &
as W. — I. P. L. you get nothing but disgrace, whether
successful or unsuccessful.— No one can say you deserted your
post, you must stand acquitted from any evil that results from your
removal, your opposers have to bear all the weight of responsibility.
Do not raise objections to Mr. F. among your friends on Hopkinsian
ground, what are those differences worth, if you begin a contro-
versy on their points, it seems to me your troubles will cease
only with your life, let those that settle him bear all the re-

Sunday.
My Dear Mother
I arrived safely last evening in this city,
much fatigued and with a severe cold upon me,
but this morning feel entirely well and in good
sprits. I found Papa at Mr. Coils looking I
feeling remarkably well, he will probably leave
N.York for N.Haven on Tuesday. I was disappoint
ed in not meeting him at N.Haven but think upon
the whole that the business of the house can be ar
ranged by us here as well as at N.Haven, I went
up into town at N.Haven while waiting for the other
boat, and in walking about, I asked what houses
were for sale. I found among others that Mr.
Woolley's house was to be disposed of and Papa
thinks that is just the thing. it would be a
fine situation for us and would make a double
house. I shall leave N.York for Washington on Thursday
in company with Mr. Caldwell of Washington. I miss
Lucetia if little Susan more than you can think, and
shall long to have us all together at N' Haven in
the Spring. We are all going to chch so good bye
for the present
Yr Affectionate Son
Sam'l P: B: Morse

Washington Dec. 17th 1819.
My Dear Parents.
It did not occur to me till just now that
I had not written you since my arrival in this city;
I have written 5 or 6 letters, but they have been to Charleston S.C. & to Lucenia; I have been here nearly a fortnight; I commenced the Presidents Portrait on Monday, and shall finish it to morrow. I have succeeded to my satisfaction, and what is better to the satisfaction of himself & family, so much so that one of his daughter's wishes me to copy the head for her; they all say that mine is the best that has been taken of him, the daughter told me, (she said as a secret) that her father was delighted with it and said it was the only one that in his opinion looked like him, and this too with Stuart's in the room, the Presd. has been very kind and hospitable to me I have dined with him 3 times and taken tea as often, he, and his family have been very sociable and unreserved. I have painted him at his house, next room to his cabinet, so that when he had a moment to spare he would come in to me.— Wednesday evening Mrs. Moonroe held a drawing room, she was splendidly and tastily
made my bow, she was splendidly and tastily
desped, the drawing room, and suit of rooms at the
Presidents are furnished and decorated in the most
splendid manner, some think too much so, but I do
not, something of splendour is certainly proper about
the chief magistrate, for the credit of the nation, plain-
ness can be carried to extreme, and in national build-
ings and establishments, it will with good reason be styled
meanness. I understood after I returned from the
drawing-room that John Lowell was there, as I never saw
him, I should have been curious to have seen him.
I am painting, Dr. Sewall, he will pay by note
for a year, in consequence of his friends not being at
command at present, as he is removing to settle in
this city with his family; he is a man with whom I
have become intimate, a pious man, eminent in his pro-
fession, and moving in the first rank in society; I have
no other portrait as yet engaged but presume when
the Poets and Dr. Sewalls become known I shall have
as many as I want, to employ me till the middle or
perhaps end of next week. I am doubtful how
I shall go on to Charleston, I am just going to write
to Baltimore to know if there are any packets ready
for Charleston if there is one I shall probably go to
Baltimore and sail for Charleston, as the best &
pensive, and least tedious, and perhaps best dan-
gerous rout. -- if however, I should not find a vessel
ready by the end of next week I shall go on as I
first contemplated, by land. -- I will inform you
before I go -- I have not heard from home since
I left it, nor from Papa since I parted from him
in N.York, nor from Concord since I left N.York.
I feel anxious to hear from all of you; do let me
hear soon; this cannot be answered, however, time
is this city. --
Remember me affectionately to all
Yr Affectionate Son
S: J: Blmoryz:
P.S. I really forgot to ask how the great folks
come on in Charleston, I hope they will pardon my re-
glect and my slighting them by putting them at the tail of
the letter: -- The President certainly must have forgotten
his accustomed politeness for he never has asked after Lot
Pool, John Soley, the Dean -- not James Warren the shoemaker, nor
Black Polidore nor Caleb Sweetser. -- unpardonable neglect. --

Washington Dec. 23. 1819.
My Dear Parents,
I received Pat's letter of 17th inst. this
morning, and snatch a few moments to answer it; I
have thought a good deal on the subject of staying
until the 10th Jan'y but conclude on the whole that it will
not be well; board is very high where I am, 2d class for
day, and I have no applications for Portraits except
Dr Sewall's & the copy of the Pres' for the family, the
former of which is completed, and the other commenced
and will be done this week, I have but one piece of
canvas left, and my materials, colors &c. running short,
so that I should be more than a fortnight without
any thing to do paying a great price for board, besides
this I find Henry has arrived at Charleston, and will
feel long pained until I join him; he writes me that
all my things arrived in good order, it is thus obviously
for my interest to hasten to Charleston, as I shall there
be immediately at work, and this is the more necessa-
ry as there are a fresh gang of adventurers in the
brush line, gone to Charleston before me.
You mention having written me from N.Haven
I have not received the letter, and therefore cannot
say anything on affairs in N.Haven. — Perhaps any
purchase or lease had better be deferred until my
return in the spring, if arrangements could be
made to board Lucretia & myself & little Susan
with you for a short time previous to my returning
and so let me find Lucretia & Susan at N.Haven
when I return northward, it would perhaps be
best under existing circumstances. — I am sorry
your letter from N.Haven is missing as I have been
anxiously expecting it ever since I have been in Wash-
ington, it may be delayed and I may yet get it —
All monies, as you request, that I shall not im-
mediately want, shall be remitted, I fear I shall not
be able to send any from here; my stoppages on this
journey have consumed my funds pretty fast — as soon
as I get to Charleston I will endeavor to send you some of
what is due promptly paid to me. —
I miss my dear Lucretia & little Susan more than
you can imagine, I did not think I should find it
so hard to part from them, it is a new experiment,
and I don't care to try it again. —
I wrote you but a day or two since, telling you
all about my success with the Portrait of the Presd.
it is acknowledged by all that have seen it to be
the best ever taken of him.— my taking a copy for
the family proves how they estimate it.—
In taste but with sincere affection
Yr Son & F. H. Mott
Love to all the family, Edwards,
Nancy, Betsy O'Sally — I shall probably leave this
city next Monday.
Rev. Judt. Morse. D.D.

Fredericksburg Virginia Dec. 31st 1861.
My Dear Father,
I left Washington Wednesday last at 4 o'clock
on my way to Charleston, arrived here yesterday much fatigued and cold with a severe cold on my lungs, but
am better to day; I am in Company with Mr. Silliman of
New York brother to Prof. S. P. we stop here to day, and
shall proceed to tomorrow to Richmond stay the Sabbath, and
then to Petersburg and so on I shall be with Mr. S. till I
arrive at Fayetteville N.C. where we separate, he for Augusta
Geo. and I for Charleston -- we had a dreadful time yesterday
in the severest Snow storm I have experienced for a long
time. It is pleasant here to-day -- I direct this to Math.
supposing you will be there in a week or two -- I left the box
containing the large canvas with the Pres. had upon it at Davis'
hotel in charge of Mr. King the painter to forward to Boston,
I will thank you to see me King on the subject, and if not forwarded to Boston let it be sent to me in Charleston -- I have
as I think it will be easier transported from Charleston than from
Boston to N.Haven, -- my funds will but barely hold to Charleston,
and if I had not painted the portrait of the Pres. and
sec. 80 doll. from him for it I should have been compelled to
have borrowed to carry me through; I have however the note of Dr. Swall
for 80 doll. to be paid in a year. -- By the way, Dr. Swall with
me to leave him a line of introduction to you, which I promised
but forgot. You will find him a very worthy, pious man
and I hope you will see him, he is at Mr. Queen's boarding
house, nearly opposite Davis' hotel, Pennsylvania Avenue.
I will remit you all I possibly can as soon as I get to
Charleston.
Good bye my dear Father and
believe me your affectionate Son
Sam'l F B. Mosby

My Dearest Wife
I wrote you a letter from Fredericksburg a
day or two since, and according to my promise I sit down
to inform you of my safe arrival in this city, we left Fredericksburg
yesterday morning at 3 o'clock, a most bitter cold
morning, but clear, with a bright moon. With all my precautions of
leggings, gloves, & mocassins, I suffered a great deal from the severity of the
cold; we had scarcely rode a mile before our hats, the bows of our
cravats, our hair, whiskers, eyebrows and eyelashes were covered with frost and icicles.
I actually found upon shutting my eyes for a little time that
my eyelashes were frozen to my cheek, we ascertain upon our arrival that the thermometer indicated the temperature at 4 degrees below 0, this is the coldest weather ever known in Virginia, (so we are told) it
has been a very fine day to-day, and although very cold has moderated some. We attended church to-day I heard Mr. Turner, an excellent sermon on the New Year, Mr. J. and his wife were at our house last summer if you recollect, I spoke to him after church and called upon him. Mr. James Dwight we found in this city also, endeavoring to establish himself in business here, he has closed his concern in Charleston: he was very glad to see me, and inquired particularly after you a gentleman by the name of Proctor, I also found here who travelled with us in the Steamboat from N. London to
New York last year, he also enquired after your ladyship.
I find contrary to my expectation a very fine hotel in
Richmond, Kept by Mr. Butler of Haven, where we are
very comfortably situated; we shall set out to-morrow
for Petersburg at 11 o'clock 25 miles, where I shall finish
my letter.— By careful nursing and precaution I have succeeded in throwing off my cold, which was a very severe
one, and I am now entirely well. I have now and then
a twinge of the defective tooth which gives me a gentle hint
that I shall soon have to throw that off also.—
I find it a great comfort having a companion with
me, especially such a man as Mr. Silliman, an intelligent
prious man, and one whose feelings and views are congenial
with my own; we are also similarly situated, both having
left wives whom we ardently love and sigh after, and children that make us long for home; he has the advantage however of one in Britain to my one; he sends his
compliments to you and says he hopes to see you one of these
days. 10 o'clock P.M.
I called and sat a little while this evening with
Mr. Turner & his wife & Mrs. Burd.
Petersburg Virginia, Jan'y. 4. 1820.
Thanks to a kind Providence, I have safely
advanced another step on my journey, and am comfortably housed
in a very fine hotel established since Mr. S. was last here, so that
we are agreeably disappointed again; we rest here till to-morrow
morning, when, at 3 o'clock in the morning, we set out again on the
most unpleasant part of our whole route, we shall not stop again
till we reach Raleigh N.C. where we shall probably arrive at
room on Thursday, riding all night, I find it very expensive
travelling on this route and I therefore doubt whether I shall
ever go to Charleston again by land; Richmond is a very
pleasant place, containing about 17,000 inhabitants, in sum-
mer I think it must be very beautiful in the vicinity, it is
on the banks of James river, this place is similarly situated it
contains about 10,000 inhabitants and is on the banks of the Appomat-
tox river, the scenery immediately in this vicinity is very
picturesque, we had quite a pleasant ride yesterday the week
or having moderated, it is a delightful day to-day and the
snow begins to disappear. We are favored with the moon
at night which we feel to be a great security.—
I shall write you next from Raleigh Friday.
at 11. I do long, my dear wife, to see you again, I miss
you more than you can imagine.— what do you think of
going with me to Boston next winter, if our lives should
be spared and we are all well? I cannot do without you
another season, I want my dear affectionate service to make
much of, and to make much of me, and dear little Susan to
May with; time will pass heavily till I see you again, dearest.
Don't forget to write me often, at least once a fortnight, wont
you dear? I forgot to tell you that I saw Dr. O'MeRl Wager
in N.York they had a fine little boy about a month
older than little Susan, they sent a great deal of love to
you and congratulations, until I reciprocated.— Good bye
my dearest wife. Have you any expectation of another Susan? I wish to

Suppose you are now left alone at home
as father is probably on his way to Washington, and Ed-
wards at Andover; I therefore sit down a few moments to
entertain you with the wanderings of your elder son, and to
congratulate you with the intelligence that he is thus far on
his journey (by the blessing of God) safe and well; I believe
I wrote you from Fredericksburg, Virginia, informing
you that I left Washington on the 29th day of December
in company with Mr. Silliman of N.York, brother to Professor
Silliman of N.Haven, an excellent, pious, intelligent
man, with whom I have travelled till now, we part at
this place, I shall set out to-morrow (Sunday) for Chas-
tor, and he next week for Augusta Geo. I have found
his society a great comfort and security throughout this
long, tedious, uncomfortable journey; and we now part
with mutual regret; I arrived here this morning at 3 o'clock
from Raleigh (N.C.) having rode all night, the place from which
I write is the best hotel in the city, but it is a miserable, dirty,
uncomfortable place; I find that the stage goes to-morrow for
Charleston, and then not till Tuesday again, so that I have
the choice of travelling on the Sabbath or staying in this
dirty hole 3 days doing nothing but spend in time & money.
in this predicament I have consulted with Mr. Silliman,
and we both think that it is best to choose the former
of these two evils; I have found this journey much more
expensive than I had imagined; I am under the necessity of
borrowing 10 doll. from Mr. Silliman which will leave
something over. I presume at the end of the journey.— I
set out to-morrow morning at 5 o'clock ride all day and the
night, the next day I next night and reach Charleston prob:
ably on Tuesday morning, at 10 o'clock, when I shall be
glad to rest in good earnest.—
I have written four letters to Lucretia on the
way and requested her to inform you as I proceeded; I
thought this was better than to write 2 letters each time
one to you & one to her each cost me 25 cents, when by writing
to her yours would cost but 10 cents, you see I understand
economy! "Have at the Spicket and let out at the Burg," I think
I hear you say, among other proverbs; Well I can't help
it; I hope soon to begin to fill the barrell at the burg, as
soon as I can get to Charleston.—
I shall write you again when I reach Charleston
in the mean time I must bid you adieu! give my love
to Edie? and the family Nancy, Betsey, & Sally if with you
and believe me as ever, your affectionate Son
Sam. F. P. Morie.
I always close without enquiring after the Charleston
herd of nobility; what are they doing now? have they turned
you into the streets yet? I see by the papers that Mr. Mead
is dead. I hope he has gone to a better place, I believe he
was a good man, though misled in his business. — I should
like to know a little of the state of affairs at home, or
your account and the family's; I hope by the blessing of
Providence we shall all be safely settled in N.Haven
next spring. — I long for the time, for I do miss my dear
wife and child and Parents & brothers very, very
much.
Again good bye, remembering me
who enquire after me.
Mr. E. A. Morse.

My Dear Husband
This day and tomorrow I presume you will spend in New
York if nothing has intervened to delay your arrival there agreeable
to your letter of the 6th from Albany which was received last Monday.
We were much pleased to find you had succeeded agreeable to your
expectations and sincerely pray that if the Undertaking is calculated
to promote the Glory of God as we trust it is he will graciously smile
on it and bless it. – This day took up the Newspaper and the
first thing that caught my eye was the death of our much loved
and excellent Father Geer my dear Husband he has entered into
his rest with respect to him we may say He is well he hangs
above the wicked care from troubling and where the weary
are at rest may we be daily prospering to follow him and all
who through faith and patience are inheriting the Promises
the paper says he died the 29 of Decr aged 94, this was the third
week day before you left home why none of the family should
have let us know it is astonishing to us all I should have
thought they would have sent an purpose but perhaps they
are anxious to satisfy us when known. – We have not heard a word from Finley or Richard since you left
us but are expecting to soon I had a letter from Secretia last week
she and little Susan were well though the latter had been sick with
a cold I say they send a great deal of love to me all and Grandpa
in particular and that little Susan sends many kisses & that she
is the best company in the world they think in their family
Yesterday Edwards went to Dr. Worcester in the Street in Boston who told me
that the council had dismissed Mr. Jay from the ministry but said nothing
about Charlestonion, We presume that he will give his answer to
next Sabbath and have no doubt it will be in the Affirmative
We do most earnestly hope you will feel it to be in your own
duty to agreeably submit to & rejoice in it as ordered in Infinite Wisdom
and come home resolved to get away with your family as early as in the
Spring as possible this will be a real comfort to your family, and in order
to it will you enquire whether our goods can be transported direct to
Newhaven if it will be best to charter a vessel at Newhaven or here
and what the expence of transportation will probably be & where our
things can be stored and the expence of storage that we may
make our calculations accordingly also please to look out for good lodging
for us see if Mrs. Deforest can accommodate us all viz. Junius
and his wife & child till they get a house to their minds and
provision made & if we shall need three bedrooms & a Parlour &c &c. Mr. G.
Dwight & Mr. Leffingwell can no doubt advise us what is best to
be done and who are trust worthy and have some Conscience
give my love to Mrs. Dwight and tell her we shall draw largely on her
for kind & friendly advice on our removal to Newhaven and hope
she will not be backward in giving it; our Friends will be able to save as a
great deal if they are disposed without any injury to themselves
in any manner but enough of this you will pass & perhaps through Philadelphia
give a great deal of love to Aunt H. & Betsey K & Mrs. & Mr.
Ralston & family and any remaining Friends there on any were
else in particular to Mr. L Coits family who have been so very kind
to you may the Lord reward them in bitter Blessings than any we
can bestow I hope if we keep home in North that we shall have
it from them often
Edwards has received one of the pamphlets you mention in your letter from
Albany it is the one you sent he got that by going to the post office himself
We have received Mr Sargent's journal and his bill on Scotland a letter
from him the postage amounting to 8/2-44 I have put them all in your
desk he says that the Quaker Woman that you mentioned has changed
her mind since you was there and is acting against your plan with
respect to the Indians His words are "The Quaker woman of late, I understand
is discouraging the Indians about the White river country if you should go to Albany
Edwardson is much en courage'd about the Geography & will do his best I hope
he will find it as well to stay with me as to go to Andover.- Mr Brooks
who preached at the Old South preached the Lecture - and Mr Jenkins
preached last Sabbath very well I was told he called in to see
me after meeting he says the business you are gone on has lain
near his heart this ten years and that he had written to the
Pendential Committee sometime ago and that at St Louis ought to
have been the place to have had a Colledge & Mission house &c &c and
were it not for his family counting 14 Children under 17 years old
he would engage in it with all his heart he thinks your situation
very favourable to such an enterprise and hopes you will succeed
We are all well and send love hope to hear from you soon remain
as ever. Your sincerely affectionate wife E D Morse

My Dearest Ladies,
Through the blessing of a kind and indulgent Providence I have been kept from all harm and have
at length arrived safely in Charleston; I left Fayetteville the morning I mentioned in my last, it was a very disagreeable
day, rainy & foggy, the coaches were watched beyond description most ingeniously contrived for inconvenience, we were as
much exposed as if out doors, the seats were wet, and the top leaked through every crack, so that in a short time
we were wet through; as night approached, the stages grew worse, and the weather more unfavorable; no moon, and
the darkness so great as to prevent our seeing our white horses, we proceeded without accident till about midnight, when our
leaders took fright at something and started out of the road, and in a moment the stage struck against a tree and stopped
with such violence as to throw us from the backseat to the front seat, we found on examination that the swingletree
was lost and the tongue broken, this detained us half an hour in a hard rain; we had a sleepless night, a miserable break-
fast at a log hovel for which we had to pay 75 cents, all the next day was rainy till towards night, it then cleared off fine
we got to Georgetown at 5 o'clock and set out immediately again, rode all night, very cold, but clear & pleasant, and
arrived without accident or sickness safely in Charleston.
ton yesterday at 9 o’Clock.
I went immediately to Aunt Finley’s, the moment
they saw me they all burst into tears I were silent; I never felt
more depressed than at this time, jaded out by a long, fatiguing
steeples ride, finding Aunt and little cousin in a different
house; in black; Aunt so altered I should scarcely have
known her, every thing reminding me of Uncle’s absence, this
too combined with the absence of my dear Lucretia, at Mr.
Munro’s, the room where we slept, and dined, and supper
the places where we walked, all, all made me; dear wife,
feel most miserably, I felt by anticipation, what might
take place, were we taken from each other by death, Oh!
may this day be far removed in mercy, but especially
dearest may we prepare at any time to say, “the Lord save
and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the
Lord.” I went early to bed, slept soundly 12 hours &
waked entirely refreshed and well, every one says I have
grown more fleshy, I have not an ache or pain; what
shall we render to the Lord for all his benefits?”
I have got excellent rooms over Dr. Bux-
baum’s Apothecary shop, it is as we had heard, he lost
his wife and partner in business, and was at death’s door
himself with yellow fever; the rooms are very conven-
ient and large I pay 33 dollars for them – I am
very busy in getting all things ready, so dearest excuse
the brevity of this letter, I have every thing to say but
must defer till next letter.— Thank you dearest
for your good long letter of Christmas eve, it comforts
me much, I recieved it yesterday, I am glad to hear
of the health of you all; what grieved me most was
the loss of your hair, but it was necessary; will it grow
out pretty long before I come home? I regret I did
not paint you before I left home, if we live I
shall certainly do it when I return.—
Aunt and cousins & the Peronneaux send
love to you & a great deal of it, they say
you must come next winter, so I say, I
have very much to say but must defer till another
opportunity as I am in the greatest haste.
Henry is well. Rick? I have not seen.—
Give a great deal of love to all father mother sisters
& brothers; and kiss the dear child for me often; I
am glad to hear she grows; don't make any more
apologies for writing of her improvements, you are
not particular enough, I want to hear of everything
write often good bye — your most affectionate
Husband
Thirley

My dear Son I arrived here last evening af-
ter a very fatiguing ride from Phila with
sleep & in feeble health -- it was necessary
to fulfil an appointment that I should be here
yesterday -- I found here your letter from
Fredericksburg but had heard from you
by Mr James Dwight, as far on your way
to Richmond -- letters from home to
the 15th inform that all are well at Charleston
& Concord -- I long for the time when we may
all be settled together at N. Haven Mr Hay
is dismissed from his people, a letter from
Dr W -- writes me that the P. Ch. Cen lies
with him installed in my place on the
9th of Feb. -- I shall look out for a board &
place for you on my way home as I have
written you that you will it -- I think Mrs
Hazard & Mrs Rockwood will settle in N.H
by us next Summer pleasantly
I spoke kindly of you, favorable of your
faithfulness I shall look after it if you
request I send at the same time
to either land any other place
I have the Presid.t's approbation of my plan for
the benefit of the Indians -- The prospects are
at present good, as I am reasonably expect.
I send you this by Mr Wm H. Mitchell,
a Yale scholar from Charleston, now a student
in divinity for the Episcopal Syn. -- I wish
to introduce you to him, as a pious young
man, a fellow lodger with me for a day or
two -- His funds being short, I have lent
him $15 -- with he will pay to you -- You
may inform me when you receive it, I
will remit it with any you may send me
Remember me affectionately to Richd. -- &
to all Charleston friends, as you see them
God bless you, prosper you, my dear son
from every affectionate
father J. Mosse
I presume you will have heard of the death
of your good Grandfather on the 29th ult. through
the hands of a spy from your mama. He was a
good man -- his spirit I trust now rests in heaven.

My dear Wife,
I arrived here last evening 5.30
& this morning was handed me your acceptable
1 King letter of the 19th in the 18th in the 18th done
from Gen Warren, the 13th. The information contained
in these letters is interesting in no common degree.
The die is cast -- The will of the Lord be done &
acquiesce with cheerfulness. The consequences as
to us will be well & I earnestly hope, to the old
& congregation also -- As to the men engaged in
objecting this change & thin measures, my opinion
of them remains unaltered. -- I shall answer Gen W's letter this evening
My last was from Phila. I remained there a day longer than expected. The stage was
full & I was not well enough to travel. On Wednesday morning I was better at 7 a.m. started in a very
cloudy stage trade on day night to Baltimore, where I arrived at 6 o'clock Thursday morning the roads in
many places bad go. I proceeded to President Munroe's office in his bed & then proceeded to his
city 36 miles in what may be called the slow stage.
This forenoon called I spent an hour with President
Munroe & opened to him my whole plan which has
his very cordial approbation in every part of it he
says, that Mr Baltimore, thinks with him I hope some
good plan will be ripened before I leave this
City— But as I may be disappointed, as at Albany,
where I was encouraged to expect a gratifica-
tion of my wishes, it may see so here & therefore
you had better say nothing particular, till you
hear ag r from me. I have felt too feeble fatigued
to make much exertion to day & shan't therefore
make this letter long as I intend writing
you ag r to morrow even. My appetite &
digestion are not good— These complaints keep
me feeble, of course— After a little resting I
think I shall feel better.
I am glad Edw d is entering so spritively
into the Abridgent & doubt not he will make
a rich & valuable book— He had better look at
Worcester's new geo f & his object shd be to have
the book contain as much permanent unchanging
matter, as can be made consistent with the
nature of the work & to place the changing
matter in a situation to have it altered with
the least injury to the whole work. I shall
bring home with me Breckinridge's new work on S t
America & some other works to assist him
The information from Lucania is very gratifying to me & I long for the time
when we shall (with leave of Providence) be all
all settled at N. Haven. I like the idea of Finley's
boarding with us, if there is room -- with I will ascertain
on my return -- I think Mrs Hazard &
my Rockwood will settle in N. Haven with us near
Summer -- They seem much pleased with the idea.
I wish you to write Mrs Hazard, & give her your
thoughts on the subject -- The w d be glad to
hear your opinion.
I have been called away to spend the
evening with the Vice President. It seems of the
Navy, which has taken up so much time
as to prevent my answering Dr W's
-- till next mail -- You may, or may
not, let him know this, as you shall judge
best. I am too tired to sit up late --
I have heard a part of Mr Pinkney's
great speech on the slavery question. I have
heard speeches, not a few, which I have thought
abler more logical, & more eloquent -- I
was less pleased than some others. He is to continue
it on Monday -- I find here many
Gentlemen, whom I know, & am spending my
time pleasantly & hope usefully in very comfortable
lodging -- You shall soon hear from me as a
lover to all as usual -- Your aff ct husband
Morse

My dear Wife,
As I promised I will to you again today – I am now lodged very comfort-
ably & hospitably at Rev Dr Lawry's one of the Ministers in this city (for whom I will preach tomorrow PM) who about 14 yrs ago
was at our house. He is a very pleasant man – has a pleasant family – it is a great
relief to know I already feel the benefit of the change, to my health – I am evidently
better to day –
I have had to day a most satisfactory interview with the Secy of War, & Col Stilts
Steph Calthous & Adams – The former is the principal man I have to do with – By
the bye the Mrs Calhous, with whom we are acquainted, who was so kind to Mrs Bird
is here (Mrs C, mother in law I believe) – & I am to drink tea with them this afternoon.
Both the Secretaries enter cordially into my plan – The business of the Stockbridge Indians
(who have gone home) is yet in good train – Lame here in good time & circumstances to help them
I have all the attentions here, that I could wish
or am capable of enjoying. More difficulty
with me is the want of a subject to write
about. I have not yet had in one instance
witnessed nothing of the influence which we suspected might be extended here. The Cavalcade you
mentioned, is coming on from C. I have heard
nothing of it. I think they are not yet here.
I have just had a letter from Mr. Sidney - he says
the mortgage is sufficient seventy-half the
original debt having been paid.
I wish Edw. to find in the Vol of Tracts
Dr. Edw. Treatise on the Mahunka new language - & look it over, & ascertain whether he
gives a history of the tribe - or people says & anything which goes to show that they are or are not
a part of the Delaware tribe - whether their
languages are the radically the same or radically distinct. It is impossible if the fact,
to prove, that they are distinct nations having
no natural relation to each other. I will
request Edw. to send me the result of his enquiry as
early as possible.
I have no time to add God bless
you all Accept my best earthly love for
yourself - Love to Mrs. & the family of your
ever affable husband I know
from
