My Dear Parents,
Your letter to Edw. & Rich and the
Bundle arrived safely by Miss Whittlesby; she left no
word where she stays in New-York so I cannot call on
her, — I don't understand mothers short and touchy
letter, as far as it concerns me. I wish mother would
not write when she is in such a mood, it is not right.
As to my coming to New Haven on the 25th inst.
I wrote the College Committee that it was absolutely im-
possible, and sent a verbal message to you by Mr. Joe-
clyn to the same effect, I am therefore at a loss to know
what you mean when you say that the Senior Class &
Mr. Silliman, and all will be disappointed if I don't
come, and that you will expect me certainly in
Saturday's boat; Now I understand my own business
best, and if they take the ground of being offended or
put out because I can't do impossibilities, then they may
find some one else to paint the picture, for my business
here is worth double what that picture will be to me in
New Haven, and if they take that ground, after what I have
stated to them, I shall have nothing to do with the thing.
I wrote them my reasons for not coming up before the 1st
I wish, when the blossoms begin to swell on the large
apple tree, just before they open into blow, that one or two
of the middling sized limbs might be carefully girdled
by taking out a ring of bark, completely round the limb,
a quarter of an inch in width; the ring should be made
on that part of the limb nearest the body of the tree; this
process performed at the time I mention (which is prob-
ably now,) will make those limbs bear larger fruit than
the rest of the tree and ripen sooner; I am anxious to pro-
duce this year the largest apple.—
Give my love to all friends and neighbors, and
many Kisses to the dear boys.—
Your affectionate Son
Sam'l L. V. Moss

My Dear Parents,
I arrived safely with all my
furniture the morning after I left you, and what
is remarkable, have all the articles without an
injury to the value of 25 Cents, the sofa, the dining
table, and the breakfast table particularly are safely in
their places without the slightest new scratch upon them,
my cast also, are without a single new break, so
that I have every reason to be thankful.—
I should have written you before, but have had
no breathing time till now.—
I send this by Mr. Durand, firm of North
Kiss and Durand who has in charge the bandbox
containing little Charles' new hat, and some things
also I believe with Susan left.— Mrs Eder says
with respect to coming to N.Haven that she will
not be able certainly to come before the last
of June, so that your arrangements will probably
suit all round. they are all well at

expected -- I hope to send the money to pay

To Gen. Lafayette,
In asking your acceptance of the enclosed
Poetic tribute, I have not the vanity to suppose
It can contribute much gratification, but if it shall
be considered as an endeavor to show to you some
slight return of gratitude for the kind sympathy you
evinced towards me at a time of deep affliction, I shall
have attained my aim. Gladly would I offer to do
you any service but while a whole nation stands
waiting to answer the expression of your smallest
wish, my individual desire to serve you can only be
considered as contending for a portion of that kind honor
which all feel in deserving you.
Believe me with the highest consideration
Tho. O. Lentz

Dear Brother
I wrote you several days since saying that
I had received a letter from Professor John Maclean,
of Princeton N. T. requesting to know your
views for a portrait of the "head size" as he
terms it. - To day one of the tutors of the college
called on me to know why the letter had not been
answered. I told him that I had written you I was
waiting your answer, as I did not wish to
burden Mr Maclean with the portage of a letter
merely to say that I did not know. - I told him
further that I would write again to you &
request you to communicate directly with
Professor Maclean on the subject. He says that
it is a portrait of Dr Horack that they want,
for the college, as he has been a benefactor to
the institution. -
The prize essays have done coming in. I have
a small cart load of them. What shall I do with
them.
The letter by Mr Brinkerhoff came
but no peaches. He had carried them by mistake to his
house & forgotten to bring them in with him. Will
bring me a basket of fresh peaches from his own
Garden on Monday to pay for them.
I shall not come up to New Haven till
fortnight or three weeks from this. When I come, I want
to spend three or four weeks, & Mr Dodd is not yet
sufficiently initiated.
Richard sends in names continually. About 40 this week. The whole number since he commenced
this tour 184. He A letter received this morning says
Direct to me at Champlain, what I find by Morris gazetter,
the best authority, is in Clinton N.Y.
Love to all,
In haste
Your affeessed brother

New York Nov. 3. 1825.
My Dear Parents,
You know just before I left you
I told you that I should be unable to write
you often, as every leisure moment must
be devoted to my lectures, which I hope to
complete by March if possible, but I have
made it conditional altogether whether I lecture
or not; I devote only my evenings to this
purpose and if I cannot complete them by
devoting this time to them I defer them until
another season. — My finger and leg are
(I may say) entirely well, they are a little tender
but give me no uneasiness; I am fainting
away with all my might; Our house keeper
is exactly what we could wish, a good econ-
omist and faithful in every thing; we are
getting along comfortably; I was professed
for money a few days since but have got through
the pressure for the present, by pumping hard
I expect to keep my head above water.
I was sorry to hear that mother is not well.
I hope she will regain her health, and long be
spared to be a blessing to her family who all
love her very, very much; I hope dear little
Finley has got over the difficulty with his
finger, and that the rest of the children are
well, I long to see them again but dare not think
of it at present. Give my love to Richard
to Nancy and all neighbors & friends.
Cousin Sarah Landing was on the point
of being with you with Richard, I arrived in
the carriage with her at the Steamboat wharf
just in time to see the boat clear from the
wharf. She hopes to be able to spend one day
with you yet. I wish you would invite her
in one of your letters to me, she will be here
about ten days longer.
In great haste, tomorrow being
Grand Canal celebration all is in confusion
Our love to mother
Yr Aff Son
Sam J. B. Mosse

My Dear Parents,
I received your letter by Mr. Goodsell;
I was very sorry to hear of dear mother's continued illness; I feel almost tempted to break away from New-York, and return to N.Haven if I thought by so doing I could be of the least service to her in relieving her cares; and Nancy too I feel exceedingly for her, she has been very kind to my dear little ones, and I can only pray, that, if it is not in my power to show her how much gratitude I feel towards her, by some more substantial token, than mere thanks, that He in whom is all fullness of blessing, will reward her abundantly here and hereafter;
I want not the inclination, you all well know to believe you all, but the way to do it is mysteriously hedged up; after weighing well my duty; it seems to be clearly pointed out that I remain where I am; reputation in abundance is flowing in upon me which in the end
will, with the blessing of Providence, be wealth; but
for the present I seem most peculiarly situated
as to commanding money; my great pictures, as I
have often told you are not profitable in com-
parison with smaller, they take much time and oblige
me to wait for my money till they are finished.— I am
industrious, and shall make sufficient to clear me from
debt and I hope transmit you something in the end;
but as for immediate cash I am upon the last
10 dollars also, and expect to be dunned for some
debts of long standing, but I must say to my creditors
have patience with me and I will pay you all; I
have almost completed Miss Horis picture for which
I shall receive $250.— but 100 must immediately be
transmitted to London to M. Bromfield, and the
other 150 will just about pay the greater debts I owe
in N-York; I am determined (Providence permitting)
to contract no new debts, but the most pressing domestic
necessary debts such as fuel & food, not even clothing
until I see every great debt paid that I now owe
and this I hope to accomplish this winter.— I am
paining Gov. Clinton for an engraver $60.— Lafayette
I shall soon commence and go directly through with
It mentioned that reputation was flowing
me. — The younger artists have formed a
association at the Academy and elected me
President, we meet in the evenings of 3 days
to draw, and it has been conducted thus
with such success, as to have trebled the number
of our association and excited the attention, and affection
of the community; there is a spirit of harmony
among the artists, every one says what never before
was said, and which augurs well for the success of
the artist. The artists are pleased to attribute it to
my exertions, and I find in them expressions and
feelings of respect which have been very
interesting to me. I have had, however, in producing
a pleasant state of things I think there was the preparation
to the state of mind of the artists themselves; I find a liberal
feeling in the younger part of them, and a refinement of
manners which will redeem the character of the art from the
degradation to which a few dissipated interlopers, have tamper
with it. A literary society, admission
to which must be by unanimous vote, and to which many
respectable literary characters of the city have been denied ad-
mission, have chosen me a member, together with W. Hillhouse
and W. Longfellow, poets. — these indicate good feeling towards me
to say the least and in the end will be of advantage. I have no doubt
God gloria! —
Yr Aff. Son Sam P. Mose

My Dear Mother,
By Mr. Converse who goes to New
Haven this afternoon I drop you this hasty
line, just to say that I received yours of the
2d of April yesterday. I immediately called
on Mr. Jappan as you requested; he took the
list which I made out, and said he would
show it to Mr. Jappan, as she had the whole
management of that part of the business. I
have not heard from him since. You put the sofa
down among the furniture to be disposed of, I
had rather not part with that, as I shall want
it here. Every thing of that kind you do not
wish for your own use, send down to me I shall
eithe use it myself or dispose of it at auction.
I cannot come to N.Haven, as I am to move myself
this season, and I am otherwise very much engaged.
You ask for the bill of the sugar, you will please accept
the triple as a present from me, and if there is any
thing else you may at any time want, just inform me
and if I am in funds you shall have it. I was
very much rejoiced to hear of the religious state of
New Haven, and most cordially say amen to your
prayer that we may all partake of the fruits of the
spirit of peace. I have constantly held myself
ready and willing to forget & forgive, the moment I
am permitted; until then I have nothing to reproach
myself with in the attitude which I have assumed
and shall maintain, towards my brothers, as long as
the course so wounding to my feelings remains un-
explained, and not the slightest expression of regret
manifested in consequence of it; if after the state

course and state of feeling towards them at that time, I can

I must say no more. Yr Aff Sam M. Mosse

My Dear Parents,
I have just heard from Mother and
feel anxious about Father; nothing but the most
imperious necessity prevents my coming immediately
to N.Haven; indeed as it is, I will try and break away
sometime next week if possible, and pass one
day with you, but how to do it without detriment
to my business I don't know; I am engaged on my
Lafayette which the Corporation are anxious to have
and in the prosecution of which picture I have met
and still meet with the most unexpected and con-
stant interruptions; I have many times resolved
to let every thing else suffer and finish it, but
some unforeseen event has from the very commen-
cement, constantly broken in, and obliged me to
delay it.— I am for a day or two now, enga-
ged in our first Exhibition of our new Academy
which is in a flourishing condition, and receives
the approbation, of most of the influential char-
acters in the city and State;— I have longed
for some time from a little respite, but like our
good Father all his sons seem destined for most
busy stations in Society, and constant exertion not
for themselves alone but for the public benefit.
I have not written you on account of such a
pressure of business in various ways, that I cannot
find a moment's leisure, I have just got settled
after moving, my No. is now 124 Broadway
corner of Cedar St. opposite City Hotel; I board at
the National Hotel. I am now called away
by 50 people. Rise my dear little ones, I feel
depressed often that I must spend so much of my
time from them; Love to all. —
I will write again soon
Y Affectionate Son as ever
Sam. J. S. Morgan

New Haven Sept. 20. 1826.
Dear Mother,
I arrived safely home after leaving you
yesterday, and found that neither the house nor the
folks had run away. Dear little Charles was taken
sick a few hours after we had left home, and
Nancy felt anxious about him; he complained of
his leg, which was swollen, and broke out with an
eczema which the doctor thought at first was Epi-
silis but afterwards thought it occasioned by rheu-
matism; he was confined to the bed all day last Sun-
day, and could not walk on Monday, but yesterday
he played about quite lively, and to-day is as great
a fly about as ever; he is now in bed fast asleep
after being well tired with his day's romping all over
the house. Little Finley is gaining very fast, he
begins to acquire his numerous little arts and tricks
which he had before his sickness; I can't but hope
he will yet be a well child. Susan is as usual,
occasionally has a little of humpee, but for the
most part a good girl.— All are well at home,
and I shall set out in the morning at 8 o’clock for
Wethersfield to Paint Judge Mitchell &c.— I heard
from N.York yesterday Edwards & Charles Walker
are well, all prosperous.—
Persevere in your travels, mother, as long as
you think it does you good, and tell Dick to
brush up his best bows and bring home some lady
to grace the now desolate mansion.—
I have no fears about home, I shall
let you know the worst always when I write,
so never think that matters are worse than I
represent; as to little Charles, once more, he is
as well as he ever was, or I should not leave home
as I shall to-morrow morning without the least fear
of any relapse.—
Nancy and all send love, Nancy says
she is glad you are gone, and shall be glad when
you come back again.—
Remember me very kindly to Aunt Salisbury and
thank her, for her generous hospitality to me when in
Boston; and give my love to my dear cousin Elizabeth
Weese, I shall soon forget her, I hope we shall
see her in NewHaven why can't you bring her on?
To cousin Hazard Sproudia if he is in Boston, give
my love, and to all kind friends in Boston or Casle-
town give my regards.
In haste but as ever
Your affectionate Son
Finley.
Mrs Eliz. Ann Morse.
care of
Mrs Josiah Salisbury.

S. D. P. Morse Esqr
Dear Sir
On my return from
New York, I received the official notice of what you
had previously informed me had been done by the
Academy in regard to myself i.e. that I had been
elected an Artist of the Institution.
I did not think it worth while to express to you
my mind on this subject, at the time when I saw you
in New York, but after mature reflection, finding
my instinctive feelings confirmed by sober reason, I do
not hesitate, confidentially, to make them known to
you.
From the first I feared you would not easily
hit upon a plan in the organization of a
National Academy, by which you would enlist the
feelings and estimation of Artists generally, residing
out of the City of New York. The only mode of doing
this I take to be, a judicious conferment of the honours
of the Institution wherever they are merited. The difficulty
by which I apprehended, was, that you would confine
your election of Academicians and Associates to resident
Artists, and that, from a laudable desire to maintain
the importance of the Honorary Membership, none
but a few Artists in the country, of the highest standing,
could be consistently united with you as Members.—
This would many respectable Artists be excluded
from the only marks of honour or consideration, which
can be valuable as coming from a body of men devoted
to the same pursuits as themselves, some of whom
perhaps of no greater attainments, though adventitiously
advanced to the grade of Academicians.
I say these are the only grades which are objects
worthy of the consideration of a professional Artist
and why?— Because the customs of Society, and the
relations in which men exist to one another in the commu-
nity as men, are such, that no one whatever may, be
his attainments will consent to a connexion with an
Institution in which he is publicly classed in the lowest
of many grades as those you have established.—
However just the discrimination may possibly be,
it is a thing at which the self-love of every individual
will revolt.
97911
I might here allude to the usages of professional
men generally in support of the foregoing remarks,
but I shall pass on
The place of Academician, so far as the honour of
it may be properly esteemed, is worthy of the ambition
of all Artists, however eminent. The same may be said
of the Honorary membership. The Associate is in
a class very way inferior to these, and is elected from
among his fellow Artists, as a preparatory step to
the ultimate honour of the Academy. What remains
is the bulk of professional men, who will not feel them
selves complimented by any farther subdivision of
their ranks.
To be sure of having a compliment valued, it
should be seen that it is valued by those who
confer it. Now it seems to me that the Body of Artists
of your Academy, (I speak plainly) is a sort of
common receptacle, to be filled with those whom you
may think best to attach to the interests of the
Academy, and yet, in doing which you hazard
nothing of the dignity of the standing grades.
I make this remark, notwithstanding I know that
this body embraces some persons of talent, of whom
it is not worth while to speak lightly. How some
of them appreciate their rank may be easily imagined.
There seems to be the imprint of littleness on every
thing relating to this grade. All the other elections
are to be made with much circumspection, at particular times, by unanimous vote. The Artist may
be either professional or Amateur; he may be proposed
and voted for at any time, and elected by a bare
majority. And even in the Catalogue, his subordinate connexion to the Academy is significantly
hinted by a little A.
This grade, soutions, so indefinite, embracing
persons of so widely different views as must
respectively belong to Artists and Amateurs, appears
to me to be alike unfit for either.
To the one it is barely an acknowledgement of his
professional character as an Artist, as distinguished
from a Student or Copy-while the other is thereby
furnished with a technical character which he seldom
wishes to avow.
The remedy (if you should wish my opinion) would
be very simple, and most consistent with the proposed
design of the Academy -- It is thin -- The Academicians
possessing the whole Executive power, might be
resident Artists (though in London the Royal Academy
there was an exception in the case of Raeburn who never
lived in London) and their number ought to be limited.
The Associates might or might not be limited
and there cannot be the least inconvenience in leaving
the number of them unlimited. -- Now the very term,
Associate, is one peculiarly adapted to such a relation
as Artists, in various parts of the country ought to sustain,
in an Institution professibly national; and by conferring
this where you might not choose to confer the honorary
membership, you would find an opportunity of
discriminating, without belittling or offending any --
In this way, and by the Honorary membership, how resident
Artists would sustain a parallel standing with the
resident Academicians and Associates, subject, however,
to the rule which requires a residence of one year
in New York, before they would be eligible to an election
into the body of Academicians.
While on this subject I will just notice an improvement
which might be made in the initial letter of the
Associate membership. -- The N.A. is definite and will
be easily understood, but the more it is not intelligible
if used in any other place than in the Catalogue.
Why not A.R.A. as properly as A.R.A. -- I think the
initials should not only distinctly indicate the
particular membership, but should also convey
a positive idea of the Academy with which the Artist
is connected.
You will perhaps think I have enlarged beyond
all bounds in the remarks I have made. I certainly
should not have done so, but for the hope of promoting
the interests of the Academy; my personal wishes could
have been expressed in few words -- From what I have
already said, you will not be surprised when I tell you
that I cannot consistently return my thanks for the
vote of membership which has been announced. --
I would not think more highly of myself than I
ought to think -- and I submit my views on this
subject with full confidence in your candour
and brotherly feeling, and in the belief, that if you
do not agree with me in sentiment now, you will
one long be convinced of the soundness of the objections
I have urged.
If a reply from me to the letter of the Secretary is
essential to my being considered fully a member, my
purpose will be accomplished by silence. but if
that should be insufficient, then I would request
you to hint my wish to be left out in such
a manner as will excite the least remark.
I make this communication confidentially, and
should not be willing to have it seen by any
member, excepting Mr Towns & Mr Durand, if you
should have occasion to show it to them.
With sincere gratification at the success of
the Academy, and with hopes of its increasing
prosperity I am as ever
Truly Your Friend

$75. from the Corporation the rest not till after
May probably, in the mean time I have taken
20 dollars from Mr. Ripley and endorsed it on the
due bill of Edward to me for $157 odd.— I don't think

set down to my credit in the family expenses.—
I have purchased three quarts of the white
mustard seed to send you by private opportunity
and one of the English handbills respecting it which
have been so extensively circulated through England a-
mong the poorer classes.— The book, (of which this

had better be planted at least a little bit in a part

Give Kisses to the children, it gratifies me very

I had the pleasure, to day, of receiving your
Circular communication to which, I must mention the
7th but dated on the 4th inst. under other circumstances
and considerations than those in which I am now
placed, I should have been pleased to contribute
to the support of your infant institution My
attention was directed towards it from its first
commencement, I watched its progress with
intense interest, and as I had been labouring
long on a similar project in this City which
I intended to establish with a view to an
improvement of the Public Taste and rendering the
artist independent of an arbitrary existing tax,
which it lays the least of it, stood in the way of improvement
and knew only to debate the profession with a
view to effect my purpose, I commenced a series of
communications in the United States Gazette under
the signature of Natural Truth, in which I endeavoured
to prove that the arts and Public Taste were
almost stationary, owing to the paralysing influence
of the Directors of the Pennsylvania Academy of the
fine Art, whose sole object was a Missionary one
in every sense of the word, arrogating to themselves
all the Prophets, and placing themselves first in
Public view, claimed and absorbed all the Honor,
too — The artist is considered as a wear
underling, a tool suited for their purposes —
However I did not succeed, and have been persecuted
for my good wishes, to the utmost of their police —
These Communications have to my knowledge
read by several artists in this State, as the Papers
containing them have sent for to your City, and
as they succeeded your formation into a society
I sometimes thought they were found in some
way or other useful — after your society was
formed I did it least expect some small
attention — They have paid to other artists of this
City, but not to me, not even a Circular till
now — It is true I am but an indifferent artist
and I neither wish nor expect your society
to alter its opinion of, or change its conduct
towards me — I wish the society all possible
success. It has done itself honor, and
will confirm, I am sure, what I predicted
would follow, if the same experiment had been
made in Philadelphia — I had therefore long since
come to the conclusion, that as I was not an object of
sufficient notice to warrant first attention, and
that at the time your respect was paid to my Friends in
this City — My Views would of course be but secondary
consideration, and therefore I did not send any
to you. Thank you for your kind and memorable
letter. I can only interpret it as a compliment, at least
for the present, I shall not, I hope, incur the displeasure
if I fail to send any of my works — I respect
its earnestness, and shall not fail to admire
the enterprise and talents of its Members
respectively and collectively, in all of which, you
will perceive that I also have some respect for myself
whatever may be the opinion entertained by others —
I am very respectfully yours at
Jascha Shaw.

writing a defence of Mr. Morse's Lecture, in

My dear Sir,
I send you for your perusal the second edition of Maria Monk's
disclosures. I think the additional matter is very important and con-
clusive of the truth of her story. The fact that she has accompanied
her volume with a plan of all the rooms in the Convent is very strong
in favor of her sincerity and integrity. Were she an impostor I cannot
believe she would have dared to put forth a document of this kind, which,
if materially incorrect, cannot fail in the course of a few days from
its publication of exposing the whole cheat. You will see in the papers
an announcement of her abduction. From a variety of secret and very
suspicious manoeuvres, there was every reason to believe that a plot was
ripened for the purpose of getting possession of her. She had had inter-
views with various persons from Canada, against whom she was warned by
her friends, and on Wednesday evening she was missing. Her guardian,
Mr. Slocum, was in much trouble about it, applied to the police and could
get no assistance, the only method left was to advise the public of the
state of the case and get the public eye directed to the matter. The next
day she returned, and her absence was satisfactorily explained. Would
you not write a short notice of the second edition (even two or three
lines would answer,) for one of the Cooperstown papers, sufficient to draw
attention to the subject of her book?-
I send you a little work for Master Paul which if you approve please
present him in my name, I find it has interested my own boys very much, and
I think it will him also.-
I also ask your acceptance of a work of one of Dr. Beecher's
daughters. It strikes me as possessing great originality and enlarge-
ment of thought, and she combats infidelity in a masterly manner. But
there is a vindication of New England character in it at page 14 and on-
ward which is so just that your candid mind I am sure will give it its just

weight in removing some of your anti puritanic feelings.—
I want to come up and see you, but I don't know that I can force
myself away from New York. Our exhibition is yet doing bravely. We
have had a few wet days, and yet the average daily receipts is not greatly
lessened; we made a calculation that if we received 17.50 pr day for the
remaining days of Exhibition, (36 in number,) our receipts would be 3000
in all, but yesterday with unfavorable weather our receipts were 79
dollars.— Nothing yet from Horace.—
I am reading your Switzerland, I like it much, but this is doubtless
to be set down by the American et omne id genus as prejudice.— Please
present my best respects to Mrs. Cooper and the young ladies. In haste
but with real respect & esteem
Yr friend & servt.
Saml. F. B. Morse.

Dr Sir,
Well, our friend Horace has come, and he looks in fine health
and spirits. He goes to Washington today and must see his mother in
Boston before he can come to Cooperstown. I have told him that when-
ever he is ready I will go to the Hall with him.-
I send you by Mr. Pratt a small parcel of books. I am inclined
to think you will be pleased with Mrs Beecher's book, there is such a
fairness and truly liberal spirit (and unaffected) throughout, at the
same time there is such a masculine character of reasoning, freed from
masculine asperity of manner, as I think will commend itself to you.
I confess myself so far sectarian as she is, and no farther, her last
chapter contains my own sentiments in regard to other denominations per-
fectly.- In great haste but with real esteem
Your friend and serv.

The strange coincidence of some, and the rapid succession of other quite striking circumstances, induces me to mention them to you by writing, as I was not so happy to find you at your residence:
1.) Ludwig enumerates, since a few weeks, among the names of subscribers to his paper that of a certain Merrick, Esq., in Columbian, Col. C. Ohio (if I am not mistaken) and of Anderson, Esq., editor in Ohio, both names of individuals that probably putted my ruin on board of the Hudson. Merrick brought my trunk to the Philadelphia Restaurant-Hotel, N.Y. the day after I had one on shore, for I was scarcely able to save my papers, and left trunk behind. I considered my help to Capt. Edis. Insurance.
2.) The "Allegemeine Zeitung" of to-morrow will contain an article on the Orange Party in Ireland, wherein the editor compares the English Protestants pretty hardy.
3.) A few days since I was requested by my landlord (bookbinder, Fred Kamp), a man who formerly belonged to the Church of the Jesuitical preacher (Rizzotto from Vienna, now in Philadelphia) to write his address on a small piece of paper, which I did, as he pretended to have no ink.
4.) Yesterday afternoon Mr. Ludwig retreated with his foreman (Westall) into a corner of the composing room, where he opened something like a respectable library of my maps of London, which I had left at home in my room, on the table.
5.) In the evening, when I went home, I found my map in its place, but missed several pages of extracts I lately made from the German "Lexicon" (Encyclopedia) for some literary purpose, and which I had likewise left on the table.
6.) Yesterday afternoon, the pressman Richards, who has quitted Ludwig's office, came there again with the singular intention to offer me a volume, entitled "the mutiny", which he recommended me to read. I positively declined it, telling him, I was too much engaged to squander my time away with such things.
7.) On Monday or on Tuesday evening I had met that young German, Stoller, out of whose hands I received, at 7 o'clock, $20, or account of the $100. D. Kaemmer in Pittsburgh. He surprised me with the news that he had quitted the company of Mrs. Mueller and Oppenheim. I returned, at the door of his house, a book (a vol. of the Engl.) which he had lent to me, cautiously avoiding seeing him in his room.
8.) To-day, Ludwig ordered me to hardly half a dollar he gave to me to his apprentice Theodore and tell him, it was for those newspapers (ports) which, to-morrow will have to be sent to Philadelphia. I objected, that I did not like
To Prof. S.F.B. Morse, N.Y.

to speak to him, being on bad terms with him. He consented then, I should give it
to Mr. Angell, his proof reader and ask him to give it to the boy. Angell, as soon as he
had the 50 cents piece between his fingers, put on hat and coat and went off. —
Ludwig, as he several times had done before, ordered me illiterate to copy some
account in his book, on a piece of paper, I did so.
9.) This evening I was told Ludwig and his former partner, Packmann, book binder,
a very double-faced man, by whom I was introduced to my present lodgment, had
gone to Albany. The deaf man, with whom I quarrelled before, went yesterday
away to Connecticut.
10.) I heard, this afternoon, several of the composers, in a low voice, talk
about Ludwig's offering money for false reports against me. "But," said one
voice, "it is a considerable risk," in I would not open my mouth, said old
Mr. Westall, but for a --, I did not understand the rest. — One of them,
the man who was present when the deaf man and Ludwig depreciated and
assured me that they always liked and esteemed me, — showed to me an eagle
and a sample in gold, and asked me, if I ever had seen such money. I replied,
"Yes," but I never had any of them in my possession. — Afterwards I met
these two men with a third one, Ogg, in the street; they invited me friends,
to accept a glass of beer of them. I did not like to offend them, and therefore
did not decline; but went immediately thereafter up to the eating-house,
of --, where I took tea, whence directly to the university. — Some of the
composers had (in the office) spoken the words: "He won't carry it on further
than till the 4th of July. — If they can get him once to the State prison,
he'll never get off."
11.) A few weeks past, an unavoidable snare was laid to me. My land-
lord, Heikhamm, told me, that a young woman, of a very good family (!!),
and arrived in his neighbourhood (in Germany) had arrived here, and was wait-
ing for her uncle, a farmer in Lyons, N.Y. She was entirely unacquainted
with the English language, and, for this reason, would stay in his, not in a
boarding house. They more than once invited me to take a walk with them,
but I always refused. At last, however, I said that my refusals provoked
them very much, so that I was in real danger of losing my little room; this
would have been an extremely disagreeable occupation even a fatal thing
to me; — consequently, I chose, among two evils, the smallest, and accom-
panied them once to the battery, and once to Hoboken.
One of these little matters might, in their connection with others,
gradually become important; thus, I dare to take the liberty of making
you acquainted with them.
I see daily more that nothing is so dangerous as to be, among
r- s, an honest man. Yet, I solemnly assure you, Sir, that, with
the only exception of my affair against my officer in Heidelberg,
I never did, nor shall do, any thing of which I could have the remotest
reason to be ashamed.
With true admiration of your noble character,
I have the honour to be forever,
Sir,
Your most grateful and
obedient servant
L. C. Henninger-Kausing.
New-York, June 20th, 1836.

Dear Sir,
Your favor of Jul. 8, confirming a report, which I
had heard before, of Mr. Henniger's death, was received a few days
ago. The statement, contained in the Journal of Commerce, which you
had so kindly as sending to me, would certainly be curious and
interesting, if the matter communicated were real facts instead
of being, as I am inclined to think, a great measure of offspring
of poor Henniger's limited imagination. That you may not con-
sider this a mere assertion, I will point out some of the improbable lies,
anachronisms, exaggerations and erroneous statements.
First as to his name. Louis C. Henniger Hanning. If Hanning was
his family name, Henniger could never have been a part of his name,
as it is a custom altogether foreign in Germany to use a family name,
such as Henniger for example, as a Christian or middle name. He
may have substituted it for Hanning, but it certainly never was
a part of his own name.
The account says: "Young Hanning was at this time under arrest,
during the time of Napoleon's assassination and its immediate effects.
Sord, who was however never a student of Feudalism, assassinated
Napoleon in April 1819, now then seventeen years old. Henniger
was a boy of eight years. As to the effect which the deed of Sord pro-
duced upon especially upon the government of Baden, I am able to
express an opinion, in as much as I resided at Feudalism at Diff-
rent times from 1819 to 1822. Even in that short time, immediately
successing the deed of Sord, the vigor of the Baden government limi-
ted considerably, and then was in that state as well as in others, a very
rapid progress towards a more liberal state of things, until it came under
98348
by the apprehensions caused everywhere by the revolution of 1830. It was in spring 1834 that a plan was formed to make a simultaneous attack upon the government of the southern German states with the cooperation of the allied Solo thus residing in France. The explosion in Frankfurt was premature, and caused the failure of the allied plan, even if otherwise practicable. Henninger was one of the many who died at Heidelberg, and succeeded to cross the Rhine at Strasburg, before he could be arrested. This is his own statement made to me last October. With regard to the occurrence at the religious procession, I am unable to say, without the fact of the insult offered to the Peninsular and his attempt at revenge is true or not; I confess, however, that it appears to me highly improbable. If true at all, it was certainly an individual act alone, altogether unconnected with religious factions. The inhabitants of Heidelberg are pretty equally divided between the protestant and catholic churches, if there is a superiority of number, it is on the side of the Catholics. There as well as in most parts of Germany, these two parties are mingled, the best feeling prevails, and nothing of that animosity is perceptible which exists between the same and other denominations, in many cases between the same family, comprises members of both churches. The festival, the procession of the Lord, has been celebrated from time immemorial, the protestants making every intention to higher the effigy of that in many respects beautiful celebration, and the Catholics receiving the neighbors assistance with due gratitude. Such is the spirit in Heidelberg, as to the condition of the Catholic church in the whole state of Baden, it is a well known fact that the Bishop of that diocese, von Wessenberg, has never been confirmed by the Pope or movement of his liberality, that there is among the catholic clergy of southern Germany a quiet and respectable party, as in France, opposed to the supremacy of the Pope, to celibacy and many other institutions of the catholic church, certainly a very strong indication of a spirit of reformation. It was in 1822 Henninger, a catholic priest, in the south of Baden, with his entire parish renounced catholicism, and took up, giving himself to any persecuted creed, although
the stage naturally caused great sensation.
With regard to the conversion of catholicism and despotism on it is well known
that many of the leading liberals in the southern states of Germany, which
have as representatives Goethe, Bismarck, Windischgrätz, Baden, Hessen-Darmstadt
etc., are Catholics. I mention these circumstances to justify my opinion
that the part of Henninger's account, relating to his persecution by the
Seruits, is the production of his diseased imagination; it is in our ward
a case of monomania. I could, I think, even with my slight knowledge of Mr.
Henninger and the few facts before me, point out the general progress of his ideas,
but there is no occasion for this at present.
I became acquainted with Mr. St. last October, when he brought me a letter
from Dr. Follen. His object was to find a publisher of his work on the Seruits.
Although I was then, as I am now, fully convinced of the treasonable and
injurious of his views of the power and extent of that body, and of the
catholics in general, yet the difference of opinion did not prevent
me from asking him if his undertaking. He was, however, unacquainted
with, and left Boston, again after a few weeks. He told me then that he
was here in a small town a few leagues South of Philadelphia, at the usual
time desired that university for the purpose of studying canonical, a course
of study comprising chiefly political economy and some portions of law,
intended to qualify the candidates for the various offices in the administration
of the government. It was during that time that he
became a member of a political association, in consequence of which he
was obliged, before the termination of his studies, to quit Philadelphia and
his country. With him I gained at once my good will and that of my
family by his apparent uprightness and purity of character, and I could
not entertain that his erroneous and extravagant opinions would be a
serious obstacle to his happiness of mind and success in life.
I must beg your pardon for this long letter. I wished to state fully my
opinion of Mr. Henninger to you also from motives of humanity and principle
to deprive him of an unfortunate young man who, living, and enduring to
product his memory after his death. -- I should have communicated your
letter to Dr. Follen, but he is at present on a tour to the West. -- Referring to
accept the assurance of my great regard, and believing me yours, Charles Dick.

I know nothing particulars of Henninger more than you have told. He came hither about a year since, from Pittsburg; I addressed myself first to Dr Follen, whether with letter I do not know. Dr F. sent him with a bustle to Dr Best; the latter sent him with a note to me. As my engagements did not permit me to look at his manuscript, -- & as I knew that the Rev. Mr Cozzell had taken an interest in the publication of "Six months in a convent", I think the liberty of affording Henninger to hear, with the note which has been published.
Henninger was several times at my house; he addressed intelligent & well informed sentiments on all subjects except the subject of liberty; -- Poor, I must say, he appeared to us all to labour under a very strong hallucination of mind, amounting for half to monomania. He had come hither direct from Pittsburg, he said, rather than from any of New York, because the Society were on the watch for him in N.Y. would defeat the publication of his book. I mentioned your name to him as the author of Breton; I was sure at the point of giving him a note began; but did not, because he said he had letters for New York; -- & there were in him here a something of a Jesuitism with which I hesitated to hinder you.

Professor Morse.
Dear Sir,
I thank you for your kind letter of the 8th inst
which I received only three days ago, on my return from a journey
to the West, to this place which I have made my summer residence.
It was about ten days ago, at Pittsburgh, that I received the
sad information of the death of young Claving in whom you
have taken so generous an interest. My acquaintance with
him began last summer when he called upon me at
Watertown, near Boston. He told me his story, and handed
to me part of a manuscript work on the Jesuits which I
read with great interest and returned to him with some criticisms
which he thought just. I then endeavored to find a publisher
for him, but did not succeed. He left Boston in order to
return to Pittsburgh, as he told me, and since that time I
did not learn anything with regard to him, until my recent
visit to that town.
I know of no particulars of his history except those which
he undoubtedly made known to you, and which are summarily
mentioned in the newspaper which you sent me. His residence
at and near Pittsburgh I do not see mentioned in this account.
There are at Pittsburgh some persons who know Clavering
very well, and who probably are able to give you some
interesting information concerning him. I mention
particularly a German apothecary, I believe his name
is Braun though I do not feel quite sure. The person
I mean may however be easily ascertained by applying
to Mr Leo Wolf, a young merchant at Pittsburgh
who during my short residence in that town introduced
me to him for the purpose of giving me the information
I desired concerning Clavering. You have probably
acquaintances in Pittsburgh who could easily collect
what information may be obtained there.
The whole manner and appearance of this unfortunate
young man impressed me with a perfect faith in his
sincerity; and however extraordinary some of the
incidents in his life, I believe he told what he
conscionately believed true. Real persecutions, however,
had evidently so much affected his imagination that
he often saw secret plots and machinations in mere
accidents; and I thought it my duty to tell him so,
and to warn him against giving way to vague suspicions
which could not fail often to create the evil which he
apprehended, and must prove as injurious to the state
of his mind as to his prospects in the world.
I am very glad to learn from you that he left his
papers as a legacy in your hands. Whatever mistakes
of judgment there may be in them mixed up with important
truths, I think they ought to be made known as forming
a part of the moral portrait of a man who under different
circumstances would have taken a very different stand
in society, and whose example would probably be looked upon
as an encouragement rather than a warning to others.
Yours very respectfully & truly
C. Follen.

My dear sir,
I am a good deal troubled by a
pain in one of my eyes, from over-use of
them; so that I do not intend to write
what is called a letter. But I send
you these few lines, to let you know
that I have not been unmindful of you
on the subject of your two last letters.
I saw Mr Jarvis soon after I received
your first letter which, thinking it
would come well in aid of what I had
to say for you, I showed him. I then
spoke of you as you would wish, and
as I honestly think you deserve. He
was not here when I got the second
letter. But I have lately written to
him about you -- and the letter, though
not long, will, I think, carry some
weight with it. Among other things
I observed, "that much as I wish to speak
Morse as a friend whom I highly value,
I would not say a word in his favour,
had I any doubt of his competency;
but I can conscientiously say that I do
believe him competent to the task.” This is
plain language, and I think more to the
purpose than a whole sheet of flourishes;
and Jarvis, who has known me for forty
years, knows that I would not have risked
my own life to serve it my own brother, if he did not
deserve it. Keep a good heart, my friend,
at all events. God bless you.
Yours affectionately,
Wm. Allston.
I shall no doubt see Mr. J. again when
he returns to Boston.

let me know how he passed the vacation and
how little Timley is?
Remember me to Aunt Salisbury & Cousins
and all New Haven friends. — I am in great haste
but as ever Your Affectionate
Sister
Sam. J. B. Mosher

great want of the Blake Whites. You remember
that I requested them to be sent to the care of Mr
Pendleton. but Have they been sent? My Nephew
informs me that Pendleton, the believer, has left
Boston; at any rate he has removed from
his store in Washington Street. Now is Mr P.
has left the city, and the Colours have been
sent to Boston with his former address, sent
to his care, they must be now on a wild goose
chase. Do let me know something about them,
as I am sadly in need of them; and send me at
the same time Mr Rovers address, that I may
know how to get a letter to him. In case the
colours should not yet have been forwarded,
I will thank you to request Mr Rover to direct them
to the care of Mr Edmund T. Hastings,221 Merchants
Row Boston; and also that he will inform me by
mail, how to send in what way I am to transmit
the money for them. — By the way, would not
Mr Verplanck be a good person to consult with
about the subscription for Mr Stuart? — I have

My dear Sir,
I have received your letter in reply
to my last, and thank you for the efforts which
you have so kindly made, at my suggestion, in
behalf of poor Stuart Wilson: on which subject
I shall say more at another time, my object now being
to say a few words concerning myself.
I find to my utter surprise a paragraph
giving the words of the Newspapers stating that I
had accepted the Commission, offered by the Committee
of Congress, for one of the pictures which they have
ordered for the Capitol; and moreover, that I had
accepted it under certain conditions namely, of
executing it at my own time &c. This statement
it seems appeared more than a month ago in the
New York Mirror; from which it has been copied
into the papers here. And it has worried me more
than you can imagine; and the more so that I
could not notice it at the time without delay
anticipating my answer to the Committee which
I did not send until the third of this Month (Feb.
1837). I had delayed my answer until this
time, as I observed in my letter to Mr Jarvis, in
order that I might give the subject the fullest
consideration. Now that the answer is at last
sent, it is proper that I correct the mistake. I
will therefore thank you to have the following
paragraphs, which are enclosed in brackets, inserted
in the New-York Mirror: First however, sparing
the Editor, that I have no ill feeling whatever
towards the writer of the paragraphs alluded to;
indeed I could not reasonably entertain any

now more than two months.
much feeling (however the mistake might have troubled me ) since it was certainly couched
in very complimentary terms, harshly never doubted that it was written and was evidently written
with a very friendly motive or rather, I should say, in a very friendly spirit. — You need make
no other preface to the following than this: Extract
of a letter from Washington Allison to a Friend in

[There having appeared, nearly two months ago,
an article in the New-York Mirror, stating that I
had accepted a Commission for one of the National
Pictures, voted by Congress, I must request the
inserted in that journal.
When the article alluded to appeared in the
Mirror, I had not made up my mind on the subject
farther than that I would not, under any circumstances,
accept more than a commission for one picture,
should I conclude in the affirmative; and that I had
formed this impression (as is well known to my friends
here) so long ago as when Mr Vanplanck was in
Congress: that I did not send my answer to the
subject down to the Committee until the third of this
month [February]; and that, in that answer I have
altogether declined the proposed Commission:
that I did not rectify the article at the time it
first appeared, because I could not have done so
without anticipating my answer to the Committee
— which would have been, to say the least, not respect-
ful; finally, that I had delayed the answer
until the time above-mentioned in order to give the
subject the fullest consideration. My reasons for the
result being wholly of a private nature, I shall
not speak of them here. — I trust it is hardly necessary for me to add, that I duly appreciate the honour
which I have thus been obliged to decline. I shall ever gratefully remember it; nor shall I soon forget the peculiar favour with which the Committee have
honoured me on this occasion.]
I cannot imagine how the story should have taken the shape in which it appeared in the Mirror. Could it have grown out of what I requested you to say concerning my resolution (so long ago formed) on no account to accept more than one of the offered pictures? If so, it seems to me strange logic, that because I had resolved not to accept two, that people should conclude I must therefore have accepted one! When I made this request of yours, it was with reference to the artist, that they might know the kind of feeling which I had towards them: not that I wished to be commended for a "good" feeling, but to claim for myself what I considered a proper one. This was had been long made known by myself. — Do not suppose that I think the refusal came from you. I know it could not be what passed between us concerning the future was altogether contingent and hypothetical, and expressed merely my wishes, not my intentions, for the latter I did not know myself, as they would depend on future circumstances; and, besides, they took no definite shape, as I was merely building castles with you in private conversation. But now that I have sent my answer to the Committee, I have done with castle-building on public ground. In this matter my resolution is fixed; it is the only way in which I can hope to secure my peace. So there's an end on't.
The above was written (as you will have seen by a note on the first page) about more than a fortnight ago. I have now learned the disappointment of the "Pictures." I had hoped to have found your name amongst the commissioned Artists, but I was grieved to find that all my efforts in your behalf have proved fruitless. I know what your disappointment must have been at this result, and most sincerely do I sympathise with you. That my efforts were both sincere and conscientious I hope will be some consolation to you. But let not this disappointment cast you down, my friend. You have it still in your power to let the world know what you can do. I pray you to think from your mind, and determine to haunt all the better for it. God bless you. Your affectionate friend.
Washington Allston.

NEWLY INVENTED TELEGRAPH.—We take the following from a Washington letter in the Baltimore Patriot.
Mr. Gomon and his associate, Mr. Servell, have, after many years application to the subject, invented an important system of Telegraphs, which puts into the hands every one of the two kinds that has yet been attempted. By this admirable plan, they can communicate every kind of information, word by word, and punctuate the same, without using more signals than words, and with as much certainty as if they were written. The system of Mr. Gomon has received the most flattering encouragement from those literary and scientific gentlemen to whom they have explained the system, and it is not a doubt in their minds that it will accomplish the purpose of the invention, and realize all that has been anticipated from it. Mr. Gomon assures me that he will be able to communicate a despatch of one hundred words from New York to New Orleans in half an hour;—and those who are thoroughly acquainted with the system confirm his promises. How elementary does every other system appear in comparison of that which is described in the preceding paragraph. This system is so powerful in contemplating the consequences of such an achievement of human ingenuity. Distance is annihilated. Thousands of miles no longer divide us. We know on the instant what it is in the affairs of the world, and determination of our fellow citizens of other countries. Furthermore, it is that we live in an age for whose intellectual progress nothing is too ripe.
We know nothing of the telegraph of Messrs. Gomon and Servell except what is related in the above paragraph; but we do know that a gentleman of our acquaintance, several years since, suggested that intelligence might be communicated almost instantaneously, hundreds, if not thousands of miles, by means of very fine wires, properly coated to protect them from moisture, and extending between places thus widely separated. It is well known that the electric fluid occupies no perceptible time in passing many miles on a wire; and if it is possible, by connecting one end of the wire with an electrical or galvanic battery to produce any sensible effect whatever at the other, it is obvious that if there are twenty four wires, each representing a letter of the Alphabet they may be connected with the battery successively in any order; and if so connected in the order of the letters of any word or sentences, the word or sentences could be read at any station by a person standing at the other end of the wire. All the letters of a paragraph in a newspaper could thus be touched successively by a man in Philadelphia and the contents, verbatim et literatum, be conveyed to New York as fast as a composer could set up the type! It is not impossible that the time may be near when speeches in Congress taken down by reporters, and conveyed by these "electric telegraphs" to New York or New Orleans, may be in type, printed, circulated, and read, within a few hours after the voice of the speaker has ceased at Washington. The wire necessary for a distance of a hundred miles need not weigh many pounds, and if enclosed in an iron or rubber tube, and supported at high points along the route at intervals of 4 or 500 feet, could be extended through an immense distance at a trifling expense. The feasibility of the project depends entirely upon the practicability of producing any sensible effect at one end of a long wire by connecting the other and with an electrical or galvanic battery.

MAGNIFICENT TELEGRAPH OFFICE,
Washington, February 9, 1848.
Editors: Your London correspondent in this
morning's Intelligence says: "The electric telegraph has
commenced operation in London, and transmits messages
to all parts of England. The price charged for sending a
message of one hundred words to Liverpool is £5. ($22.20.)
This is considered so high that great dissatisfaction is ex-
pressed. The time occupied in forwarding such a message
is about ten minutes. Do you not do this business quicker
and cheaper? The distance between London and Liverpool
is two hundred and twenty miles.
I can satisfactorily answer your correspondent's question.
The distance from Washington to New York is two hundred
and twenty-five miles, and a message of one hundred
words is transmitted ordinarily in five minutes, but sometimes
in three and a half minutes, at a charge of five dollars for the
first hundred words, but only three dollars and thirty-three
cents for the second and for each following hundred words.
The comparative efficiency of the American and English systems
of electric telegraphs is therefore easily stated and comprehended:
English telegraph, 100 words, 220 miles, 10 min. $22.20;
American telegraph, 100 words, 225 miles, 5 min. $25.00.
That England is not now reaping the vastly superior advantages
of the American telegraphic system is owing to the injustice of
her Attorney General, in 1838, in most unscrupulously refusing
to grant Professor Morse's application for a patent at that
time, on a plea false in fact, but, had it been a fact, illegal in
its application. An illustration of the old adage that "might
make might right" will now more forcibly exhibit than
its own force the counsel pursued by the English Attorney
General upon the application of Professor Morse at that time.
It is hoped for the credit of Great Britain, that she will yet
do that justice to the Professor which is due by all the
world to a public benefactor.
With high respect, your friend and obedient servant,
B. B. FRENCH,

TARIFF OF CHARGES BY THE WASHINGTON
AND NEW ORLEANS TELEGRAPH COMPANY.—We have received a tariff of charges by the
Washington and New Orleans Telegraph Company from the telegraph office in Washington,
and the respective intervening points. It is published by the company, and we find that for
the first ten words sent to the first nearest point, Georgetown, two miles from Washington,
the charge is fifteen cents for each additional word; to Alexandria, 10 miles,
16 cents for ten words; to Charleston, S. C. 644
miles, the charge is 79 cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word; to Mobile,
1,262 miles, the charge is 16 cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word; to New Orleans,
1,716 miles, the charge is $2, and 10 cents for
each additional word. Between Mobile and New
Orleans the charge is fifteen cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word. From Charleston to New Orleans 110 miles. Editors
and proprietors of newspapers receiving news for
their own paper are only charged one quarter of
the above rates. All other communications are
written in our language and sent to us. No
charges are added for signature and date, and communications prepaid.
LINES OF ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH.—There are being erected two or three new lines of electric telegraph between Washington, New York and Boston,
by different companies and individuals. From the
abundance of things, there will, we fear, be a
great deal of quarrelling about these new lines. A
new enterprise of the same character in the West
has been stopped, and is now a subject of litigation, and we much fear that similar proceedings
will take place concerning the Atlantic lines, before
managers are settled down, and the companies or individuals who are contracting them will be permitted to enjoy their own rights or inventions.
Professor Morse certainly, thus far, has given good
work, and has been a model of industry. His patent
was the first to carry it into practical operation; and
although it might be advantageous to the public
to encourage rivalry in this business, still it ought
to be done with due regard to the rights of original inventors.

Be it known that I, Samuel W B morse of New York in
the county and State of New York have invented a new
method of transmitting and recording intelligence by means of
Electric magnetism, and I hereby declare that the following
is a full and exact description of it as it is at present conducted
or may be made

or ships of copper or iron, Property insulated in the ground

To convey to the party to which the said visible signs of electricity, have invented the following apparatus, namely,
1. A system of signs by which numbers, and consequently words are signified.

Third; The Post-rule.
The Post-rule, is for the purpose of carrying the Rule when
prepared with its type, it consists of a small lever like the
lever to the key of a horse collar, but with a
shaping rule with its type at the intersection of single cogs.
The lever falls into a notch, and rises upon the
notch, and rises upon the type. The lever is a
portion of the circuit by affixing a portion of the conductor to it
with a point of the post-rule, and otherwise connected so that the circuit will close
at the end it always. The other end is at the end of
the lever which has the most motion, and is made to break or close
the circuit at the end of its motion. The point of the con-
ductor is connected by a turnbuckle to the post-rule, at
the other extremity of the circuit, or upon a plate of copper
silver or other metal attached to the said extremity.
2. The rule is made to pass with regularity as to space and time, beneath
the lever, by means of a pinion wheel fitting the cogs, which wheel
is made to revolve either by a crank moved by the hand, or by
other power in any of the usual methods.
3. The Rule is kept in its channel or way made for that purpose.
The Post-rule sends the intelligence.

constructed, 1st An Electro-magnet made in any of the usual modes

Dear Sir I received yours of
the 11th in the 10th and am much pleased to learn of the
succsess of a contract if our water experiment succeeds I presume nothing can be done in that way until we have made a trial. I have some directions to give you in regard to opening the boxes. You will find on the sides of the top cover four screens, two on each side by which the uppermost cover is fastened.
When they are taken out you can lift the top off, and you will find the reels in order for immediate use. I would suggest to you to have them remain in the lower story of the University (Perhaps you can obtain Prof. Beckers room) as they will be very heavy and difficult to take up and down from this Hall as soon after they are filled with wine. I am very busy with our Machines. I find there is considerable work to do upon them. But we have not got very well with them and I see nothing in the way of completing them next week
my father goes to the City next week and will stay but
a few days. However I hope, that will not deter you from
visiting us as early as possible. I have acquainted Mrs Rail
of your offered service and she regards me to say that she
will be happy to receive them, and that she will be greatly

I have disposed with the large spiral wheel, and have con-
cluded to use one smaller on the opposite end of the shaft. The
reason for doing so, was that three inches was not more than
enough for the magnet, and that the large spiral would be
in the way of the magnet. Now, the space between the drum
will be clear, and free. I think you will like the last plan
the best.
I have completed as far as head work is concerned my
letter Machine and shall make the pattern for it, as I have
leasure from the attention due the writing Machine. This is
not, I presume, objectionable, I should rejoice to try it a
well watered at Washington this winter, and produce an extra
astonishment, would it not be fine?
What has become of Mrs Patterson will the leave the City before
the wire is all wound? I hope not, or we will meet with further delay, which is horrible to think of just now, as I have
my eye still intently fixed upon Europe. I fear we shall lose
our advantage over European discoveries if there is much delay.
The secret shall be well kept.
I assume you will scarcely recognise me when you come
out. For you must know I have something else to do besides
ride clean my boots, and wear a clean face, and besides the
shop present a different scene from the Pastor or Study,
and wears a somewhat different appearance. However there
are some clean beds in Spedwell to which I sometime
resort, and which I hope you will be able to find on your
arrival. The remainder of the sheet I will serve for Monday
Monday morning.
I am inclined to think that my father will not visit
the City this week: -- I am think of nothing more to com
mandate. I shall wait with great interest to hear
from you by your next. Remember me of your
prof. gall.
I remain yours truly
Alfred Vail

My Dear Brother,
This will be handed you by Mr. Stephen
Vail the father of Mr. Vail who is engaged with me in the
Telegraph. He wishes to have some conversation with you on
the subject of Paper, as he has just become possessed of a
paper mill which is manufactured first rate paper. You
will of course know best whether it is desirable to make
a contract with him for a regular supply. Mr. Vail
is well known as a faithful man in his contracts and
entirely responsible.
You will perhaps be surprised to learn that I
came out here to be sick; I caught a severe cold the day
I left New York from the sudden change of temperature, and
was taken down with one of my bilious attacks, which under
other treatment and circumstances might have resulted seriously.
But through a kind providence, I have been thrown among
most attentive and kind and skillful friends, who have treated
me more like one of their own children than like a stranger.
Mr. Vail has been a perfect mother to me; our good Nancy
Thazard can alone compare with her. Through her nursing and
constant attention I am now able to leave my room and have
been down stairs to-day, and hope to be out in a few days. This
sickness well of course detain me a while longer than I intended,
for I must finish the portraits before I return. I may possibly, if
strong enough, come in on Saturday, and return here again on Tuesday
following. I have learned a good deal about a bilious habit by this sickness
so that I think I could now be a pretty good nurse to you if you
should have a serious attack. The truth is we are all of a bilious habit.
poor Richard seems to be the greatest sufferer from it, and I should like
to see him well through a good course of medical treatment. How is
he? I called to see him the evening before I left town, but could make
no one answer at the door, so I was obliged to go without laying good bye.
give my love to him and his family.
The machinery for the Telegraph goes forward daily; slowly
but well and through. You will be surprised at the strength and quantity
of machinery, greater doubtless than will eventually be necessary, yet
it gains the main points, certainty and accuracy.

W. S. is of opposite politics to yourself.
Yours as ever

Spindletop Jan. 13th
Dear Brother,
Mr. Alfred Vail is just going in to N.York and will
return on Monday morning; The machinery is at length complete
and we have thrown it to the Missouri people with great
delight. It is the talk of all the people round, and the principal
inhabitants of Newark made a special expedition on Friday to
see it. The success is complete. We have tried the experiment of
sending a pretty full letter, which I got up from the members given
me, transmitted through two miles of wire and deciphered with but
a single unimportant error. — I am staying only to perfect a
modification of my fortune, and hope to see you on Saturday or
on the earliest on Wednesday when I shall tell you about it.
The matter looks well now, and I desire to feel grateful to him
who gives success, and he always surprised for any disappointment
which he in Infinite wisdom may have in store.—
I long to hear also about your doing in the upper story.
give my regards to them all. Love to Richard and family.
Your great brother & wife Brotten
Sam. P. Brotten

public estimation. I sent you sometime since a pamphlet

Patton, Hackley Norton Burt & Davis Linne which the Faculty
have now organized with new professors and one of these professors
namely Professor Dwight Rogers of the Chem. Dept. has since resigned
the Medical Faculty has been since you left appointed and cure
on the eve of being organized in all 18 professors but in consequence

they have resigned in a body and are going to publish their
transactions and history in a pamphlet form stating they have kept together

The Sub-Committee, from the Committee of Science and Arts appointed
to examine the Electro-Magnetic Telegraph of Professor Samuel F.
B. Morse.
Report, That this instrument was exhibited to them in
the hall of the Institute, and every opportunity given by Mr. Morse
and his associate Mr Alfred Vail, to examine it carefully, and to
judge of its operation; and they now present the following as
the result of their observations. [The instrument is here described]
The instrument may be briefly described as follows;
1st There is a galvanic battery of sixty pairs of plates 7 by 8 1/2
inches each, arranged according to the very convenient plan
suggested by Prof. Howe, and set in action by a solution of sulphate
of copper
2d The poles of this battery can be connected at pleasure,
with a circuit of copper wires, which in the experiments with
ed was ten miles in length. The greater part of the wire was
wound round two cylinders, and the coils insulated from one
another, by being covered with cotton thread.
3d In the middle of this circuit of wire, that is, at what
was the Regulator. In this there is an electro-magnet, made
of a bar of soft iron bent in the form of a horse-shoe, and
surrounded by coils of the wire, which forms the circuit.
The keeper of this magnet is at the short arm of a bent
lever, at the end of the longer arm of which is a
fountain pen. When the keeper is drawn against the
magnet, the pen comes in contact with a roll of paper
wound round a cylinder, and makes a mark with
ink upon this paper. While the telegraph is in operation,
the cylinder which carries the paper is made to revolve
slowly upon its axis by an apparatus like the kitchen jack

It may be proper to state that the idea of using electro-
magnetism for telegraphic purposes has presented itself to sev-
eral different individuals, and that it may be difficult to
settle among them the question of their originality. Gauss has
a telegraph of this kind, in actual operation, for communicat-
ing signals between the University at Göttingen and his magnetic
Observatory in its vicinity. Mr. Wheatstone of London has
also been for some time engaged in experiments on an electro-
magnetic telegraph. But the plan of Professor Morse is, so
far as the Committee are informed, entirely different from
any of those devised by other individuals, all of which act
by giving different directions to a magnetic needle, and
would therefore require several circuits of wires between the
stations.
In conclusion, the Committee beg to state
their high gratification with the exhibition of Professor
Morse's telegraph, and their hope that means may begin
to him to subject it to the test of an actual experiment
made between stations at a considerable distance from each
other. The advantages, which this telegraph, would present
if successful, over every kind hitherto used, make it
worthy of the patronage of the Government. These are,
that the stations may be a distance asunder far exceeding
that to which all other telegraphs are limited, and that
the signals may be given at night and in rains, and
fogs, when other telegraphs fail.

Dear Sir:
A Committee of the House of Representatives
has been appointed, to consider the expediency of purchasing
Gilbert Stuart's portraits of the five first Presidents
of the United States; in behalf of which Committee I
address you, as a competent & disinterested judge, for in-
formation on the subject.
It is desired, in the first place, to ascertain the
mechanism of these portraits as works of art and as
portraits;
And, secondly, their pecuniary value as articles of
sale, upon a fair & liberal estimate.
May I ask you to favor me with your views
on each of these points, to be laid before the Committee?
I am very respectfully yours &c
C. Cushing.

Yours of the 4th came to hand
yesterday. A compliance with your proposal would be
exceedingly agreeable to me & my family, & since the re-
ception of your request we have talked it over & stuck
to make provision for it. On the whole, however,
we regret to say, it will not be convenient for us to
accommodate your daughter as a boarder. We
already have a young lady with us who rooms with
Harriet, & whom we have engaged to keep till the 1st

take Susan in her place, you are only sorry we can
not do so. But, as it is, we have only one spare
room & subject, as we are, to company which we
must accommodate, we think it our duty to deny

to the Institute on my invitation, to be exhibited to the Committee of Science

and Stanton.

timing that it is "to examine Professor Morse's electric-magnetic
telegraph."

preparations and arrangements; and as the instrument is of great

by the Institute.

Dear Sir Your
favour of the 15th came to hand on Friday but
on account of our pressing affair I have not
attempted to answer it until now. I have delayed
informing you of the progress of the Machine expecting
you out every day. But I can now assure you that we are getting on very well
The Battery will be ready on Monday to put together
I have concluded to make it of 30 plates 4in by 5
It will be a beautiful one, and no doubt powerful
enough for a circuit of 2 miles, perhaps more though
I wont'd throw all the plate which I had made into
one battery instead of making two batteries, and hope
you will not object to giving me the battery when
you return from Europe if it returns -- It is about
15 inches long. I have no materials for the joints, will
you send or rather bring it out with you, and also
inquire of Dr Gale what are the parts of the composition
he used for cementing the plates -- The wheel for
the register and port rule are now almost all out, and
other parts in progress -- I need several rolls of the
insulated copper wire, to make magnets with and experiment
upon the form of the magnet -- I also need
some of the flat ribbon in my return from the city
I tried a straight magnet, but not satisfactorily to
myself, as the battery I used was poor, and the acid
weak, — I have been waiting to hear from you respecting
the type — that is, their exact proportion, — I cannot
do any thing until I know — I wish steel trasp to
make them of about the thickness of the little catet
on the port rule, which holds the lever up, — I would
thank you to get about 6 feet of it, of the ordinary
width, — also a cord for the weight — a little less than
the one we used for the old machine, and 6 feet in
length, — I have contrived a new port rule, which I
think must answer, and which will not require sticks
or rather but one stick, — It was brought forth after
much study and perplexity; the port rule is a difficult
affair — I shall make it to run by machinary; I have
had today three hands to work at the Telegraph, and shall
use every effort to get it done in time, — We have tried
the new printing machine, and find that it succeeds
in its imperfect state very well, — I think Mr Smith
better take a look at it, and he will no doubt desire
an interest in it, — I think that if he should see it he
will make up his mind to take out a patent for it
in Europe, — In case he should, I do not think that
it would in the least hinder the progress of the Telegraph.
Both might be attended to with ease, as the Printing
machine will require no experimenting, — I would not
for a moment suppose it, did I think our interest would
be neglected or slighted, — the all would be very glad to
see him here either on his return from Maine or
Washington, — The Great expectation I had on my return
home of joining into partnership with George founded
a semi-founded on the premises made by my father
have burst — I am again on vague premises for three months
and they resting upon the sweep of the printing machine — I feel Prof. More that if I am ever worth any
thing, it will wholly attributable to your kindness —
I now should have no earthly prospect of happiness and
domestic bliss had it not been for what you have done,
for which I shall ever remember with the liveliest emotion of gratitude, whether it is eventually successful or not,
I can appreciate your reasonable and appropriate
that there is nothing certain in this life, that it is a to
of care, anxiety, and trouble, and that our dependence
must be placed upon a higher power than of earth, I
do not to love this world above my Country — I think
of I know my own heart that I had rather live a life
of poverty and toil, than roll in wealth and loose my
conscience and conviction, — Hoping to see you soon I bid you always
remember me to Prof. Galt if you please
I am yours truly
Alfred Bail
