I hope you will bear with me a moment, while I take the liberty to address you
for a few lines. I have seen by your publication of the
Confessions of a French Catholic priest, that the author is now
in New York. I myself am a Frenchman ordained Priest
by Bishop Foleyt of Bardstown Ky. in 1830. I have
acted in the capacity of a Priest, nearly five years, on the
two most conspicuous stations of the Diocese. But in consequence of an injustice done me by theadjutor Bishop,
I have ceased to officiate, and, in all probability, I will never
officiate again — and because I suppose to be bullied — into
what I conceived to be a flagrant wrong, they have attempted
to injure me in public opinion. Still in the camp, I have
lettered the gaulet, and taught them with their own means
I have already published from members in the Western Protestant, a religious paper of this place, in which, I have
confuted their charges with their own official Documents.
I have in my possession, letters of five Bishops,
and two archbishops of the United States, and several love letters of the men to their Priest, which go to confirm the
Statements made in the "Confessions". The Catholic clergy
of this place, in a paper edited by them, have noticed the work
and, as a matter of course, denounce it as "a vile fabrication"
which they say "was never written even by an apostate priest" I am
perfectly content with the details made in the "Confessions", as
a recommendation from me might have some weight with the
public in this great Western region. I would, therefore, beg of
you, to consider me the bearer of the author, you may
say, by any word that he will never be betrayed. Your
disgraceful attempt to produce a reciprocal service
to each other -- and of a beneficial result to the public --
there is only one copy of the "Confessions" in this place -- a
number of strong words will very rarely.
The materials in my possession, could make a
handsome volume, and it has been my design for some
time past to undertake the task; but my constant engagement
for the last six months, has prevented me, for this, to do so; besides,
being a stranger, I feel the necessity of an experienced
hand. Your kind kindness to the French gentleman who
published the "Confessions" you have revived, has induced me to address
you, most humbly requesting, that you would be good
enough to extend the same favour to me -- and to
advise me of the best means to take, in my present
situation, to carry my contemplated work, successfully
to an end.
In the expectation of an answer, as speedy as
your communication will allow, I remain,
Respectfully yours
Birot

Since my return,
I have been very busily engaged in finishing
the machine, and have now got it so far com-
pleted, as to assure you of its being sent to the
City this week. I have been entirely "non plus" with
the battery, and how to remedy the evil I know
not. On my return, I procured more Sulphuric -- but
found that, although the action of the solution
on the plate was as good as ever -- that is, that
the Sulphate of Copper was as readily decomposed,
yet, the Magnetic effect was not so great, or which
is the same thing, the electric effect -- I washed the
plate, thoroughly cleaning them several times, and
renewed the solution, with no better effect -- then
I tried Sulphuric acid, both to try the effect of it
upon the magnet, and also to clean the copper
plates, but without success. -- There was however
on every trial a feeble effect upon the magnet, and
a very small spark visible on breaking the circuit.
After spending two days in this way, and using
almost 3 lbs of Sulphur -- I resolved to send it together
with the Machine to you, that you might with
the assistance of Dr. Gale discover the cause, and ap-
ply the remedy -- After all my experience of two days
the only cause I can assign for its acting thus, is that
the copper plate is covered with a minute film of copper
which I cannot get off. -- Perhaps it may be some
thing else -- Our large battery never served me this
time, and I am afraid it will not do so again. I am
your very obliged servant
Samuel F. B. Morse

Dear Sir,
I cannot but express the high gratification with which I witnessed the operation of your
beautiful and ingenious Electro magnetic Engine. It performed more than promised. I was told
that it would raise 500 pounds of steel in one minute. It raised 523 pounds of steel in a minute. From these
data any one can calculate the power which an erection of machinery on this principle, can be able to avail
I have seen a number variety of electro magnetic engines in operation, among which I have also
had submitted to my inspection examination several plans not yet completed. Of these latter I need not speak, as trial
alone will test satisfactorily the principles on which they are constructed, but of the former I can say with truth
Yours is the most powerful, and contained within the smallest compass of any I have seen. The peculiarities
which pleased me in your engine, are the novel construction and arrangement of the magnets and armatures, and the
ingenious mode of breaking and closing the circuit.
and the individual connections of each Plate of the battery with its own conductor.

TO ALL TO WHOM THESE PRESENTS SHALL COME:
BE IT KNOWN, that I, Samuel F. B. Morse, now of Poughkeepsie, in the county of
Dutchess, in the State of New York, have invented a new and useful apparatus for, and
a system of transmitting intelligence between distant points, by means of Electro-Mag-
netism, which puts in motion machinery for producing sounds or signs, and recording
signs upon paper or other suitable material, which invention I denominate the Ame-
rican Electro-Magnetic Telegraph, and that the following is a full, clear and exact de-
scription of the principle or character thereof, which distinguishes it from all other Tele-
graphs previously known, and of the manner of making and constructing said apparatus
and applying said system, reference being had to the accompanying drawings, making
part of this specification in which Examples 1, 2, and 3, show my system of signs consisting
of a combination of dots and spaces, and of dots, spaces and horizontal lines intended to
represent—Example 1, signs for numbers; Example 2, signs for compound numbers; Example
3, signs for letters; all which signs may also represent words or sentences. Examples 4,
5 and 6, are specimens of the form of type used for regulating the imprinting of the signs.
Example 7, is the type rule; Example 8, apparatus for connecting and breaking the
Electrical or Galvanic circuit. Example 10, Fig. 1, is a perspective view of the regis-
tering apparatus, Fig. 2, a top plan, Fig. 3, a side elevation of the train of wheels moving
the paper and regulating its motion, Fig. 4, a sectional elevation of the Registering lever
and parts appended thereto, Fig. 5, alarm apparatus. Example 11, is a diagram, show-
ing the relative positions of the different parts of an approved form of apparatus, including
a combination of circuits.
Prior to my first application for a patent, it had been essayed to use the currents of
Electricity or Galvanism for Telegraphic purposes, either by decomposition or the action
or exercise of the deflective force of a current upon a magnetized bar or needle, which de-
composition or deflection required to be noted by ocular inspection at the instant the sign
was made.
By my invention the intelligence can be transmitted, and imprinted on paper or other
suitable substance, without requiring the aid of any person at the station to which the
communication is transmitted, so as to be read at any time thereafter.
My apparatus for this purpose consists of two principal parts or combinations.
The first part consists of a Galvanic Battery, or any known generator of Galvanism or
Electricity, a Galvanic or Electric circuit, composed of any known conductors of Electricity,
a port rule and signal lever or other contrivance for closing and breaking the circuit, all in
combination with an Electro-Magnet, or device by which the motive power of the Electric or
Galvanic current, which I call Electro-Magnetism, may be developed and applied to give
motion to other machinery for the purpose of marking or imprinting intelligible characters,
signs or letters at any distances; the conductors may be suspended in the air upon posts
or otherwise, or buried in the ground, being always well insulated at the posts or in the
ground. This combination is illustrated in the annexed drawings in Example 11, Fig. 2,
where D indicates the battery; a, a, the circuit; B, the signal lever; and
C the Electro-Magnet.
The new parts and the operation of this portion of my apparatus, I thus further
describe, viz: at any convenient point in the circuit, (generally near the generator) a
break is made in the conductor, and the two ends thereof are immersed in mercury cups
as shown in the drawings at E, E, Fig. 1, example S. To connect the circuit, I employ
an inverted V formed piece of metal or other proper connector A, suspended over the
mercury cups E, E, in the end of a horizontal lever denominated in said drawing the “signal
lever,” whose fulcrum is at a, so that when the connector A is dipt into the cups, the cir-
cuit is completed. Between the fulcrum and connector A, there is affixed to the under
side of the lever and projecting downward a triangular tooth b, which bears on the upper
surface of the types about to be described, and is raised or lowered by them.
The lever may be counter-balanced by a weight or its equivalent as at C, to make it
move easily. The types are composed of flat straight strips of metal, as shown in exam-
pies 4 and 5, of the drawings herunto annexed, having their upper edges indented to suit
the character to be represented, and which will be hereinafter more fully set forth in the
description of the operation of the machine. The indentations are made of sufficient
depth to allow the connector A to be plunged into the mercury cups, and the highest sur-
face raises it from them. It is obvious that the forms of the upper surface of the types
may be reversed, and the cog b placed on the other side of the fulcrum, and the same
effect would be produced. The types are set up and confined in a Rule to form any re-
quired sentences in one long line. This rule, denominated in the drawings, Example 8,
“Type Rule,” has on its under side a rack that gears into a pinion x, on a shaft under the
grooved railings D, of common construction, on which said rule slides, and is directed
under the cog b, on the lever; the types are advanced at a regular speed by the applica-
tion of any convenient power to the pinion x, and bring the notches, or raised and de-
pressed parts successively under the cog b.
The mercury cups may be dispensed with, and any other convenient metallic con-
98760
taet be made to accomplish the same end, and the closing and breaking of the circuit may
be effected by applying the hand or any other machinery to the signal lever, or by any
other mode adapted to the same end. The closing of the circuit by the depression of the
signal lever, causes the electric current to run upon the circuit a, a, Ex. 11, Fig. 2, and
through the helices of the Electro-Magnet C, which is thus charged with power to move
any machinery which may be connected with it in a proper manner.
The second part of my invention, consists of a Register for Recording the characters,
signs or letters transmitted from any distance, and is composed of the following parts in
combination, viz: a bent lever A, as shown most distinctly in example 10, Fig. 4. To
one arm of this lever there is attached one or more pencils, fountain pins, or other suit-
able marking instruments, B, directly under which is placed a suitable cylinder, D, over
which the paper passes on which the marking for signs are made.
This cylinder turns on its axis, and is connected by a train of wheels and pinions with
a barrel m, Fig. 3, example 10, of common construction which is driven by a weight and
cord wound thereon, and also with a fly K of same Fig. which regulates its motion. To
the other arm of the lever (which is also an armature) is affixed a spiral spring i, as seen
in Example 10, Figs. 1 and 4.
Near the cylinder D, a reel or spool, d, is placed, on which a strip of paper or other
markable material is wound, the end of which is carried over the cylinder D, and is confined
thereon by means of two tapes and endless bands or their equivalents, one at each edge
which pass around two pulleys b, b, one on each side of cylinder D. This is clearly
represented in Figures 2 and 4, Example 10. The clock work is kept at rest by a detent
g, in contact with the fly wheel k, in Fig. 3, and connected with the lever as shown in
Figure 5.
To the Register may be attached an alarm bell as shown in Example 10, Fig. 5, the
machinery for striking which may be variously modified and therefore need not to be
described.
The Register, or second part of my Invention, is operated upon by the first part, in the
following manner, viz: the short end of the pen lever in the second part as seen in example
10, Fig. 4, is an armature f, which is brought in proximity to the Electro-Magnet C, in
the circuit a, a, as shown in Example 11, Fig. 2, and in Example 10, Fig. 4. The Electro-
Magnet C, being charged by closing the circuit, attracts the armature, bringing it nearly
in contact, thus imparting a movement to the lever A. By this movement of the lever,
the detent, Fig. 5, Example 10, is removed from the fly wheel, and the clock work begins
to move, carrying the paper over the cylinder D, and at the same time the fountain pen,
pencil, or other marking instrument is, by the action of the lever, set in motion.
The circuit being broken, the lever is brought back to its position by the spiral spring
i, and by the closing and breaking of the circuit, more or less rapidly, dots and spaces and
marks of any required length are made upon the paper and in any required combinations.
My system of characters consists of dots, spaces and lines, variously combined, to form
letters and other characters, a specimen of which is represented in Examples 1, 2, and 3.
To make a dot, a notch or indentation is required in the types, into which the cog or
tooth on the "signal lever" will fall and instantly rise from, as the types move onward and
when a line is to be formed on the paper at the Register as a sign, the notch in the type is
extended, so that the lever will remain down for a space of time, sufficient to make the
line required.
The alarm bell shown at A, Example 10, Fig. 5, may be struck by means of a ham-
mer, actuated by a supplementary Electro-Magnet placed in the same circuit as that first
named. Any convenient number of Registers and Registering stations, may be connected
with the same circuit, all constructed and operating as above described.
To extend more effectually the communication by my apparatus, I adopt the following
arrangement, whereby I can use any number of additional batteries or generators of Elec-
tricity, and by which I can connect progressively any number of consecutive circuits,
viz: I place at any point in the first circuit an Electro-Magnet, and opposite its poles I
place an armature on a lever, like that described for Registering, but instead of using the
said lever to mark with, I use it to close and break a second circuit, precisely as the
signal lever is used to close and break the first circuit.
The second circuit has an independent battery, and may be used to work a Register
or other apparatus for Registering, or to close and break a third circuit or both, and thus
by a combination of circuits the requisite power can be obtained at any distances, ad-infi-
num. This combination is shown in Example 11, Fig. 1.
It will be observed that my vocabulary system of signs or secret writing by cypher
can be conveniently used in communicating by this Telegraph, and any mode of closing
and breaking a circuit may be adopted, the object being to do so at proper intervals.
CLAIMS.
First. Having thus fully described my Invention, I wish it to be understood that I
do not claim the use of the Galvanic current or currents of Electricity, for the purpose of
Telegraphic communications generally, but what I specially claim as my Invention and
Improvement, is making use of the motive power of magnetism, when developed by the
action of such current or currents, substantially, as set forth in the foregoing description of
the first principal part of my Invention, as means of operating or giving motion to machi-
nery, which may be used to imprint signals upon paper or other suitable material, or to
produce sounds in any desired manner for the purpose of Telegraphic communication at
any distances. The only ways in which the Galvanic current has been proposed to be
used prior to my Invention and Improvement, were by bubbles resulting from decomposi-
tion, and the action or exercise of Electrical power upon a magnetized bar or needle, and
the bubbles, and the deflections of the needles thus produced, were the subjects of in-
spection and had no power, or were not applied to record the communication. I there-
fore, characterize my Invention as the first Recording or Printing Telegraph by means of
Electro-Magnetism.
There are various known modes of producing motions by Electro-Magnetism, but
none of these had been applied, prior to my Invention and Improvement, to actuate or
give motion to printing or recording machinery, which is the chief point of my Invention
and Improvement.
Second. I also claim, as my Invention and Improvement, the employment of the
machinery called the Register or Recording instrument, composed of the train of clock
wheels, cylinders and other apparatus or their equivalents, for moving the material upon
which the characters are to be imprinted, and for imprinting said characters substantially,
as set forth in the foregoing description of the second principal part of my Invention.
Third. I also claim as my Invention and Improvement, the combination of machinery
herein described, consisting of the generator of Electricity, the circuit of conductors, the
contrivance for closing and breaking the circuit, the Electro-Magnet, the pen or contri-
vance for marking, and the machinery for sustaining and moving the paper all together,
constituting one apparatus or Telegraphic machine, which I denominate the American
Electro-Magnetic Telegraph.
Fourth. I also claim as my Invention, the combination of two or more Galvanic or
Electric circuits, with independent batteries substantially by the means herein described,
for the purpose of obviating the diminished force of Electro-Magnetism in long circuits, and
enabling me to command sufficient power to put in motion registering or recording ma-
chinery at any distances.
Fifth. I claim as my Invention, the system of signs consisting of dots and spaces,
and of dots, spaces, and horizontal lines, for numerals, letters, words, or sentences sub-
stantially, as herein set forth and illustrated, for Telegraphic purposes.
Sixth. I also claim as my Invention, the system of signs, consisting of dots and
spaces, and of dots, spaces and horizontal lines substantially, as herein set forth and
illustrated, in combination with machinery, for recording them as signals for Telegraphic
purposes.
Seventh. I also claim as my Invention, the types, or their equivalent, and the type
Rule, and Port Rule, in combination with the signal lever or its equivalent, as herein des-
cribed, for the purpose of closing and breaking the circuit of Galvanic or Electric con-
ductors.
Eighth. I do not propose to limit myself to the specific machinery, or parts of ma-
chinery described in the foregoing specification and claims, the essence of my Invention
being the use of the motive power of the Electric or Galvanic current, which I call Elec-
tro-Magnetism, however developed, for marking or printing intelligible characters, signs
of letters at any distances, being a new application of that power, of which I claim to be
the first Inventor or discoverer.

New Haven, June 31st 1840.
My dear Father,
I suppose you would like to be informed of your
news. I suppose my daughter Susan's safe arrival, is it down to
write you the very next day after I arrived. -- We had a delightful
passage up the Sound. -- Mr. Luelton introduced another lady,
who was placed in his care, with three little boys. Her name
is Mrs. Richards, a very sweet lady from this city, and I became
quite well acquainted with her, before we reached N.Y. Heaven.
The sun came out quite bright, when we were about half way
here, so after all we had a delightful day. -- Mr. Luelton rode
up with me to Mrs. Deverson's, when we arrived about half past
one, and found a warm welcome. I am sure I thought to be
very thankful that I found such good company, for Mr. L.
was very attentive to me, and I felt as if I was well provided
for. The family were at dinner when I arrived -- they said
they had quite given up in despair of seeing me, but were very
glad to see me. The father, you do not know how beautiful
New Haven looks, from an unvarnished view, and the fine elm
trees in their glory; the new houses that have been erected since
I was here, are very handsome. Give me N.Y. Haven for my home.
After dinner I laid down & took a short nap, and
towards nine -- Henrietta Silliman called in. She came to see
98767
Maria, not knowing that I was here, but seemed very glad to
see me. She does not expect to go West in four or five days
as she is waiting for her brother in law, Mr Currah. After
Maria and myself took a stroll up in the avenue and as we
were coming back met Hemmen, who insisted upon our calling
us, a few moments, so we went in, and saw Mrs Fillman,
and Julia. They enquired particularly after you, & Uncle
We have came back and stopped in to Dr Taylor, a few
moments found them & her mother he only said now at
Home. They gave me a warm welcome, and wanted to hear
all about your mission, and the rest of the Morris. Mrs Taylor
says, I must write Uncle Sidney, that she wishes him to come
back and make her a visit this Summer, for she longs to see him
again & hopes he will not fail to accept her invitation.
The boys, she has thought for some time of writing him a
letter, especially to invite him, and hopes to hear that he has
accepted it. - Mrs Bethany Whittlesey was over there, and told
me I must come over and see her.
I am going over to see about Salisbury this morning.
should have gone yesterday, but heard Mr Elias Edwards I
was going to visit on a journey that afternoon, and concluded
I would wait till after the trouble of departure was over,
before I went.
Every thing looks so delightful to me, father, the streets are

the Division has just put her head in, & says I must give

see me - I must hasten come at all too early, and hopes you will

family, and I already begin to feel quite at home.
While Uncle Sidney, I sent Uncle Whittlesey's letter, to
Mrs. Merrick's to same afternoon I arrive at
it looks very much like rain, this morning, and is quite
clampt and foggy. - How do you get along without your
tending them? - I have much love to this Washington for me, when you see
them. - If you will allow me, I will add a few words to
Brantley before I close. - Love to Uncle Sidney - & write Sara - Dear
father to your very aff. daughter Susan.
To Chas. W. More-
Dear Sister- Your wanting Toby is at last out of the way, &
how do you get along without him & we are going to take up lodging
until letter to P. Haines to day, if it does not rain.
Do not forget to send me observis every fortnight by Mr Stanley

I hope you will write me from also, for I want to hear how

But I have not time to say more at present, must go

New Haven July 20th 1840.
My Dearest Father,
Your letter dated the 9th only reached me, if you
will believe it, last Sunday eve; and to day, upon returning from a
delightful ride to East Rock I was rather very happy by the receipt
of another epistle from you, which was delivered by Mr Davis, during
my absence. I have been wondering for a long long while, why
your father did not write me, but presumed it was owing to your
being so busy. While I thought Charley might have at least sent me a
few lines, to let me know you had not quite forgotten your runaway
daughter. I was so disappointed in the other day in regard to sending you, in
several of my friends, a letter. My package was all in readiness to be
sent by Boston Edward Salisbury and Cally, who were going to the
city, I shall very probably appeared to take letters, when they went.
They were entertained for a three days on account of the illness of two
Worleys little daughter Agnes - do I keep my package for them when to
my surprise and disappointment on calling the same day, I found
they had gone. It seems Captain C. Hall sent me word by his man, that
he should go on the morrow - but the servant says it to the men - as
thus they were all written for nothing. - I wrote Charley until
you a letter together - but as it was full of inquiries why you did
not write etc. I understand upon receiving yours of the 9th not to
send it, but write another - so here I am at my third epistle.
I mean to send this in the office to make sure sending it.
Genius or Catty went to Morris Corn for a little while -- and then returned
to their house -- when I had the pleasure of seeing them very often. They
sent in for me twice to dine with them -- the first time I was engaged
to spend the day at Mr. Thalledens' Hermitage, and the second
I went -- and had a very pleasant visit -- They think your
letters an excellent one & consider he hopes to see you if he
stays long enough in the city. They have now gone to Princeton
in N. Jersey to stay some length of time, as the physicians think
sea bathing will be good for his Catty.-- About Calisburg is very
much taken up in attending to Cadie Martha who is now able to
talk out -- I am in their glee, & she is very kind to me, -- always
ingenuous when I have heard from you -- & it was not three
evenings to tea sociably, last week -- to the Taylor -- Prof. Filliman
& a Mrs Hotchkiss -- a cousin of the Denisons. -- We met Mrs Hubbard,
her daughter (Faith that was) and she is very pleasant to have me come
and visit her in Hanover, another season -- Her husband is Josephus
Van. Do she used to be a dear friend of my mother's? I should be
delighted to go -- and old
time friends to have me come and visit her in Hanover, another
season -- I am very happy here, dear father -- and friends are around
me -- and my home at Olds Denisons is delightful. The tall stately
Elms -- despite it quite cool, even during the vexing weather we
have had for a week past -- I hardly trust, I shall not in the
mildest of terms complain, forget the quiet of home -- and trust I may
use them right. -- I attend the Center Church & sit with Aunt
Lucy's family morning -- & in the afternoon go with Miss Susan Taylor to
the Village Chapel to hear Prof. Ficker -- sometimes attend the Episcopal
with the Miss Denisons.--
Now give it was in Uncle Charles to send me your
money -- was he not, dear father -- how can I ever repay him
for his many kindnesses to me -- I was thinking how would
it do to let it remain in the Bank, and then, as I wantell
it -- Can any one do so? Then when I want any little
article a little out of the common line -- it can suit for the most -- or if I
wish to contribute to Benevolent Soc. can draw from that. If you
think however father, that it would do better in Harriet's hands -- I
will abide by your opinion -- I have wanted for some time past
one of those large black red Skirts with fringe -- that the Ladies wear
so much in their cloys. Almost every young lady has one been, & I
find they are very convenient indeed -- still as it was more a luxury
I concluded I would do without one -- seeing I must draw up on Harriet's
liberty for the Unit. I think now I can afford to get one, and dear
father, if it is not too much to ask -- some day when you are going down town
with you get one one -- I should like to have Harriet Pitts judgement
about that dress -- not so much if you would call on her -- she would
accompany you, & know with pleasure. -- I do not wish one over
seven or eight dollars -- and please take the money from Harriet. Much will
& Charles would take it to Albany -- she would send it next day by Mr
Tucker -- I feel very to trouble you -- perhaps if you give the money to Harriet,
she would give it to some one, and purchase it, without troubling you to ask
-- pay her -- I must write Harriet Charles again -- and thank her for
this very pleasant & unexpectative present -- You speak of a letter you
have sent me -- I have not yet it yet, but presume I shall be informed
when the penny post comes -- We have had very hot weather here for
a week past, but last Sunday there was a Local Thunder Showers -- & the
day the air is cool & invigorating -- Early this morning Miss O's cousin called
in a carriage & took us all out to the Rocks we rolled half way up the
Mr -- then got out & walked up to the top, & the little house there is built
then for the recreation of visitors -- We came back, Branch pleased with
our game -- The Taylors say, after I have done here -- I must come &
make them a visit & then Margaret Sherman wants me to visit her,
do you must not expect, dear father -- that Miss Davis will be ready
to return quite so soon, as part often commerce -- You had better
let me remain till cool weather -- for my health is so good here --
But we will talk about that, when you come up -- We have plenty
of fine tea -- & flowers as Mrs J. has a fine garden --
do not, think I forget you, dear father, Annie so many friends. Do you

permit me to express to you, individuals, my regret at the
unsuccessful result of the negotiations between our committee
of conference. From the propositions aspires under which we
convened our meetings, I had intimated the hope, that
our Cabiny would have terminated in promoting such
a course of harmonious action between the Institutions
we represented, as should greatly contribute to the prosperity
of both. At the close of our conferences last summer, from
which grew your liberal offer, to our cordial acceptance, of the
guaranties use of your rooms in Clinton Hall for our talks
exhibition, the difficulties, which have now so unexpectedly
barred further progress in negotiation, had not been even
suggested. At our last meeting on July 4, when our labour was
unprecedented for the season, you remarked, that the only point
remaining to be adjusted, which presented any difficulty, was
the terms of admission of the members of the Association
to the Exhibition, of the shade my, & that you were confident, from the liberal & friendly disposition already evinced by your Council, this matter could be easily arranged.

not only on grounds of equitable reciprocity, but in the
most liberal spirit of compromise, I did not doubt our
negotiations would result in securing the objects we
had in view. I can now only regret that our recent
difficulties have prevented this happy issue.

expressing the hope, that, as the Academy of Design & the
Metalls Association were both founded for one object, &
are both seeking one & the same grand result, & as the
members of each can have no personal interest to serve
that can come in competition with the public good,
they may both move on harmoniously in their respective spheres, & that their arduous labour may be
crowned by the happy event of making our City, as distinct
from the other cities of the United States, as it is already eminent for her commercial enterprise.
With high considerations of respect,

Dear Father,
I was just going to put a letter in the office
saying you might expect me in the city on Tuesday morning
next, with Linlin Joe when your truly welcome letter
arrived, and changed all my plans completely.
Sincerely do I hope you will come on -- and let it
be, your father as near the 28th as possible, because
Charles' vacation is only Wednesday, and it will be keeping
him from College. I am really sorry that I cannot
return with you for I shall have to go with
any opportunity that presents itself -- as Cousin Joe will return
on Monday, because his vacation is out on Wednesday.
I should like to return at least two days before
he will go. I have many little things to do -- and
arrange, that can only be done in the city --
you know I can stay at the Kittilans, who
now live in Grand St -- and they will be very
happy to have me too.
By the way, dear father - there has a poor woman been
making me some under garments, and I was to pay
her Wistham. & she would see to it. Will you let Charity
take them 1s 70d - and say it was for the place?
It will oblige me much if you will.
I have a flying report that my friend & school mate
Sam Shepherd of Bengal, thinks of accompanying me to
Bordeaux - so if there has a letter come to the office post marked
Washingtoon, Co - I shall begin to think it true. Please bring
on all letters that may have come - dear father. I hope
the will go - and am very anxious to ascertain the truth
of such a report. As to Lord Charles, I fear I shall
have to give him up. It seems very strange that he
has not wrote.
I shall not engage myself dear father, and indeed
he does not seem to think I would be doing myself
justice to do so. I have always been strongly opposed
to long engagements - especially of such a length as one
would necessarily be - four and even five years.
Though I think now my affection for him would not
change, by a voyage across the ocean - still I think
you engaging myself - but some improvement change
my feelings entirely, for I know I am rather fickle.
He has sent me a long letter for you, this morning
under the belief that I was to leave on the morning
but as that plan is changed I presume he will
prefer taking it back & waiting to see you himself.
The family have been very polite to me. Still they discourage
him, by telling him he stands but a poor chance -- so long
an interval must elapse before we can be united -- and I
Shall be placed soon, in such different circumstances.
I know that he loves me truly -- and would be willing to
make any sacrifice for me. Lewis he wrote that letter, I
have received some more notes from him -- and he is willing
to have me go abroad free, and if my affection does not
change, to be engaged on my return.
Then is brother Charles? Why will you not let him come
to us with you, dear father, and leave me home to
see him? His friends and relatives would be delighted
to have him. -- So bring on your Daguerreotype -- for
then are a good many want to have their portraits
taken, by you. -- I hope you will at last call

Your petition in relation to the Electro-Magnetic Telegraph having been before Congress for many Long Years and no final action
having been had thereon, I thought I would write you on the subject and inform you that nothing had ever been done by Congress at any of the subsequent Sessions and propose to obtain this claim for you for the Patent Right as I am confident I could render you services of great
value towards obtaining it. The Printed Journals of the House of Representatives show that nothing has transpired on the subject. The opposition that will be made on account of the great expense attendant on laying down the wire and constructing the appurtenances of the Telegraph is the greatest difficulty that will have to be contended with. It appears by the newspapers (some time since) that an Association was about to be formed for the purpose of establishing a line of Electrics Magnetic Telegraph, but as I have never heard that this Association was formed or effected anything which if they had would have been known, I presume there was not a sufficient subscription for the effectuation of the design of forming a Company. The Committee of Commerce of the Senate last Session reported a Bill for $50000 to make an experimental test of Genon's plan of Telegraphs. This Telegraph of Genon's being on the Semaphoric plan can be established with much greater economy than yours, which may cause much opposition from that score, to yours, and a preference for Genon's with many members and no doubt there will be a hard struggle by the friends of that plan in Congress in favor of that. There is so possibility that this claim can be obtained, although it would be an extremely difficult task, from the very low state of the Treasury which causes a severe scrutiny of claims, and from the struggle of both parties to cut down all expenditures to the lowest possible point, and from the fact that so great is the delay that any claim which is admitted on all hands to be perfectly just has very little chance of passing, so great are the delays so very numerous the forms which a claim has to go through -- first through one House and then through the other, and only on Sundays and Saturdays are claims taken up, and very often they are passed aside even on three days by the press of the National business. of other Committees on National Matters, or not reaching the particular claim in his long list
to report to the Committee during the whole Session, and if he should be ready to report to the Committee,
of there may not be a quorum present (and if so they cannot act as they are very careful in their
attendance on Committees, and if a quorum is present, they may debate it for many successive
meetings, until even if they report in favor of it, there is such an immense number of public
and private Bills already on the Calendar that it cannot be even reached during the whole Session,
much less have time to pass one House and then to pass through the Committees of the
other House and be read three times in each House and debated, and then only in its turn
on the docket. And without the principles of a claim and the grounds on which it is claimed
and the proof carefully explained to the members of the Committees, and they fully impeded
with all its grounds and points (and even then if they are in favor of it, they often retain the
papers in their hands too long for its passage) they will from some frivolous objection, or
pretended want of liability on the part of the United States report against it. A claim
therefore needs the most constant, unceasing and vigilant attention to see
that it is not neglected, or rejected on false grounds. In your letter of February 15th 1838
to the Committee on Commerce of the House of Representatives (printed in the Documents of the House
of Representatives) it is stated as follows: "If the Government is disposed to test this mode of
télégraphic communication by enabling me to give it a fair trial for one hundred miles, I will
engage to enter into no arrangements to dispose of my rights as the inventor and patentee for
the United States to any individual or company of individuals, previous to offering it to the
Government for such a just and reasonable compensation as shall be numerically agreed upon."
The first movement of course, as thus suggested would be to obtain the appropriation of $20,000
estimated then to be necessary, as until its practicability was demonstrated, Congress would
do nothing further, even if they would then. Being acquainted and having the warm
friendships of many Members of Congress, and having had much experience in the business
of presenting claims, gives me very great facilities for obtaining the claim, and in addition to
this I am acquainted with the precedents of their purchasing useful inventions, am thoroughly
acquainted with the Science of Mechanics and Electric Magnetism & understand the Patent
Laws the principles of which are included in this claim -- and am well versed in the rules of the House
and Senate and the best modes to forward a claim. For a person to depend (even if there was
a Report in favor of paying him a claim) on the mere justice of the claim, without having it
vigorously attended to, would be entirely useless as there are just claims of 20 years sending

My Dear Kathen,
I have this moment read the dress
and letter you were so kind as to send me by Uncle
Lancry. Many thanks for the dress, although not the
kind I meant, it is very pretty & suits me well.
As to the letter, the father it was read with various
emotions -- you are indeed a better parent than I deserve,
thus to accede to my wishes, when so contrary to your
attitude -- But I must all will come right one of these
days. George, I well know, is not so healthy as some,
Still he has a strong constitution and these rheumatic
attacks are practically wearing off. If I have written him
that I shall not marry him, unless he becomes a Chris-
tian and dear father you may rely upon it, even if
what it will, I shall adhere to my resolution.
I will also follow your advice in regard to engaging
myself dear father, George is coming up in the Monday
evening boat to pass a day or two -- I tell you this
because I wish to keep nothing concealed from
you, and I intend to behead with the utmost
prudence -- in all my intercourse with him. I feel
dear father, as if I could never thank you enough
for your kindness, in thus gratifying my wishes -- but
if I am to travel a thorny path as you fear, then
it will come all on my own head.
Do you believe Uncle Charles has not come yet? I am
tried of being kept in suspense. He very long ago left
I received quite a long letter from him saying he made all
arrangements to come Monday but the rain prevented,
suspecting you Uncle did went to New York the next
day, he concluded to finish his visit at the Springs,
(as I died out about four o'clock) and come to see
me Friday at 2 o'clock. As to a journey with him, he has
engaged to visit Cambridge and Hampshir e and
be present at Knowl Park's graduation. After that
he says he shall be at liberty to attend me where I
want, I will expect me to the Falls. He is so hard to
be got at, that I much fear whether I shall see
Dragaria or not. What would you say, dear father,
to my going on to Boston with him, or remaining with
Uncle Bartlett while he goes north? I only suggest this,
but do not know as it would be best if I went with
him, you were would be a greater chance of my seeing
the Falls this season. We have been on the constant
look out, but no Uncle Charles as yet. I do not dare
take the five o'clock train, but if not, all hope of seeing
him will vanish. My friend Wm Shepherd writes me
he is to be in St. Louis on at 6 o'clock and urges me strongly to
come on there, for she longs to see me. I hardly know what
to do, one pulling me here, and another there.
You speak of coming up again if the weather continues warm.
I hope you will dear father, and I should be delighted
to accompany you West if you go. There seems a spell
but refuse my ever seeing, Demondora.
Why do you not go up to Sun Haven to live
with Uncle Barney, father? They would all be so glad
to see you thus. I suppose Uncle has told you of
this sitting room in it Broadway for the Winter. I was
going to find I was got to be deprived of a home,
but I am a boarding house too, but I suppose all
is for the best, this I must say. It was quite a disappointment to me. I shall be even more cheerful and Dr. Peter
George says with God's help, she has determined to be come a
better man. That he knows presidency is not becoming a Christian
it must come from the heart, and he will pray for a new
heart, not because it will win me but that it may save
his soul from another death. I have prayed for him's sake
but I need prayers greatly on my behalf for I want to
live nearer to God to become a better Christian, & be resigned
& God's will in all things.
We are well here, and we go on the same as usual.
Monday morning.
I have kept my letter open, the father in
hope Uncle Char will arrive before the post falls
off but still he disappoints us.
Uncle Richard only accompanied him to
Jersey for fun as Potash will soon be back
tomorrow. I will write you again by
the return of 9 and let you know if
Uncle Char has come thus. We are all
well this season. Please excuse this
shortness of words.
From the room off Chytn.
Isaac

dollars were collected, leaving a deficit on the second quarter of.................... 55 dollars
On the third instalment but...................................................... 135
dollars were collected, leaving a deficit on the third quarter of.................... 90 dollars.
thus making on the three installments a Total deficit of...................... 165 dollars!!
This diminution in such a rapid ratio of the collections of a quarterly sum, small at most, alarmed me, and I found it ne-
cessary seriously to calculate the cost of the enterprise in which I had embarked. Having no means aside from this subscrip-
tion, it was indispensably necessary to be assured of sufficient capital before I could advance another step. At this junc-
ture, my attention was directed by a letter from the Secretary of the Treasury at Washington, to my invention of the Electro-
magnetic Telegraph, made several years before. The attention of the government being directed to this subject, the Telegraph
offered in the opinion of my friends, the readiest and quickest mode of supplying myself with means for a future prosecution of
my commission. Accordingly at once requested the Secretary to give me an order for a loan of $5000 to be applied to the
three installments, until I had ascertain the proceeds with the Telegraph. I need not give the details of more than three years
labors, hopes, and disappointments, in waiting for the action of our own and foreign governments. It is sufficient to say that my
expectations, or rather those of my friends, so far as pecuniary profit is concerned, have been vain. I have as yet not realized
one cent, and I thus find myself farther from my object than ever. Upon deliberately considering the matter, the late winter and
spring, I came to the determination, in the first place, to free myself from the pecuniary obligations under which I had long
lain to my friends of the Association, and I commenced a systematic economy and penchance by which I had gradually to
amass the money for that purpose, which sum it would have been impossible for me to raise to $510. Three hundred dollars
of this sum I had already laid down when an article in the N. York Mirror of the 16th Oct. determined me at once to commence
the refunding of the funds received. In compliance with this determination, I have the pleasure herewith to send you
five dollars being the amount collected from you for one instalment on one share according to the
Treasurer's account rendered to me.
I return this sum with many thanks for your kind intentions, sincerely regretting that circumstances beyond my control should
have prevented the accomplishment of my wishes and those of my friends. Although as yet frustrated, I do not entirely
despair; a system of financial obligation is of all things to me most fatal to that independence of mind which is absolutely
necessary to a free exercise of its higher powers, and in thus freeing myself from this obligation, I hope you will see in it the
evidence, not that I abandon my enterprise, nor that I am insensible to those other obligations which gratitude towards each, and
all of the Association imposes, but, (as matters now stand,) that I have taken the first necessary step to the final accomplish-
ment of my design.
With sincere respect, your most obedient servant,
Samuel F. B. Morse.

My dear Sir.
I have just received another letter from Mr. Isaac
A. Coffin from Washington in relation to the Telegraph.
I gave him to understand last Summer that it was
favorable to his proposition but that I could do nothing
without consulting the other proprietors. From you I
received a definite answer and power to propose certain
terms, but not from Mr. Alfred Vail who wished to con
sult his brother. It is perhaps my fault that he has
not answered definitely as I penciled on recently read
ing his letter he waited for a reply to my letter, so that
I have not a power of Attorney to act for him. From Mr.
Galt I expect one in a few days. Indeed my dear Sir
Something ought to be done to carry forward this enterprise
that we may all receive what I think we all deserve. The
whole labor and expense of moving at all, devolves on me,
and I have nothing in the world (completely crippled
in means, I have scarcely, (indeed I have not at all,) the
means even to pay the postage of letters on the subject.
I feel it most tantalizing to find that there is a move
ment in Washington on the subject to know that the Telegraph
will be before Congress this session and from the means
possessed by Lord & Wheatstone (yes Wheatstone who
successfully headed us in England) one or the other of
their two plans will probably be adopted Wheatstone
Samprase you know has a patent here and has expended
$1000. to get every thing prepared for a campaign to carry
his project into operation, and more than this his patent
is dated before mine! My dear Sir to speak as I feel,
I am sick at heart to perceive how easily others, foreign
ers can manage our Congress and can contrive to cheat
our Country out of the honor of a discovery of which the
Country boasts, and our countrymen out of the profit, which
are our due; to perceive how easily they can find men
and means to help them in their plans, and how difficult, may
impossible for us to find either Is it really so?
or am I deceived. What can be done? Do write immediately
and propose something. Will you not be in Washington
this Winter? Will you not call on me as you pass
through New York if you do go?
Genox has his Telegraph on
the Capitol, and a Committee of the Senate reported in
favor of trying him for a short distance, and will pass a
bill this Session if we are not doing something. Some means
some how must be raised. I have been compelled to stop
my machine just at the moment of completion. I cannot
move a step without running in debt, and that I cannot
do.
As to the Company that was thought of to carry the Telegraph
into operation here, it is another of those ignes fatui
that have just led me on to waste a little more time,
money and patience. The gentleman who proposed the matter
was doubtless friendly disposed, but he lacks judgement and perseverance in
98873
a matter of this sort.
If Congress could but pass the bill of 300000 before
them there would be no difficulty. There is no difficulty
in the scientific or mechanical part of the matter,
that is a problem solved. The only difficulty that
remains is obtaining funds which Congress can furnish
to carry it into execution. I have a great deal to
say, but must stop for want of time to write more.
Everything done by me in regard to the Telegraph
is at arms length. I can do nothing without consultation,
and when I wish to consult on the most trivial
thing, I have three letters to write, and a week or ten
days to wait before I can receive an answer. I feel,
at times, almost ready to cast the whole matter to the
winds, and turn my attention forever from the subject.
Indeed I feel almost inclined at times to destroy
the evidences of priority of invention in my possession,
and let Wheatstone and England take the credit of it.
For it is tantalizing in the highest degree to find the
papers and the lecturers boasting of the invention as
one of the greatest of the age, and as an honor to America,
and yet to have the nation by its representatives,
leave the inventor without either the means to fruit
his invention fairly before his Countrymen, or to defend
himself against foreign attack. If I had the means
in any way of support in Washington this winter, I would
go on in the middle of Jan st and push the matter

Dear Sir
Your letter of the 3d inst. was received,
in which you offer me five per cent commission to attend to your claim before Congress.
As from the extreme uncertainty of a claim ever passing Congress after years of
immense labor trouble anxiety variation; it is common to allow even one half, but even the
lowest commission is twenty per cent. But I will vigorously attend to the claim for only
one half of the lowest amount given for ten per cent if it is ever obtained, and if not
obtained after years of trouble, time, labour, expense and fatigue nothing. This certainty
is low enough most especially as I have to take the risk after infinite labor of having no
renumeration. As the appropriation reported by the Committee was much lower than your
estimate which was $20,000, as contained in printed document No 153, and the estimate of
$26,000 comprised compensation for the services of yourself, Mr. Galt & Mr. Vail the
larger sum of $30,000, will, even deducting my commission in case of success leave more than
a full remuneration according to the estimate for yourself and Mr. Galt & Vail, as you
will have a right to apply the additional $4,000 to the contingency of increased payment for the
services of the experiment, as well as to any other item in the estimate; and it being the application
of principles of profound science, you have a right to charge a much higher remuneration than
that in the estimate. Therefore you can afford to allow this commission out of the $30,000
appropriation, but even supposing for a moment that which will not be the case, that it did
not leave enough to compensate the proprietors, you should waive compensation for the present
for services in the experiment, until the Government purchase the Invention, which its
testing it will be a strong step towards. The obtaining the appropriation is Herculean
(and the risk of not doing it after next elections great) compared to the trouble of the experiment
and the undying honor and eternal applause which will be your lot in case it being carried
into effect will alone be a glorious reward for you for the trouble of the experiment. five
per cent as a contingent commission is too little and after spending years of effort might not
succeed: there are hundreds of kinds of businesses where there is no contingency where five per cent
is allowed, but nothing on earth so extremely contingent or uncertain as the passage of a claim
before Congress. Congress being the Legislature of a Nation of over 17,000,000 of population
with a Republican form of Government causes an enormous and unparalleled amount of
business of a National character to be constantly before it. Every Session therefore, it
necessarily leaves an extremely long Calender of unfinished business. The thing is new
untried, and being a matter dependent on the principles of profound Science, it will be
extremely difficult to impress members with its principles. This is a claim, too, more than
ordinarily difficult, in consequence of the rivalry of other plans, and the very powerful in
and influence and headway which those plans have already gained, thus generating
and violent opposition to this. If it should ever get to pass the House, it would meet
the most powerful opposition from the Committee of Commerce of the Senate a Committee
of surpassing talent and energy, who would contend that it was wrong at a time when the
Government was borrowing money, to attempt the most expensive plan, and which was untried, when
this plan was economical and for all practical purposes unsufficient; that their was a plan that
had been demonstrated, and would ridicule this plan as visionary and theoretical; -- and their powerful
opposition is seriously apprehended as an insuperable obstacle to the passage of this
Bill. Therefore, in addition to the two Houses being generally disposed to all claims, and the
State of the Treasury, here is all this tremendous influence which will be directed against
it, which adds infinitely to the difficulty and vastly lessen the chance of obtaining it. I ought in
fair justice if I undertake it, to have the chance of at least ten percent, after many years
of intense labor, many nights during which I shall set up all night relative to this claim,
always laboring days, to advance it, and writing very late at night to promote it -- it may
be obtained -- there being indisputable claims which have been pending for twenty years, is the vast amount and great pressure of the National business. Or claims about which
is no hesitation twenty per cent is allowed, and ten percent on one half the lowest amount
allowed, or a claim to which there is such powerful opposition is certainly low and rarer
and as I should, necessarily from the fact of the favour with which Governor's plan has been
by the Senate (one of its most powerful Committees having made a formal Official Report
strongly in favour of it) be compelled to make every far greater election than usual in relation
to this claim, it would be very hard that I should not have that per centage, and I can
undertake to make the immense exertion, which I know are absolutely necessary for even a
remote possibility to get this claim through, at the risk of obtaining nothing -- and not have
the chance of one half the amount that those do where the amount is admitted by Congress
be due and only awaits legislative authority to settle it. Congress are fearful to allow a
claims from the precedents they set, -- and this will be most violently opposed from the precedents
that it will set -- will be objected that this precedent will draw a large amount from the
Treasury in future to purchase future Patents, for Public Improvements for the Army or Sea
-- and object that it will be quoted as a justification of intolerable appropriation for such purposes
From the very low state of the Treasury from the Tariff coming down to the lowest
state at this time -- and as the Government have confessed their Estimates into the narrowest
profitable limits, and have come into power with the pledge of Reform of expenditure, and the
other party violently oppose all expenditures for fear of consequence of a high Tariff, -- these facts
show that both parties are striving every nerve to cut off expenditures, which will naturally give
the opposition to the claim from both parties, and difficulty of obtaining it. Under all the
circumstances if the above remuneration will be allowed only in case the claim is obtained, and if
not obtained, notwithstanding whatever trouble, time, expense or fatigue, -- it will
make the greatest exertions possible to procure the passage of a Law for the claim, through all
the Committees and all the Stages of both Houses -- infinitely greater exertions I am sure than
any other person whatever ever has, but otherwise I cannot go on, for it is useless for me to
wear out my life on the mere chance for a claim to which there must be the most powerful opposition,
and which therefore whatever may be the efforts, is highly probable to fail
of passing. Please reply immediately on the reception of this on the
above subject of the per-centage, as if I go on with it I wish to state
to you immediately at great length the systematic mode, method, and
exertions which I should adopt to forward it in the most efficient manner
-- that I may know whether I am to go on or not as if I go with this
claim, I wish to commence immediately to make every arrangement necessary to
promote it: and your courtesies in so doing will be at all times reciprocated.
I am With the Highest Esteem & Regard
Your Obd Servt

My D: Sir.
I am endeavouring to do something with the Telegraph
at Washington &c. We all seem somewhat
supplied, and I most of all, being obliged
to superintend the setting up of a set of machinery complete,
and to make the greater part myself, and without a cent of
means -- I am now at work upon it, and feel to propose of be-
sturing upon it. If I should get it completed I may visit you with it
in Phila. sometime before the winter closes. Mr. Smith is without
means and cannot advance any thing. He suggests that if I could raise
200 or 300 dollars to enable me to visit Wash. with the new machines,
it would be well and he expects to my receiving the first receipt
from the Telegraph to repay the sum. If I give my time and
attention to the matter, is it not fair that I should receive
a compensation? All the burden now rests on my shoulders after
years of time devoted to the enterprise, and I am willing to offer as
I am able to bear my share, if the other proprietors will lend a
helping hand and give me facilities to act, and a reasonable
recompense for my services in case of success. -
Truly your friend, I am
Samt B. Morse

My Dear Sir
Yours of the 15th came
to hand this morning, I reply to your
letter of some months since, and cannot
divine the reason you have not received
it. In that I stated my perfect willingness
to grant your request, on my own part but
as my brother is interested with me, and has
bome for me much of the expense, indeed
almost all. I could not do any thing in
the matter with out consulting him. I
reply to your letter to that effect and have
received no answer from you. I apprehend
however no objection on his part to grant
you any power in the matter which you
may desire. And I would suggest to you
the propriety of just dropping him a line to
that effect, and you may state to him
my perfect consent to any arrangement you
may be pleased to make for the good of
the whole Co.
I have recently given considerable thought
to the subject of the Telegraph, and was
intending to get permission of you, if there
is any thing to the contrary in our articles
of agreement, to build for myself and my private use, a Telegraph upon your plan. Now I
should be glad to have your consent to it. It
will be some time before I could make it at
any rate, and therefore can do the general cause
no harm. I will write to my Brother that
he will give my consent for him to give you the
power of attorney to act for us. I hope there
will be no embarassment thrown in the way
of your and our ultimate success in the
Telegraph. I should be very much pleased
to have you come to Philadelphia and invade your
stay at my house, and I will endeavour
to render you every assistance in my power.
My Father is frequently in New York and
you may be able to transact the whole
business through him and George. He will
convey any message to G and get the requisite
papers. You may show Father this letter
which will answer the purpose of my writing.
He, I think, always puts his name upon the
books of the Commercial Hotel Courtland St.
on the South side, near Greenwich St. within City.
Let me hear from you by return of mail
if this is satisfactory. I remain yours truly
Alfred Bait

By S.F. B. Morse,
Dear Sir:
Having recently returned to this
City after an absence of nine months, I deem it a duty
I should have discharged longer than this, to inform you of
the reasons why I have not fulfilled the pecuniary
obligation I am under to you for instructing me in the
use of the Daguerreotype. Notwithstanding all my efforts
I found the constant humidity of the atmosphere counter-
quent on incessant rains, baffled all my attempts
to succeed. I then relinquished that employment and
took a small school in the County which has furnished
me with a bare subsistence till now. My prospects,
however, are brightening somewhat as I have recently been
elected Classical teacher in the Cokesburg Manual
School School in this State. My labor in that Insti-
tution will commence with the 1st of February next, and
as soon as I receive the first payment of my Salary I will
forward the amount due you.
Yours with sincere regard and esteem
Charles Taylor

"The diff erence between practical knowledge and theoretical
knowledge is this. The
one contains the elements of an immediate
application, the other not. The one asks what
use can be made of this truth? The other,
what is this truth? Wherein does it consist?
"The former seeks truth on account of the ben e
efit to be derived from it, the latter desires it
on its own account, and not for the sake of
something else, which it is to serve as means.
"In the one case truth is rendered subservient
to selfish interests, in the other it is consid er
ered more valuable than any thing else, the
supreme good. Practical knowledge having only
usefulness in view, must spread itself over a
large field; it thus becomes superficial. But true
knowledge is less practical than that which does
not exhaust its subjects. Truly practical know l
ledge is solid and thorough; but all solid kno w
ledge must be theoretical, must be acquired for its
own sake, and as it is in itself since every relation to something else renders it impure. We will exhibit in a few words two kinds of theory.
Both are united in having the same principles but they differ in the manner of representing them.
The one begins with single facts, observes and examines them, unites such as exhibit essential affinities under a common head, and as those excluded will show something common with each other new classes will be formed, and a number of classes more allied to each other than other will again become subordinate to a higher one. Every day adds new facts, and as the whole exists in its parts, this cannot be seen until all the latter have been collected. No one can say when this will be effected. According to this theory all heads & classes, or rather principles seem to have been gained by observation and by uniting those facts, that show similarity. Yet unless man had formed an idea of union previous to his making experiments, he would I could not think of investigating single cases, since his investigations could not have any Scientific object. This object is the union sought for. The other theory begins, therefore, with the principle of Science, and experience is to corroborate & prove it. It has not suffered itself to be drowned in the constantly increasing number
80
"number of facts, nor to become confused by them. The principle
"is the life of all experiments, and is the same to Science, that the
"centre is to a periphery. All the parts of Science are organized
"by it, and filled with it, as every member of the body indicates
"the presence of the soul. It attracts, what belongs to Science
"and arranges it, and excludes what is foreign to it. This principle
"giving Science a systematical character, throws light
"upon all its parts by the mutual support, they afford to each
"other and which proceeds from their position & relation to each
"other. This theory it cannot be denied, has little reference
"to practice; it will exhaust truth, it will exhibit Science
"as a whole; it does not deduce its rules for action.
"What then is its value? The former theory is engaged with single
"actions, for which it gives the rules, the latter examines the
"general nature of these rules. The former theory reduces
"the many instances of language to general rules,
"the latter unfolds before us the principles of grammar, gives
"us the philosophy of it, and shows the necessity & connexion
"of the many single rules. Both kinds of grammar are necessary.
"They are related to each other as History & the Philosophy of History,
"the latter cannot be written without the former; yet the former
"is a mere collection of dry bones without the latter. The one de-
"mands exact discrimination, and penetrating acuteness; the other
"a productive genius. The one makes fine distinctions in given
"facts; the other derives deep & fruitful ideas from them."

the rest of your communication, Shapow enclosed,

netic Telegraph; and to assure you that my

Dear Sir,
The Geological survey of this state has been completed, and the
final report is in proof. The first volume will appear on the 16th of August.
It has been thought very desirable to give an introduction setting forth the
history of the progress and present condition of literature, science and the arts
in the State of New York. May I duly give to furnish you with notes for a memoir
of this undertaking as relative to the arts of design? The more full the notes
should be, the more useful; yet it is my opinion that such notes as shall be
submitted by the Scientific and literary Gentlemen throughout the state,
shall render it into a brief compendious article. The magnitude of the final
report of the Survey and the interest it is expected to excite seem to favor the
design of making better known to the world the scientific and literary
achievements of the citizens of this State.
Sam. Sis. with my high respect.
Your humble servant.
William H. Severance

To the Honorable Senate and House of Representatives
of the United States.
The petition of Levi S. Bartlett of Kingston in the county
of Rockingham and State of New Hampshire respectfully represents
that on the 10th day of June last past he entered into a contract with
the U. States to do and perform certain services at a fixed rate
of compensation therein named.
Said contract is in writing and herewith submitted.
By its terms he was to be enabled to fulfill the same between
the first day of August and the 1st day of December last. But by
repeated failures on the part of the U. States as will fully appear
from correspondence herewith submitted he was delayed in the
progress of said work to his great damage until even past
the period assigned for its completion.
That having at very great expense and labor prepared
to fulfill his part of the contract as rapidly as the Agent of the
United States would furnish the means, and while progressing
therein, and after the greatest difficulties, risks, and labor, incident
to such complete fulfilment on the rail road between
Baltimore and Washington cities had been incurred by your
petitioner although not the half in distance had been completed
your petitioners received on the 18th day of December last past the
written order of the Agent of the U. States arresting him in the
future execution of the work and directing a small fractional
portion of work (not in fact covered by his contract) to be executed
under the circumstances which will appear by said written
order, a copy of which is herewith submitted marked A,
and by your petitioners answer thereto marked B.
Your petitioners willing as in said paper marked B to
accommodate himself to the request of the governments agent
99371
removed his team men and implements to Washington City expecting
to be accommodated and indemnified therefor, and after many fruit-
less efforts to arrange the contract proposed to be postponed, a writing
was agreed on between the Government agent and your petitioners agent
and submitted to the said Comptroller of the Treasury for approval.
Said Comptroller suggested a modification thereof as stated in doc-
ument herewith submitted marked C, and the modification was
made accordingly and submitted to said Comptroller, and he endea-
fved his approval thereof in writing on the back of the same, as will
appear by the paper herewith submitted marked C and the Govt.
said Agent S.B. Morse did the same as will appear by the same
document.
Thereafter, the Govt. Agent, to wit, on the 29th of December
returned to your petitioners agent said document, with his own
letter of explanation herewith submitted marked D and a copy of
a letter from the Secretary of the Treasury also herewith submitted
marked E disallowing said modification under the pretense
that an alleged assignment of the contract by your petitioners
justified the government in treating the contract as at an end,
and proposing to adjust the damages under an admission that the
Government had violated the contract on its part as will appear
by said paper marked E.
In reply to the positions thus taken a letter herewith sub-
mitted marked F was addressed to the Secretary of the Treasury by
your petitioners agent illustrative of the error and injustice of
the Secretary's position in the case. Yet professing to yield thereto
if the Govt. would pay the amount of the contract then admitted
to be violated on its part deducting only so much as the complete
fulfilment of the remaining part will cost him (the petitioners) under
the preparation he has made for its fulfillment, and deducting of
course payments already made. To this as will be seen by
the Govt.'s letter herewith submitted marked G the new ground was
that the military control was thoroughly by the Congress
maintained. The army was given to the administration
for an adjustment of the demands in the army of the
United States.

was established by the President of the United

Washington, Jan. 19th 1844.
Si I have the honor to report that, in compliance with my
instructions from the Department of War , to ascertain whether
any damages or loss, and if so the extent, has been sustained by the
"Govt." growing out of any contract or agreement entered into between
"Mr. Smith & Faltham & brothers to supply the Telegraphy of pipe under
"Surrells Contract," I have gone into an examination of the quality of
the pipe delivered by F.O.J. Smith the contractor with Mr. P. Faltham
and brothers to furnish lead pipe for the Telegraphic Conductors, and
I find it defective in many points, but particularly in the destructive
effect that has been produced upon the insulation of the wires by the
hot process of manufacture. The wires will should be taken out of the
pipe, be rewarmed, and returned to the pipe. From the report of
my Assistant the expense of these repairs will fall within the sum of
Twice hundred dollars but as this sum is saved to the Government
between Mr. Smith and the the Telegraphs, and credited to the United States,
on the final settlement of their bill for pipe, the aggregate sum allowed
for lead pipe is not exceeded. Part of the damage which the pipe and
wires have sustained ought to be borne by the Messrs. Faltham & they
relinquish Fifty dollars. The principal damage sustained is one of
that a kind not chargeable to their neglect, but to a great degree
to the neglect of my Assistant Prof. Fitcher who has since been dismissed
for all the pipe has been delivered under these circumstances I ask permission to pay
the balance of their account.
Respectfully I am
Yr Obd Servt
Geo. W. Mason

Princeton Jan 24th 1844
My Dear Sir
I am anxious to hear from you
in reference to the telegraph and I have
intended to write to you on the subject
for a month past but extra college
duties have occupied all my thoughts
and all my time since the beginning of
the present term. During the last
vacation I occupied myself as usual
with my investigations in electricity
and among other results I arrived at
an idea which I think may have an
important bearing on the success of
the telegraph. It is this, while a
current of electricity is passing through
a wire one part of the conductor
is constantly plus to any other part which
exceeds it, the difference in the
degree of the electrical state constantly
increasing as the distance of the two points
is greater. The maximum difference is thus
at the two ends and hence when the two
extremities of a long wire are brought
into near approximation there is a
great tendency in the electricity to cut
across from the one to the other. This
tendency is not due, as has been supposed
narrowly to the great resistance of the
long wire and the cross cut opening of
the operating channel, but to the fact
of the one part being positive and the other
negative and the consequent great
attraction of the electricity in the one
part for the unattained matter in
the other.
According to this view the insulation
which would be sufficient to separate two concentric portions of the
same wire which had been divided, would
entirely insufficient to prevent the cutting
across. I consider the fact I have stated
as one of considerable importance in
a theoretical point of view and I do
not wish it to be made public before
the publication of my paper in the
transactions of the American Philosophical Society.
On sending you letters on the subject
of the telegraph in the newspapers
I was struck with the idea that you
had probably met with the very difficulty
my researches have led me to
anticipate. If this is the case and
your insinuation is not founded sufficient
to suspect such a condition
of things. With much respect
Yours Truly
Joseph Henry

Sometime since received from you a
letter enclosing a draft on your brother for $30. some cents for

which you had promised to pay me. I have waited some time in expectation
of hearing from you on the subject, but have as yet had no answer
to my last letter, as it is possible that you may have in the hurry of your
business had it pass from your mind, I have concluded to write to you again
on the subject. I trust you will see the necessity to me at least of not
to yourself of attending to it. I am unwilling to suppose that the paragraph
in your letter to me offered to done, in which you put a case where
your firing have been inflicted the obligation of gratitude cannot
have been intended by you to mean that you did not intend to comply with
your promise reflectively made to me, because I believe you to be a Christian
or gentleman, I cannot for a moment think that you would want to
act as a substitute to about the fulfillment of your becoming obligations.
I do not ask any thing from you on account of gratitude I have lived long
enough to know that gratitude is a very feeble claim to one easily satisfied
where the disposition exists to do so, but I do ask from you as a matter
of justice that you should remit to me without delay the amount due
me for my board in Washington during the last winter, Whether I was
of any service or not in preventing the oppression for you, or whether
it was a weakness in me, or you say, to suppose that I was instrumental in

of concern. I doubt which I do not care a stone. Though others may have a differ-
ent opinion of the matter, as I know they have. All I wish is that you would
do a simple matter of justice & right & comply with your promise & I am
perfectly willing to relieve you from all obligations of gratitude to me if you
can relieve yourself why we shall both be satisfied. I send you therefore
to and the amount due me on acct of board & in a draft directed to me at this
place by return of mail. I have waited I think sufficiently long to enable you

I remain very respectfully yours
Colt Secrt

My dear Sir,
Baltimore Feb 7. 1844
You must think it strange that I have not answered your
letter of the 24th ult. before this but I have this moment received it in passing though
this place on my way to N.York which I trust will be a sufficient apology for my
apparent neglect. I have read your letter with much interest and it has determined
me to make a visit on my return from Mulberry which will be the beginning of the
week perhaps on Tuesday morning 13th inst. If any thing in N.York should prevent
me from being with you then, I will drop you a line on Monday morning.
Spiritual questions occur to me in this hurried moment, (as I have in
the morning and carry this with me to Princeton on my way to N.York) suggested
by your results.
1st How does the result you have arrived at affect the experiments made
on my 80 feet of wire of 160 miles?
2d. What distance apart must the wires of a circuit be to prevent
the cross cut? Will any insulation in a tube prevent it?
3d. If my conductors are placed or poles suspended in the air, will there
then be any danger of cross cut?
4th. Now is it that Wheatstone, who has extended his conductors
for 20 miles and more, has not discovered this difficulty of cross cut?
I found the difficulty which you apprehend in the insulation of
my wires, but this I will explain when I have the pleasure of seeing you.
In the mean time believe me
With sincere respect Your obliged
Sam T Brown
