Dear Sir
I regret what S did not happen
to beat my lodging, when you called the other
day, both because it would have given me pleas-
ure to meet you, and because S wished to con-
duct you in relation to a matter of some
public interest, which has been referred to
me for examination. S called at the
telegraph office this morning after you left
and, but in inquiring for you learned that
you had left the city. The subject on
which S wished to ask your opinion is this,
Mr. Kening of New York, late a paymaster
in the army, issues the government about
$35,000 of which not more than $1000 is
subject to be sevance. By way of additional
security, he has assigned to the U. States
fifteen or twenty pictures lately exhibited
in a few days in the National at the
Capital, and now at the Patent Office.
The proposer that the Government shall
take these pictures towards the debt at
a price to be fixed by valuation, and make them
as the nucleus of a national gallery. The
Government, having no alien security, will
of course be obliged to take them, but by the
conditions of the assignment, unless they are
accepted at some fixed price, they must
be converted into money by sale. The
question then resolves itself into this. Is
it in the public interest to retain these pictures
or to sell them for what they will
bring at public auction? Supposing that
you may have seen them, I should be glad
to have your opinion, in regard to their
genuineness and merit. (One Herring
estimates at their value is very high, &
he is an exponent of certificates, tending to
establish the authenticity of some of them,
Among them, ascending to him, one works
of Andrea del Sarto, de Moza, Titian, Rubens,
Claude, Poussin, Rembrandt, and other
artists of occasional inferior celebrity. That

Washington March 4th 1844.
Dear Sidney,
I have just received letters from the
children at Pats Rice, and I presume you have
letters also by the same arrival. They are well, except Mr. Lind whose health seems not quite established
They advise me of a barrel of oranges for me,
if they arrive in good order please ship them to me
to Baltimore to the care of D. Barback Esq. 14
Commerce St., but also direct the one at Washington
at Hon. H. L. Ellsworth's. They also say that there
are some sweetmeats coming by the "Joseph" in about
10 days, if these arrive, they are for my friends the
Ellsworths, please direct them in the same way.
I have nothing new. Smith continues to annoy
me, but I think I have got him in check, by a
demand for compensation for my services, for seven
months for doing that for him which he was bound to do.
The agreement stipulates that I give my services for
"three months and no longer", but at his earnest solicitation I remained seven months longer, and was his
Agent in "negotiating the sale of rights," which by
the articles he was obliged to do; consequently I have
a right to compensation, and Mr. E and others think
my claim a valid one; if it is sustained, the table
is completely turned on him, and he is debtor to me
for the amount of 6 or 700 dollars. I have commenced my operations with posts which promise
well at present. I have no time to add only
that I am well, give much love to all at home,
if I have such a place, and your house and Richards
seem more like it than any thing else or earth at present.
Susan speaks of returning when the "Joseph" makes
her next trip after the present.
Good bye
Y. Aff. brother
Finley.

Dear Sir
I never since since given to understand that
there was a drawing Department belonging or attached to the
University and that you had resigned the Professorship
and that nothing more was doing there; or that present of consideration
but a copy of the list of Professor Students published a few
days since was put into my hands, by which I dismissed my
mistake as regards your resignation, yet as there was no
drawing School in operation I visited on Dr. Darling Langson
the Chancellor who though confined to his Chamber by a
sprained or broken Arm, gave me away agreeable audience
he informed me there were no such Department in operation
at present that some of the young gentlemen occasionally took
lessons of some artist residing in the Building, in short as he
could not act on the subject, he recommended me to write
to you, for it belonged to your Department and that every
arrangement you might suggest would meet with attention.
I then waited on Mr. Dunner related my difficulties with the
Chancellor he strongly urged me to write you immediately
would write himself that deemed it necessary as you know
me well and would do all for me that was possible & proper
It had been suggested in the council of that Academy to have
an elementary School, for me to experiment in it though I
was aware of the kind intentions of Mr. Homan Cummings
& Chapman &c it was found they had no room requisite to
execute a plan -- Now as the University have plenty of
room and it seemed in your power to put a Drawing School
in operation, I make this application to ascertain your sentiments
in regard to my acting in such Department under your control
and whether, while striking the Institutions principal
line in drawing, I could also undertake such elementary
class, as would become as much an auxiliary to the
Nat'l H. as if the Schools were their own, and above all
a prospective class or permanent school might be
made either useful to every Branch of the State
Government or to the whole State. I have informed you, that since you first heard my
illustrations, that by improvements in Machinery
and long practice in knitting, I have rendered the
Attainment of Perspective a simple and easy affair
and could do much more to improve & expedite the facilities
of its Machinery if I were permanently attached and
continued by Authority in a Public Institution.
It is true the Council of the Nat'l H. appointed
a committee to examine my apparatus & method of
Instruction, they attended to that Duty and their Report
tho' not approved & accepted in a manner gratifying
to me, they furnished me with a Copy from their Minutes
which with their former kind offer of a Room to Lecture
in has proved an availling though in circumstances beyond
their control (the winter Technique School in blazing so
as to leave no room) but if you feel confidence in
my zeal & Talent, you situation as professor at the
University enables you to open that Department
and which I feel will the object contemplated in
that Institution, will become a powerful assistant
to the parents of the Nat'l Academy upon which you
have so successfully prided from its infancy —
I have omitted hastily put the Two together
(between principal of a small class of Ladies on drawing
and now to get out top apparatus for Perspective
Lecture this evening) in order to attain your
sentiments therein as far as regards myself
I am deprived of rendering myself useful
in that vacation which has given much
appreciation from all quarters during
a life of practice —
I should be happy to have gone early enough
because it will probably have a decided
influence on my locality at the opening May Day
I have not yet engaged any place and have
declined continuing where I am after May Day
at the time approaching when every one is on a scramble
I hope it will be some apology for disappointment
you for an early reply which will greatly
oblige yours respectfully
John Robbins Smith

Dear Sir,
In compliance with your request that I would give you
my opinion of the pictures recently placed in the Patent Office
I would say that I have this day examined them and find none of
my notes, as they were taken on the spot, I had no Catalogue, and
No. 1. is a picture of some merit but of its originality I could not
judge from the distance I was compelled to see it.
No. 2. Christ standing a good copy.
No. 3 has some good points in color, --
No. 4. Dead Christ, apparently a good copy.
No. 5 Adoration of the Magi, a fair copy.
No. 6. A poor thing.
No. 7. Some good points about this landscape, freely touched
with a full pencil, but ostentations in the display of
this technical excellence.
No. 8. The best picture in the whole collection; full of sunlight,
rich and silver-toned; architecture well painted, the
shipping Claudeslike, but the Sky not Claude.
No. 9. a fair copy, I believe from Nouvermans
No. 10 of the same character as No. 9.
No. 11. A poor thing
No. 12. Christ in the Garden, an indifferent work.
No. 13. A Magdalene, mediocre. -- a copy
No. 14 St Sebastian, a very fair picture, but unequal in the
execution, and bears evidence of its being a copy.
No. 15. Winter scene, good, but not remarkably so.
As a collection it is very indifferent, No. 8 is the only picture
I should select for my collection.
I have been very free, in condemning, Exce ption ly, but to be honest
I cannot avoid it.
Believe, me dear Sir,
With sincere respect
Y. O. B. Sent.
Sam. B. B. Mordy

to the Distribution of my Posts between Wash. & Baltimore,
I understood from him that freight might be charged for
carrying them to the various termini, but from thence they would
be distributed gratuitously, but he advised to my correspondence
with you on the subject. On the belief that by your letter to
me of Decr. 15th. 1843, "the materials for my operations would
be transported between intermediate points on the road, free
of Charge," although "transportation throughout the entire distance"
would be subject to a different law, I had sent in
my estimates to the Treasury Department, (on this understanding)
[on the operation between Wash. & Baltimore,] As I sent in a very
low estimate, and am making every exertion for an economical
experiment I should be much embarrassed if a different
understanding has been put upon your permission of the
15th. Decr. 1843, I would take this occasion to say that the
Distribution of my materials for the present experience
will be much less trouble to the Company than the Distribution of my Posts between Wash. & Baltimore.

Washington March 21. 1844.
Dear Sidney,
I am going to trouble you to compare the
accompanying copy of a letter of Mr Smith's to Messrs Tatham
& brothers lead pipe manufactures on Water st. and certify or
get them to certify that it is a true copy. It is a letter of
great importance in the claim of Smith before Congress. I
took a copy of it, before it was sent, but the Secy of State I
had better have a certified copy from N.York. I wrote
the Tathams on the 14th inst. requesting a copy but have
received no answer; and I fear they think that there is
something in it which implicates them. I assure them
that this is not the case; it is merely to show the
relation of Smith to the pipe contract. -- I think they
will not object to your comparing it with them, nor
to their or your certifying to the correctness of it.--
Smith is greatly haste, enclosing two letters*
received from Susan. If oranges and box of sweetmeats
come please forward them with as little delay as
possible.-- Telegraph matters look a little more
encouraging, I hope two or three weeks will enable me to show a successful experiment as far as
Belleville 12 miles.--
Give much love to Katherine & Richard's family
and Gilbert and little Lucetta, and to Finley.--
Yr Aff. brother as ever
Finley.
Keep the drawing of the house & building
of the Henrietta, carefully.
Washington March 23. 1844
Dear Sidney.
I have just received the letter you sent
from Susan with the endorsement respecting Richard's
son Richard, I hope his illness will not be serious, yet I am
preparing for a different issue. Tell them to
yield their hearts in perfect submission to the will of
God, and all will be peace. Give my love to them all
and to Catherine & the children & Sidney.
Susan says in her letter she shall return in May
with Charles, and the baby, and leaves Mr. Sind behind
to follow some time after. What arrangements can be
made for them when they arrive? I wish you would
cast in your mind and let me know what you think on
the subject. – I hope to be able to be in New-York when
they arrive, but where can she be, since you & Catherine will
be absent, and Richards house will be overflowing. –
Perhaps she may find it agreeable to board in
New Haven. –
The Rev. Mr. Spole has just said to me that in Nov. he
sent $5. to pay for the Obviance, and has just received
a bill which gives no credit for that amount. He wishes me
to mention it when I wrote you. Mr. Spole is our minister
here, from Carlisle (I think) in Penn.
My telegraph letters go on well at present, the whole matter
is now critical, or as our good father used to say, there is a
crisis at hand. I hope for the best, while I endeavor to prepare
my mind for the worst. Smith if he goes forward with his claim
is a ruined man in reputation, but he may sink the telegraph
also in his possession; but when he retires, we hope through his
friends to persuade him to withdraw it, which he may do from fear of the
consequences. As to his claims privately on me, I think I have him
in check but he is a man of consummate art, and in principle
he will, therefore, doubtless give me trouble.
I wrote you yesterday giving you a little trouble to
verify the copy of a letter of Smith's to Sathan V brothers
which it is important I should have. — Please drop one
line respecting the oranges which Susan says she sent me in
the "New Haven", and the box of sweetmeats sent by the "Joseph"
I am anxious to have them especially the former lest they
spoil.
Sove to all again,
Truly Yr Aff. brother
Finley.
Sidney E. Morse, Esq.

The following is an extract from a letter which I received from Mr H. C. Smith on the subject of his claim for damage on the Bartlett Contract, that I refer to in a conversation with you this morning.
"I am willing at any time to refer the whole question to the two Comptrollers of the Treasury, and abide by their report as to the damages which ought to be allowed on the contract, and thus withdraw all further cause of angry feelings between all parties. If Morse and the Secretary will agree to refer the whole question over to Judge Parris (2d Comptroller) and Comptroller McCallough (1st Comptroller) both are honest men impartial judges of the law and the fact, and you may so say to Prof. Morse - I will not open my mouth against any man they shall make on a proper hearing of the case - In that event, the petition and all the papers can be formally withdrawn from the Senate, and when the award, if in favor of the contract, shall be made, the Secretary if he does not feel authorized to pay the amount, shall make a report to Congress of the amount due, if he will do this and attend to it immediately, and if Prof. Morse and myself cannot be found, we will cease to be enemies. Can any proposition be fairer? I will moreover say, that I will consent that Prof. Morse shall have full liberty to use any letter, however private or confidential, I ever wrote him touching the contract, and not consider such use any breach of confidence, for I am so unacquainted with any wrong, or shadow of dishonour in the matter that I will impose no restraint upon him."
I hope this may result in a satisfactory adjustment of all differences.
Yours Respectfully
E. Correll

Dear Sir,
During our late interview in this City, you informed me
that you contemplated making an experiment with your telegraph between Washington & Beltsville, in two or three weeks.
I had the pleasure this morning of seeing two of my friends (Editors of the Baltimore
American) Messrs. Dobbin & Bose who are highly pleased with all they have heard concerning the Electro-Magnetic telegraph,
and will take great pleasure in being present whenever you make a public
exhibition.
You also mentioned to me while here that the government shortly contemplated
organizing a telegraphic Corps; should they do so I shall feel under many
obligations if you can assist me towards receiving an appointment under you
as regards my knowledge of the science you have had practical information; and
the large circle of friends I have here, and at the seat of the General Government
I may be of some service to you.
The Station at Baltimore would suit
me better than any other, inasmuch as
my family reside in this City.
If you should find it necessary to con-
nect the optical telegraph at any time
with your system, my invention and
knowledge may be of service.
I observe that your appropriation is to
be expended under the direction of the
Post Master General, and if he has the
organization of the telegraphic Corps, my
connection as Agent for the Great Southern
Mail Line will give me sufficient influence
with him through your nomination
to get an appointment.
If the foregoing meets your approbation
I should be pleased to hear from you.
I am very respectfully
Your faithful Servt
Henry J. Rogers

In addition to the interest which Mr Smith now in the
Telegraph in the United States, I know that he would be unwilling to exchange it for that abroad. But
if Professor Moser could persuade him to exchange his interest in the United States, which is one
quarter, he would receive such a proposition from me with a favorable consideration,
or if Smith made a distinct offer of ten thousand dollars in cash, and as much
money when Professor Moser shall have reported that he has made a successful experi-
ment between Washington & Baltimore, as far as to render the probability of
it no longer doubtful, he will relinquish to me all claim to the United States
with an addition that he be represented from all existing agreements between him and other proprietors; and if such an arrangement be effected,
I could not likely for myself, or by the opinion of a friend, obtain of
him his part of the Telegraph in France, being so to say 3/8th -- that he
would then be out of the concern entirely. Mr Smith
does not mention to me his offer with any idea of his opinion as to the
value or success of the invention, but I infer that he feels it would be a fatal
relation that to him have become incompatible. -- While on the other hand,
the time has been when the concern would have in done him to withdraw,
I have 15 days from 2 of April to accept his proposition, all of which I should
have a reasonable time, if that were not enough. -- Now I do not think I
can gain a company here to take it up -- but I thought I might as well let you
know that Dean has Mr Smith put, as you may have found it out
you would like it or not it, I think could all together this -- and if so
please let me know -- I have the modest done -- and I should

know that you will not use it to my advantage --
Yours respectfully
David Bunker

Prof: S. F. B. Morse
Dear Sir,
Yours of 10th and I have
received, and pleased to hear that my "Tele-
graphic dispatch" was understood.
I have read with great pleasure the articles
on your Telegraph experiments which no
doubt is satisfactory to your friends.
We are looking anxiously for the comple-
tion of your line to this City.
I called on Dr. Dunbar to day but was
unsuccessful in seeing him - I expect to
visit him tomorrow, and shall present
respects to D.C.
I will be in Washington on Monday
morning next, and it will afford me pleas-
ure to meet you.
Very respectfully
Your faithful Servt
Henry J. Rogers
P.S. When you visit this City, I can be
found at the ticket office of Baltimore
& Ohio Rail Road; & any communication
from Washer left with Mr. Stehmins or either
of the Conductors will be forwarded to me.

My dear Sir Baltimore April 16th 1844,
Goods of yesterday is received, and with
it was in my power to wake up some of our people here
to what I really think would be benefit them; but they came
different from many other business men, and only use
when it is too late, & behind the age, I presume without
out my accomplishing the sale of all, I can make no arrangement with Mr S for a part, - How would it
answer for you to write some of your friends in New York, stating
as you may deem practicable that there may be an opportunity to obtain through one a seat of Mr S - claim in
the State - I wish it was so that you could have 2 or 3 days,
I have forwarded your letter to Bragman, it
will probably reach there in a week or 10 days, the chance for
sending thither from him is good - When you have such occasion you must command me here & I will attend to it.
I had very much some information, that a
Mr Knowles, a clerk, or rather the person who conducts
visitors about the room containing models of Machinery,
in the Patent office - bring on the first floor to the left as we
enter the building from the street - can impart - I had
a machine made for splitting & shaving out hoops from
hoop poles - and Mr H in conversation told me how it could
be made - also said there was a model in the Office of one
that would answer, and gave me the name, (name
that I have written this letter (paying my postage) but have
not yet sent to you)
received no answer. so that I must give that up -- and
am trying to have one made here, and should be
very much obliged if Mr Knowles would proceed out on so
some kind of a draft according to his views as to what
need -- size of knife. If the knife should move through
the wood or the wood into the knife I am a stranger
to Mr Knowles. I probably you may be also an acquaintance
with him -- but if it be not incompatible with the rules, I do
not know but it might be imparted to you through your
friend Mr Ellsworth -- I would remark that since
Mr Knowles seemed to understand at once independent of
anything in the office, what was wanted -- if you can
obtain this for me I shall be under an additional
obligation.
I am sending glad to hear that your improvement
appears so encouraging -- and that your perseverance
and patience will accomplish what you desire.
Mr King says there will be some lead on the
way soon -- if no order come with it, perhaps I
as well put it away cheap as I can, & be doing
as of opportunity presents -- but I shall probably be
the pleasant spring you soon --
Yours truly
David Burtank

Washington, D C,
Sir.
I take the liberty of addressing you
in the purpose of requesting a favor in behalf of my brother,
Richard W Hattard. He is now in Boston engaged in painting
and teaching and we are desirous of obtaining business here
for him in the instruction of a school in which a vacancy
exists. The only obstacle of any moment to our obtaining the
situation for him is the want of testimonials as to his qualifications
for the post which we are afraid we should not have
sufficient time to obtain if we write to him in regard to them.
I have therefore taken the liberty of requesting your kind
services in the matter by giving me your opinion in such
form as you see proper so as to be applicable to the purpose
we have in view. He has devoted himself entirely to drawing
& painting since he left you and has been for the last 8 months
engaged in teaching those arts in Boston. If you think you
can meet our wishes on this subject we shall regard it as
a very great favor.
As the urgency is somewhat pressing may I request so far
as to request as early a reply as your engagement will permit.
Very respectfully yours
Samuel G B Morel

New York April 26th 1844
My Dear Sir.
The first thought which occurred to me on the morning after our late
mid- pol election was the pleasure with which
you would hear the results of that election.
During the campaign, also, your name was
the subject of frequent mention among our
old and tried friends; and I often endeavored
to induce the Judicating Committee, late in
the month, to say that some of the men of the
day were not such as to recognize the long
arduous and faithful services of the best friends
of the principles at issue; and the recent loss born
respecting those friends having told the National
American Party etc! It is true, no respectable
or high minded person has thus demanded him
self, but the story having been put in circulation
by Byett and one or two others, it was in
justification eliculated to our prejudice. It was
also said that I had written a letter from
Albany stating that I had changed my sentiments
in relation to American principles. This
of course, was as malicious as it was false.
None of these malicious things, however bad
they affect with their poison, have you yourself
ever read the history of the party. But since this
call was made on me and desired that a complete revision
of these things should be made, and they
proposed a meeting of that party for that purpose. Now, I wish you to pay, in a letter
addressed to Mr Joseph A. Davis, Secretary of
the Executive Committee, that nothing of the
kind, or any intention of it, was made or thought of, unless by Long Meadgett, Green or Savage; that the friends of the party and principles adhered to
to our position with constant devotion and
ab quietisatis. And, as regards myself,
you know I will well my own closing devotion
to the cause and my great sacrifices in it, from
first to last; and this you will here mention. Also, if you please
My personal and American friend has
continually solicited me to take office under the
powers that he; and since both of the parties, all
well as I can judge, are warmly in favor of this,
for no such reasons as those I have mentioned
have at all affected me with that proportion of
the party which I have, accordingly, been actively
engaged during the whole of your party. Among the things
I have written, besides editing the Time Tribune,
has been a pamphlet, which being issued just prior
to the election, had a great effect, I am flatly obliged to
the officers named to secure
me from Police justice, or death of the
Board of Aldermen. The former being present,
several letters from both members of Congress and
the most respectable of our citizens, will be handed
the members elect of the Common Council; and if
it is perfectly agreeable, I would be pleased with one from
you, as to my capabilities and my unswerving allegiance
and sacrifices in the party. I would be glad of this
in receipt, to them a favor of the Aldermen elect. You
favor me this particular with gratitude, and you may make
it as strong as you please.
I remain, truly, your friend
J.D. Chapin

Dear Sir - I have delayed writing for a few days,
in the hope that I might find an opportunity to use the
same and as soon as I could not do any better
with it than as bad - I have offered to him where
able, if there was anything to be made on it, in dispute
shape over the price of land they would buy it - and
I find that land commands as high a price here as in any
other place - Mr. Avery laid some of it down for the
purchase of knowing if it would answer for water:- yesterday
he told me he finds it will not answer for it -
After making up about 10,000 of the first sale - 2 1/8th
I think I shall be able to get 3d for all the remainder
knowing your anxiety I desire to turn every thing to the
best possible account - I have him very particular in
regard to the sale - and as time is considerable
of an amount now ready to be taken away, perhaps
I may as well be disposing of it - I have made a
sketch of an offer that you may know how we stand - the
fight of the two last loads has not yet come in which will
probably be about the same as the other - 32 1/2 barrels
of Alphaltein got to come probably about 13d - One
barrel of Algeafatin was forwarded to you on the 30
of April, which hope you have received - I shall continue to pay the rent on the House in Whitney Street
until you
otherwise doubt -- I have the accounts all made
out & if you wish will forward them any time, but
I though I might as well drop a line to you with
a view to school myself -- Mr. King says he is
progressing very well and it is certainly pleasant to
see your assistant manifest so much interest for your
succeff --
Yours truely
David Bunker.

Washington May 7th 1844
Dear Sidney,
I have a moment just before retiring to
bed very much fatigued, to write a few lines.
This morning my young friend Miss Annie G.
Elsworth left Washington with her cousin Mr.
Goodrich Smith for New York to pass a week or
two in the city. She will be at Mr. Manning's
No. 107 Second Avenue, 4 doors above 5th Street
I gave her a letter to Sister Catherine, and for my
sake and her father's & mother's I wish you and
Sister would become acquainted with her, and
particularly my Susan if she arrives in New York
soon, as I expect she will be with you in a day or
two at latest.* Let me know when Susan and
the Charles arrive, for if they come within the
next fortnight, I think I can contrive to run
on and pay a visit of two or three days, unless
my marplot Smith should prevent again, as he
is likely to do if he comes on here. As yet there
is no settlement of that matter, and he seems de-
termined (in his nos.) to be as ugly as he can and
defeat all application for an appropriation if
I am to have the management of it; he chases
like a wild bear, but when he finds he can effect
nothing by such a temper, self interest may often
him into terms. — You will see by the papers
I had a letter from Susan yesterday in which she says she
shall be in New York by willin' to leave Washington, and it is
your four weeks.
that the Telegraph is in successful operation for
22 miles to the Junction of the Annapolis road
with the Balt. & Wash. road. The nomination
of Mr Frelinghuysen as V. Pres. was written, sent
on, and the receipt acknowledged back, in 2 minutes
and 1 second, a distance of 44 miles.— The news was
spread all over Washington, one hour & 4 minutes
before the cars containing the news by express trains.
In about a fortnight I hope to be in Baltimore
and a communication will be established between
the two cities.—
Good bye I am almost asleep from overtax-
tion so course abrupt closing. Love to Catherine
Hinley, and the Children and to Richard, Louisa and
family.—
Your affectionate brother
Sam J. D. Mosby
P.S. I sent you a few days ago one of Mr. Ellsworth
Reports. Did you get it?

Dear Sir
Baltimore May 10th 1844
I wrote on Saturday regarding the sale of the
lead pipe, and was in hopes to have the pleasure of a reply by
the return of mail. I have an opportunity to sell this
lead pipe, as had - as I stated in my last to you - but
as it is different from what we had hoped, I thought I
would rather consult you again before parting with it -
I find it impossible to sell it for any thing but lead, and
have offered every inducement I can to purchase it but
it is some other purpose but it being so small I think they
decline - Mr Avery says he put down a pipe
200 feet long for drawing off the waste water, of a fall
of 8 or 9 feet I found the tube too small, consequently
took it up - put down a pipe of Fathoms pipe
which he makes answer the purpose.
I will thank you for any advice you may
please to communicate, although as you remarked you
only expect what the market will pay.
Mr Avery is industriously at work, I came out this
morning - and he remarked, as I am writing you, that he
finds in own hacking, much bad wire that is barred &
bodily wound & he has to cut out but his work ofspan
the progress will.
Yours Truly
David P. Barbour

New York May 15. 1844.
Next September I shall be, I hope, at Milan. The scientific Congress of
Italy will meet there on the 12th of that month. I intend to present to it
an Account of the Sentimentary System of the U.S. if you, dear
Professor, are willing to help me, I will lay before it also an account
of your wonderful Telegraph. I think that the description of the
process which led you to the application of the magnetic power to
telegraphic purposes, and of the telegraph itself, would prove highly
interesting and acceptable to my countrymen. I am willing to do my
utmost in this business, but my utmost will amount to very little
indeed: for I have no knowledge of the scientific principles of
language of your electromagnetism, a mechanism. If you can not
spare time enough to draw up a full account, tell me where
I may find the materials out of which a competent person
could make one, & give me the necessary direction.
I write, Professor, because I am not certain whether I shall be able
to come to Washington to see you, before my departure. I am
trying now to collect here money enough to begin the business
of the Christian Alliance; then I shall visit for the same
object New-Haven, Hartford, Boston, & Providence. I have
strong hopes to succeed in this pecuniary mission, & I am
certain that the experiment will be gratifying to all our
friends.
I intend also to publish in Italy a Statistical Account of the U.S.
for 1843. To this end I have collected many documents; but
99532
the most important ones, those of the present Congress, are
wanting. I am told that the Clerks of the two Houses of Congress,
& of the Executive Departments have always spare copies of
all the printed Messages, Reports of the Heads of the
several Departments, of the several Committees of Congress,
etc. etc., & that Members of Congress can get them
for their friends, etc. etc.
I have no acquaintance with M. C. I suppose you have with
many; and could you not make use of it in my behalf?2
could you not get for me copies of all the said Messages,
Reports, Accounts, Statements, etc. of the President, Sec-
retaries, Committees, Departments, Public Institutions, etc.
that have any bearing on the Statistics of the United
States for the year 1843, 44?
I read some time ago that a Mr. Zadok Pratt, I believe, had
prepared some very valuable Statistics; this man, if you
have access to him, might be requested to make a collec-
-tion and selection of such papers as I may want. I
have read also that Mr. Ellsworth of the Patent Office
presented a very interesting Report to
You, dear Professor, may wonder at my indirection in mak-
-ing so many requests. But I am on one hand very
anxious to turn to some account my voyage to Europe,
on the other I have no means to do myself what I
want, & must be done in order to be able to carry out my
designs. Hence it is a moral necessity that I should seek
for assistance. And where must I look to for it, if I do
not look to my friends, to Italy's, to Christianity's?
As this letter will not be the last, and it is long enough, I hope.
Pray God, that my exertions may be successful, as I do pray
that your health, & cheerfulness may never forsake you; my
dear friend, addio.
Your
P. L. Barynemi

Washington.

edition of at least 5000. copies of d'Aubigné's History of the Reformation. I have
already translated, into Italian, the first volume; and shall complete the rest within
sea. 2. Do you see a large edition of Mr. Civi's History of the Nof in Italy. This

Washington May 27th 1844
Sir,
I have the honor to request from the Dept.
advice, in respect to my duty as Sup't of the U.S.
Telegraphs, touching the claim of Levi Bartlett for
damages alleged to be sustained by him under his Contract
with the Govt for trenching.
Mr. F. O. J. Smith the Assignee of the Contract
in question particulars strongly insists that I as Superintendent
now the power to refer to the judgment and arbitration of any Disinterested men
have it in my power to settle this claim, and that
refrain from application to the Department it would be
injustice.
I enclose a copy of questions which I have
hardly omitted to ask Mr. Smith for his opinion, and
which gives in his own words the matter received from the Department I cannot find that
I have any power of this kind, Virginia Smith . In the letter of the Dept. under date of 29th Dec.
1843. The Bartlett "Contract is declared to be vitally at
an end," and I am directed "to advertise for offers to make
the trenching required," and "to open negotiations with
Mr. Bartlett for adjusting the amount of damages he has sustained."
"By reference to the letter of the Department
of Janr. 9. 1844, the course pursued by me for ascertaining
this claim has been as follows: I had the claim submitted by Mr. Smith, and
who chose to make his own representations to the Dept."
I am instructed in the same letter in these words, "You
must expressly understand to Congress." -- In compliance
with these instructions I have endeavored to ascertain the
amount of damages, and the result is in the Report I had the
honor to transmit Feb. 23. 1844 -- Mr.
Smith laid his claim before Congress, and it is undergoing
investigation by the Com't of Claims of the Senate.
I respectfully request, therefore, to know if
you understand that you are only instructed to
inquire into and ascertain the amount of damages which may
have been sustained by the parties referred to, and as not authorized to
make any statement for the parties, as in demarcation for location of any trench
or on the part of the Govt a line can only be made by Congress
and
if the Supreme Court appears to liquidate claim for
damages
any discretion allowed me to settle this claim, and if so in
what form it can be presented. I feel satisfied that the
matter was wholly in the hands of the Committee of Claims
and of Congress.
Very Respectfully, J. D. S.
to the Hon. M. Clintock, Secretary of the Treasury
ad interim.
S. F. B. Morre

Baltimore May 28th 1844
Professor S. J. B. Morse
Dear Sir:
The electric tele-
-graph being now in successful operation,
you will find it necessary to appoint an
assistant at Baltimore, provided Mr Vail
leaves this for the station at Washington City.
Will you do the favor to inform me what
time you will require my service, and the
probable amount of salary allowed by the
government.
My engagement with you, will govern
some negotiations now pending between
Stockton Falls, and myself in reference
to my agency for them.
The service I now perform of being up
at 12 o'clock at night waiting the arrival
of the Eastern Mail, and dispatching
the Southern Mail at 2 o'clock in the morning,
is rather too arduous for a married
man; inasmuch as the duty has to be performed
nightly; which is one cause
for my wishing to change my situation.
My fondness for the Science of Telegraph
is another and the most important one.
I think it advisable for me to practice
the signals under yours or Mr Vails direc-
tion. Cannot we succeed in getting Con-
gress to organize a telegraphic Corps with
you as chief.
Very respectfully
Your obedient Servant
Henry J. Rogers

Illinois City, May 29, 1844
My dear Mr.
I have by the papers of this morning that
your magnetic telegraph is now in successful operation
between Washington and Chicago. I hasten to acquaint
you on occasion of your complete success in this most
inpatient and interesting invention, and to add the
expression of my warmest wishes that what has been so
succcessfully commenced, may be continued by the govern-
ment, until the main lines of our railroads throughout the
lands may be applied with the telegraph. If so I hope it
may give you an interesting and profitable employment
for years to come.
We have recently commenced knocking at no
54 Bond St. a short distance from Mrs. Bruce, who
will remain at 35 Broadway. And as you must be
fagged out with your duties anxieties and labour, and
ought to have a little relaxation, I beg that you
will pack your trunk and make an visit for as
many weeks as you may find it agreeable. Mrs B.
will probably drain half of your time, but that is our
little between ourselves.
I sent your book according to the request of
the N. A. Academy to N.York, and much to my Surprise
a few weeks afterwards received it back again.
It was only glad to welcome it back again, but it
was quite unspectable -- The best therefore remaining
in my possession subject to your devotions -- Is there
not a copy of the Critic? Anything on Sale in
New York --
I have been amuring myself with recently by copying
a very secret subject from Carlo Dolci "the Savion in the Garden"
I think it from a very small engraving, enlarging it eight
or ten times more than the print -- The subject is one
of the most graceful and lovely Confronting, which I ever
saw, and for a mere amateur, I think I have made
quite a tolerable Copy --
With the kind wishes of all your relations Friends
in Utica, I remain
Very Truly
Your
P.R. Walker

Dear Sidnus,
You will see by the Papers, how
great success has attended the first efforts of
the Telegraph. That sentence of Annie Ellsworth's was divinely intited, for it is in my thoughts
day and night, "What hath God wrought." It is his
work, and he alone could have carried me thus
far through all my trials, and enabled me
to triumph over the obstacles physical and
moral which opposed me; Not unto us, not
unto us, but to thy name O Lord be all the
praise! — I begin to fear now the effects of public fame, lest it should kindle that pride of heart
and self sufficiency, which dwells in my own, as
well as in others' hearts and which is so ready to be inflamed by the slightest spark of praise. I do indeed feel gratified, but I rejoice with fear, and I desire that a sense of dependence upon and increased obligation to the
Grain of every good and perfect gift, may keep me humble, and circumspect.
The Conventions at Baltimore happened most opportune for the display of the powers of the Telegraph, especially as it was the medium of correspondence between the Convention and the first candidate elect for the
Vice Presidency. The enthusiasm of the
crowd before the window of the Telegraph Room
in the Capitol, was excited to the highest pitch, at
the announcement of the nomination of the Pres-
idential Candidate, and the whole of it afterwards
summitted upon the Telegraph. They
gave the Telegraph 3 cheers, and I was called to
make my appearance at the window, when three
cheers were given by some hundreds present, composed
mainly of members of Congress. — Such is the feeling in Con-
gress that many tell me, they are ready to grant any
thing. Even the most inveterate opponents, have changed
to admirers and one of them Hon. Cave Johnson, who sat
in the last session by associating my system animal magnetism with the
many tricks of animal magnetism, came to me and said, "Sir
I give in, it is an astonishing invention." When I see all this
and such enthusiasm everywhere manifested, and contrast
the present with the past season of darkness and almost
despair, have I not occasion to exclaim "What hath God wrought?"
Surely none but He who has all hearts in his hands, and
turns them as the rivers of water are turned, could so
have brought light out of darkness. sorrow may con-
tinue for a night but joy cometh in the morning.—
Pray for me then, my dear brother, that I may have a
heart to praise the Great Deliverer, and in future
when discouraged or despairing be enabled to remember
His past mercy, and in full faith rest all my cares on
him who careth for us.—
private Mr. L. still embarrasses the progress of the in-
vention, by his stubbornness, but there are indications
of giving way, mainly I fear because he sees his premium
interest in doing so, and not from any sense of the gross
injury he has done me. I pray God for a right spirit
in dealing with him.
June 2d.
I enclose a letter received a few days ago
from Mr. Fisk of Concord N.H. which please
see answered. It seems a little singular that Mr.
L. should select Charles & Finley, and leave out
Susan. Ask Susan if she recollects any offence
ever given to Mr. Livmore? She was a
singular woman in many respects, and
took offence at me at one time, which I
know not that she ever forgave, and which as Susan
will tell you was as causeless as any thing well could be.
But I hope she was prepared for a better world. She was
certainly a kind hearted and benevolent woman.
I have just received Susan's letter of the 30th. I am
glad to hear her health is improving. If she thinks best to
go down to Staten Island and be at the Wickhams I should
like it well enough. Mr. Wickham owes me $20. and when
I was last in N.York spoke to me about it. Perhaps it would
be agreeable to him to pay me in this way, and Susan can
settle with me. Susan says she thinks my expectations were
not realized in regard to Charlie my grandson, and that it
made her sometimes sad; Tell her to dispel all such sadness for
99588
they were more than realized. She had led me to believe
he was not a handsome boy, whereas I think him a very
handsome child, and have boasted of him as such, but
I think his disposition which is of most ca-
lculated to his advantage and his appearance to have a fine disappointment
sequence. I tell her I would write, but she will see
that Congress has but a few days more of session, and I
must devote every moment to get my matters through in
season. Love to all, to Richards family and your

from Wash. to Bath, but see no notice of it.
Richard E. Morse Esq.

Lix - I take the liberty of handing you
one of my Circulars, by which you will see, that the
Natural Asphaltum rock, is a cement completely, impervious
to air and water, and is universally used in Europe &
also in the United States, for works which require protection
from air and dampness - Therefore I have no hesitation
in recommending the Asphaltum to you, as a material
for building Pipes to serve as a Cover for your Magnetic
Telegraph which will be the Cheapest, and the most
durable material you can use for that purpose -
I believe that the Asphaltum has been used
in England for the same purpose - I refer you to the
Engineers mentioned in my circular, and particularly to
the Chief Engineer Col J. G. Lotten in Washington, who
has published a Book on the subject of Bitumen, called
"Papers on practical Engineering, Bitumen, its varieties, pro-
perties, and uses" - and by calling on Col Lotten, you
can easily get a copy of it, which will give you all
the necessary information on the subject.
The price of the Asphaltum is $32. per 2000 lbs
and the mineral Tar $6. per 100 lbs - The proportion of
Tar necessary for working the Natural Asphaltum
is 12 lbs of Tar to 100 lbs of Asphaltum and 5 lbs
of this mixture will cover one square foot of half
an inch in thickness - from this statement you
can easily learn, how much material will be
required to a running foot of pipe of any
thickness - if you should decide on trying this article,
I shall feel pleasure in giving you a detailed account as
regards the mode of working it - hoping to hear from
you soon I remain
Your most obedient Servt
John Lowitz
NATURAL ASPHALTUM.
The ASPHALT ROCK is a Bituminous Limestone, found only in the mines of Seysel and Val Du
Travers, and is pulverized by subjecting it to the action of heat. By mixing with it ten per cent. of Min-
eral Tar, it forms a Cement of great adhesion and durability, and is completely impervious to air and water.
It was first adopted by the War Department in France, and is now universally used in Europe for the
following purposes.
First, In building FORTIFICATIONS—to preserve Casements which are covered with earth, to prevent
dampness from penetrating the walls, and to keep the basement rooms dry.
Second. To keep Powder Magazines, and Arsenal walls and floors dry.
Third. For RAIL ROADS—the wood used for the support of the iron rail, if covered with a thin coat of
this Asphaltum, will be preserved from decay.
Fourth. In constructing new buildings by the river side, and docks, where the ground is liable to inunda-
tion from spring tides or any pressure of water, the cellars can be made water tight by a brick floor laid in
Asphaltum. Old cellars can also be made water tight in this way.
Fifth. It can be used to great advantage in warm climates upon ICE HOUSES, and renders them air tight.
Sixth. For foundations in general—a layer or two around the building will preserve the masonry as well as
good work.
Seventh. For CISTERNs and TANKS—a coating of this Cement will preserve the water clear and good.
Eighth. For TERRACES and ROOFS—also for Garden and Side-walks, and Street Pavements, Canals,
Bridges, Piers, Wharfs, Baths, Aqueducts, Sewers, Market and Slaughter Houses, and in all cases where it
is desirable to preserve Wood Work and Masonry, and keep out vermin.
Ninth. To fix Iron Clamers in rocks, instead of with lead, to bind masonry work with wood or rock, cast-
ing ornaments of all descriptions, and for enclosing Iron, Copper, Lead, and other metallic pipes, to prevent
corrosion and decay.
The Subscriber has spent considerable time and money to introduce the Asphalt Rock into this Country,
and is now prepared to execute orders to any extent, furnishing the material and superintending the work
himself. It has been used upon the principal fortifications in this country, and Public Buildings at
Washington. And the Subscriber refers to the following Engineers who have seen the application of this
Cement, and who are satisfied that it is superior to any other known material for the above purposes.

use for telegraphic purposes, by

New York June 1st 1854
My Dear Sir
It is now something since I have heard from
you directly though I hear from your works through the public
prints that you are pushing the Telegraph more vigorously.
The impression in N.Y. is very strong that it will be extended until
it shall spread every important key town in the U.S. My Brother
has just returned from Boston and tells me that it was the most
frequent topic of conversation wherever he went.
It seems you have finally got to Baltimore. Did the appropriation
hold out and what is the condition of the enterprise before Congress?
that is, what sort of a proposition have you made, and what pro-
gress has it made in Congress? I am the more anxious to know as
I have recently received a lengthy communication from Mr. Riggs
attempting to vindicate his own acts relative to the Telegraph and
showing wherein he blames you. I at first thought I would include
to you the communication but on reflection decided otherwise. I will give
in brief his complaint. It is that 1. you will not come to any terms
to settle his claim against the government in the trenching contracts
2. you will not determine even on the mode by which you may
ascertain the amount of any payment which he the contractor ought to
receive and which you as Superintendent ought to apply for
3d. that you have referred him over to the Sec'y of the Treasury for
payment and he cannot to his fault – that the Secretary, without notifying
Mr S. had decided on the case and reported it to government.
Mr S. goes on to say that in consequence of this state of affairs
Can any one blame me for refusing to enter into any new engage-
ments concerning the Telegraph until the old claim is secured?
He also states that he has proposed to leave the whole subject
to the 3 Lieutenants Avery Cornell Tail and himself
to abide by their decision.
May I ask how far will his opposition under present 400
flagrants influence government's action in the funding application,
and whether his refusal to participate in such application can
be legal course put on injunction on the proceedings.
May I ask what is the substance of your application, to what dis-
tract does it extend and what amount is asked for from government?
Have you in case an appropriation should be made fixed on your
assistant or assistant? Do you suppose I should be needed,
I do not make application to influence your mind in this matter
in any manner. I know all your kindness of heart to do favors
for others has resulted in personal demeriture to yourself, I wish
you to understand I do not desire to come into the Telegraph to turn
ear of employment away one you already have, nor to come
under any circumstances unless I can be of as much benefit
to the Telegraph as the Telegraph is to me.
I am still engaged in my Sugar of Lead works at present very
much enlarged. I have my brother with me who acts as foreman
We have 2 Buildings 100ft by 25., one 70 by 25., one 30 by 25, besides a
shed or two and are making 800 lbs of lead and shall soon make 1400-
suppose you should need me what salary would you think of giving
and how long would it continue?
I ask these things that I may better understand your views.
One thing I will add while it is on my mind, Mr. S. says he thinks
"I feel that under the impressions which a reliance on Prof. Hordis's
supposed knowledge of Electic Currents gave rise to great injustice was done to Prof. Simon in accusing him of negligence in attempting the wire line and laid upon their failure to work satisfactorily in fields & I design so far as I have been thus made
the instrument of injustice by reliance upon erroneous theories, to make ample amends to him whenever an opportunity shall offer" &c. &c.
I do not write these things to find fault but to let you know what is going on - I have the same confidence in your sense of justice that I have always had.
Dr F has behaved very badly towards me, not only has he robbed me of all my plans & continuances for the manufacture of Sugar of Lead but in order to justify his glaring and palpable misconduct he has represented to his friends that I had promised him a partnership in the manufacture for the aid and improvements he had afforded and the only hold he had on me was to rob me of my improvements to build up himself.
The first and only time I ever said anything about this to Fraternal relation to my factory or business was when I learned you had discharged him and then I wrote F stating that it was possible I might be able to make some arrangement with him to take charge of my factory and accordingly when I reached home last Christmas I went directly to see Dr F to profess an arrangement when I was repulsed with a "Much obliged I can do better"
I shall be glad to hear from you soon
Respectfully
Ed Lisle

Dr. C. J. Smith Esq.
Dear Sir,
Mr. Vail and myself as proprietors of
the Telegraph in common with yourself have given to
the Memoranda of agreement which you handed in yesterday,
such consideration as the limited time we had at command
would allow. And the better to understand its legal
bearings, we took council of a legal gentleman in Baltimore
M. Latrobe, who has promised to send down by the
morning train a draft of such a memorandum as will
embody our views. A transaction of this kind we do not wish
to act upon hastily, and the press of other engagements at a time
when what we have to do must be done quickly, compels us to
propose some simple mode of promoting our general interests
without interfering more than is necessary with our individual
preferences. I have a great repugnance to the management of
such a contract as is proposed, even in its most unobjectionable
form, and while I would accord to enter into such contracts
with the Govt. as you and it can for the mutual benefit of the
proprietors arrange, we wish ourselves to be free from its
moral and as well as pecuniary responsibilities. Now can not this be brought about by the adoption of one
of the following propositions.
1st We propose to sell to the Government the whole
Patent, for a definite sum.
2d We will sell to Genl. the use of the Telegraph
for its own purposes, leaving to us the right to
sell rights to others.
3d We will sell rights at so much per mile,
4th Let Government go on and construct, and
leave it to Genl. to say what compensation shall be given
us for the use of it.
Very Respectfully
Yr Obser
S.J. Morse

Dear Sir
I saw Mr. Stella of Solomons on
his return, & enquired as to the nitrous acid, he
does not seem to understand what state it is in,
or what it may be considered or called, after using it
for your purpose -- but will like to know --
I said to him -- that the last is too weak, here
replies, that the last is of the same as this other for
market sent, and is of the usual fair "commercial
strength," & he can increase it 1/2 as strong again perhaps
more so -- for 20 to 25c while he thinks might
suit your purpose very well --
If it will be convenient, please let me
know at what sum you would be willing to sell
your part of the interest, being on -- & in the
Telegraph, as I might by having a reasonable
time, accomplish what you desire, as well as
benefit myself a little -- also if you please and an
opportunity presents that I might some how be useful in future
operations -- I shall be grateful if you will bear me in mind,
so far as you may deem suitable -- Yours truly
David B. Braden,

Dear Sir,
The bill you drew, I find is liable to
the following objections, and therefore a different
bill had better be drawn, and I am willing that
Mr. Choate or any other Honorable Member should
draft a bill to be presented, against which I
will state no objections.
I am advised by my Counsel at Baltimore
that each Proprietor becomes liable under the
contract you have drawn as a Partner, and
therefore, as I am not willing to assume the
such an obligations I am opposed to signing the
Contract.
I am willing to sell the whole right of the
Telegraph, or I am willing to sell the right
to construct and use it for a given distance
at a certain rate per mile and as the Govt. are not
likely in your opinion now to pay us the full
value this last may be the best.
1. It compels the Govt. to contract with the
Proprietors of Telegraphs for the Construction
of the Telegraph, as well as for the use of
the right (of the proprietors) -
2. It makes one Superintendent, while he is
also Contractor, and owns one half of the Telegraph.
3. No sum is definitly appropriated from the
hearing, but the P.M. General is authorized
to take money ad libitum for the object.
4. No sum is fixed for the right to use the
Telegraph.
5. The proprietors may sell to companies & individuals
viduals, and yet a penalty of imprisonment for
years is annexed for a slight damage to private
property by enacting that the penalty shall attach
to all times of Telegraph hereafter made in the U.S. §
6. To prevent all competition arising from bids and
while the work may be done as appears by the estimate
of Mr. Cornell for $192. per mile the proprietors
might demand a much larger sum over and above
a liberal compensation for the right.
Now, however, objecting you may have sufficient
reason to satisfy your own mind in relation
to the soundness of your own views, you cannot expect
that they will be placed before Congress and not
undergo the most rigid scrutiny. You know
I objected in the outset to any such proposition as
would in the short time in which Congress now
have at Command, lead to discussion, and so defeat the
bill. The straight forward simple way is undoubtedly
best for all concerned.

Respectfully yours,

Philadelphia June 10th 1844
Professor F B Morse
Lincoln
I have been writing to
hear of the intention of the Telegraphic association
as regards the disposal of the funds to the government
from Alfred. But have been disappointed and
I would therefore desire you to inform me if it is
consistent with your feelings and the interest
of all concerned. (not without) that project is now
on foot and if its ultimate success is more possible
you may rest assured that although apparently
not with you my heart is there -- In my presence
at Philadelphia I lost all of my available property
and I have lifted up a pretty good heart until this year
when and other circumstances have broken up for me
to such an extent that sometimes I feel I would rather
not have been born -- The connection with the Telegraph
now is my only hope -- and hence the intense anxiety
I feel is occasioned -- You will please excuse me for saying
so much of myself -- and please do not mention it
to anyone except to and to him I have never told so
much as is contained in this letter --
I would add that although I feel reluctant to mention it
that if nothing but an appropriation is made
of a situation could be given to me for the purpose
of laying it down I would be very glad to have
the offer of it. if in your opinion I could perform the duties required.
I am through the Journal of Commerce heard somewhat
of the general operation of the Telegraph but not enough
to satisfy. I would have written it but want of funds prevented me. I would there take the opportunity to express
to you my gratitude for the kindnesses which you have
extended to me in way of employment and I hope
that he has not been backward in doing his part
in the laborious task which you have had to endure.
I know that as to honesty he knows nothing else.
and from what I have heard from him. I know
his whole existence was in the object which you have
attained.
I am the Servt

6 o'clock Tuesday.
Dear Rail
I have but a moment to say that your faith as
a Christian will be tried as well as my own, in the blow
up which has taken place. I go before the Committee
this morning. Mr. S. Smith has written me a passion-
ate letter accusing my friend Mr. Ellsworth in the most
offensive terms. Depend upon it, such feeling cannot
cover any but the darkest designs upon us all. I am
sick at heart and can only find relief in that refuge,
which in the hour of seeming hopelessness, has appeared
so often to turn sorrow to joy. Let Him be your hope
and trust, and all will come right. I have no fear
for the result. No time to add
Truly Yours
S.D.B.Morris

6 o'clock
To
Dear Vail -- (at City Baltimore)
I have but a moment to say I am faithful as a
Christian will be tried, as well as my son, in the blow up
which has taken place. I go before the Court this morning.
Mr S. has written me a passionate letter, accusing my friend
Mr Elsworth in the most offensive terms. Defend upon it
such feeling cannot cover any but the darkest designs, upon
us all. I am sick at heart, & can only find relief in that
refuge, which in the hour of seeming hopelessness, has appeared
so often to have done me joy. Let this be your hope & trust,
& all will come out right. I have no fear for the result.
No time to add. Truly Yours - S P B More.

The proprietors of Morse's Electric Mag-
netic Telegraph feel grateful to bankers
for its past liberality in testing the practi-
cability to the satisfaction of the public.
The proprietors did not need such
a test to satisfy themselves merely.
In consideration of that liberality, they
have felt under obligations to tender the
right of extending the Telegraph to NewYork,
to the Government, before yielding to any
of the opportunities offered of placing it
in the charge of private associations.
But many years of expense and
toil have been spent in perfecting it, and
the proprietors cannot afford to suffer
a year to be lost for the decision of Congress
on its acceptance or non-acceptance
by the Government, to the exclusion of
private associations.
Their motto is obscure obscure . If
bankers is not prepared to extend it, by
advancing only the means of construction, the
proprietors cannot be blamed for suffer-
ing the enterprise of individuals to die
to, though its effect upon the revenues
of the P. O Department, be disastrous.
It requires no argument, nor complication
of facts, to demonstrate, that for the purposes
of carrying intelligence, neither horse power,
nor steam power, nor the enterprise of private
express riders, nor the best efforts of the
P. O Department, cannot compete

about even private expenses
cannot be the damage of the P. O.

The proprietors have no other

If Congress shall elect to make

at liberty to accomplish such their
damages they desire in the enterprise

with a serious wound in my leg from a fall, and a probability
of a long confinement which must be my apology for not answering
your letter immediately on its receipt. I am unable at this moment
to reply to your queries. The proprietors of the Telegraph are
dispersed one of them being in Maine, and I shall be compelled
to wait for answers from them previous to giving you
definitely the answers you desire. I will write to them
however immediately and hope in the course of a few
days to be able to give you all the information
you wish.
In the mean time
Believe me with great respect
Y. Mothens

Dear Prof. Thomson
I arrived safely this
morning and in about 2 hours after had
the car unloaded and Mr. Avery is now
cleaning up the dirty sines and putting
them in order (all that were dirty) -- While
I was very much engaged this morning I got
Mr Burbank to inquire about the copper dies
Mr. McKin will furnish the dies at 50cts
per lb. cut out, which is 5 cts advance on
sheet copper. This would make a great saving.
The holes in the centre Mr. McKin cannot do
But Mr Burbank can punch the holes at
a cost of $2 per day & $1.00 for a tool to punch the
holes. -- The labour will not I think exceed much
of over a day -- The acids is with Stabler & Lanby
and they will do what they can with it. Mr B
will take the acid elsewhere if SL & C will not do
the thing that's nice -- Mr Burbank has balls of
cotton thread and will do the best he can.
Mr Avery is extremely anxious to see his family
and would receive as a great favour of you
would grant him a furlough -- will you
be kind enough to drop a line as soon
as you can. I trust your leg is fast
improving and that soon I shall see
you hoping about as brisk as usual
I remain yours affectiony
Alfred Vail

S. S. B. Morse Esq
Dear Sir
I have been expecting you
in the City, but learned yesterday from
your British Sidney that you might not be
here for some time -- I have witnessed the
succes of your Telegraph with great gratifica-
tions, and most heartily congratulate you
on your perfect triumph -- It has secured
to you as much fame as you could de-
rive, and will bring you as much money
as will make you independent for
the rest of life -- I am domiciled with
my family in the family of your friend Doctor
Gale, and so far am only pleasantly situated -- I have conversed with him much
about the Telegraph, and he informs me
that he has a small interest in it, but
has given you a Carl Blanch for any arrangement for its disposal Which you may
think proper to make -- I did suppose
that your proposals to Congress would have received a final action, notwithstanding
ing the influence of the Evil genius, which
has presided over the Nation the State system.
But since it has failed for the time being,
it has thrust me that possibly you would
like to sell it, or the right to use it between
Baltimore and New York, and would construct
the same between the places for fair
consideration -- If you would do so, I
heard of some parties to whom I should
like to apply for the means, and if you
will give me terms, I will make the application
in such a way that if nothing comes
of it the matter shall not be known.
I suppose that the mail road companies would
allow it to be constructed through their lines
for moderate compensation. Had the Congress
voted it, construction that day, your calculation
as to procuring the right of way for
it -- If you would like to do any thing in
the premises, please say so by early mail
that you will construct the telegraph for
between the two places including or excluding
the expense of the right of way, and dilate it in
complette order for operation making the suitable
number of stations between the two places -- and
had much you will charge in
additional for an absolute and exclusive
right to use it between said places for the
term of the patent - My impression is, that
I could secure a company in a short time,
and have it completed before Congress
shall meet again - The money being
raised, how long would it take you
to complete the structure through the Ohio
distance? Please address me at 215-8th and
11th St.
I am very sincerely
Jenny S. Leonard

Washington June 23, 1844
My dear brother,
I am still in the bed, and from appearances I
am likely to be held here for many days, perhaps weeks. The
wound on the leg was worse than I at first supposed. It seems
slow in healing and has been much inflamed although now
yielding to remedies. My hope was to have spent some weeks
in New York, but it will now depend on the time of the healing
of my leg. The ways of God are mysterious, and I find prayer
answered in a way not at all anticipated. This accident as
we are apt to call it, I can plainly see is calculated to effect
many salutary objects. I needed rest of body and mind, after
my intense anxieties and excitations, and I might have neglected
it and so perhaps brought on prematurely disacle of both, but
I am involuntarily laid up, so that I must keep quiet, and
although the fall that caused my wound was painful at first
yet I have no severe pain with it now. But the principal
effect is doubtless intended to be of a spiritual character, and
I am afforded an opportunity of quiet reflection, on the wonderful
dealings of God with me. I cannot but constantly exclaim
What hath God wrought? When I look back upon the darkness
of the last winter, and reflect how at one time every thing seemed
hopeless, when I remember that all my associates in the enter-
prise of the Telegraph had either deserted me or were discouraged
and even Mr. Vail who has held fast to me from the beginning
felt like giving up, just in the deepest darkness of all, when I
remember that giving up all hope myself from any other
source that than his right arm, which brings Salvation, his salvation did
come in answer to prayer, Faith is strengthened, and did I not know
by too sad experience the deceitfulness of the heart, I should say that
it was impossible for me again to distrust or feel anxiety, and due anxiety
for the future. But he who knows the heart, knows its diseased, and
as the Good Physician, if we give ourselves unreservedly into his hands
to be cured, he will give that medicine which his perfect knowledge
of our case prescribes. - I am well aware that just now my principles
ring from one end of the country to the other, I cannot take up a paper
in which I do not find something to flatter the natural pride of the
heart. I have prayed, indeed, against it, I have asked for a right
spirit under a trial of a new character, for prosperity is a
trial, and our Saviour has denounced a woe on us "when all
men speak well of us," may it not then be in answer to this
prayer, that he shoots me up, to strengthen me against the temptations
which the praises of the world present, and so by meditation
on his dealings with me, and reviewing the way in which he has led
me, showing me my perfect helplessness without him, is preparing
to bless me with stronger Faith, and more unreserved trust in Him.
To Him, indeed belongs all the glory. I have had evidence enough
that without Christ I could do nothing, all my strength is there,
and I fervently desire to ascribe to him all the praise. -
I know not what is before me, nor would I feel any
joy for He who hath led me thus far will not now desert me. If
I am to have influence, increased influence, I desire to have it for
Christ, to use it for his cause; if wealth, for Christ, if more
knowledge, for Christ. I speak sincerely when I say, I fear pros-
perity, lest I should be proud and forget, whence it comes.
I send you a copy of Niles' Register which has a good
account of Telegraphs and of mine, but containing some errors
which ought to be corrected if unpublished.—
Give much love to my dear Susan, and her fine boy,
and to Catherine with her fine boy, & dear little Lucretia;—
I hope Charles is settled, and determined to exert all his
abilities to be useful in an honorable business.—
I think of you and your difficulties with Cousin Samuel
I wish that you could see Uncle Sidney, perhaps
a free conversation with him would set matters
right, at present, I fear an unpleasant family
breach. Uncle Sidney is a man of strict integrity and I
think when your representations are made to him, he will
perceive how unjustly and improperly you have been treated.
As it now stands Cousin has had the whole telling of the story
and with the natural bias of parents towards their children
they will think of course that you have wronged him.—
Love to Finley and to Richard & family
Truly your affectionate brother
Sam. F. B. Morse

Washington June 24th. 1844
Dear Sir;
Your of the 25th inst. is received and in reply I would say that I have not from the
part with the Government, without leave of the Department; I shall be in NewYork in a week or two
probably and can perhaps span you the quantity you want from some of my own which is stored there.—
In regard to my opinion of the failure of the first trial lead pipe I think the failure due to the
injury the insulation received in putting it into the pipe, such was the injury that not a single coil that I tried was
free from the fatal defect of having the electricity cross from wire to wire and to the pipe, so that my pipe has turned out
a dead loss, and has been sold for simple lead. It is its being tested before it left your premises; if it is true, it was my
misfortune to have trusted this testing to an unfaithful assistant, who passed it all as sound, leaving it to me to discover
when too late to remedy the evil, the fatal defect I have mentioned.
I congratulate you on your safe return, and thank you for the information respecting the extent of the English
Telegraph; The extent in pipe is or was greater than you mention. From London to Dayton on the G. Western R. way 13 miles
was laid down two or three years since. I am very respectfully

Dear Sir,
In the other letter I have copied a letter just received from Phila. What can we say in answer? I have expressed
that if we gave permission to construct the line for $10,000, or say $100,000 mile that sum to be secured and
paid to us six months after the work is commenced that this would be a simple and easy mode of arranging the
whole matter. Please give me your own views of what you think best. I think myself if we at once
fix the rate at 100 cents as our price for the construction of the line, we shall soon have orders from all parts of the Country, and our profits
will come in rapidly, and sure. If you think any of us should desire further to increase our own profits by contracting with any company or companies this might
be done without embarrassment to the rest. I think that $100 per mile might be substituted for $50 in forming a
company for the N.York & Boston line. I am still confined by my leg, but hope to be able to go out in a few days.
Respectfuly, J. Mose
By granting a privilege on a particular line we do not have ourselves from granting a privilege on another line between two points, so that unless we sell right in states (which we ought to avoid)
we can have a good profit from God at the same time that we accommodate private companies.

Professor S. F. B. Morse,
Dr Sir,
Mr. Vail informed
me the day he passed through this city
from Washington to Philadelphia, that
you contemplated engaging me as
one of your assistants, provided I
would be willing to embark in the enter-
prise at the risk of your getting an ap-
propriation from the Government next
winter.
He also informed me you would be
willing to have my salary stipulated at
$2.50 per day out of the present ap-
propriation.
I have no doubt that an appropriation
will be made to extend your telegraph,
and it is the opinion of several gentle
men of my acquaintance who are at-
tached to the Post Office Department,
that it must be done; among the
number are Doctor Howard Kennedy &
Major Robbie -- at all events I am wil-
ling to sink my risk & sink
or swim with the Telegraph, I hereby
inform you of my decision.
If you still contemplate having
attached to your department will you
be kind enough to use the necessary
means to have me appointed.
The necessity of having a complete
vocabulary by the next meeting of Con
gress may decide your immediate action
in the case, I thus can during this
summer and coming fall, finish the
one I submitted to you some time ago,
and which when completed can be
published by us jointly, provided you
purchase Capt. Black's interest in
the Optical Telegraph.
Very respectfully
Your faithful servt
Henry S. Rogers
P.S. I hope you have got well & will
be soon in Baltimore.

Dear Sir,
As soon as you hear from your partner
I would be obliged to you to let me have answer
to the queries contained in my brother's letter, as well as
to those I made verbally when I saw you.
From what I have done since I returned I am sanguine of success in establishing
a telegraphic line between here and New York, but
I cannot consent to put the means I have for the
purpose into operation without some guarantee that
I shall not waste money and time in the attempt.
Within thirty or forty days I think with the peculiar
means in my power I can doubtless obtain the
Capital, provided it is not a greater sum than
that you mentioned to me. Therefore I would be
obliged to you if you would give me in legal form
the right to purchase if I choose to do so within
say forty days, for the sum you and your partners
agree upon an electro magnetic telegraph to be
erected between this city and New York upon the
line of the rail road, and the patent right to the
exclusive use of the telegraph to erected by you
and to any number of additional wires or additional telegraphs hereafter erected on the same
route, or between the cities of Philadelphia and
New York. The consent of the rail road Company
to the erection of the Telegraph to be obtained and
paid for by me in addition to the sum to
be paid to you.
I make as I explained to you this proposition,
in order that I may secure for myself the
office of agent or director of the line, as there will
be such a person needed to superintend the
postage arrangements &c as well as the
working of the telegraph, -- and I wish par-
ticularly to make such an agreement with you
in order that after I have obtained for you
the means of erecting the line, (a service worthy
of done acknowledgment) I may not, by parties
who may become interested be put aside and
the office bestowed on another.
If you agree to my proposition I would
be glad if you would write to me imme-
diately, and I will set to work without delay
With great respect
From ofst Servt
Edward P. Fry

Dear Prof. Moone
I wrote to you this morning
stating that I would be ready tomorrow for
experiment. I however shall not be ready
so early as I contemplated in consequence
of all the stores being shut up, and I have
not been able to get the acid I want for
the experiments, I shall however be early at
7 in the morning and as your east &
Ground circuit is closed you will know
when I am ready by the ringing of the bell
if it is in a condition to be rung when I am
ready — If at 11 o'clock no action takes place
send to the cars for a letter, as I will write
if any thing is wrong — wire broken &c — and
at 11 o'clock I will change to West & Ground.
Then after we get started you can order the
experiments to suit yourself — write if you can
not attend yourself by tomorrow mornings train
I do hope that no impediment will be put in
our way towards continuing the Telegraph in
operation during the Summer & Fall, by stopping
the appropriation — I presume Sec. Babb will
leave it to the discretion of Mr. Young who will
I feel assured yield to the wishes of several here
% whom he is indebted for his place, and who will
see him whenever you desire it. Mr. Rogers tells me
this — The wires which were broken at Bladenburg
were untwisted. The ends of her with and you
the breaks which Cleveland mended on Tuesday,
were occasioned by lightning he says
as the two posts on either side of the break were
marked along the bark with the streak or cut
made by the fluid descending to the ground, as
I also the trees in the immediate neighborhood
The breaks were not at any joint, but of whole
cloth as he says, -- between the same posts
but not directly opposite each other. They were
6 or 8 feet apart, one on each wire, and about
3 miles beyond Beltsville toward Washington.
I hope your leg has entirely healed and that
you have had a long siege, but I trust
it is all for the best although it does not
appear so -- Will you leave for New York
soon? -- Cleveland is now cleaning up the old
vine's -- and Brown may send me the other
which he has cast. -- I have not yet got from
Dr Page the thinktop of the Copper state for the
Dixie's, and I can therefore do nothing until
he sends me a sample of the thinktop.
Your Most Obest Servt
Alfred Bait
